abstract: 1024 distributed-neuron synapses have been integrated in an active area of 6.1mm x 3.3mm using a 0.9p.m, double-metal, single-poly, n-well CMOS technology. The distributed-neuron synapses are ar(cid:173) ranged in blocks of 16, which we call '4 x 4 tiles'. Switch matrices are interleaved between each of these tiles to provide programma(cid:173) bility of interconnections. With a small area overhead (15 %), the 1024 units of the network can be rearranged in various configura(cid:173) tions. Some of the possible configurations are, a 12-32-12 network, a 16-12-12-16 network, two 12-32 networks etc. (the numbers sep(cid:173) arated by dashes indicate the number of units per layer, including the input layer). Weights are stored in analog form on MaS ca(cid:173) pacitors. The synaptic weights are usable to a resolution of 1 % of their full scale value. The limitation arises due to charge injection from the access switch and charge leakage. Other parameters like gain and shape of nonlinearity are also programmable.

paragraphs: This paper describes an analog neural chip whose connections can be rearranged to support different network layouts. It integrates 1,024 distributed-neuron synapses in a 6.1 by 3.3 millimeter active area. Groups of sixteen synapses form tiles, with programmable switch matrices placed between them.

The switches allow the same hardware resources to implement different layer arrangements, including 12–32–12 and 16–12–12–16 networks, or two 12–32 networks. The numbers specify units per layer, including inputs. Providing this flexibility adds a reported 15 percent area overhead. The design therefore makes network structure a programmable choice within the resources available on the chip.

Weights are stored as analog values on MOS capacitors and are usable at a resolution of one percent of their full-scale value. Charge injected by access switches and charge leakage set this limit. Gain and the shape of the nonlinearity are also programmable. Together, these features show how reconfiguration can extend beyond wiring to the numerical behavior of an analog network, while remaining constrained by physical storage effects.
summary.tldr: A tiled analog neural chip supports multiple network configurations through programmable switches, with additional control over weights, gain, and nonlinear response.

title: A Reconfigurable Analog VLSI Neural Network Chip

abstract: The conventional Bayesian justification of backprop is that it finds the MAP weight vector. As this paper shows, to find the MAP i-o function instead one must add a correction tenn to backprop. That tenn biases one towards i-o functions with small description lengths, and in particular fa(cid:173) vors (some kinds of) feature-selection, pruning, and weight-sharing.

As this paper shows, to find the MAP i-o function instead one must add a correction tenn to backprop. That tenn biases one towards i-o functions with small description lengths, and in particular fa(cid:173) vors (some kinds of) feature-selection, pruning, and weight-sharing.

paragraphs: This paper distinguishes two possible targets for Bayesian neural network training: the most probable weight vector and the most probable input-output function. A weight vector specifies the network's adjustable numbers, whereas an input-output function describes the behavior those numbers produce. The paper argues that the conventional Bayesian interpretation of backpropagation addresses the first target.

To optimize the probability of the function instead, the author derives an additional correction term for backpropagation. This matters because changing the object whose probability is maximized changes the learning objective. The result connects a question about what Bayesian learning should select to a concrete modification of the training procedure.

The correction favors functions that admit shorter descriptions. In particular, it encourages some forms of feature selection, pruning, and weight sharing, linking these structural choices to the function-level Bayesian objective. The qualification matters: the abstract does not claim that every version of those techniques follows from the correction. Its central finding is that a preference for compact functional descriptions emerges when inference targets network behavior.
summary.tldr: Optimizing Bayesian probability over network functions requires a backpropagation correction that favors compact descriptions and certain structural simplifications.

title: Bayesian Backpropagation Over I-O Functions Rather Than Weights

abstract: In supervised learning, learning from queries rather than from random examples can improve generalization performance signif(cid:173) icantly. We study the performance of query learning for problems where the student cannot learn the teacher perfectly, which occur frequently in practice. As a prototypical scenario of this kind, we consider a linear perceptron student learning a binary perceptron teacher. Two kinds of queries for maximum information gain, i.e., minimum entropy, are investigated: Minimum student space en(cid:173) tropy (MSSE) queries, which are appropriate if the teacher space is unknown, and minimum teacher space entropy (MTSE) queries, which can be used if the teacher space is assumed to be known, but a student of a simpler form has deliberately been chosen. We find that for MSSE queries, the structure of the student space deter(cid:173) mines the efficacy of query learning, whereas MTSE queries lead to a higher generalization error than random examples, due to a lack of feedback about the progress of the student in the way queries are selected.

paragraphs: This paper studies query learning when a student cannot perfectly learn its teacher. Instead of receiving random examples, the learner selects queries intended to gain information. The authors examine a linear perceptron student learning a binary perceptron teacher, using this mismatch to investigate whether information-seeking queries actually improve generalization.

They compare two ways to reduce uncertainty. Minimum student space entropy queries target uncertainty in the student's possible models and are appropriate when the teacher's model space is unknown. Minimum teacher space entropy queries target uncertainty about the teacher and assume that its model space is known, even though a simpler student has deliberately been chosen.

For student-space queries, effectiveness depends on the structure of the student's model space. Teacher-space queries produce higher generalization error than random examples in the studied setting because query selection lacks feedback about the student's progress. The finding shows why acquiring information about the teacher can be poorly aligned with improving a learner whose representational capacity is more limited.
summary.tldr: Queries that maximize information about a teacher can hurt a simpler student's generalization when selection ignores the student's progress.

title: Learning from queries for maximum information gain in imperfectly learnable problems

abstract: Graphical models provide a broad probabilistic framework with ap(cid:173) plications in speech recognition (Hidden Markov Models), medical diagnosis (Belief networks) and artificial intelligence (Boltzmann Machines). However, the computing time is typically exponential in the number of nodes in the graph. Within the variational frame(cid:173) work for approximating these models, we present two classes of dis(cid:173) tributions, decimatable Boltzmann Machines and Tractable Belief Networks that go beyond the standard factorized approach. We give generalised mean-field equations for both these directed and undirected approximations. Simulation results on a small bench(cid:173) mark problem suggest using these richer approximations compares favorably against others previously reported in the literature.

paragraphs: This paper develops approximations for probabilistic graphical models, whose computations can become prohibitively expensive as graphs grow. Variational methods address this by replacing a difficult distribution with a more manageable one. The paper focuses on enriching that substitute distribution beyond the standard factorized approach, which represents variables without retaining their dependencies.

The authors introduce two tractable families: decimatable Boltzmann machines and tractable belief networks. These provide undirected and directed approximation structures, respectively. They derive generalized mean-field equations for both families, giving procedures for using the richer structures within the variational framework. The aim is to preserve useful relationships while keeping the approximation computationally accessible.

Simulations on a small benchmark suggest favorable performance compared with previously reported alternatives. That result supports the value of retaining more structure in an approximation, within the scope of the reported problem. The contribution combines a choice of manageable distribution families with the equations needed to use them, expanding the available options between fully factorized approximations and the original difficult model.
summary.tldr: Two structured variational families retain dependencies beyond factorized approximations while allowing tractable graphical-model computations.

title: Tractable Variational Structures for Approximating Graphical Models

abstract: I consider the problem of calculating learning curves (i.e., average generalization performance) of Gaussian processes used for regression. A simple expression for the generalization error in terms of the eigenvalue decomposition of the covariance function is derived, and used as the starting point for several approximation schemes. I identify where these become exact, and compare with existing bounds on learning curves; the new approximations, which can be used for any input space dimension, generally get substantially closer to the truth.

paragraphs: A learning curve describes how average prediction performance changes as a model receives more training data. This paper studies how to calculate such curves for Gaussian process regression. The goal is to understand expected generalization performance across training data, beyond the predictions produced by one particular fitted model.

The analysis begins with an expression for generalization error based on the eigenvalue decomposition of the covariance function. This decomposition provides a mathematical description of the covariance structure that can be used to analyze learning. The author then develops several approximation schemes from that expression and identifies circumstances in which the approximations become exact.

The proposed approximations are compared with existing bounds on Gaussian process learning curves and generally track the true curves substantially more closely. They can also be applied regardless of the input-space dimension. The contribution is therefore a more accurate analytical route from a Gaussian process's covariance specification to its expected learning behavior as training data accumulates.
summary.tldr: Covariance eigenvalues yield approximations that more closely describe how Gaussian process regression improves with additional training data.

title: Learning Curves for Gaussian Processes

abstract: In 1986, Tanner and Mead [1] implemented an interesting constraint sat(cid:173) isfaction circuit for global motion sensing in a VLSI. We report here a new and improved a VLSI implementation that provides smooth optical flow as well as global motion in a two dimensional visual field. The com(cid:173) putation of optical flow is an ill-posed problem, which expresses itself as the aperture problem. However, the optical flow can be estimated by the use of regularization methods, in which additional constraints are intro(cid:173) duced in terms of a global energy functional that must be minimized . We show how the algorithmic constraints of Hom and Schunck [2] on com(cid:173) puting smooth optical flow can be mapped onto the physical constraints of an equivalent electronic network.

paragraphs: The paper presents an analog integrated-circuit implementation for estimating motion across a two-dimensional visual field. It extends an earlier circuit for global motion sensing by also providing smooth optical flow. This means the implementation addresses a spatial pattern of apparent motion as well as the overall movement of the visual field.

Optical flow is an ill-posed problem: the available visual information does not by itself uniquely determine motion. The abstract identifies this ambiguity with the aperture problem. The approach addresses it through regularization, adding constraints expressed as a global energy function whose minimum corresponds to the desired motion estimate.

The key contribution is mapping the smoothness constraints of the Horn and Schunck algorithm onto physical constraints in an equivalent electronic network. This connects an algorithmic formulation of motion estimation with a feedback-connected analog implementation. The work shows how additional constraints used to resolve visual ambiguity can be embodied in circuit behavior, yielding both smooth optical flow and global motion estimates.
summary.tldr: The paper maps smooth optical-flow constraints onto an analog circuit that estimates both local flow and global motion.

title: Computation of Smooth Optical Flow in a Feedback Connected Analog Network

abstract: The problem of developing good policies for partially observable Markov decision problems (POMDPs) remains one of the most challenging ar(cid:173) eas of research in stochastic planning. One line of research in this area involves the use of reinforcement learning with belief states, probabil(cid:173) ity distributions over the underlying model states. This is a promis(cid:173) ing method for small problems, but its application is limited by the in(cid:173) tractability of computing or representing a full belief state for large prob(cid:173) lems. Recent work shows that, in many settings, we can maintain an approximate belief state, which is fairly close to the true belief state. In particular, great success has been shown with approximate belief states that marginalize out correlations between state variables. In this paper, we investigate two methods of full belief state reinforcement learning and one novel method for reinforcement learning using factored approximate belief states. We compare the performance of these algorithms on several well-known problem from the literature. Our results demonstrate the im(cid:173) portance of approximate belief state representations for large problems.

paragraphs: In partially observable decision problems, an agent can represent uncertainty through a belief state: a probability distribution over underlying states. Reinforcement learning with this representation is promising for small problems. For larger ones, computing or storing the complete distribution can become intractable, making the representation itself a central obstacle to learning useful policies.

The paper investigates two reinforcement learning methods using full belief states and a new method using factored approximate belief states. The approximate approach builds on work showing that useful belief estimates can often be maintained while leaving out correlations between state variables. Factoring the belief representation addresses the burden of representing their full joint uncertainty.

The authors compare these methods on several established problems and report results demonstrating the importance of approximate belief representations for large problems. The contribution is to study approximation as part of the learning system, where its value depends on supporting policy learning as well as representing uncertainty. The stated findings support this direction without claiming that removing correlations preserves all information relevant to every decision problem.
summary.tldr: A new reinforcement learning method uses factored approximate beliefs to address the difficulty of full belief-state representations in large partially observable problems.

title: Reinforcement Learning Using Approximate Belief States

abstract: In this paper, we use mutual information to characterize the dis(cid:173) tributions of phonetic and speaker/channel information in a time(cid:173) frequency space. The mutual information (MI) between the pho(cid:173) netic label and one feature, and the joint mutual information (JMI) between the phonetic label and two or three features are estimated . The Miller's bias formulas for entropy and mutual information es(cid:173) timates are extended to include higher order terms. The MI and the JMI for speaker/channel recognition are also estimated. The results are complementary to those for phonetic classification. Our results show how the phonetic information is locally spread and how the speaker/channel information is globally spread in time and frequency.

The Miller's bias formulas for entropy and mutual information es(cid:173) timates are extended to include higher order terms. The MI and the JMI for speaker/channel recognition are also estimated. paragraphs: The paper investigates where different kinds of information are located within speech across time and frequency. It distinguishes information about phonetic labels from information about the speaker or channel. This matters because a speech feature can be informative for one recognition task without having the same role in another.

The authors estimate mutual information between phonetic labels and individual features, along with joint mutual information for groups of two or three features. These calculations examine information available from features separately and together. They also extend Miller's bias formulas for entropy and mutual-information estimates with higher-order terms, addressing the estimation procedure used in the analysis.

Corresponding information estimates are made for speaker and channel recognition. The findings describe complementary spatial distributions within the time-frequency representation: phonetic information is spread locally, while speaker/channel information is spread globally. The result provides a task-dependent picture of informative speech components, showing why the scale over which features are considered matters when characterizing what a speech signal reveals.
summary.tldr: Information estimates reveal local spreading of phonetic information and global spreading of speaker/channel information across speech time and frequency.

title: Search for Information Bearing Components in Speech

abstract: Competition in the wireless telecommunications industry is rampant. To main(cid:173) tain profitability, wireless carriers must control chum, the loss of subscribers who switch from one carrier to another. We explore statistical techniques for chum prediction and, based on these predictions. an optimal policy for identify(cid:173) ing customers to whom incentives should be offered to increase retention. Our experiments are based on a data base of nearly 47,000 U.S. domestic subscrib(cid:173) ers, and includes information about their usage, billing, credit, application, and complaint history. We show that under a wide variety of assumptions concerning the cost of intervention and the retention rate resulting from intervention, chum prediction and remediation can yield significant savings to a carrier. We also show the importance of a data representation crafted by domain experts. Competition in the wireless telecommunications industry is rampant. As many as seven competing carriers operate in each market. The industry is extremely dynamic, with new services, technologies, and carriers constantly altering the landscape. Carriers announce new rates and incentives weekly, hoping to entice new subscribers and to lure subscribers away from the competition. The extent of rivalry is reflected in the deluge of advertise(cid:173) ments for wireless service in the daily newspaper and other mass media. The United States had 69 million wireless subscribers in 1998, roughly 25% of the population. Some markets are further developed; for example, the subscription rate in Fin(cid:173) land is 53%. Industry forecasts are for a U.S. penetration rate of 48% by 2003. Although there is significant room for growth in most markets, the industry growth rate is declining and competition is rising. Consequently, it has become crucial for wireless carriers to con(cid:173) trol chum-the loss of customers who switch from one carrier to another. At present, domestic monthly chum rates are 2-3% of the customer base. At an average cost of $400 to acquire a subscriber, churn cost the industry nearly $6.3 bilIion in 1998; the total annual loss rose to nearly $9.6 billion when lost monthly revenue from subscriber cancellations is considered (Luna, 1998). It costs roughly five times as much to sign on a new subscriber as to retain an existing one. Consequently, for a carrier with 1.5 milIion subscribers, reduc(cid:173) ing the monthly churn' rate from 2% to 1 % would yield an increase in annual earnings of at least $54 milIion, and an increase in shareholder value of approximately $150 million. (Estimates are even higher when lost monthly revenue is considered; see Fowlkes, Madan, Andrew, & Jensen, 1999; Luna, 1998.) The goal of our research is to evaluate the benefits of predicting churn using tech(cid:173) niques from statistical machine learning. We designed models that predict the probability 936 M. C. Mozer, R. Wolniewicz. D. B. Grimes. E. Johnson and H. Kaushansky of a subscriber churning within a short time window, and we evaluated how well these pre(cid:173) dictions could be used for decision making by estimating potential cost savings to the wireless carrier under a variety of assumptions concerning subscriber behavior.

abstract: We study the problem of combining the outcomes of several different classifiers in a way that provides a coherent inference that satisfies some constraints. In particular, we develop two general approaches for an im(cid:173) portant subproblem - identifying phrase structure. The first is a Marko(cid:173) vian approach that extends standard HMMs to allow the use of a rich ob(cid:173) servation structure and of general classifiers to model state-observation dependencies. The second is an extension of constraint satisfaction for(cid:173) malisms. We develop efficient combination algorithms under both mod(cid:173) els and study them experimentally in the context of shallow parsing.

In particular, we develop two general approaches for an im(cid:173) portant subproblem - identifying phrase structure. The first is a Marko(cid:173) vian approach that extends standard HMMs to allow the use of a rich ob(cid:173) servation structure and of general classifiers to model state-observation dependencies. The second is an extension of constraint satisfaction for(cid:173) malisms. We develop efficient combination algorithms under both mod(cid:173) els and study them experimentally in the context of shallow parsing.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to combine outputs from several classifiers into a coherent inference that respects constraints. Its central application is identifying phrase structure. The issue is how individual classification decisions can jointly form a valid structured interpretation, rather than being considered only as separate predictions.

The authors develop two general approaches. The first extends hidden Markov models to support a rich observation structure and general classifiers for dependencies between states and observations. This provides a Markovian framework in which classifier outputs can contribute to sequential inference. The second approach extends constraint-satisfaction formalisms, providing another route for combining decisions under structural requirements.

For both approaches, the paper develops efficient combination algorithms and studies them experimentally in shallow parsing. The contribution brings together flexible local classifiers and mechanisms for making their outputs jointly consistent. Presenting both Markovian and constraint-based formulations also makes the combination problem explicit: successful phrase-structure inference requires a procedure for coordinating the available predictions with the constraints on the final interpretation.
summary.tldr: Two efficient frameworks combine classifier outputs into constrained phrase-structure predictions using extended HMMs and constraint satisfaction.

title: The Use of Classifiers in Sequential Inference

abstract: There exist many different generalization error bounds for classiﬁcation. Each of these bounds contains an improvement over the others for cer- tain situations. Our goal is to combine these different improvements into a single bound. In particular we combine the PAC-Bayes approach intro- duced by McAllester [1], which is interesting for averaging classiﬁers, with the optimal union bound provided by the generic chaining technique developed by Fernique and Talagrand [2]. This combination is quite nat- ural since the generic chaining is based on the notion of majorizing mea- sures, which can be considered as priors on the set of classiﬁers, and such priors also arise in the PAC-bayesian setting.
originalAbstract: There exist many different generalization error bounds for classiﬁcation. Each of these bounds contains an improvement over the others for cer- tain situations. Our goal is to combine these different improvements into a single bound. In particular we combine the PAC-Bayes approach intro- duced by McAllester [1], which is interesting for averaging classiﬁers, with the optimal union bound provided by the generic chaining technique developed by Fernique and Talagrand [2]. This combination is quite nat- ural since the generic chaining is based on the notion of majorizing mea- sures, which can be considered as priors on the set of classiﬁers, and such priors also arise in the PAC-bayesian setting.

paragraphs: Generalization bounds often improve different aspects of learning, so choosing one can mean losing an advantage offered by another. This paper combines PAC-Bayesian analysis with generic chaining. The goal is a bound that benefits both from averaging classifiers and from a refined treatment of complexity across the hypothesis space.

PAC-Bayes uses a prior over classifiers to assess data-dependent distributions of predictors. Generic chaining organizes increasingly fine comparisons through majorizing measures, which can also be interpreted as priors. That shared structure makes the combination mathematically natural rather than simply taking the minimum of unrelated inequalities.

The contribution is a unified theoretical tool for classification generalization. It connects two ways of controlling a large collection of possible predictors: distributional averaging and multiscale complexity analysis. The work focuses on strengthening the form of the bound, so its significance is in what can be proved about learning procedures rather than a new classifier architecture or empirical benchmark result.
summary.tldr: PAC-Bayesian generic chaining combines classifier averaging with multiscale complexity control in a unified generalization bound.

title: PAC-Bayesian Generic Chaining

abstract: A mixed-signal image filtering VLSI has been developed aiming at real-time generation of edge-based image vectors for robust image recognition. A four-stage asynchronous median detection architec- ture based on analog digital mixed-signal circuits has been intro- duced to determine the threshold value of edge detection, the key processing parameter in vector generation. As a result, a fully seamless pipeline processing from threshold detection to edge fea- ture map generation has been established. A prototype chip was designed in a 0.35-µm double-polysilicon three-metal-layer CMOS technology and the concept was verified by the fabricated chip. The chip generates a 64-dimension feature vector from a 64x64-pixel gray scale image every 80µsec. This is about 104 times faster than the software computation, making a real-time image recognition system feasible.

paragraphs: This paper develops a chip that converts grayscale images into compact descriptions of their edges. These image vectors are intended to support recognition fast enough for real-time use. A central challenge is choosing the edge-detection threshold, which controls which image changes count as edges and therefore influences the features passed to recognition.

The design uses a four-stage asynchronous median-detection architecture built from a mixture of analog and digital circuits. This architecture determines the threshold and connects that calculation directly to edge-feature-map generation. The contribution is therefore an integrated processing pipeline, with threshold selection included in the hardware path that produces the image representation.

The authors fabricated a prototype using 0.35-micrometer CMOS technology and verified the concept on the chip. It produces a 64-dimensional feature vector from a 64-by-64-pixel image every 80 microseconds. The reported speed advantage over software makes real-time image recognition feasible, although the demonstrated output is the feature vector that such a recognition system would use.
summary.tldr: A mixed-signal chip generates compact edge-based image vectors every 80 microseconds, supporting real-time image recognition.

title: A Mixed-Signal VLSI for Real-Time Generation of Edge-Based Image Vectors

abstract: We initiate the study of learning from multiple sources of limited data, each of which may be corrupted at a different rate. We develop a com- plete theory of which data sources should be used for two fundamental problems: estimating the bias of a coin, and learning a classiﬁer in the presence of label noise. In both cases, efﬁcient algorithms are provided for computing the optimal subset of data.

In both cases, efﬁcient algorithms are provided for computing the optimal subset of data.

paragraphs: This paper studies learning when several sources provide limited amounts of data and each source may have a different corruption rate. The central decision is which sources to use. A source contributes observations, but their quality also matters, so the learning problem includes choosing the data as well as estimating the desired quantity.

The authors analyze two basic tasks. The first is estimating a coin's bias, meaning its probability of producing one of its two outcomes. The second is learning a classifier when some training labels are corrupted. These settings let the paper examine source selection for both probability estimation and prediction from noisy labels.

For each task, the authors develop what they describe as a complete theory of which data sources should be included. They also provide efficient algorithms for computing the optimal subset of data. The contribution is therefore both a characterization of the selection problem and a way to carry out that selection, with optimality established for the two studied problems rather than for arbitrary learning tasks.
summary.tldr: The paper gives theory and efficient algorithms for selecting data sources with different corruption rates in two learning problems.

title: Learning from Data of Variable Quality

abstract: We provide a provably efficient algorithm for learning Markov Decision Processes (MDPs) with continuous state and action spaces in the online setting. Specifically, we take a model-based approach and show that a special type of online linear regression allows us to learn MDPs with (possibly kernalized) linearly parameterized dynamics. This result builds on Kearns and Singh's work that provides a provably efficient algorithm for finite state MDPs. Our approach is not restricted to the linear setting, and is applicable to other classes of continuous MDPs.

paragraphs: This paper addresses online learning in Markov decision processes with continuous states and actions. Such a setting calls for learning about a system while interacting with it, rather than working only with a finite list of possible situations and choices. The authors provide a provably efficient algorithm using a model-based approach.

The main technical connection is to a special form of online linear regression. The authors show that this regression method enables learning MDPs whose dynamics have a linear parameterization, potentially using kernels. This places learning the system’s dynamics at the center of the reinforcement-learning procedure and gives regression a role in obtaining an efficiency guarantee.

The result builds on earlier work by Kearns and Singh for finite-state MDPs. The abstract also states that the approach applies beyond the linear setting to other classes of continuous MDPs. The significance is a bridge from efficient learning in finite systems to structured continuous systems. The explicit regression-based result concerns linearly parameterized dynamics, while the broader approach has further stated applicability.
summary.tldr: A specialized online regression method enables provably efficient model-based learning of continuous MDPs with linearly parameterized dynamics.

title: Online Linear Regression and Its Application to Model-Based Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Motor primitives or motion templates have become an important concept for both modeling human motor control as well as generating robot behaviors using imitation learning. Recent impressive results range from humanoid robot movement generation to timing models of human motions. The automatic generation of skill libraries containing multiple motion templates is an important step in robot learning. Such a skill learning system needs to cluster similar movements together and represent each resulting motion template as a generative model which is subsequently used for the execution of the behavior by a robot system. In this paper, we show how human trajectories captured as multidimensional time-series can be clustered using Bayesian mixtures of linear Gaussian state-space models based on the similarity of their dynamics. The appropriate number of templates is automatically determined by enforcing a parsimonious parametrization. As the resulting model is intractable, we introduce a novel approximation method based on variational Bayes, which is especially designed to enable the use of efficient inference algorithms. On recorded human Balero movements, this method is not only capable of finding reasonable motion templates but also yields a generative model which works well in the execution of this complex task on a simulated anthropomorphic SARCOS arm.

This paper addresses both requirements using human movement trajectories recorded as multidimensional time series. Its organizing principle is similarity in movement dynamics, connecting the grouping process to how a motion unfolds.

The method uses Bayesian mixtures of linear Gaussian state-space models. It automatically determines the number of motion templates by encouraging a parsimonious parameterization. summary.tldr: Bayesian dynamical models cluster human demonstrations into motion templates that support task execution by a simulated robot arm.

title: Using Bayesian Dynamical Systems for Motion Template Libraries

abstract: In this paper we introduce a new algorithm for updating the parameters of a heuristic evaluation function, by updating the heuristic towards the values computed by an alpha-beta search. Our algorithm differs from previous approaches to learning from search, such as Samuels checkers player and the TD-Leaf algorithm, in two key ways. First, we update all nodes in the search tree, rather than a single node. Second, we use the outcome of a deep search, instead of the outcome of a subsequent search, as the training signal for the evaluation function. We implemented our algorithm in a chess program Meep, using a linear heuristic function. After initialising its weight vector to small random values, Meep was able to learn high quality weights from self-play alone. When tested online against human opponents, Meep played at a master level, the best performance of any chess program with a heuristic learned entirely from self-play.

paragraphs: A game-playing program uses a heuristic evaluation function to assess positions during search. This paper develops a way to improve that function using values produced by alpha-beta search. The idea is to train a relatively direct position evaluator toward the assessments obtained through deeper exploration of possible play.

The algorithm differs from earlier approaches in two stated ways. It updates the evaluator using every node in the search tree, rather than one node. It also takes the result of a deep search as its training signal, rather than waiting for the result of a subsequent search. Both choices determine how information generated by search becomes learning data.

The authors implement the method in the chess program Meep with a linear evaluation function. Starting from small random weights, Meep learns high-quality weights entirely through self-play. In online games against humans, it reaches master-level performance. The paper reports this as the strongest performance among chess programs whose heuristics were learned wholly through self-play, supporting the usefulness of deep-search assessments as training targets.
summary.tldr: Training a chess evaluator on deep-search values across all search-tree nodes enables Meep to learn master-level play through self-play.

title: Bootstrapping from Game Tree Search

abstract: We consider regularized stochastic learning and online optimization problems, where the objective function is the sum of two convex terms: one is the loss function of the learning task, and the other is a simple regularization term such as L1-norm for sparsity. We develop a new online algorithm, the regularized dual averaging method, that can explicitly exploit the regularization structure in an online setting. In particular, at each iteration, the learning variables are adjusted by solving a simple optimization problem that involves the running average of all past subgradients of the loss functions and the whole regularization term, not just its subgradient. This method achieves the optimal convergence rate and often enjoys a low complexity per iteration similar as the standard stochastic gradient method. Computational experiments are presented for the special case of sparse online learning using L1-regularization.

paragraphs: The paper studies learning objectives made from two convex pieces: a loss measuring task performance and a simple regularizer expressing a preference such as sparsity. Its focus is stochastic and online learning, where parameters are updated as information arrives. The challenge is to make those updates use the regularizer's structure explicitly.

The proposed regularized dual averaging method keeps a running average of all previous loss subgradients. At each iteration, it solves a simple optimization problem involving that average and the complete regularization term. Keeping the whole regularizer in the update is the defining feature, allowing its mathematical form to influence the new parameters directly.

The method achieves an optimal convergence rate and often has per-iteration complexity comparable to standard stochastic gradient methods. The authors also present computational experiments for sparse online learning with L1 regularization. The contribution therefore combines a convergence guarantee with a potentially inexpensive update rule. Its practical appeal is that directly handling regularization need not require abandoning the low-cost iterations useful in online learning.
summary.tldr: Regularized dual averaging combines past loss subgradients with the full regularizer to obtain optimally convergent, often inexpensive online updates.

title: Dual Averaging Method for Regularized Stochastic Learning and Online Optimization

abstract: Synaptic plasticity underlies learning and is thus central for development, memory, and recovery from injury. However, it is often difficult to detect changes in synaptic strength in vivo, since intracellular recordings are experimentally challenging. Here we present two methods aimed at inferring changes in the coupling between pairs of neurons from extracellularly recorded spike trains. First, using a generalized bilinear model with Poisson output we estimate time-varying coupling assuming that all changes are spike-timing-dependent. This approach allows model-based estimation of STDP modification functions from pairs of spike trains. Then, using recursive point-process adaptive filtering methods we estimate more general variation in coupling strength over time. Using simulations of neurons undergoing spike-timing dependent modification, we show that the true modification function can be recovered. Using multi-electrode data from motor cortex we then illustrate the use of this technique on in vivo data.

paragraphs: Changes in synaptic strength are central to learning, but observing them in living brains is difficult because intracellular recordings are challenging. This paper develops two methods for estimating changes in coupling between pairs of neurons from extracellular spike recordings. The goal is to use the timing of observable neural activity to infer how the relationship between neurons changes.

The first method uses a generalized bilinear model with Poisson output and assumes that all coupling changes depend on spike timing. Under that assumption, it estimates the modification function describing spike-timing-dependent plasticity from paired spike trains. The second method uses recursive point-process adaptive filtering to estimate a broader range of time-varying coupling, relaxing the restriction to exclusively timing-dependent changes.

In simulations of neurons undergoing spike-timing-dependent modification, the authors show recovery of the true modification function. They then illustrate the technique using multi-electrode recordings from motor cortex. These two forms of evidence serve different purposes: simulations support recovery against a known process, while the recordings demonstrate application to in vivo data.
summary.tldr: Two methods infer changing neural coupling from spike trains, including timing-dependent plasticity under an explicit modeling assumption.

title: Inferring spike-timing-dependent plasticity from spike train data

abstract: In regression problems over $\real^d$, the unknown function $f$ often varies more in some coordinates than in others. We show that weighting each coordinate $i$ with the estimated norm of the $i$th derivative of $f$ is an efficient way to significantly improve the performance of distance-based regressors, e.g. kernel and $k$-NN regressors. We propose a simple estimator of these derivative norms and prove its consistency. Moreover, the proposed estimator is efficiently learned online.
originalAbstract: In regression problems over $\real^d$, the unknown function $f$ often varies more in some coordinates than in others. We show that weighting each coordinate $i$ with the estimated norm of the $i$th derivative of $f$ is an efficient way to significantly improve the performance of distance-based regressors, e.g. kernel and $k$-NN regressors. We propose a simple estimator of these derivative norms and prove its consistency. Moreover, the proposed estimator is efficiently learned online.

paragraphs: The paper considers regression problems in which the target function changes more strongly along some input coordinates than others. For methods that predict using distances between examples, this uneven sensitivity matters: the coordinate system used to compare inputs should reflect how the output varies. The paper develops a way to estimate and use that information.

Its proposal assigns each coordinate a weight based on an estimated norm of the target function’s derivative in that direction. The derivative norm summarizes the function’s sensitivity to that coordinate. These weights are then used by distance-based regression methods, including kernel regression and nearest-neighbor regression, to improve how input differences are assessed.

The authors give a simple estimator for the derivative norms and prove that it is consistent. They also show that it can be learned efficiently online. Their stated finding is that this weighting can significantly improve regression performance, connecting the choice of input distance to estimated properties of the function being learned.
summary.tldr: Estimating how strongly a target function varies along each coordinate provides effective distance weights for kernel and nearest-neighbor regression.

title: Gradient Weights help Nonparametric Regressors

abstract: Abstract Given samples from distributions $p$ and $q$, a two-sample test determines whether to reject the null hypothesis that $p=q$, based on the value of a test statistic measuring the distance between the samples. One choice of test statistic is the maximum mean discrepancy (MMD), which is a distance between embeddings of the probability distributions in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space. The kernel used in obtaining these embeddings is thus critical in ensuring the test has high power, and correctly distinguishes unlike distributions with high probability. A means of parameter selection for the two-sample test based on the MMD is proposed. For a given test level (an upper bound on the probability of making a Type I error), the kernel is chosen so as to maximize the test power, and minimize the probability of making a Type II error. The test statistic, test threshold, and optimization over the kernel parameters are obtained with cost linear in the sample size. These properties make the kernel selection and test procedures suited to data streams, where the observations cannot all be stored in memory. In experiments, the new kernel selection approach yields a more powerful test than earlier kernel selection heuristics.

paragraphs: A two-sample test asks whether two groups of observations provide evidence that their underlying distributions differ. This paper focuses on tests using maximum mean discrepancy, which compares distribution embeddings defined by a kernel. Because the kernel determines the comparison, its choice affects the test's ability to detect a real difference.

The authors propose choosing kernel parameters to maximize test power at a given test level. The level bounds the probability of falsely declaring a difference, while greater power reduces the chance of missing one that exists. This ties parameter selection directly to the statistical purpose of the test rather than relying on an earlier kernel-selection heuristic.

Computing the statistic, determining its threshold, and optimizing kernel parameters all have cost linear in sample size. These properties make the procedure suitable for streams whose observations cannot all remain in memory. Experiments show greater power than earlier selection heuristics, supporting the value of optimizing the kernel for detection while keeping the overall testing procedure scalable.
summary.tldr: Power-focused kernel selection improves large-scale MMD two-sample tests while keeping selection and testing costs linear in sample size.

title: Optimal kernel choice for large-scale two-sample tests

abstract: We study the average case performance of multi-task Gaussian process (GP) regression as captured in the learning curve, i.e.\ the average Bayes error for a chosen task versus the total number of examples $n$ for all tasks. For GP covariances that are the product of an input-dependent covariance function and a free-form inter-task covariance matrix, we show that accurate approximations for the learning curve can be obtained for an arbitrary number of tasks $T$. We use these to study the asymptotic learning behaviour for large $n$. Surprisingly, multi-task learning can be asymptotically essentially useless: examples from other tasks only help when the degree of inter-task correlation, $\rho$, is near its maximal value $\rho=1$. This effect is most extreme for learning of smooth target functions as described by e.g.\ squared exponential kernels. We also demonstrate that when learning {\em many} tasks, the learning curves separate into an initial phase, where the Bayes error on each task is reduced down to a plateau value by ``collective learning'' even though most tasks have not seen examples, and a final decay that occurs only once the number of examples is proportional to the number of tasks.

paragraphs: This paper studies how prediction error changes as multi-task Gaussian process regression receives more examples. Its learning curves track the average Bayes error for one task against the total training examples across all tasks. The analysis assumes a covariance formed by multiplying an input covariance function with a freely specified matrix of relationships between tasks.

For this model family, the authors obtain accurate learning-curve approximations for any number of tasks and investigate behavior with large amounts of data. They find that multi-task learning can become essentially unhelpful asymptotically: examples from other tasks help only when inter-task correlation is close to its maximum. This effect is strongest for smooth target functions, such as those described by squared exponential kernels.

With many tasks, the curves exhibit two phases. Collective learning initially lowers errors toward a plateau even though most tasks have no examples. A later decline occurs only when the example count becomes proportional to the task count. These findings distinguish early benefits from sharing information from the conditions needed for continued improvement.
summary.tldr: Learning-curve analysis shows early collective benefits but potentially negligible asymptotic gains from multi-task Gaussian process regression unless tasks are highly correlated.

title: Learning curves for multi-task Gaussian process regression

abstract: Multiple Kernel Learning (MKL) generalizes SVMs to the setting where one simultaneously trains a linear classifier and chooses an optimal combination of given base kernels. Model complexity is typically controlled using various norm regularizations on the vector of base kernel mixing coefficients. Existing methods, however, neither regularize nor exploit potentially useful information pertaining to how kernels in the input set 'interact'; that is, higher order kernel-pair relationships that can be easily obtained via unsupervised (similarity, geodesics), supervised (correlation in errors), or domain knowledge driven mechanisms (which features were used to construct the kernel?). We show that by substituting the norm penalty with an arbitrary quadratic function Q \succeq 0, one can impose a desired covariance structure on mixing coefficient selection, and use this as an inductive bias when learning the concept. This formulation significantly generalizes the widely used 1- and 2-norm MKL objectives. We explore the model’s utility via experiments on a challenging Neuroimaging problem, where the goal is to predict a subject’s conversion to Alzheimer’s Disease (AD) by exploiting aggregate information from several distinct imaging modalities. Here, our new model outperforms the state of the art (p-values << 10−3 ). We briefly discuss ramifications in terms of learning bounds (Rademacher complexity).

paragraphs: Multiple kernel learning jointly trains a classifier and selects how to combine several base kernels. Conventional regularizers control the vector of mixing weights, but they do not explicitly use information about relationships between kernels. This paper asks how those relationships can guide the choice of weights when learning a predictive model.

Q-MKL replaces the usual norm penalty with a quadratic penalty defined by a positive semidefinite matrix. This allows a desired covariance structure to influence the mixing coefficients. Information about kernel interactions can come from similarities, correlations between prediction errors, or domain knowledge about the features used to build each kernel. The formulation generalizes commonly used one-norm and two-norm objectives.

The authors apply the method to predicting conversion to Alzheimer's disease using several imaging modalities. It outperforms the state-of-the-art methods considered, with reported p-values much smaller than 0.001. This supports using relationships among information sources in that prediction task. The paper also briefly discusses learning-bound implications through Rademacher complexity.
summary.tldr: Q-MKL uses a quadratic regularizer to encode relationships between kernels and improves the reported neuroimaging prediction results.

title: Q-MKL: Matrix-induced Regularization in Multi-Kernel Learning with Applications to Neuroimaging

abstract: It has been long argued that, because of inherent ambiguity and noise, the brain needs to represent uncertainty in the form of probability distributions. The neural encoding of such distributions remains however highly controversial. Here we present a novel circuit model for representing multidimensional real-valued distributions using a spike based spatio-temporal code. Our model combines the computational advantages of the currently competing models for probabilistic codes and exhibits realistic neural responses along a variety of classic measures. Furthermore, the model highlights the challenges associated with interpreting neural activity in relation to behavioral uncertainty and points to alternative population-level approaches for the experimental validation of distributed representations.

The neural encoding of such distributions remains however highly controversial. Here we present a novel circuit model for representing multidimensional real-valued distributions using a spike based spatio-temporal code. Our model combines the computational advantages of the currently competing models for probabilistic codes and exhibits realistic neural responses along a variety of classic measures. Furthermore, the model highlights the challenges associated with interpreting neural activity in relation to behavioral uncertainty and points to alternative population-level approaches for the experimental validation of distributed representations.

paragraphs: Ambiguous and noisy information motivates the idea that the brain represents uncertainty as probability distributions. How neural activity might encode those distributions remains disputed. This paper presents a circuit model for representing distributions over several real-valued quantities using a code spread across neurons and across time.

The model uses spikes to implement this spatio-temporal representation. According to the authors, it combines computational advantages of competing proposals for probabilistic neural codes while producing realistic neural responses on a variety of classic measures. The contribution is thus a concrete circuit-level proposal that links uncertainty representation with recognizable features of neural activity.

The model also highlights difficulties in interpreting neural recordings in relation to behavioral uncertainty. A distributed code makes the relationship between recorded activity and represented probabilities an experimental question requiring suitable measurements. The authors point toward population-level approaches for validating these representations. Their result offers both a candidate encoding mechanism and guidance for studying it, while remaining a model of how uncertainty could be represented.
summary.tldr: A spiking circuit model represents multidimensional uncertainty across neurons and time, combining advantages of competing codes and motivating population-level validation.

title: Spatio-temporal Representations of Uncertainty in Spiking Neural Networks

abstract: Given samples from an unknown distribution, p, is it possible to distinguish whether p belongs to some class of distributions C versus p being far from every distribution in C? This fundamental question has receivedtremendous attention in Statistics, albeit focusing onasymptotic analysis, as well as in Computer Science, wherethe emphasis has been on small sample size and computationalcomplexity. Nevertheless, even for basic classes ofdistributions such as monotone, log-concave, unimodal, and monotone hazard rate, the optimal sample complexity is unknown.We provide a general approach via which we obtain sample-optimal and computationally efficient testers for all these distribution families. At the core of our approach is an algorithm which solves the following problem:Given samplesfrom an unknown distribution p, and a known distribution q, are p and q close in Chi^2-distance, or far in total variation distance?The optimality of all testers is established by providing matching lower bounds. Finally, a necessary building block for our tester and important byproduct of our work are the first known computationally efficient proper learners for discretelog-concave and monotone hazard rate distributions. We exhibit the efficacy of our testers via experimental analysis.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to test a structural claim about an unknown probability distribution from samples. The goal is to distinguish distributions belonging to a specified family from distributions far from every member of that family. The families considered include monotone, log-concave, unimodal, and monotone-hazard-rate distributions.

The authors develop a general approach that yields computationally efficient testers with optimal sample requirements for all these families. A central component compares an unknown distribution with a known candidate: it distinguishes closeness in chi-squared distance from being far apart in total variation distance. The use of two different distance notions is part of the testing problem solved by this component.

Matching lower bounds establish that the sample requirements cannot be improved for the tested problems. The construction also produces computationally efficient proper learners for discrete log-concave and monotone-hazard-rate distributions, meaning that their learned distributions belong to the target family. Experiments illustrate the testers' effectiveness. The work thus combines optimal testing guarantees with learning procedures needed to make those tests computationally practical.
summary.tldr: A general testing approach achieves optimal sample complexity and efficient computation for several structured distribution families.

title: Optimal Testing for Properties of Distributions

abstract: Efforts to automate the reconstruction of neural circuits from 3D electron microscopic (EM) brain images are critical for the field of connectomics. An important computation for reconstruction is the detection of neuronal boundaries. Images acquired by serial section EM, a leading 3D EM technique, are highly anisotropic, with inferior quality along the third dimension. For such images, the 2D max-pooling convolutional network has set the standard for performance at boundary detection. Here we achieve a substantial gain in accuracy through three innovations. Following the trend towards deeper networks for object recognition, we use a much deeper network than previously employed for boundary detection. Second, we incorporate 3D as well as 2D filters, to enable computations that use 3D context. Finally, we adopt a recursively trained architecture in which a first network generates a preliminary boundary map that is provided as input along with the original image to a second network that generates a final boundary map. Backpropagation training is accelerated by ZNN, a new implementation of 3D convolutional networks that uses multicore CPU parallelism for speed. Our hybrid 2D-3D architecture could be more generally applicable to other types of anisotropic 3D images, including video, and our recursive framework for any image labeling problem.

These broader uses are proposed possibilities rather than reported demonstrations.
summary.tldr: Deeper mixed 2D-3D networks and a second prediction stage substantially improve neuronal boundary detection in anisotropic electron microscopy images.

title: Recursive Training of 2D-3D Convolutional Networks for Neuronal Boundary Prediction

abstract: We revisit the choice of SGD for training deep neural networks by reconsidering the appropriate geometry in which to optimize the weights. We argue for a geometry invariant to rescaling of weights that does not affect the output of the network, and suggest Path-SGD, which is an approximate steepest descent method with respect to a path-wise regularizer related to max-norm regularization. Path-SGD is easy and efficient to implement and leads to empirical gains over SGD and AdaGrad.

We argue for a geometry invariant to rescaling of weights that does not affect the output of the network, and suggest Path-SGD, which is an approximate steepest descent method with respect to a path-wise regularizer related to max-norm regularization. Path-SGD is easy and efficient to implement and leads to empirical gains over SGD and AdaGrad.

paragraphs: This paper revisits how stochastic gradient descent measures changes to the weights of a deep neural network. Its starting point is that some rescalings of weights leave the network's output unchanged. The authors argue that the geometry used for optimization should respect these transformations, so equivalent rescaled descriptions are treated consistently by the optimization framework.

They propose Path-SGD, an approximate steepest descent method defined using a path-wise regularizer related to max-norm regularization. Here, the choice of geometry determines what counts as a steep update. The path-based regularizer provides the basis for that choice, connecting the optimization step to the rescaling behavior the authors want it to respect.

The paper describes Path-SGD as straightforward and efficient to implement and reports empirical gains over SGD and AdaGrad. Those findings support the practical value of reconsidering optimization geometry, alongside the conceptual argument for rescaling invariance. The stated performance result is empirical: the contribution offers a particular efficient update method and evidence of benefits over the two named alternatives.
summary.tldr: Path-SGD uses a path-based optimization geometry motivated by output-preserving weight rescalings and reports empirical gains over SGD and AdaGrad.

title: Path-SGD: Path-Normalized Optimization in Deep Neural Networks

abstract: New silicon technology is enabling large-scale electrophysiological recordings in vivo from hundreds to thousands of channels. Interpreting these recordings requires scalable and accurate automated methods for spike sorting, which should minimize the time required for manual curation of the results. Here we introduce KiloSort, a new integrated spike sorting framework that uses template matching both during spike detection and during spike clustering. KiloSort models the electrical voltage as a sum of template waveforms triggered on the spike times, which allows overlapping spikes to be identified and resolved. Unlike previous algorithms that compress the data with PCA, KiloSort operates on the raw data which allows it to construct a more accurate model of the waveforms. Processing times are faster than in previous algorithms thanks to batch-based optimization on GPUs. We compare KiloSort to an established algorithm and show favorable performance, at much reduced processing times. A novel post-clustering merging step based on the continuity of the templates further reduced substantially the number of manual operations required on this data, for the neurons with near-zero error rates, paving the way for fully automated spike sorting of multichannel electrode recordings.

paragraphs: Large multichannel neural recordings need automated spike sorting that is accurate, fast, and economical to review manually. KiloSort addresses these requirements with an integrated framework that uses waveform templates during both spike detection and clustering. This gives the two stages a shared way to describe the recorded electrical signals.

The framework models voltage as a sum of template waveforms occurring at spike times. That additive representation allows it to identify and resolve overlapping spikes. KiloSort works on raw recordings instead of first compressing them with PCA, which the authors report supports more accurate waveform modeling. Batch-based optimization on GPUs reduces processing time.

Against an established sorting algorithm, KiloSort shows favorable performance with much shorter processing times. A subsequent merging step uses template continuity to reduce manual corrections further. The reported substantial reduction concerns the evaluated data and neurons with near-zero error rates. The findings support progress toward fully automated sorting, rather than establishing that manual review has already become unnecessary.
summary.tldr: KiloSort uses raw-signal template matching and GPU optimization to sort neural spikes quickly while reducing manual curation.

title: Fast and accurate spike sorting of high-channel count probes with KiloSort

abstract: A capsule is a group of neurons whose activity vector represents the instantiation parameters of a specific type of entity such as an object or object part. We use the length of the activity vector to represent the probability that the entity exists and its orientation to represent the instantiation parameters. Active capsules at one level make predictions, via transformation matrices, for the instantiation parameters of higher-level capsules. When multiple predictions agree, a higher level capsule becomes active. We show that a discrimininatively trained, multi-layer capsule system achieves state-of-the-art performance on MNIST and is considerably better than a convolutional net at recognizing highly overlapping digits. To achieve these results we use an iterative routing-by-agreement mechanism: A lower-level capsule prefers to send its output to higher level capsules whose activity vectors have a big scalar product with the prediction coming from the lower-level capsule.

paragraphs: The paper represents an object or object part using a capsule, a group of neurons with a vector-valued activity. The vector's length expresses the probability that the entity exists, while its direction expresses the entity's instantiation parameters. This lets a representation convey both presence and information about how an entity appears.

Lower-level capsules use transformation matrices to predict the parameters of higher-level capsules. A higher-level capsule becomes active when multiple predictions agree. The proposed iterative routing mechanism directs a lower-level capsule's output preferentially toward higher-level capsules whose activity vectors align strongly with its prediction, measured through their scalar product.

This agreement-based communication connects the representations at different levels: supporting evidence depends on whether their predictions fit together. The authors train a multilayer capsule system discriminatively and report state-of-the-art performance on MNIST. They also find it considerably better than a convolutional network at recognizing highly overlapping digits. Those results support the proposed representation and routing mechanism in the evaluated digit-recognition settings.
summary.tldr: Capsules represent entity presence and parameters as vectors, using agreement-based routing to achieve strong digit-recognition results.

title: Dynamic Routing Between Capsules

abstract: Most online optimization algorithms focus on one of two things: performing well in adversarial settings by adapting to unknown data parameters (such as Lipschitz constants), typically achieving $O(\sqrt{T})$ regret, or performing well in stochastic settings where they can leverage some structure in the losses (such as strong convexity), typically achieving $O(\log(T))$ regret. Algorithms that focus on the former problem hitherto achieved $O(\sqrt{T})$ in the stochastic setting rather than $O(\log(T))$. Here we introduce an online optimization algorithm that achieves $O(\log^4(T))$ regret in a wide class of stochastic settings while gracefully degrading to the optimal $O(\sqrt{T})$ regret in adversarial settings (up to logarithmic factors). Our algorithm does not require any prior knowledge about the data or tuning of parameters to achieve superior performance.

paragraphs: Online optimization algorithms must make successive decisions while learning from the losses they encounter. This paper addresses a tension between handling unpredictable, adversarial losses and exploiting favorable stochastic structure. Methods designed for adversarial robustness had typically retained square-root regret even in stochastic settings where faster rates were possible.

The proposed algorithm achieves O(log⁴(T)) regret across a wide class of stochastic settings. In adversarial settings, it degrades to the optimal square-root dependence on T up to logarithmic factors. Regret measures accumulated shortfall relative to a comparator, so these rates describe how the cost of learning grows over repeated decisions.

The algorithm obtains these guarantees without prior knowledge of the data or parameter tuning. That matters because the learner need not know in advance which kind of environment it will encounter to obtain the stated adaptation. The stochastic rate is polylogarithmic rather than the O(log(T)) rate mentioned for specialized methods, while the adversarial guarantee retains its logarithmic qualification. The contribution is combining these behaviors in one untuned procedure.
summary.tldr: An untuned online algorithm achieves polylogarithmic stochastic regret while retaining near-optimal adversarial regret up to logarithmic factors.

title: Stochastic and Adversarial Online Learning without Hyperparameters

abstract: Instance level video object segmentation is an important technique for video editing and compression. To capture the temporal coherence, in this paper, we develop MaskRNN, a recurrent neural net approach which fuses in each frame the output of two deep nets for each object instance - a binary segmentation net providing a mask and a localization net providing a bounding box. Due to the recurrent component and the localization component, our method is able to take advantage of long-term temporal structures of the video data as well as rejecting outliers. We validate the proposed algorithm on three challenging benchmark datasets, the DAVIS-2016 dataset, the DAVIS-2017 dataset, and the Segtrack v2 dataset, achieving state-of-the-art performance on all of them.

Due to the recurrent component and the localization component, our method is able to take advantage of long-term temporal structures of the video data as well as rejecting outliers. We validate the proposed algorithm on three challenging benchmark datasets, the DAVIS-2016 dataset, the DAVIS-2017 dataset, and the Segtrack v2 dataset, achieving state-of-the-art performance on all of them.

paragraphs: MaskRNN addresses instance-level video segmentation: assigning pixels to individual objects across successive frames. This task matters for video editing and compression, where an object's identity and shape need to remain coherent as the video changes. The paper builds temporal information directly into its segmentation approach.

For each object in each frame, the model combines two neural network outputs. A binary segmentation network predicts a pixel mask, while a localization network predicts a bounding box. A recurrent component integrates these outputs over time. This joins detailed information about object shape with a more compact estimate of where the object is located.

The authors attribute the method's ability to exploit long-term temporal structure and reject outliers to its recurrent and localization components. They evaluate it on DAVIS-2016, DAVIS-2017, and Segtrack v2, reporting state-of-the-art performance on all three. The findings support combining temporal memory, object localization, and pixel-level prediction for maintaining individual object segmentations across a video.
summary.tldr: MaskRNN recurrently combines object masks and bounding boxes to achieve strong instance-level video segmentation across three benchmarks.

title: MaskRNN: Instance Level Video Object Segmentation

abstract: We investigate the non-identifiability issues associated with bidirectional adversarial training for joint distribution matching. Within a framework of conditional entropy, we propose both adversarial and non-adversarial approaches to learn desirable matched joint distributions for unsupervised and supervised tasks. We unify a broad family of adversarial models as joint distribution matching problems. Our approach stabilizes learning of unsupervised bidirectional adversarial learning methods. Further, we introduce an extension for semi-supervised learning tasks. Theoretical results are validated in synthetic data and real-world applications.
originalAbstract: We investigate the non-identifiability issues associated with bidirectional adversarial training for joint distribution matching. Within a framework of conditional entropy, we propose both adversarial and non-adversarial approaches to learn desirable matched joint distributions for unsupervised and supervised tasks. We unify a broad family of adversarial models as joint distribution matching problems. Our approach stabilizes learning of unsupervised bidirectional adversarial learning methods. Further, we introduce an extension for semi-supervised learning tasks. Theoretical results are validated in synthetic data and real-world applications.

paragraphs: Bidirectional adversarial learning trains mappings in two directions while trying to match a joint probability distribution. The paper examines a difficulty called non-identifiability: the matching objective may leave ambiguity about which relationship the model should learn. This matters because satisfying a distribution-matching goal can still leave multiple possibilities for the learned correspondence.

The authors use conditional entropy to organize their analysis. Conditional entropy describes uncertainty about one variable when another is known, making it relevant to the ambiguity of a learned relationship. Within this framework, they propose both adversarial and non-adversarial methods for learning desirable joint distributions in supervised and unsupervised tasks. They also bring a broad family of adversarial models under a common distribution-matching interpretation.

The proposed approach stabilizes unsupervised bidirectional adversarial learning, and an extension addresses semi-supervised tasks. Experiments on synthetic data and real-world applications validate the theoretical results. The contribution therefore combines an explanation of ambiguity in these models with methods intended to guide training toward more useful matched relationships.
summary.tldr: ALICE uses conditional entropy to analyze ambiguity in bidirectional adversarial learning and guide more stable joint distribution matching.

title: ALICE: Towards Understanding Adversarial Learning for Joint Distribution Matching

abstract: Many real world dynamical systems are described by stochastic differential equations. Thus parameter inference is a challenging and important problem in many disciplines. We provide a grid free and flexible algorithm offering parameter and state inference for stochastic systems and compare our approch based on variational approximations to state of the art methods showing significant advantages both in runtime and accuracy.
originalAbstract: Many real world dynamical systems are described by stochastic differential equations. Thus parameter inference is a challenging and important problem in many disciplines. We provide a grid free and flexible algorithm offering parameter and state inference for stochastic systems and compare our approch based on variational approximations to state of the art methods showing significant advantages both in runtime and accuracy.

paragraphs: Stochastic differential equations describe dynamical systems whose evolution includes randomness. Learning about such a system involves estimating both its parameters and its states: the quantities governing its behavior and the system's evolving condition. The paper addresses these two inference tasks together, motivated by their importance across disciplines that model real-world dynamics.

The authors propose a flexible, grid-free algorithm based on variational approximations. The approximation is central to the approach: inference is carried out using an approximate representation rather than being presented as an exact solution. Its scope includes both parameter inference and state inference, so the method addresses uncertainty about the governing model as well as the system being modeled.

Comparisons with leading methods show significant advantages in both runtime and accuracy. Those findings matter because computational efficiency and inference quality are separate practical concerns; the reported method improves both in the comparisons presented. The contribution is therefore an algorithmic approach for stochastic-system inference whose stated evidence combines computational savings with more accurate estimates.
summary.tldr: A grid-free variational algorithm jointly supports parameter and state inference for stochastic systems, with reported gains in speed and accuracy.

title: Efficient and Flexible Inference for Stochastic Systems

abstract: Despite significant accuracy improvement in convolutional neural networks (CNN) based object detectors, they often require prohibitive runtimes to process an image for real-time applications. State-of-the-art models often use very deep networks with a large number of floating point operations. Efforts such as model compression learn compact models with fewer number of parameters, but with much reduced accuracy. In this work, we propose a new framework to learn compact and fast ob- ject detection networks with improved accuracy using knowledge distillation [20] and hint learning [34]. Although knowledge distillation has demonstrated excellent improvements for simpler classification setups, the complexity of detection poses new challenges in the form of regression, region proposals and less voluminous la- bels. We address this through several innovations such as a weighted cross-entropy loss to address class imbalance, a teacher bounded loss to handle the regression component and adaptation layers to better learn from intermediate teacher distribu- tions. We conduct comprehensive empirical evaluation with different distillation configurations over multiple datasets including PASCAL, KITTI, ILSVRC and MS-COCO. Our results show consistent improvement in accuracy-speed trade-offs for modern multi-class detection models.
