paragraphs: Accurate object detectors often rely on deep networks whose computation makes real-time use difficult. Compact models can run faster but lose substantial accuracy. This paper develops a framework that transfers information from a teacher detector to a compact detector using knowledge distillation and hint learning, aiming for a better balance between accuracy and speed.

Detection requires more than assigning an image to a class: it also involves regression and region proposals, with less abundant labels. The framework addresses these challenges through several components. A weighted cross-entropy loss handles class imbalance, a teacher-bounded loss addresses regression, and adaptation layers help the compact network learn from the teacher's intermediate distributions.

The authors evaluate different distillation configurations on PASCAL, KITTI, ILSVRC, and MS-COCO. They report consistent improvements in accuracy-speed trade-offs for modern multiclass detectors. These findings support adapting knowledge transfer to the distinct parts of detection, rather than assuming that a method effective for simpler classification tasks will transfer without modification.
summary.tldr: Detection-specific distillation losses and adaptation layers help compact object detectors achieve better accuracy-speed trade-offs.

title: Learning Efficient Object Detection Models with Knowledge Distillation

abstract: Despite their impressive performance, Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) typically underperform Gradient Boosting Trees (GBTs) on many tabular-dataset learning tasks. We propose that applying a different regularization coefficient to each weight might boost the performance of DNNs by allowing them to make more use of the more relevant inputs. However, this will lead to an intractable number of hyperparameters. Here, we introduce Regularization Learning Networks (RLNs), which overcome this challenge by introducing an efficient hyperparameter tuning scheme which minimizes a new Counterfactual Loss. Our results show that RLNs significantly improve DNNs on tabular datasets, and achieve comparable results to GBTs, with the best performance achieved with an ensemble that combines GBTs and RLNs. RLNs produce extremely sparse networks, eliminating up to 99.8% of the network edges and 82% of the input features, thus providing more interpretable models and reveal the importance that the network assigns to different inputs. RLNs could efficiently learn a single network in datasets that comprise both tabular and unstructured data, such as in the setting of medical imaging accompanied by electronic health records. An open source implementation of RLN can be found at https://github.com/irashavitt/regularization learning networks.

paragraphs: Deep neural networks often trail gradient boosting trees on tabular learning tasks. This paper explores whether assigning a separate regularization strength to each network weight can help the network make better use of relevant inputs. The obstacle is that this creates an enormous collection of hyperparameters, making ordinary tuning impractical.

Regularization Learning Networks address the tuning problem with an efficient scheme that minimizes a new Counterfactual Loss. The resulting models significantly improve on the tested neural networks and achieve performance comparable to gradient boosting trees. The strongest results come from an ensemble combining the two approaches.

The learned networks are extremely sparse, removing up to 99.8% of edges and 82% of input features. This sparsity also helps reveal which inputs the network considers important, making its use of the data easier to interpret. The authors further suggest that RLNs could efficiently handle tabular and unstructured inputs within one network, such as medical images accompanied by health records; this is presented as a possible application.
summary.tldr: Learning a regularization strength for each weight produces sparse neural networks with tabular performance comparable to gradient boosting trees.

title: Regularization Learning Networks: Deep Learning for Tabular Datasets

abstract: Leverage score sampling provides an appealing way to perform approximate com- putations for large matrices. Indeed, it allows to derive faithful approximations with a complexity adapted to the problem at hand. Yet, performing leverage scores sampling is a challenge in its own right requiring further approximations. In this paper, we study the problem of leverage score sampling for positive definite ma- trices defined by a kernel. Our contribution is twofold. First we provide a novel algorithm for leverage score sampling and second, we exploit the proposed method in statistical learning by deriving a novel solver for kernel ridge regression. Our main technical contribution is showing that the proposed algorithms are currently the most efficient and accurate for these problems.

paragraphs: Leverage score sampling offers a way to approximate computations involving large matrices while adapting the computational effort to the problem's structure. Its attraction is that a carefully chosen sample can retain information needed for a faithful approximation. The difficulty is that obtaining the sampling probabilities can itself be expensive and require approximation.

This paper addresses that difficulty for positive definite matrices defined by a kernel. Its first contribution is a new algorithm for leverage score sampling. Its second is a kernel ridge regression solver that uses the proposed sampling method, connecting the matrix approximation problem directly to a statistical learning task.

The main technical result establishes efficiency and accuracy advantages for these algorithms, which the authors describe as the strongest available for the problems considered. The contribution therefore concerns both generating useful samples and turning them into an effective learning procedure. It targets the computational work needed to obtain the approximation, as well as the quality of the resulting solution.
summary.tldr: A new leverage score sampling algorithm supports an efficient kernel ridge regression solver with technical guarantees on efficiency and accuracy.

title: On Fast Leverage Score Sampling and Optimal Learning

abstract: Learning low-dimensional embeddings of knowledge graphs is a powerful approach used to predict unobserved or missing edges between entities. However, an open challenge in this area is developing techniques that can go beyond simple edge prediction and handle more complex logical queries, which might involve multiple unobserved edges, entities, and variables. For instance, given an incomplete biological knowledge graph, we might want to predict "em what drugs are likely to target proteins involved with both diseases X and Y?" -- a query that requires reasoning about all possible proteins that might interact with diseases X and Y. Here we introduce a framework to efficiently make predictions about conjunctive logical queries -- a flexible but tractable subset of first-order logic -- on incomplete knowledge graphs. In our approach, we embed graph nodes in a low-dimensional space and represent logical operators as learned geometric operations (e.g., translation, rotation) in this embedding space. By performing logical operations within a low-dimensional embedding space, our approach achieves a time complexity that is linear in the number of query variables, compared to the exponential complexity required by a naive enumeration-based approach. We demonstrate the utility of this framework in two application studies on real-world datasets with millions of relations: predicting logical relationships in a network of drug-gene-disease interactions and in a graph-based representation of social interactions derived from a popular web forum.

paragraphs: Predicting a missing relationship in a knowledge graph is simpler than answering a question involving several unknown relationships and intermediate entities. This paper addresses conjunctive logical queries, which combine requirements that must hold together. The goal is to make useful predictions about such queries even when the graph does not contain all the relevant connections.

The framework places entities in a low-dimensional space and represents logical operators through learned geometric operations, such as translations or rotations. A query can then be evaluated through operations on those representations. This avoids explicitly enumerating all possible assignments to its variables, which becomes expensive as the query grows.

The authors report time complexity linear in the number of query variables, compared with the exponential complexity of naive enumeration. They demonstrate the framework on two real-world datasets containing millions of relations: drug–gene–disease interactions and social interactions represented from a web forum. These studies support the usefulness of learned query representations for predicting compound relationships, extending the role of graph embeddings beyond individual missing-edge prediction.
summary.tldr: Learned geometric operations on graph embeddings support efficient prediction of conjunctive logical queries in incomplete knowledge graphs.

title: Embedding Logical Queries on Knowledge Graphs

abstract: Feed-forward neural networks can be understood as a combination of an intermediate representation and a linear hypothesis. While most previous works aim to diversify the representations, we explore the complementary direction by performing an adaptive and data-dependent regularization motivated by the empirical Bayes method. Specifically, we propose to construct a matrix-variate normal prior (on weights) whose covariance matrix has a Kronecker product structure. This structure is designed to capture the correlations in neurons through backpropagation. Under the assumption of this Kronecker factorization, the prior encourages neurons to borrow statistical strength from one another. Hence, it leads to an adaptive and data-dependent regularization when training networks on small datasets. To optimize the model, we present an efficient block coordinate descent algorithm with analytical solutions. Empirically, we demonstrate that the proposed method helps networks converge to local optima with smaller stable ranks and spectral norms. These properties suggest better generalizations and we present empirical results to support this expectation. We also verify the effectiveness of the approach on multiclass classification and multitask regression problems with various network structures. Our code is publicly available at:~\url{https://github.com/yaohungt/Adaptive-Regularization-Neural-Network}.
originalAbstract: Feed-forward neural networks can be understood as a combination of an intermediate representation and a linear hypothesis. While most previous works aim to diversify the representations, we explore the complementary direction by performing an adaptive and data-dependent regularization motivated by the empirical Bayes method. Specifically, we propose to construct a matrix-variate normal prior (on weights) whose covariance matrix has a Kronecker product structure. This structure is designed to capture the correlations in neurons through backpropagation. Under the assumption of this Kronecker factorization, the prior encourages neurons to borrow statistical strength from one another. Hence, it leads to an adaptive and data-dependent regularization when training networks on small datasets. To optimize the model, we present an efficient block coordinate descent algorithm with analytical solutions. Empirically, we demonstrate that the proposed method helps networks converge to local optima with smaller stable ranks and spectral norms. These properties suggest better generalizations and we present empirical results to support this expectation. We also verify the effectiveness of the approach on multiclass classification and multitask regression problems with various network structures. Our code is publicly available at:~\url{https://github.com/yaohungt/Adaptive-Regularization-Neural-Network}.

paragraphs: This paper studies how regularization can adapt to relationships among neurons, especially when training data is limited. It views a feed-forward network as an intermediate representation combined with a linear predictor. Rather than concentrating on diversifying that representation, the authors use an empirical Bayes motivation to construct a data-dependent prior over weights.

The prior is a matrix-variate normal distribution whose covariance has a Kronecker product structure. Under this factorization assumption, it captures correlations among neurons through backpropagation and encourages them to share statistical information. The resulting regularization adapts to the data. An efficient block coordinate descent algorithm, with analytical solutions for its updates, is used to optimize the model.

Empirically, the approach leads networks toward local optima with smaller stable ranks and spectral norms. The authors interpret these properties as suggesting improved generalization and provide experimental support for that expectation. Evaluations cover multiclass classification and multitask regression with different network structures, supporting the usefulness of correlation-aware regularization across the tested settings.
summary.tldr: A structured, data-dependent weight prior lets neurons share statistical information and empirically improves generalization across the tested learning tasks.

title: Learning Neural Networks with Adaptive Regularization

abstract: We introduce a region-specific diffeomorphic metric mapping (RDMM) registration approach. RDMM is non-parametric, estimating spatio-temporal velocity fields which parameterize the sought-for spatial transformation. Regularization of these velocity fields is necessary. In contrast to existing non-parametric registration approaches using a fixed spatially-invariant regularization, for example, the large displacement diffeomorphic metric mapping (LDDMM) model, our approach allows for spatially-varying regularization which is advected via the estimated spatio-temporal velocity field. Hence, not only can our model capture large displacements, it does so with a spatio-temporal regularizer that keeps track of how regions deform, which is a more natural mathematical formulation. We explore a family of RDMM registration approaches: 1) a registration model where regions with separate regularizations are pre-defined (e.g., in an atlas space or for distinct foreground and background regions), 2) a registration model where a general spatially-varying regularizer is estimated, and 3) a registration model where the spatially-varying regularizer is obtained via an end-to-end trained deep learning (DL) model. We provide a variational derivation of RDMM, showing that the model can assure diffeomorphic transformations in the continuum, and that LDDMM is a particular instance of RDMM. To evaluate RDMM performance we experiment 1) on synthetic 2D data and 2) on two 3D datasets: knee magnetic resonance images (MRIs) of the Osteoarthritis Initiative (OAI) and computed tomography images (CT) of the lung. Results show that our framework achieves comparable performance to state-of-the-art image registration approaches, while providing additional information via a learned spatio-temporal regularizer. Further, our deep learning approach allows for very fast RDMM and LDDMM estimations. Code is available at https://github.com/uncbiag/registration.

paragraphs: Image registration seeks a spatial transformation that aligns images. This paper introduces RDMM, which represents the transformation through velocity fields that vary over space and time. Its central change concerns regularization: different regions can have different deformation constraints, and those constraints move with the regions as they deform.

The framework supports predefined regional regularization, directly estimated spatial variation, or regularization predicted by an end-to-end deep learning model. A variational derivation shows that RDMM can ensure diffeomorphic transformations in the continuum, meaning smooth transformations with smooth inverses. The existing LDDMM formulation is included as a special case, connecting the new model to an established registration approach.

Experiments use synthetic two-dimensional data, three-dimensional knee MRI, and lung CT. RDMM achieves performance comparable to state-of-the-art registration methods while additionally providing a learned regularizer that describes spatial and temporal variation. The deep learning version also enables very fast RDMM and LDDMM estimation. The contribution is thus a more region-sensitive account of deformation with competitive alignment performance, with the stated mathematical guarantee specifically applying in the continuum.
summary.tldr: RDMM aligns images using region-specific regularization that moves with deformation, achieving competitive registration while exposing additional deformation structure.

title: Region-specific Diffeomorphic Metric Mapping

abstract: Sum-product networks (SPNs) are flexible density estimators and have received significant attention due to their attractive inference properties. While parameter learning in SPNs is well developed, structure learning leaves something to be desired: Even though there is a plethora of SPN structure learners, most of them are somewhat ad-hoc and based on intuition rather than a clear learning principle. In this paper, we introduce a well-principled Bayesian framework for SPN structure learning. First, we decompose the problem into i) laying out a computational graph, and ii) learning the so-called scope function over the graph. The first is rather unproblematic and akin to neural network architecture validation. The second represents the effective structure of the SPN and needs to respect the usual structural constraints in SPN, i.e. completeness and decomposability. While representing and learning the scope function is somewhat involved in general, in this paper, we propose a natural parametrisation for an important and widely used special case of SPNs. These structural parameters are incorporated into a Bayesian model, such that simultaneous structure and parameter learning is cast into monolithic Bayesian posterior inference. In various experiments, our Bayesian SPNs often improve test likelihoods over greedy SPN learners. Further, since the Bayesian framework protects against overfitting, we can evaluate hyper-parameters directly on the Bayesian model score, waiving the need for a separate validation set, which is especially beneficial in low data regimes. Bayesian SPNs can be applied to heterogeneous domains and can easily be extended to nonparametric formulations. Moreover, our Bayesian approach is the first, which consistently and robustly learns SPN structures under missing data.

paragraphs: Sum-product networks estimate probability distributions while supporting attractive inference operations. Choosing their structure is harder to justify systematically than learning their numerical parameters: many existing methods rely on heuristic design choices. This paper introduces a Bayesian framework that treats learning the effective structure and learning the parameters as parts of one inference problem.

The approach separates the computational graph from its scope function, which determines the effective structure over that graph. Learning this function must preserve the network's completeness and decomposability requirements. For an important, widely used special case, the authors introduce structural parameters that can be included directly in Bayesian posterior inference.

Experiments show that Bayesian networks often achieve better test likelihoods than greedy structure learners. The framework also supports choosing hyperparameters through a Bayesian model score without a separate validation set, which matters when data are scarce. The authors additionally report consistent, robust structure learning with missing data and describe applicability to heterogeneous domains and extensions to nonparametric models.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian framework jointly learns sum-product network structure and parameters, often improving test likelihood and supporting missing data.

title: Bayesian Learning of Sum-Product Networks

abstract: Wide neural networks with random weights and biases are Gaussian processes, as observed by Neal (1995) for shallow networks, and more recently by Lee et al.~(2018) and Matthews et al.~(2018) for deep fully-connected networks, as well as by Novak et al.~(2019) and Garriga-Alonso et al.~(2019) for deep convolutional networks. We show that this Neural Network-Gaussian Process correspondence surprisingly extends to all modern feedforward or recurrent neural networks composed of multilayer perceptron, RNNs (e.g. LSTMs, GRUs), (nD or graph) convolution, pooling, skip connection, attention, batch normalization, and/or layer normalization. More generally, we introduce a language for expressing neural network computations, and our result encompasses all such expressible neural networks. This work serves as a tutorial on the \emph{tensor programs} technique formulated in Yang (2019) and elucidates the Gaussian Process results obtained there. We provide open-source implementations of the Gaussian Process kernels of simple RNN, GRU, transformer, and batchnorm+ReLU network at github.com/thegregyang/GP4A. Please see our arxiv version for the complete and up-to-date version of this paper.

paragraphs: Wide neural networks with random weights and biases can correspond to Gaussian processes, giving a probabilistic description of their outputs across inputs. This paper extends that correspondence beyond previously studied fully connected and convolutional cases. Its result covers a broad range of modern feed-forward and recurrent architectures within a shared mathematical framework.

The supported components include multilayer perceptrons, recurrent units such as LSTMs and GRUs, ordinary and graph convolutions, pooling, skip connections, attention, and batch or layer normalization. The authors introduce a language for expressing neural-network computations, and the theorem encompasses networks expressible in that language. This makes the scope precise through the computation framework rather than through a short list of architectures.

The paper also serves as a tutorial on tensor programs, the technique underlying the result. Implementations of Gaussian-process kernels are provided for a simple RNN, a GRU, a transformer, and a network using batch normalization with ReLU. Together, the theory and implementations broaden the range of random wide networks that can be understood through Gaussian-process descriptions.
summary.tldr: Tensor programs extend the Gaussian-process correspondence for random wide networks to a broad range of feed-forward and recurrent architectures.

title: Wide Feedforward or Recurrent Neural Networks of Any Architecture are Gaussian Processes

abstract: We study linear approximate value iteration (LAVI) with a generative model. While linear models may accurately represent the optimal value function using a few parameters, several empirical and theoretical studies show the combination of least-squares projection with the Bellman operator may be expansive, thus leading LAVI to amplify errors over iterations and eventually diverge. We introduce an algorithm that approximates value functions by combining Q-values estimated at a set of \textit{anchor} states. Our algorithm tries to balance the generalization and compactness of linear methods with the small amplification of errors typical of interpolation methods. We prove that if the features at any state can be represented as a convex combination of features at the anchor points, then errors are propagated linearly over iterations (instead of exponentially) and our method achieves a polynomial sample complexity bound in the horizon and the number of anchor points. These findings are confirmed in preliminary simulations in a number of simple problems where a traditional least-square LAVI method diverges.

paragraphs: Linear approximate value iteration represents future rewards with relatively few parameters. Even when that representation can accurately express the optimal value function, repeated updates can fail. Combining least-squares projection with the Bellman operator may amplify errors until the estimates diverge. This paper studies that instability with access to a generative model.

The proposed algorithm builds value estimates by combining Q-values estimated at selected anchor states. Its aim is to preserve the compactness and generalization of linear models while obtaining the more controlled error behavior associated with interpolation. The anchors provide a set of reference estimates from which other states are represented.

The central guarantee has an explicit condition: every state's features must be a convex combination of anchor features. Under that condition, errors propagate linearly across iterations instead of exponentially, and sample complexity is polynomial in the horizon and number of anchors. Preliminary simulations on simple problems support the analysis, including cases where conventional least-squares value iteration diverges. The result identifies a sufficient geometric condition for more stable approximation.
summary.tldr: Anchor-based value approximation controls error propagation when every state's features are a convex combination of anchor features.

title: Limiting Extrapolation in Linear Approximate Value Iteration

abstract: End-to-end models for raw audio generation are a challenge, specially if they have to work with non-parallel data, which is a desirable setup in many situations. Voice conversion, in which a model has to impersonate a speaker in a recording, is one of those situations. In this paper, we propose Blow, a single-scale normalizing flow using hypernetwork conditioning to perform many-to-many voice conversion between raw audio. Blow is trained end-to-end, with non-parallel data, on a frame-by-frame basis using a single speaker identifier. We show that Blow compares favorably to existing flow-based architectures and other competitive baselines, obtaining equal or better performance in both objective and subjective evaluations. We further assess the impact of its main components with an ablation study, and quantify a number of properties such as the necessary amount of training data or the preference for source or target speakers.

paragraphs: Voice conversion changes the apparent speaker in a recording. Training such a system becomes particularly challenging when the available recordings are non-parallel, meaning they do not provide matched utterances across speakers. This paper introduces Blow, an end-to-end model that performs conversion directly on raw audio under that training setup.

Blow uses a single-scale normalizing flow with hypernetwork conditioning. The conditioning mechanism lets speaker information influence the model through a speaker identifier. Training operates frame by frame, and the same framework supports many-to-many conversion across speakers. These choices bring raw-audio modeling and speaker-controlled conversion into one trainable system without requiring parallel recordings.

The reported comparisons find equal or better performance than existing flow architectures and other competitive baselines in both objective measurements and subjective evaluations. An ablation study examines the contribution of the main components. The authors also investigate training-data requirements and whether converted speech favors source or target speaker characteristics, giving the evaluation a focus on both conversion quality and the behavior of the model.
summary.tldr: Blow performs many-to-many voice conversion directly on raw audio using non-parallel recordings and speaker-conditioned normalizing flows.

title: Blow: a single-scale hyperconditioned flow for non-parallel raw-audio voice conversion

abstract: Convolutional neural networks require significant memory bandwidth and storage for intermediate computations, apart from substantial computing resources. Neural network quantization has significant benefits in reducing the amount of intermediate results, but it often requires the full datasets and time-consuming fine tuning to recover the accuracy lost after quantization. This paper introduces the first practical 4-bit post training quantization approach: it does not involve training the quantized model (fine-tuning), nor it requires the availability of the full dataset. We target the quantization of both activations and weights and suggest three complementary methods for minimizing quantization error at the tensor level, two of whom obtain a closed-form analytical solution. Combining these methods, our approach achieves accuracy that is just a few percents less the state-of-the-art baseline across a wide range of convolutional models. The source code to replicate all experiments is available on GitHub: \url{https://github.com/submission2019/cnn-quantization}.

paragraphs: Convolutional networks require substantial computation, storage, and memory bandwidth, including for intermediate values. Quantization reduces the numerical precision used to represent these values, but recovering the resulting accuracy loss often requires access to the full training dataset and further training. Those requirements complicate deployment of an already trained model.

This paper introduces a practical approach to four-bit post-training quantization for both weights and activations. It requires neither fine-tuning of the quantized network nor the complete dataset. The authors propose three complementary techniques that minimize quantization error at the tensor level. Two of these techniques have closed-form analytical solutions.

Combining the methods produces accuracy only a few percent below the state-of-the-art baseline across a broad range of convolutional models, according to the reported results. The contribution is a deployment-oriented tradeoff: substantially reduced numerical precision with a relatively small reported accuracy loss, achieved without another training stage. Targeting both stored weights and intermediate activations addresses two sources of the memory demands described in the paper.
summary.tldr: Three complementary techniques enable four-bit quantization of network weights and activations without fine-tuning or access to the full dataset.

title: Post training 4-bit quantization of convolutional networks for rapid-deployment

abstract: Compressing word embeddings is important for deploying NLP models in memory-constrained settings. However, understanding what makes compressed embeddings perform well on downstream tasks is challenging---existing measures of compression quality often fail to distinguish between embeddings that perform well and those that do not. We thus propose the eigenspace overlap score as a new measure. We relate the eigenspace overlap score to downstream performance by developing generalization bounds for the compressed embeddings in terms of this score, in the context of linear and logistic regression. We then show that we can lower bound the eigenspace overlap score for a simple uniform quantization compression method, helping to explain the strong empirical performance of this method. Finally, we show that by using the eigenspace overlap score as a selection criterion between embeddings drawn from a representative set we compressed, we can efficiently identify the better performing embedding with up to 2x lower selection error rates than the next best measure of compression quality, and avoid the cost of training a separate model for each task of interest.

paragraphs: Compressing word embeddings saves memory, but a compression-quality score is useful only if it helps predict performance on subsequent language tasks. This paper finds that existing measures often fail to distinguish useful compressed embeddings from weaker ones. It proposes eigenspace overlap as a new way to assess how well compression preserves relevant structure.

The authors connect this score to downstream performance through generalization bounds for linear and logistic regression. They also derive a lower bound on eigenspace overlap for a simple uniform quantization method. This provides a theoretical explanation for that method's strong empirical performance by linking its compression behavior to a measure with downstream guarantees.

The paper then uses the score to choose among a representative collection of compressed embeddings. In those comparisons, selection error rates are up to two times lower than with the next-best compression measure. This offers a way to identify better-performing embeddings without training a separate model for every task of interest. The result concerns selection quality on the tested collection, while the theoretical connection is established in the stated regression settings.
summary.tldr: Eigenspace overlap helps predict and select compressed word embeddings that retain downstream performance without repeatedly training task-specific models.

title: On the Downstream Performance of Compressed Word Embeddings

abstract: We obtain global, non-asymptotic convergence guarantees for independent learning algorithms in competitive reinforcement learning settings with two agents (i.e., zero-sum stochastic games). We consider an episodic setting where in each episode, each player independently selects a policy and observes only their own actions and rewards, along with the state. We show that if both players run policy gradient methods in tandem, their policies will converge to a min-max equilibrium of the game, as long as their learning rates follow a two-timescale rule (which is necessary). To the best of our knowledge, this constitutes the first finite-sample convergence result for independent policy gradient methods in competitive RL; prior work has largely focused on centralized, coordinated procedures for equilibrium computation.

paragraphs: In a two-player zero-sum stochastic game, each player learns while facing an opponent who is also changing. This paper studies an episodic setting in which players independently choose policies. Each observes the state and its own actions and rewards, so learning does not rely on a centralized procedure with access to both players’ experience.

The authors prove that when both players use policy gradient methods, their policies converge to a minimax equilibrium under a two-timescale learning-rate rule. The requirement governs how the two players’ update rates relate, and the abstract identifies it as necessary. The convergence claim therefore depends on this specified relationship between learning rates.

The guarantees are global and non-asymptotic, providing finite-sample results rather than only a statement about limiting behavior. The authors describe this as, to their knowledge, the first such result for independent policy gradient methods in competitive reinforcement learning. It shows that equilibrium learning is possible through independent updates in the studied setting, extending analysis beyond centralized, coordinated computation.
summary.tldr: Independent policy gradients have finite-sample convergence guarantees in two-player zero-sum games when their learning rates follow a necessary two-timescale rule.

title: Independent Policy Gradient Methods for Competitive Reinforcement Learning

abstract: There is a growing interest in societal concerns in machine learning systems, especially in fairness. Multicalibration gives a comprehensive methodology to address group fairness. In this work, we address the multicalibration error and decouple it from the prediction error. The importance of decoupling the fairness metric (multicalibration) and the accuracy (prediction error) is due to the inherent trade-off between the two, and the societal decision regarding the ``right tradeoff'' (as imposed many times by regulators). Our work gives sample complexity bounds for uniform convergence guarantees of multicalibration error, which implies that regardless of the accuracy, we can guarantee that the empirical and (true) multicalibration errors are close. We emphasize that our results: (1) are more general than previous bounds, as they apply to both agnostic and realizable settings, and do not rely on a specific type of algorithm (such as differentially private), (2) improve over previous multicalibration sample complexity bounds and (3) implies uniform convergence guarantees for the classical calibration error.

paragraphs: Multicalibration provides a way to assess calibration across groups, making it relevant to group fairness. This paper separates the error in that fairness measure from ordinary prediction error. The distinction matters because choosing a trade-off between accuracy and fairness is a separate decision from determining how reliably either quantity has been measured.

The authors derive sample complexity bounds for uniform convergence of multicalibration error. These bounds specify how much data is sufficient to ensure that the error measured on samples is close to its population counterpart. The guarantee applies regardless of predictive accuracy, allowing confidence in the fairness estimate without tying it to a particular accuracy level.

The results cover both realizable and agnostic settings and do not depend on a specific algorithm category, such as differentially private methods. The authors also report improved sample complexity bounds over prior work. As a further consequence, their analysis yields uniform convergence guarantees for classical calibration error, extending the usefulness of the results beyond the multicalibration setting.
summary.tldr: The paper bounds the samples needed to estimate multicalibration error reliably, independently of prediction accuracy and a specific learning algorithm.

title: Sample Complexity of Uniform Convergence for Multicalibration

abstract: Obtaining generalization bounds for learning algorithms is one of the main subjects studied in theoretical machine learning. In recent years, information-theoretic bounds on generalization have gained the attention of researchers. This approach provides an insight into learning algorithms by considering the mutual information between the model and the training set. In this paper, a probabilistic graphical representation of this approach is adopted and two general techniques to improve the bounds are introduced, namely conditioning and processing. In conditioning, a random variable in the graph is considered as given, while in processing a random variable is substituted with one of its children. These techniques can be used to improve the bounds by either sharpening them or increasing their applicability. It is demonstrated that the proposed framework provides a simple and unified way to explain a variety of recent tightening results. New improved bounds derived by utilizing these techniques are also proposed.

paragraphs: Generalization bounds describe how learning from a training set relates to performance beyond that set. Information-theoretic approaches study this relationship through mutual information between the learned model and its training data. This paper develops a graphical framework for improving such bounds and understanding connections among existing results.

The authors represent the relevant random variables and their dependencies using a probabilistic graph. They introduce two operations on this representation. Conditioning treats a selected variable as given. Processing replaces a variable with one of its children in the graph. These operations provide systematic ways to change the information quantities used in an analysis.

The improvements can take two forms: a tighter bound or a bound applicable in more situations. The paper shows that the framework offers a unified explanation for several recent tightening results and uses it to derive new improved bounds. Its significance lies in organizing apparently separate advances around a shared set of techniques, while also supplying tools for developing further generalization analyses.
summary.tldr: Conditioning and processing provide a graphical framework for tightening information-theoretic generalization bounds or broadening their applicability.

title: Conditioning and Processing: Techniques to Improve Information-Theoretic Generalization Bounds

abstract: Stein discrepancies (SDs) monitor convergence and non-convergence in approximate inference when exact integration and sampling are intractable. However, the computation of a Stein discrepancy can be prohibitive if the Stein operator -- often a sum over likelihood terms or potentials -- is expensive to evaluate. To address this deficiency, we show that stochastic Stein discrepancies (SSDs) based on subsampled approximations of the Stein operator inherit the convergence control properties of standard SDs with probability 1. Along the way, we establish the convergence of Stein variational gradient descent (SVGD) on unbounded domains, resolving an open question of Liu (2017). In our experiments with biased Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) hyperparameter tuning, approximate MCMC sampler selection, and stochastic SVGD, SSDs deliver comparable inferences to standard SDs with orders of magnitude fewer likelihood evaluations.

paragraphs: Stein discrepancies help assess whether approximate inference is converging when exact integration and sampling are impractical. Their own computation can nevertheless be expensive because the Stein operator may require evaluating many likelihood terms or potentials. This paper introduces stochastic Stein discrepancies that replace the full operator with subsampled approximations.

The authors prove that these stochastic discrepancies retain the convergence-control properties of standard Stein discrepancies with probability one. This matters because reducing diagnostic cost is useful only if the diagnostic still reliably controls convergence behavior. Along the way, the analysis also establishes convergence of Stein variational gradient descent on unbounded domains, resolving a previously open question.

Experiments cover tuning hyperparameters for biased Markov chain Monte Carlo, selecting approximate MCMC samplers, and stochastic Stein variational gradient descent. Across these applications, stochastic discrepancies deliver comparable inferences with orders of magnitude fewer likelihood evaluations. The contribution combines a theoretical preservation result with evidence that subsampling can substantially reduce the computational cost of inference assessment and related procedures.
summary.tldr: Subsampled Stein discrepancies preserve convergence control with probability one and achieve comparable experimental inferences using far fewer likelihood evaluations.

title: Stochastic Stein Discrepancies

abstract: Aggregating multiple sources of weak supervision (WS) can ease the data-labeling bottleneck prevalent in many machine learning applications, by replacing the tedious manual collection of ground truth labels. Current state of the art approaches that do not use any labeled training data, however, require two separate modeling steps: Learning a probabilistic latent variable model based on the WS sources -- making assumptions that rarely hold in practice -- followed by downstream model training. Importantly, the first step of modeling does not consider the performance of the downstream model.To address these caveats we propose an end-to-end approach for directly learning the downstream model by maximizing its agreement with probabilistic labels generated by reparameterizing previous probabilistic posteriors with a neural network. Our results show improved performance over prior work in terms of end model performance on downstream test sets, as well as in terms of improved robustness to dependencies among weak supervision sources.

paragraphs: Weak supervision combines imperfect labeling sources to reduce the need for manually collected ground-truth labels. The paper examines approaches that train without labeled training data. In the existing workflow described by the authors, one model first combines the weak sources into probabilistic labels, and a separate downstream model then learns from those labels.

This separation creates two difficulties: the label model relies on assumptions that may not hold in practice, and its learning objective does not account for downstream predictive performance. The proposed approach connects the stages through end-to-end learning. It uses a neural network to reparameterize earlier probabilistic posteriors and trains the downstream predictor to agree with the resulting probabilistic labels.

The reported results show better downstream test performance than prior work and greater robustness when weak labeling sources depend on one another. Such dependencies matter because several sources can provide overlapping information rather than independent evidence. The findings support learning the probabilistic supervision and final predictor together, with the usefulness of the supervision tied more directly to the model that ultimately makes predictions.
summary.tldr: An end-to-end weak-supervision approach jointly connects probabilistic labeling with downstream learning, improving reported accuracy and robustness to dependent labeling sources.

title: End-to-End Weak Supervision

abstract: We study the problem of list-decodable linear regression, where an adversary can corrupt a majority of the examples. Specifically, we are given a set $T$ of labeled examples $(x, y) \in \mathbb{R}^d \times \mathbb{R}$ and a parameter $0< \alpha <1/2$ such that an $\alpha$-fraction of the points in $T$ are i.i.d. samples from a linear regression model with Gaussian covariates, and the remaining $(1-\alpha)$-fraction of the points are drawn from an arbitrary noise distribution. The goal is to output a small list of hypothesis vectors such that at least one of them is close to the target regression vector. Our main result is a Statistical Query (SQ) lower bound of $d^{\mathrm{poly}(1/\alpha)}$ for this problem. Our SQ lower bound qualitatively matches the performance of previously developed algorithms, providing evidence that current upper bounds for this task are nearly best possible.

paragraphs: This paper studies linear regression when most examples may be corrupted. Only an alpha fraction, with alpha below one half, are independent samples from a linear regression model with Gaussian input features. The remaining examples can come from an arbitrary noise distribution. This makes the reliable observations a minority of the available data.

The objective is to produce a small list of candidate regression vectors containing at least one vector close to the true target. The paper establishes a lower bound in the Statistical Query model, a restricted framework for studying learning algorithms. Its bound has the form d raised to a polynomial in 1/alpha, where d is the input dimension.

That dependence qualitatively matches previously developed algorithms. The result therefore provides evidence that existing upper bounds are nearly optimal for this task. Its scope matters: the lower bound is established for Statistical Query algorithms under the stated data model, so the evidence should not be read as an unrestricted impossibility result for every conceivable learning procedure.
summary.tldr: A Statistical Query lower bound suggests existing algorithms for regression with a minority of reliable examples are nearly optimal.

title: Statistical Query Lower Bounds for List-Decodable Linear Regression

abstract: Conventional supervised learning methods, especially deep ones, are found to be sensitive to out-of-distribution (OOD) examples, largely because the learned representation mixes the semantic factor with the variation factor due to their domain-specific correlation, while only the semantic factor causes the output. To address the problem, we propose a Causal Semantic Generative model (CSG) based on a causal reasoning so that the two factors are modeled separately, and develop methods for OOD prediction from a single training domain, which is common and challenging. The methods are based on the causal invariance principle, with a novel design in variational Bayes for both efficient learning and easy prediction. Theoretically, we prove that under certain conditions, CSG can identify the semantic factor by fitting training data, and this semantic-identification guarantees the boundedness of OOD generalization error and the success of adaptation. Empirical study shows improved OOD performance over prevailing baselines.

paragraphs: A representation can mix information that determines an output with variation that only happens to correlate with it in the training domain. Such correlations may change outside that domain, weakening predictions. This paper addresses that problem using a causal model that distinguishes semantic factors from variation factors, with only the semantic factor causing the output.

The Causal Semantic Generative model represents the two factors separately and supports out-of-distribution prediction from a single training domain. Its methods use causal invariance together with a variational Bayes design intended to make both learning and prediction efficient. The aim is to learn the part of a representation whose relationship to the output remains useful when domain-specific correlations change.

The theoretical results are conditional: under certain conditions, fitting the training data identifies the semantic factor. That identification guarantees a bounded out-of-distribution generalization error and successful adaptation within the theoretical setting. Empirical comparisons show improved performance over prevailing baselines. Together, the results link a causal representation design to both conditional guarantees and observed improvements beyond the training distribution.
summary.tldr: A causal generative model separates output-relevant semantics from domain-dependent variation to improve prediction beyond a single training domain.

title: Learning Causal Semantic Representation for Out-of-Distribution Prediction

abstract: A Forster transform is an operation that turns a multivariate distribution into one with good anti-concentration properties. While a Forster transform does not always exist, we show that any distribution can be efficiently decomposed as a disjoint mixture of few distributions for which a Forster transform exists and can be computed efficiently. As the main application of this result, we obtain the first polynomial-time algorithm for distribution-independent PAC learning of halfspaces in the Massart noise model with strongly polynomial sample complexity, i.e., independent of the bit complexity of the examples. Previous algorithms for this learning problem incurred sample complexity scaling polynomially with the bit complexity, even though such a dependence is not information-theoretically necessary.

paragraphs: A Forster transform reshapes a multivariate distribution to give it useful anti-concentration properties, meaning its probability mass avoids certain problematic forms of concentration. Such a transform does not exist for every distribution. This paper addresses that obstacle by showing that any distribution can be efficiently split into a small disjoint mixture of suitable components.

Each component in the decomposition admits a Forster transform, and the authors show that these transforms can also be computed efficiently. The decomposition therefore makes a useful geometric tool available piece by piece even when it cannot be applied to the entire distribution at once. This construction is the paper's central technical contribution.

The main application is learning halfspaces under the Massart noise model without assumptions on the example distribution. The resulting algorithm runs in polynomial time and has sample complexity independent of the bit complexity of the examples. Earlier algorithms required sample counts that grew polynomially with that representation complexity. The result removes a dependence that was not required by information-theoretic considerations, strengthening the computational guarantee for this learning problem.
summary.tldr: An efficient distribution decomposition enables polynomial-time learning of noisy halfspaces with sample complexity independent of example bit complexity.

title: Forster Decomposition and Learning Halfspaces with Noise

abstract: We present Multi-view Pose transformer (MvP) for estimating multi-person 3D poses from multi-view images. Instead of estimating 3D joint locations from costly volumetric representation or reconstructing the per-person 3D pose from multiple detected 2D poses as in previous methods, MvP directly regresses the multi-person 3D poses in a clean and efficient way, without relying on intermediate tasks. Specifically, MvP represents skeleton joints as learnable query embeddings and let them progressively attend to and reason over the multi-view information from the input images to directly regress the actual 3D joint locations. To improve the accuracy of such a simple pipeline, MvP presents a hierarchical scheme to concisely represent query embeddings of multi-person skeleton joints and introduces an input-dependent query adaptation approach. Further, MvP designs a novel geometrically guided attention mechanism, called projective attention, to more precisely fuse the cross-view information for each joint. MvP also introduces a RayConv operation to integrate the view-dependent camera geometry into the feature representations for augmenting the projective attention. We show experimentally that our MvP model outperforms the state-of-the-art methods on several benchmarks while being much more efficient. Notably, it achieves 92.3% AP25 on the challenging Panoptic dataset, improving upon the previous best approach [35] by 9.8%. MvP is general and also extendable to recovering human mesh represented by the SMPL model, thus useful for modeling multi-person body shapes. Code and models are available at https://github.com/sail-sg/mvp.

Multi-view Pose transformer, or MvP, instead predicts the 3D joint positions directly from the images. This removes intermediate estimation tasks from the pose pipeline and makes cross-view reasoning part of the prediction model itself.

MvP represents skeleton joints with learned query embeddings that progressively gather information from the different views. A hierarchical representation organizes queries for multiple people, while input-dependent adaptation adjusts them to the images. Projective attention uses geometry to guide which cross-view information each joint combines. A further operation, RayConv, incorporates camera geometry into the image features supporting that attention.

The authors report higher accuracy and substantially greater efficiency than previous state-of-the-art methods on several benchmarks. On Panoptic, MvP reaches 92.3% AP25. They also describe an extension to human meshes represented by SMPL, connecting the same general approach to body-shape recovery. The contribution combines a direct prediction pipeline with explicit geometric guidance rather than leaving view fusion entirely unconstrained.
summary.tldr: MvP directly predicts multiple people's 3D joints from camera views using learned queries and geometrically guided attention.

title: Direct Multi-view Multi-person 3D Pose Estimation

abstract: Hierarchical Bayesian methods enable information sharing across regression problems on multiple groups of data. While standard practice is to model regression parameters (effects) as (1) exchangeable across the groups and (2) correlated to differing degrees across covariates, we show that this approach exhibits poor statistical performance when the number of covariates exceeds the number of groups. For instance, in statistical genetics, we might regress dozens of traits (defining groups) for thousands of individuals (responses) on up to millions of genetic variants (covariates). When an analyst has more covariates than groups, we argue that it is often preferable to instead model effects as (1) exchangeable across covariates and (2) correlated to differing degrees across groups. To this end, we propose a hierarchical model expressing our alternative perspective. We devise an empirical Bayes estimator for learning the degree of correlation between groups. We develop theory that demonstrates that our method outperforms the classic approach when the number of covariates dominates the number of groups, and corroborate this result empirically on several high-dimensional multiple regression and classification problems.

paragraphs: Hierarchical Bayesian models share information among related regression problems. A common design treats effects as exchangeable across data groups while allowing correlations among covariates. This paper shows that this arrangement can perform poorly when covariates greatly outnumber groups, a situation that arises in high-dimensional applications such as statistical genetics.

The proposed alternative reverses the roles: effects are modeled as exchangeable across covariates, while correlations can differ across groups. Exchangeability specifies which effects receive a common probabilistic treatment. Changing that choice therefore changes how the model pools information. The authors construct a hierarchical model with this structure and an empirical Bayes estimator for learning correlations between groups.

Their theory demonstrates an advantage over the classic approach when the number of covariates dominates the number of groups. Experiments on several high-dimensional regression and classification problems support that result. The paper's message is tied to this dimensional regime: the direction in which a hierarchical model shares information can substantially affect statistical performance, and the conventional arrangement is not always the preferable one.
summary.tldr: When covariates outnumber groups, exchanging their usual roles in a hierarchical model can improve statistical performance.

title: For high-dimensional hierarchical models, consider exchangeability of effects across covariates instead of across datasets

abstract: This paper presents a novel discriminator-constrained optimal transport network (DOTN) that performs unsupervised domain adaptation for speech enhancement (SE), which is an essential regression task in speech processing. The DOTN aims to estimate clean references of noisy speech in a target domain, by exploiting the knowledge available from the source domain. The domain shift between training and testing data has been reported to be an obstacle to learning problems in diverse fields. Although rich literature exists on unsupervised domain adaptation for classification, the methods proposed, especially in regressions, remain scarce and often depend on additional information regarding the input data. The proposed DOTN approach tactically fuses the optimal transport (OT) theory from mathematical analysis with generative adversarial frameworks, to help evaluate continuous labels in the target domain. The experimental results on two SE tasks demonstrate that by extending the classical OT formulation, our proposed DOTN outperforms previous adversarial domain adaptation frameworks in a purely unsupervised manner.

paragraphs: Speech-enhancement systems estimate clean speech from noisy recordings. Their training and deployment conditions can differ, creating a domain shift that complicates learning. This paper addresses adaptation to a target domain using knowledge available from a source domain.

The proposed discriminator-constrained optimal transport network, DOTN, performs that adaptation without target-domain supervision. It aims to estimate clean references for noisy target speech, treating enhancement as a regression task with continuous outputs.

DOTN combines optimal transport with a generative adversarial framework. The discriminator constraint extends the classical transport formulation to help evaluate continuous target-domain labels. This addresses a setting where unsupervised adaptation methods are less developed than in classification and often require additional input information.

Experiments on two speech-enhancement tasks show improvements over previous adversarial domain-adaptation frameworks in a purely unsupervised setting. The contribution is a transport-based adaptation mechanism tailored to continuous speech outputs, with the reported results supporting its usefulness when noise conditions differ between the source and target domains.
summary.tldr: DOTN combines optimal transport and adversarial learning to adapt speech enhancement to new noise domains without target supervision.

title: Unsupervised Noise Adaptive Speech Enhancement by Discriminator-Constrained Optimal Transport

abstract: The convex consistency dimension of a supervised learning task is the lowest prediction dimension $d$ such that there exists a convex surrogate $L : \mathbb{R}^d \times \mathcal Y \to \mathbb R$ that is consistent for the given task. We present a new tool based on property elicitation, $d$-flats, for lower-bounding convex consistency dimension. This tool unifies approaches from a variety of domains, including continuous and discrete prediction problems. We use $d$-flats to obtain a new lower bound on the convex consistency dimension of risk measures, resolving an open question due to Frongillo and Kash (NeurIPS 2015). In discrete prediction settings, we show that the $d$-flats approach recovers and even tightens previous lower bounds using feasible subspace dimension.

paragraphs: A supervised learning task may be trained through a convex surrogate whose predictions are vectors. This paper asks how small those vectors can be while still allowing a surrogate consistent with the target task. The minimum such size is called the convex consistency dimension, and lower bounds establish dimensions below which a suitable surrogate cannot exist.

The authors introduce a tool called d-flats, based on property elicitation, for proving these lower bounds. The approach unifies reasoning across continuous and discrete prediction problems. Its value lies in providing a shared way to analyze the dimensional requirements of surrogate losses across domains that had used different techniques.

Applied to risk measures, the tool produces a new lower bound and resolves an existing open question. In discrete prediction, it recovers and sometimes strengthens earlier bounds based on feasible subspace dimension. These are structural results about what convex surrogate formulations require. They help characterize the possible prediction spaces before a particular optimization algorithm or model is chosen.
summary.tldr: The d-flats tool unifies and strengthens lower bounds on the prediction dimension required by consistent convex surrogates.

title: Unifying lower bounds on prediction dimension of convex surrogates

abstract: Episodic event memory is a key component of human cognition. Predicting event memorability,i.e., to what extent an event is recalled, is a tough challenge in memory research and has profound implications for artificial intelligence. In this study, we investigate factors that affect event memorability according to a cued recall process. Specifically, we explore whether event memorability is contingent on the event context, as well as the intrinsic visual attributes of image cues. We design a novel experiment protocol and conduct a large-scale experiment with 47 elder subjects over 3 months. Subjects’ memory of life events is tested in a cued recall process. Using advanced visual analytics methods, we build a first-of-its-kind event memorability dataset (called R3) with rich information about event context and visual semantic features. Furthermore, we propose a contextual event memory network (CEMNet) that tackles multi-modal input to predict item-wise event memorability, which outperforms competitive benchmarks. The findings inform deeper understanding of episodic event memory, and open up a new avenue for prediction of human episodic memory. Source code is available at https://github.com/ffzzy840304/Predicting-Event-Memorability.

This paper studies that question through cued recall, examining whether prediction should account for the context of an event as well as the visual properties of the image used as a cue. The findings concern the studied cued-recall setting and provide evidence for richer event-memory modeling.
summary.tldr: A cued-recall study introduces the R3 dataset and CEMNet for predicting life-event memorability from contextual and visual information.

title: Predicting Event Memorability from Contextual Visual Semantics

abstract: This paper focuses on training implicit models of infinite layers. Specifically, previous works employ implicit differentiation and solve the exact gradient for the backward propagation. However, is it necessary to compute such an exact but expensive gradient for training? In this work, we propose a novel gradient estimate for implicit models, named phantom gradient, that 1) forgoes the costly computation of the exact gradient; and 2) provides an update direction empirically preferable to the implicit model training. We theoretically analyze the condition under which an ascent direction of the loss landscape could be found and provide two specific instantiations of the phantom gradient based on the damped unrolling and Neumann series. Experiments on large-scale tasks demonstrate that these lightweight phantom gradients significantly accelerate the backward passes in training implicit models by roughly 1.7 $\times$ and even boost the performance over approaches based on the exact gradient on ImageNet.

paragraphs: Implicit models can represent computations corresponding to infinitely many layers. Training them has commonly involved implicit differentiation to compute an exact gradient for backpropagation, which can be expensive. This paper asks whether a cheaper gradient estimate can serve as an effective training signal.

The proposed phantom gradient avoids the costly exact-gradient computation. The authors analyze conditions under which an ascent direction in the loss landscape can be found and give two implementations, based on damped unrolling and a Neumann series. These provide concrete ways to construct lightweight gradient estimates for implicit-model training.

Experiments on large-scale tasks show backward-pass acceleration of roughly 1.7 times. On ImageNet, the method also improves performance over approaches using the exact gradient. The empirical result is therefore about both reduced backward computation and the usefulness of the resulting update direction. The paper does not establish that every approximate gradient is preferable; it supplies particular constructions, theoretical conditions, and experimental evidence for the phantom-gradient approach.
summary.tldr: Phantom gradients replace expensive exact gradients in implicit models, accelerating backward passes and improving ImageNet performance in experiments.

title: On Training Implicit Models

abstract: Deep reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms are powerful tools for solving visuomotor decision tasks. However, the trained models are often difficult to interpret, because they are represented as end-to-end deep neural networks. In this paper, we shed light on the inner workings of such trained models by analyzing the pixels that they attend to during task execution, and comparing them with the pixels attended to by humans executing the same tasks. To this end, we investigate the following two questions that, to the best of our knowledge, have not been previously studied. 1) How similar are the visual representations learned by RL agents and humans when performing the same task? and, 2) How do similarities and differences in these learned representations explain RL agents' performance on these tasks? Specifically, we compare the saliency maps of RL agents against visual attention models of human experts when learning to play Atari games. Further, we analyze how hyperparameters of the deep RL algorithm affect the learned representations and saliency maps of the trained agents. The insights provided have the potential to inform novel algorithms for closing the performance gap between human experts and RL agents.

Specifically, we compare the saliency maps of RL agents against visual attention models of human experts when learning to play Atari games. Further, we analyze how hyperparameters of the deep RL algorithm affect the learned representations and saliency maps of the trained agents. The insights provided have the potential to inform novel algorithms for closing the performance gap between human experts and RL agents.

paragraphs: A reinforcement-learning agent may perform a visual task successfully while remaining difficult to interpret. This paper examines that problem by comparing the image regions associated with an agent's decisions to those attended to by human experts performing the same task. The aim is to connect visual representations with behavior, rather than assess performance alone.

The study focuses on Atari games and compares agent saliency maps with models of expert human visual attention. It asks how similar the learned representations are and how their similarities or differences can help explain agent performance. This comparison provides a concrete way to investigate which visual information the trained systems emphasize during task execution.

The authors also analyze how reinforcement-learning hyperparameters affect the learned representations and saliency maps. This links choices made during training to the visual behavior of the resulting agent. The stated contribution is an interpretive investigation whose insights could inform future algorithms for narrowing the performance gap with human experts. The abstract presents that algorithmic benefit as a possibility, rather than reporting that the gap has already been closed.
summary.tldr: The study compares Atari agents' saliency maps with expert human attention to investigate visual representations, performance, and the effects of training hyperparameters.

title: Machine versus Human Attention in Deep Reinforcement Learning Tasks

abstract: Neural Ordinary Differential Equations (NODEs) have proven successful in learning dynamical systems in terms of accurately recovering the observed trajectories. While different types of sparsity have been proposed to improve robustness, the generalization properties of NODEs for dynamical systems beyond the observed data are underexplored. We systematically study the influence of weight and feature sparsity on forecasting as well as on identifying the underlying dynamical laws. Besides assessing existing methods, we propose a regularization technique to sparsify ``input-output connections'' and extract relevant features during training. Moreover, we curate real-world datasets including human motion capture and human hematopoiesis single-cell RNA-seq data to realistically analyze different levels of out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization in forecasting and dynamics identification respectively. Our extensive empirical evaluation on these challenging benchmarks suggests that weight sparsity improves generalization in the presence of noise or irregular sampling. However, it does not prevent learning spurious feature dependencies in the inferred dynamics, rendering them impractical for predictions under interventions, or for inferring the true underlying dynamics. Instead, feature sparsity can indeed help with recovering sparse ground-truth dynamics compared to unregularized NODEs.

paragraphs: Neural ordinary differential equations can fit observed trajectories, but that does not establish whether they recover the underlying dynamical laws or predict well beyond those observations. This paper systematically compares weight sparsity and feature sparsity for both forecasting and identifying dynamics. It also proposes regularization that sparsifies input-output connections and selects relevant features during training.

The authors curate human motion-capture and human hematopoiesis single-cell RNA-sequencing datasets to examine different levels of out-of-distribution generalization. Their empirical evaluation suggests that weight sparsity improves generalization when observations are noisy or sampled irregularly. summary.tldr: Weight sparsity can improve neural-ODE forecasting under imperfect observations, while feature sparsity better supports recovery of sparse dynamics.

title: Sparsity in Continuous-Depth Neural Networks

abstract: Probabilistic programs provide an expressive representation language for generative models. Given a probabilistic program, we are interested in the task of posterior inference: estimating a latent variable given a set of observed variables. Existing techniques for inference in probabilistic programs often require choosing many hyper-parameters, are computationally expensive, and/or only work for restricted classes of programs. Here we formulate inference as masked language modeling: given a program, we generate a supervised dataset of variables and assignments, and randomly mask a subset of the assignments. We then train a neural network to unmask the random values, defining an approximate posterior distribution. By optimizing a single neural network across a range of programs we amortize the cost of training, yielding a "foundation" posterior able to do zero-shot inference for new programs. The foundation posterior can also be fine-tuned for a particular program and dataset by optimizing a variational inference objective. We show the efficacy of the approach, zero-shot and fine-tuned, on a benchmark of STAN programs.

paragraphs: Probabilistic programs describe how observed and hidden variables are generated. Posterior inference works in the opposite direction, estimating hidden variables from observations. Existing inference methods can be computationally expensive, require many hyperparameter choices, or support only restricted program families. This paper explores learning an inference model that can be reused across programs.

The approach treats inference as a masked prediction problem. A program supplies supervised examples containing variables and their assigned values, and some assignments are randomly hidden. A neural network learns to predict the missing values, thereby defining an approximate posterior distribution. Training a single network across multiple programs spreads the training cost across those inference problems.

The resulting foundation posterior can perform inference on new programs without additional training. It can also be specialized to a particular program and dataset through a variational inference objective. Experiments on a benchmark of STAN programs demonstrate the approach in both zero-shot and fine-tuned forms. The central idea is to make approximate inference reusable through shared predictive training.
summary.tldr: A network trained to reconstruct masked variable assignments across probabilistic programs learns reusable approximate posteriors for zero-shot or fine-tuned inference.

title: Foundation Posteriors for Approximate Probabilistic Inference

abstract: Test-time adaptation (TTA) refers to adapting neural networks to distribution shifts, specifically with just access to unlabeled test samples from the new domain at test-time. Prior TTA methods optimize over unsupervised objectives such as the entropy of model predictions in TENT (Wang et al., 2021), but it is unclear what exactly makes a good TTA loss. In this paper, we start by presenting a surprising phenomenon: if we attempt to $\textit{meta-learn}$ the ``best'' possible TTA loss over a wide class of functions, then we recover a function that is $\textit{remarkably}$ similar to (a temperature-scaled version of) the softmax-entropy employed by TENT. This only holds, however, if the classifier we are adapting is trained via cross-entropy loss; if the classifier is trained via squared loss, a different ``best'' TTA loss emerges.To explain this phenomenon, we analyze test-time adaptation through the lens of the training losses's $\textit{convex conjugate}$. We show that under natural conditions, this (unsupervised) conjugate function can be viewed as a good local approximation to the original supervised loss and indeed, it recovers the ``best'' losses found by meta-learning. This leads to a generic recipe than be used to find a good TTA loss for $\textit{any}$ given supervised training loss function of a general class. Empirically, our approach dominates other TTA alternatives over a wide range of domain adaptation benchmarks. Our approach is particularly of interest when applied to classifiers trained with $\textit{novel}$ loss functions, e.g., the recently-proposed PolyLoss (Leng et al., 2022) function, where it differs substantially from (and outperforms) an entropy-based loss. Further, we show that our conjugate based approach can also be interpreted as a kind of self-training using a very specific soft label, which we refer to as the $\textit{conjugate pseudo-label}$. Overall, therefore, our method provides a broad framework for better understanding and improving test-time adaptation. Code is available at https://github.com/locuslab/tta_conjugate.

The authors find that meta-learning an adaptation loss produces something close to temperature-scaled prediction entropy for a cross-entropy-trained classifier, but produces a different objective for a classifier trained with squared loss.

They explain this dependence through the training loss's convex conjugate. Under natural conditions, the resulting unsupervised function provides a good local approximation to the supervised loss and recovers the objectives discovered through meta-learning.
