For classifiers trained with PolyLoss, the derived objective differs substantially from entropy and outperforms it. The central implication is that the model's original training objective can guide the choice of test-time adaptation loss.
summary.tldr: Convex conjugates provide training-loss-specific objectives and pseudo-labels for adapting classifiers to unlabeled test domains.

title: Test Time Adaptation via Conjugate Pseudo-labels

abstract: For predictive models to provide reliable guidance in decision making processes, they are often required to be accurate and robust to distribution shifts. Shortcut learning--where a model relies on spurious correlations or shortcuts to predict the target label--undermines the robustness property, leading to models with poor out-of-distribution accuracy despite good in-distribution performance. Existing work on shortcut learning either assumes that the set of possible shortcuts is known a priori or is discoverable using interpretability methods such as saliency maps, which might not always be true. Instead, we propose a two step approach to (1) efficiently identify relevant shortcuts, and (2) leverage the identified shortcuts to build models that are robust to distribution shifts. Our approach relies on having access to a (possibly) high dimensional set of auxiliary labels at training time, some of which correspond to possible shortcuts. We show both theoretically and empirically that our approach is able to identify a sufficient set of shortcuts leading to more efficient predictors in finite samples.

paragraphs: A predictive model can perform well on familiar data by exploiting correlations that stop being useful in a new environment. This shortcut learning creates a gap between accuracy on the training distribution and reliability under distribution shifts. Addressing the problem requires identifying which available signals act as shortcuts.

The paper proposes a two-stage approach: first identify relevant shortcuts efficiently, then use that information to train predictors that are more robust to shifts. Its key requirement is access during training to auxiliary labels, potentially a large collection, some of which describe possible shortcuts. This provides a pool from which to identify relevant shortcuts without assuming their precise set is already known or recoverable from saliency maps.

The authors give theoretical and empirical evidence that their approach can identify a sufficient set of shortcuts and produce more efficient predictors with finite samples. Sufficiency matters here: the stated result does not require identifying every conceivable shortcut. The contribution links shortcut discovery to predictor construction, while making the availability of auxiliary training labels a substantive part of the method’s setting.
summary.tldr: The method uses auxiliary training labels to identify a sufficient set of shortcuts and build more robust predictors.

title: Causally motivated multi-shortcut identification and removal

abstract: A striking observation about iterative magnitude pruning (IMP; Frankle et al. 2020) is that—after just a few hundred steps of dense training—the method can find a sparse sub-network that can be trained to the same accuracy as the dense network. However, the same does not hold at step 0, i.e. random initialization. In this work, we seek to understand how this early phase of pre-training leads to a good initialization for IMP both through the lens of the data distribution and the loss landscape geometry. Empirically we observe that, holding the number of pre-training iterations constant, training on a small fraction of (randomly chosen) data suffices to obtain an equally good initialization for IMP. We additionally observe that by pre-training only on "easy" training data, we can decrease the number of steps necessary to find a good initialization for IMP compared to training on the full dataset or a randomly chosen subset. Finally, we identify novel properties of the loss landscape of dense networks that are predictive of IMP performance, showing in particular that more examples being linearly mode connected in the dense network correlates well with good initializations for IMP. Combined, these results provide new insight into the role played by the early phase training in IMP.

paragraphs: Iterative magnitude pruning can discover sparse subnetworks that train to the accuracy of a dense network after a short period of dense training. The same behavior does not hold at random initialization. This paper investigates what that early training phase contributes, examining both the data used during pretraining and the geometry of the loss landscape.

The experiments show that, when the number of pretraining iterations stays fixed, a small randomly selected fraction of the data can produce an equally good initialization for pruning. Selecting only easy training examples can further reduce the number of steps needed, compared with using either the full dataset or a random subset. These findings distinguish the amount of data encountered from the number and character of early updates.

The authors also identify loss-landscape properties predictive of pruning performance. In particular, a greater number of examples exhibiting linear mode connectivity in the dense network correlates with better initializations. This is evidence of an association, rather than a claim that the geometric property alone causes successful pruning. Together, the observations clarify how early training prepares a network for sparsification.
summary.tldr: Experiments show that small data subsets can prepare networks for successful pruning, while easy examples can reduce the required pretraining steps.

title: Lottery Tickets on a Data Diet: Finding Initializations with Sparse Trainable Networks

abstract: Groundbreaking language-vision architectures like CLIP and DALL-E proved the utility of training on large amounts of noisy image-text data, without relying on expensive accurate labels used in standard vision unimodal supervised learning. The resulting models showed capabilities of strong text-guided image generation and transfer to downstream tasks, while performing remarkably at zero-shot classification with noteworthy out-of-distribution robustness. Since then, large-scale language-vision models like ALIGN, BASIC, GLIDE, Flamingo and Imagen made further improvements. Studying the training and capabilities of such models requires datasets containing billions of image-text pairs. Until now, no datasets of this size have been made openly available for the broader research community. To address this problem and democratize research on large-scale multi-modal models, we present LAION-5B - a dataset consisting of 5.85 billion CLIP-filtered image-text pairs, of which 2.32B contain English language. We show successful replication and fine-tuning of foundational models like CLIP, GLIDE and Stable Diffusion using the dataset, and discuss further experiments enabled with an openly available dataset of this scale. Additionally we provide several nearest neighbor indices, an improved web-interface for dataset exploration and subset generation, and detection scores for watermark, NSFW, and toxic content detection.

Studying these models at their intended scale requires billions of pairs. LAION-5B addresses the lack of openly available data at that scale by providing a resource for broader research participation.

The dataset contains 5.85 billion image-text pairs filtered using CLIP, including 2.32 billion pairs with English text. The authors demonstrate successful replication and fine-tuning of models such as CLIP, GLIDE, and Stable Diffusion using the dataset. These demonstrations establish that the collection can support substantial language-vision modeling work, beyond simply offering a large catalog of paired data.

The release also includes nearest-neighbor indices, a web interface for exploring the collection and generating subsets, and detection scores for watermarks, NSFW content, and toxic content. These supporting tools help researchers navigate and select from the dataset. The contribution therefore combines scale, open availability, demonstrated model-training uses, and infrastructure for working with the collection.
summary.tldr: LAION-5B opens access to 5.85 billion CLIP-filtered image-text pairs and tools for exploring and using them in multimodal research.

title: LAION-5B: An open large-scale dataset for training next generation image-text models

abstract: In many multi-agent settings, participants can form teams to achieve collective outcomes that may far surpass their individual capabilities. Measuring the relative contributions of agents and allocating them shares of the reward that promote long-lasting cooperation are difficult tasks. Cooperative game theory offers solution concepts identifying distribution schemes, such as the Shapley value, that fairly reflect the contribution of individuals to the performance of the team or the Core, which reduces the incentive of agents to abandon their team. Applications of such methods include identifying influential features and sharing the costs of joint ventures or team formation. Unfortunately, using these solutions requires tackling a computational barrier as they are hard to compute, even in restricted settings. In this work, we show how cooperative game-theoretic solutions can be distilled into a learned model by training neural networks to propose fair and stable payoff allocations. We show that our approach creates models that can generalize to games far from the training distribution and can predict solutions for more players than observed during training. An important application of our framework is Explainable AI: our approach can be used to speed-up Shapley value computations on many instances.

paragraphs: Teams can achieve outcomes beyond what their members could accomplish separately, but dividing the reward raises questions of contribution and cooperation. Cooperative game theory provides concepts such as the Shapley value for contribution-based allocation and the Core for reducing incentives to leave a team. Computing these solutions can be difficult even in restricted settings.

Neural Payoff Machines learn to propose allocations by distilling cooperative game-theoretic solutions into neural networks. The approach aims to retain the usefulness of fair and stable allocation concepts while replacing repeated expensive solution computations with predictions from a trained model. Fairness and stability here refer to the game-theoretic concepts motivating the learned outputs.

The authors show that the resulting models can generalize to games far from their training distribution and predict solutions involving more players than were present during training. They also identify explainable AI as an application: the framework can accelerate Shapley-value computations across many instances. These findings support learned approximation as a way to make computationally demanding allocation concepts more accessible.
summary.tldr: Neural Payoff Machines learn to predict game-theoretic reward allocations and can generalize to unfamiliar games and larger teams.

title: Neural Payoff Machines: Predicting Fair and Stable Payoff Allocations Among Team Members

abstract: Adversarial training, originally designed to resist test-time adversarial examples, has shown to be promising in mitigating training-time availability attacks. This defense ability, however, is challenged in this paper. We identify a novel threat model named stability attack, which aims to hinder robust availability by slightly manipulating the training data. Under this threat, we show that adversarial training using a conventional defense budget $\epsilon$ provably fails to provide test robustness in a simple statistical setting, where the non-robust features of the training data can be reinforced by $\epsilon$-bounded perturbation. Further, we analyze the necessity of enlarging the defense budget to counter stability attacks. Finally, comprehensive experiments demonstrate that stability attacks are harmful on benchmark datasets, and thus the adaptive defense is necessary to maintain robustness.

paragraphs: Adversarial training prepares a model to withstand malicious changes to its inputs at prediction time. It has also shown promise against attacks that alter training data to undermine learning. This paper asks whether small changes to the training data can instead manipulate adversarial training itself, leaving the resulting model vulnerable when it is tested.

The authors introduce a threat called a stability attack. Its aim is to damage the robustness obtainable from the training data. In a simple statistical setting, they prove that perturbations bounded by epsilon can strengthen non-robust features enough that adversarial training with the conventional epsilon defense budget fails to provide test robustness.

The paper then analyzes why a larger defense budget is necessary to counter these attacks. Experiments on benchmark datasets also show that stability attacks can be harmful. Together, the theory and experiments challenge the assumption that a conventional adversarial-training budget remains adequate after training data has been manipulated, and motivate adapting the defense to this threat.
summary.tldr: Small training-data perturbations can undermine adversarial training’s test robustness, motivating an enlarged defense budget against stability attacks.

title: Can Adversarial Training Be Manipulated By Non-Robust Features?

abstract: Embedded topic models are able to learn interpretable topics even with large and heavy-tailed vocabularies. However, they generally hold the Euclidean embedding space assumption, leading to a basic limitation in capturing hierarchical relations. To this end, we present a novel framework that introduces hyperbolic embeddings to represent words and topics. With the tree-likeness property of hyperbolic space, the underlying semantic hierarchy among words and topics can be better exploited to mine more interpretable topics. Furthermore, due to the superiority of hyperbolic geometry in representing hierarchical data, tree-structure knowledge can also be naturally injected to guide the learning of a topic hierarchy. Therefore, we further develop a regularization term based on the idea of contrastive learning to inject prior structural knowledge efficiently. Experiments on both topic taxonomy discovery and document representation demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves improved performance against existing embedded topic models.

paragraphs: Topic models seek interpretable themes within document collections. Embedded topic models represent words and topics in a geometric space, but the usual Euclidean space can make hierarchical relationships difficult to capture. HyperMiner changes that geometry to better represent how broad themes and more specific topics relate within a semantic hierarchy.

The framework embeds both words and topics in hyperbolic space, whose tree-like structure suits hierarchical data. This gives the model a way to exploit semantic relationships when discovering topics. The same geometry also provides a natural place to incorporate existing tree-structured knowledge rather than relying entirely on hierarchy discovery from documents.

To introduce that prior structure, the authors add a regularization term inspired by contrastive learning. It guides topic-hierarchy learning using the supplied structural knowledge. Experiments on topic taxonomy discovery and document representation show improvements over existing embedded topic models. The findings support choosing an embedding geometry that fits hierarchical organization and combining it with explicit structural guidance when available.
summary.tldr: HyperMiner uses hyperbolic embeddings and optional structural guidance to improve topic hierarchy discovery and document representation.

title: HyperMiner: Topic Taxonomy Mining with Hyperbolic Embedding

abstract: We study the problem of multi-armed bandits with ε-global Differential Privacy (DP). First, we prove the minimax and problem-dependent regret lower bounds for stochastic and linear bandits that quantify the hardness of bandits with ε-global DP. These bounds suggest the existence of two hardness regimes depending on the privacy budget ε. In the high-privacy regime (small ε), the hardness depends on a coupled effect of privacy and partial information about the reward distributions. In the low-privacy regime (large ε), bandits with ε-global DP are not harder than the bandits without privacy. For stochastic bandits, we further propose a generic framework to design a near-optimal ε global DP extension of an index-based optimistic bandit algorithm. The framework consists of three ingredients: the Laplace mechanism, arm-dependent adaptive episodes, and usage of only the rewards collected in the last episode for computing private statistics. Specifically, we instantiate ε-global DP extensions of UCB and KL-UCB algorithms, namely AdaP-UCB and AdaP-KLUCB. AdaP-KLUCB is the first algorithm that both satisfies ε-global DP and yields a regret upper bound that matches the problem-dependent lower bound up to multiplicative constants.

The framework consists of three ingredients: the Laplace mechanism, arm-dependent adaptive episodes, and usage of only the rewards collected in the last episode for computing private statistics. AdaP-KLUCB is the first algorithm that both satisfies ε-global DP and yields a regret upper bound that matches the problem-dependent lower bound up to multiplicative constants.

paragraphs: A bandit algorithm chooses actions while learning from limited reward feedback. This paper studies the additional difficulty of requiring global differential privacy. It proves minimax and problem-dependent regret lower bounds for stochastic and linear bandits, quantifying unavoidable losses from learning under both partial information and a privacy constraint.

The bounds suggest two regimes. With strong privacy, corresponding to a small privacy budget, difficulty reflects a coupled effect of privacy and incomplete knowledge of rewards. With weaker privacy, the private problem is no harder in the characterized sense than its non-private counterpart. This distinction explains why privacy's learning cost depends on the regime.

For stochastic bandits, the authors give a framework combining Laplace noise, adaptive episodes for each arm, and private statistics computed only from the latest episode's rewards. It produces private variants of UCB and KL-UCB. The resulting AdaP-KLUCB algorithm satisfies global differential privacy and matches the problem-dependent regret lower bound up to multiplicative constants, connecting the hardness analysis to an algorithm with a correspondingly strong guarantee.
summary.tldr: The paper characterizes privacy-dependent bandit difficulty and introduces a globally private algorithm matching the problem-dependent regret lower bound up to constants.

title: When Privacy Meets Partial Information: A Refined Analysis of Differentially Private Bandits

abstract: Twitter bot detection has become an increasingly important task to combat misinformation, facilitate social media moderation, and preserve the integrity of the online discourse. State-of-the-art bot detection methods generally leverage the graph structure of the Twitter network, and they exhibit promising performance when confronting novel Twitter bots that traditional methods fail to detect. However, very few of the existing Twitter bot detection datasets are graph-based, and even these few graph-based datasets suffer from limited dataset scale, incomplete graph structure, as well as low annotation quality. In fact, the lack of a large-scale graph-based Twitter bot detection benchmark that addresses these issues has seriously hindered the development and evaluation of novel graph-based bot detection approaches. In this paper, we propose TwiBot-22, a comprehensive graph-based Twitter bot detection benchmark that presents the largest dataset to date, provides diversified entities and relations on the Twitter network, and has considerably better annotation quality than existing datasets. In addition, we re-implement 35 representative Twitter bot detection baselines and evaluate them on 9 datasets, including TwiBot-22, to promote a fair comparison of model performance and a holistic understanding of research progress. To facilitate further research, we consolidate all implemented codes and datasets into the TwiBot-22 evaluation framework, where researchers could consistently evaluate new models and datasets. The TwiBot-22 Twitter bot detection benchmark and evaluation framework are publicly available at \url{https://twibot22.github.io/}.

paragraphs: Twitter bot detection increasingly uses relationships in the social network, but evaluating those methods requires datasets that preserve useful graph structure. The benchmark is designed to support methods that make use of network connections.

They combine the implementations and datasets into a public evaluation framework. summary.tldr: TwiBot-22 combines a large graph-based Twitter bot dataset with a public framework evaluating 35 baselines across nine datasets.

title: TwiBot-22: Towards Graph-Based Twitter Bot Detection

abstract: Interpretable and fair machine learning models are required for many applications, such as credit assessment and in criminal justice. Decision trees offer this interpretability, especially when they are small. Optimal decision trees are of particular interest because they offer the best performance possible for a given size. However, state-of-the-art algorithms for fair and optimal decision trees have scalability issues, often requiring several hours to find such trees even for small datasets. Previous research has shown that dynamic programming (DP) performs well for optimizing decision trees because it can exploit the tree structure. However, adding a global fairness constraint to a DP approach is not straightforward, because the global constraint violates the condition that subproblems should be independent. We show how such a constraint can be incorporated by introducing upper and lower bounds on final fairness values for partial solutions of subproblems, which enables early comparison and pruning. Our results show that our model can find fair and optimal trees several orders of magnitude faster than previous methods, and now also for larger datasets that were previously beyond reach. Moreover, we show that with this substantial improvement our method can find the full Pareto front in the trade-off between accuracy and fairness.

paragraphs: Small decision trees provide understandable predictions, but finding the best tree of a given size while satisfying fairness requirements can be computationally expensive. This paper develops a faster approach using dynamic programming. The attraction is that trees naturally split into smaller problems, allowing optimization to exploit their structure.

A global fairness constraint complicates that decomposition because choices in one part of the tree can affect whether the entire tree is fair. The authors address this dependence by maintaining upper and lower bounds on the final fairness values that partial solutions could achieve. Those bounds allow candidate solutions to be compared and pruned before a complete tree has been built.

The reported results show fair, optimal trees being found several orders of magnitude faster than with previous methods, including on larger datasets that had been out of reach. The speedup also enables computation of the full accuracy-fairness Pareto front: the set of trade-offs where improving one objective requires sacrificing the other. This makes the method useful for examining choices among competing fairness and accuracy targets.
summary.tldr: Fairness bounds make dynamic programming practical for finding optimal decision trees and mapping accuracy-fairness trade-offs much faster.

title: Fair and Optimal Decision Trees: A Dynamic Programming Approach

abstract: This work discusses tensor network embeddings, which are random matrices ($S$) with tensor network structure. These embeddings have been used to perform dimensionality reduction of tensor network structured inputs $x$ and accelerate applications such as tensor decomposition and kernel regression. Existing works have designed embeddings for inputs $x$ with specific structures, such as the Kronecker product or Khatri-Rao product, such that the computational cost for calculating $Sx$ is efficient. We provide a systematic way to design tensor network embeddings consisting of Gaussian random tensors, such that for inputs with more general tensor network structures, both the sketch size (row size of $S$) and the sketching computational cost are low.We analyze general tensor network embeddings that can be reduced to a sequence of sketching matrices. We provide a sufficient condition to quantify the accuracy of such embeddings and derive sketching asymptotic cost lower bounds using embeddings that satisfy this condition and have a sketch size lower than any input dimension. We then provide an algorithm to efficiently sketch input data using such embeddings. The sketch size of the embedding used in the algorithm has a linear dependence on the number of sketching dimensions of the input. Assuming tensor contractions are performed with classical dense matrix multiplication algorithms, this algorithm achieves asymptotic cost within a factor of $O(\sqrt{m})$ of our cost lower bound, where $m$ is the sketch size. Further, when each tensor in the input has a dimension that needs to be sketched, this algorithm yields the optimal sketching asymptotic cost. We apply our sketching analysis to inexact tensor decomposition optimization algorithms. We provide a sketching algorithm for CP decomposition that is asymptotically faster than existing work in multiple regimes, and show the optimality of an existing algorithm for tensor train rounding.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to compress tensor-structured data using random projections that themselves have tensor-network structure. Such compression can accelerate tensor decomposition and kernel regression. Earlier constructions targeted particular input structures; the authors develop a systematic approach using Gaussian random tensors for more general networks, aiming to keep both the compressed representation and the computation small.

The analysis covers embeddings that can be expressed as a sequence of sketching matrices. It supplies a sufficient condition for controlling accuracy and derives computational lower bounds for embeddings satisfying that condition whose sketch size is smaller than every input dimension. The resulting algorithm uses a sketch size that grows linearly with the number of input dimensions being sketched.

The efficiency guarantees depend on explicit conditions. With classical dense matrix multiplication for tensor contractions, the algorithm comes within an O(sqrt(m)) factor of the derived lower bound, where m is sketch size. When every input tensor has a dimension requiring sketching, its asymptotic cost is optimal within the analyzed setting. Applications include faster CP decomposition in multiple regimes and an optimality result for an existing tensor-train rounding algorithm.
summary.tldr: Gaussian tensor-network sketches compress broadly structured tensor inputs with accuracy conditions and computational guarantees, including optimal cost in a specified setting.

title: Cost-efficient Gaussian tensor network embeddings for tensor-structured inputs

abstract: We consider online prediction of a binary sequence with expert advice. For this setting, we devise label-efficient forecasting algorithms, which use a selective sampling scheme that enables collecting much fewer labels than standard procedures. For the general case without a perfect expert, we prove best-of-both-worlds guarantees, demonstrating that the proposed forecasting algorithm always queries sufficiently many labels in the worst case to obtain optimal regret guarantees, while simultaneously querying much fewer labels in more benign settings. Specifically, for a scenario where one expert is strictly better than the others in expectation, we show that the label complexity of the label-efficient forecaster is roughly upper-bounded by the square root of the number of rounds. Finally, we present numerical experiments empirically showing that the normalized regret of the label-efficient forecaster can asymptotically match known minimax rates for pool-based active learning, suggesting it can optimally adapt to benign settings.

paragraphs: The paper studies a forecaster that predicts a binary sequence while receiving advice from multiple experts. Learning which advice to trust normally requires observing the correct outcomes. Here, the goal is to request fewer of those labels while still keeping regret—the accumulated disadvantage relative to expert advice—under control. The proposed algorithms decide selectively when obtaining a label is worthwhile.

Their theoretical guarantees cover the general setting in which no expert needs to be perfect. In difficult cases, the forecaster requests enough labels to retain optimal regret guarantees. In more favorable cases, it can request substantially fewer. Specifically, when one expert is strictly better than the others in expectation, the authors bound label usage roughly by the square root of the number of prediction rounds.

Experiments further suggest that normalized regret can asymptotically match known minimax rates from pool-based active learning. This last result is empirical evidence of adaptation to favorable conditions, rather than a universal theoretical guarantee. Together, the findings show how selective feedback can reduce labeling demands without abandoning worst-case prediction guarantees.
summary.tldr: An adaptive forecaster requests fewer labels in favorable settings while preserving optimal worst-case regret guarantees.

title: Adaptive Selective Sampling for Online Prediction with Experts

abstract: We study a generalization of boosting to the multiclass setting.We introduce a weak learning condition for multiclass classification that captures the original notion of weak learnability as being “slightly better than random guessing”. We give a simple and efficient boosting algorithm, that does not require realizability assumptions and its sample and oracle complexity bounds are independent of the number of classes. In addition, we utilize our new boosting technique in several theoretical applications within the context of List PAC Learning. First, we establish an equivalence to weak PAC learning. Furthermore, we present a new result on boosting for list learners, as well as provide a novel proof for the characterization of multiclass PAC learning and List PAC learning. Notably, our technique gives rise to simplified algorithms and analysis compared to previous works.

paragraphs: Boosting builds stronger learners from learners that satisfy a weaker performance requirement. Extending this idea to classification with many possible labels requires specifying what counts as weak learning. This paper introduces a multiclass condition intended to preserve the intuitive meaning of doing slightly better than random guessing, giving the boosting process a simple conceptual starting point.

The authors provide an efficient boosting algorithm based on this condition. It does not require realizability assumptions, meaning the analysis does not demand that the learning problem admit a perfect classifier within the relevant model class. Its sample and oracle complexity bounds are independent of the number of classes. That independence concerns those resource bounds specifically, making the theoretical result attractive for multiclass problems.

The same technique also produces results for List PAC Learning, where learners can return lists of candidate labels. The paper establishes an equivalence with weak PAC learning, gives a boosting result for list learners, and supplies a new proof characterizing multiclass and List PAC learning. The authors emphasize simpler algorithms and analyses than previous work.
summary.tldr: A new multiclass weak-learning condition supports efficient boosting with sample and oracle bounds independent of the number of classes.

title: Multiclass Boosting: Simple and Intuitive Weak Learning Criteria

abstract: Many common types of data can be represented as functions that map coordinates to signal values, such as pixel locations to RGB values in the case of an image. Based on this view, data can be compressed by overfitting a compact neural network to its functional representation and then encoding the network weights. However, most current solutions for this are inefficient, as quantization to low-bit precision substantially degrades the reconstruction quality. To address this issue, we propose overfitting variational Bayesian neural networks to the data and compressing an approximate posterior weight sample using relative entropy coding instead of quantizing and entropy coding it. This strategy enables direct optimization of the rate-distortion performance by minimizing the $\beta$-ELBO, and target different rate-distortion trade-offs for a given network architecture by adjusting $\beta$. Moreover, we introduce an iterative algorithm for learning prior weight distributions and employ a progressive refinement process for the variational posterior that significantly enhances performance. Experiments show that our method achieves strong performance on image and audio compression while retaining simplicity.

paragraphs: The paper compresses data by representing a signal as a neural network that maps coordinates to values. For an image, this means mapping pixel positions to colors. Fitting a compact network to a particular signal allows its weights to serve as the compressed representation, but reducing weight precision can substantially damage reconstruction quality.

The authors instead fit a variational Bayesian neural network and encode an approximate posterior weight sample using relative entropy coding. This changes how the learned representation is compressed. Minimizing the beta-ELBO directly optimizes the balance between storage rate and reconstruction distortion, with beta controlling different trade-offs for the same network architecture.

The method also learns prior weight distributions through an iterative algorithm and progressively refines the variational posterior. These additions significantly improve performance according to the abstract. Image and audio experiments show strong compression results while retaining a simple approach. The central contribution is to connect probabilistic weight representations, coding, and the desired compression-quality trade-off within one optimization strategy.
summary.tldr: Bayesian neural signal representations and relative entropy coding enable direct optimization of compression rate against reconstruction quality.

title: Compression with Bayesian Implicit Neural Representations

abstract: Previous studies have shown that optimizing the information bottleneck can significantly improve the robustness of deep neural networks. Our study closely examines the information bottleneck principle and proposes an Information Bottleneck Distillation approach. This specially designed, robust distillation technique utilizes prior knowledge obtained from a robust pre-trained model to boost information bottlenecks. Specifically, we propose two distillation strategies that align with the two optimization processes of the information bottleneck. Firstly, we use a robust soft-label distillation method to increase the mutual information between latent features and output prediction. Secondly, we introduce an adaptive feature distillation method that automatically transfers relevant knowledge from the teacher model to the student model, thereby reducing the mutual information between the input and latent features. We conduct extensive experiments to evaluate our approach's robustness against state-of-the-art adversarial attackers such as PGD-attack and AutoAttack. Our experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in significantly improving adversarial robustness. Our code is available at https://github.com/SkyKuang/IBD.

paragraphs: This paper develops a way to improve adversarial robustness by transferring knowledge from a robust pretrained model. Its approach, Information Bottleneck Distillation, connects teacher-to-student learning with the information bottleneck principle. The aim is to shape internal features so they retain information useful for prediction while reducing their dependence on the input.

The method has two complementary distillation strategies. Robust soft-label distillation increases mutual information between latent features and output predictions. Adaptive feature distillation transfers relevant knowledge from the teacher to the student and reduces mutual information between inputs and latent features. These strategies correspond to the two optimization directions of the information bottleneck.

The authors evaluate the resulting robustness against adversarial attackers including PGD and AutoAttack. Their experiments report significant improvements, supporting the effectiveness of this combination of robust prior knowledge and information-bottleneck objectives. The work's main contribution is the coordinated design of the two transfers: one strengthens prediction-relevant information, while the other shapes how much input information the internal representation preserves.
summary.tldr: Information Bottleneck Distillation transfers robust teacher knowledge through two complementary objectives that empirically improve adversarial robustness.

title: Improving Adversarial Robustness via Information Bottleneck Distillation

abstract: A common setting in multitask reinforcement learning (RL) demands that an agent rapidly adapt to various stationary reward functions randomly sampled from a fixed distribution. In such situations, the successor representation (SR) is a popular framework which supports rapid policy evaluation by decoupling a policy's expected discounted, cumulative state occupancies from a specific reward function. However, in the natural world, sequential tasks are rarely independent, and instead reflect shifting priorities based on the availability and subjective perception of rewarding stimuli. Reflecting this disjunction, in this paper we study the phenomenon of diminishing marginal utility and introduce a novel state representation, the $\lambda$ representation ($\lambda$R) which, surprisingly, is required for policy evaluation in this setting and which generalizes the SR as well as several other state representations from the literature. We establish the $\lambda$R's formal properties and examine its normative advantages in the context of machine learning, as well as its usefulness for studying natural behaviors, particularly foraging.

paragraphs: An agent’s priorities can change as it consumes or repeatedly encounters something rewarding. This paper studies diminishing marginal utility: receiving more of the same reward can make each additional instance less valuable. That setting differs from a common multitask reinforcement learning setup, where an agent adapts among stationary reward functions drawn from a fixed distribution.

The usual successor representation separates predictions about future state visits from the rewards assigned to those states. This separation supports rapid evaluation of a policy under different reward functions. The authors introduce the λ representation to handle the diminishing-reward setting, and establish that it is required for policy evaluation within that setting. It also generalizes the successor representation and several other existing state representations.

The paper develops the representation’s formal properties and examines its advantages for machine learning and the study of natural behavior. Foraging is a particular focus because the value of continuing to seek a reward can depend on previous consumption. The contribution connects how rewards change with what information a state representation must retain to evaluate behavior.
summary.tldr: The λ representation extends successor representations to evaluate policies when repeated rewards have diminishing value.

title: A State Representation for Diminishing Rewards

abstract: Counterfactual generation lies at the core of various machine learning tasks, including image translation and controllable text generation. This generation process usually requires the identification of the disentangled latent representations, such as content and style, that underlie the observed data. However, it becomes more challenging when faced with a scarcity of paired data and labelling information. Existing disentangled methods crucially rely on oversimplified assumptions, such as assuming independent content and style variables, to identify the latent variables, even though such assumptions may not hold for complex data distributions. For instance, food reviews tend to involve words like “tasty”, whereas movie reviews commonly contain words such as “thrilling” for the same positive sentiment. This problem is exacerbated when data are sampled from multiple domains since the dependence between content and style may vary significantly over domains. In this work, we tackle the domain-varying dependence between the content and the style variables inherent in the counterfactual generation task. We provide identification guarantees for such latent-variable models by leveraging the relative sparsity of the influences from different latent variables. Our theoretical insights enable the development of a doMain AdapTive counTerfactual gEneration model, called (MATTE). Our theoretically grounded framework achieves state-of-the-art performance in unsupervised style transfer tasks, where neither paired data nor style labels are utilized, across four large-scale datasets.

paragraphs: Counterfactual generation often requires separating latent content from style, but those factors may be dependent. Their relationship can also change across domains, such as different positive words appearing in food and movie reviews. This paper addresses that dependency instead of assuming independent latent factors.

The authors derive identifiability guarantees by exploiting relative sparsity in the influences of different latent variables. Those insights lead to MATTE, a domain-adaptive counterfactual-generation model designed to handle domain-varying content-style dependence.

On four large-scale datasets, MATTE achieves state-of-the-art unsupervised style-transfer results without paired examples or style labels. The abstract does not spell out all identifiability conditions or provide performance scores. The guarantees therefore depend on the stated structural framework, rather than implying that arbitrary unlabeled data uniquely reveal their causal factors or that every generated change is a valid real-world counterfactual.
summary.tldr: MATTE identifies dependent content and style factors under structural assumptions for unsupervised style transfer.

title: Counterfactual Generation with Identifiability Guarantees

abstract: We consider the adversarial linear contextual bandit setting, whichallows for the loss functions associated with each of $K$ arms to changeover time without restriction. Assuming the $d$-dimensional contexts aredrawn from a fixed known distribution, the worst-case expected regretover the course of $T$ rounds is known to scale as $\tilde O(\sqrt{KdT})$. Under the additional assumption that the density of the contextsis log-concave, we obtain a second-order bound of order $\tildeO(K\sqrt{d V_T})$ in terms of the cumulative second moment of thelearner's losses $V_T$, and a closely related first-order bound of order$\tilde O(K\sqrt{d L_T^*})$ in terms of the cumulative loss of the bestpolicy $L_T^*$. Since $V_T$ or $L_T^*$ may be significantly smaller than$T$, these improve over the worst-case regret whenever the environmentis relatively benign. Our results are obtained using a truncated versionof the continuous exponential weights algorithm over the probabilitysimplex, which we analyse by exploiting a novel connection to the linearbandit setting without contexts.

paragraphs: The paper studies contextual bandits in which a learner chooses among K actions using d-dimensional contextual information, while action losses can change arbitrarily over time. Regret measures the learner's cumulative disadvantage relative to a comparison policy. With contexts drawn from a fixed, known distribution, the established worst-case expected regret scales roughly as the square root of K times d times T.

The authors derive more adaptive guarantees under the additional assumption that the context distribution has a log-concave density. One bound depends on the cumulative second moment of the learner's losses, V_T; another depends on the best policy's cumulative loss, L_T*. Their respective orders are K times the square root of d V_T and K times the square root of d L_T*, ignoring logarithmic factors.

These quantities can be substantially smaller than the number of rounds, so the bounds can improve on worst-case guarantees in sufficiently benign environments. The algorithm uses a truncated continuous exponential-weights procedure over action probabilities. Its analysis connects the contextual problem to linear bandits without contexts, providing a route to loss-sensitive guarantees.
summary.tldr: Under a known log-concave context distribution, new contextual-bandit regret bounds adapt to losses and can improve guarantees in benign environments.

title: First- and Second-Order Bounds for Adversarial Linear Contextual Bandits

abstract: Test-time adaptation (TTA) is a special and practical setting in unsupervised domain adaptation, which allows a pre-trained model in a source domain to adapt to unlabeled test data in another target domain. To avoid the computation-intensive backbone fine-tuning process, the zero-shot generalization potentials of the emerging pre-trained vision-language models (e.g., CLIP, CoOp) are leveraged to only tune the run-time prompt for unseen test domains. However, existing solutions have yet to fully exploit the representation capabilities of pre-trained models as they only focus on the entropy-based optimization and the performance is far below the supervised prompt adaptation methods, e.g., CoOp. In this paper, we propose SwapPrompt, a novel framework that can effectively leverage the self-supervised contrastive learning to facilitate the test-time prompt adaptation. SwapPrompt employs a dual prompts paradigm, i.e., an online prompt and a target prompt that averaged from the online prompt to retain historical information. In addition, SwapPrompt applies a swapped prediction mechanism, which takes advantage of the representation capabilities of pre-trained models to enhance the online prompt via contrastive learning. Specifically, we use the online prompt together with an augmented view of the input image to predict the class assignment generated by the target prompt together with an alternative augmented view of the same image. The proposed SwapPrompt can be easily deployed on vision-language models without additional requirement, and experimental results show that it achieves state-of-the-art test-time adaptation performance on ImageNet and nine other datasets. It is also shown that SwapPrompt can even achieve comparable performance with supervised prompt adaptation methods.

summary.tldr: SwapPrompt adapts vision-language prompts to unlabeled test images through paired prompts and predictions across augmented views.

title: SwapPrompt: Test-Time Prompt Adaptation for Vision-Language Models

abstract: This paper presents new quadrature rules for functions in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space using nodes drawn by a sampling algorithm known as randomly pivoted Cholesky. The resulting computational procedure compares favorably to previous kernel quadrature methods, which either achieve low accuracy or require solving a computationally challenging sampling problem. Theoretical and numerical results show that randomly pivoted Cholesky is fast and achieves comparable quadrature error rates to more computationally expensive quadrature schemes based on continuous volume sampling, thinning, and recombination. Randomly pivoted Cholesky is easily adapted to complicated geometries with arbitrary kernels, unlocking new potential for kernel quadrature.

paragraphs: Quadrature approximates an integral by evaluating a function at selected locations and combining those values. Kernel quadrature uses a kernel-defined function space to guide this approximation. The paper studies functions in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space, where choosing useful evaluation locations is central to obtaining accurate integration without an expensive computational procedure.

The authors construct new quadrature rules whose evaluation locations, or nodes, come from randomly pivoted Cholesky sampling. This addresses a tradeoff identified in earlier kernel quadrature methods: some offer limited accuracy, while others depend on sampling problems that are difficult to solve efficiently. The proposed sampling procedure offers a practical route to selecting nodes.

Theoretical and numerical results show that the method is fast and reaches quadrature error rates comparable to more expensive approaches using continuous volume sampling, thinning, and recombination. The authors also emphasize that it adapts readily to complicated geometries and arbitrary kernels. Its significance is the combination of competitive integration accuracy and a simpler computational path to constructing the quadrature rule.
summary.tldr: Randomly pivoted Cholesky sampling builds fast kernel quadrature rules with error rates comparable to more computationally expensive methods.

title: Kernel Quadrature with Randomly Pivoted Cholesky

abstract: Current dataset collection methods typically scrape large amounts of data from the web. While this technique is extremely scalable, data collected in this way tends to reinforce stereotypical biases, can contain personally identifiable information, and typically originates from Europe and North America. In this work, we rethink the dataset collection paradigm and introduce GeoDE, a geographically diverse dataset with 61,940 images from 40 classes and 6 world regions, and no personally identifiable information, collected by soliciting images from people across the world. We analyse GeoDE to understand differences in images collected in this manner compared to web-scraping. Despite the smaller size of this dataset, we demonstrate its use as both an evaluation and training dataset, allowing us to highlight shortcomings in current models, as well as demonstrate improved performance even when training on this small dataset. We release the full dataset and code at https://geodiverse-data-collection.cs.princeton.edu/

paragraphs: Large web-scraped image collections can carry stereotypical biases, include personally identifiable information, and disproportionately represent Europe and North America. GeoDE explores a different collection approach: asking people around the world to contribute images. The resulting dataset contains 61,940 images covering 40 object classes across six world regions, without personally identifiable information.

The researchers analyze how images collected through this process differ from web-scraped images. This makes collection strategy part of the research question, alongside the dataset's role in object recognition. Geographic coverage provides a basis for examining model shortcomings that might be less apparent in data drawn from more concentrated sources.

GeoDE is used for both evaluation and training. The experiments expose weaknesses in current models and demonstrate improved performance from training with this comparatively small collection. The findings show that a geographically diverse dataset can contribute useful training information as well as a broader evaluation resource. The paper releases the dataset and accompanying code for further use.
summary.tldr: GeoDE collects geographically diverse object images from contributors worldwide, revealing model shortcomings and improving performance when used for training.

title: GeoDE: a Geographically Diverse Evaluation Dataset for Object Recognition

abstract: Exploration is essential in reinforcement learning, particularly in environments where external rewards are sparse. Here we focus on exploration with intrinsic rewards, where the agent transiently augments the external rewards with self-generated intrinsic rewards. Although the study of intrinsic rewards has a long history, existing methods focus on composing the intrinsic reward based on measures of future prospects of states, ignoring the information contained in the retrospective structure of transition sequences. Here we argue that the agent can utilise retrospective information to generate explorative behaviour with structure-awareness, facilitating efficient exploration based on global instead of local information. We propose Successor-Predecessor Intrinsic Exploration (SPIE), an exploration algorithm based on a novel intrinsic reward combining prospective and retrospective information. We show that SPIE yields more efficient and ethologically plausible exploratory behaviour in environments with sparse rewards and bottleneck states than competing methods. We also implement SPIE in deep reinforcement learning agents, and show that the resulting agent achieves stronger empirical performance than existing methods on sparse-reward Atari games.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning agents need to explore, especially when useful external rewards are rare. Intrinsic rewards temporarily supplement those external signals with incentives generated by the agent itself. This paper argues that exploration can benefit from information about how states were reached, alongside information about the future possibilities associated with those states.

Successor-Predecessor Intrinsic Exploration, or SPIE, combines prospective and retrospective information in a new intrinsic reward. The retrospective component draws on the structure of transition sequences. Its purpose is to make exploratory behavior sensitive to the broader organization of the environment, allowing the agent to use global structural information rather than relying only on local prospects.

The authors report more efficient exploration in environments with sparse rewards and bottleneck states, together with behavior they describe as more ethologically plausible than competing methods. They also implement SPIE in deep reinforcement learning agents and find stronger empirical performance on sparse-reward Atari games. These results support combining information about past transitions and future possibilities when designing exploration incentives.
summary.tldr: SPIE combines retrospective and prospective state information to improve exploration in sparse-reward environments.

title: Successor-Predecessor Intrinsic Exploration

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are excellent in-context learners. However, the sensitivity of data contained in prompts raises privacy concerns. Our work first shows that these concerns are valid: we instantiate a simple but highly effective membership inference attack against the data used to prompt LLMs. To address this vulnerability, one could forego prompting and resort to fine-tuning LLMs with known algorithms for private gradient descent. However, this comes at the expense of the practicality and efficiency offered by prompting. Therefore, we propose to privately learn to prompt. We first show that soft prompts can be obtained privately through gradient descent on downstream data. However, this is not the case for discrete prompts. Thus, we orchestrate a noisy vote among an ensemble of LLMs presented with different prompts, i.e., a flock of stochastic parrots. The vote privately transfers the flock's knowledge into a single public prompt. We show that LLMs prompted with our private algorithms closely match the non-private baselines. For example, using GPT3 as the base model, we achieve a downstream accuracy of 92.7% on the sst2 dataset with $(\varepsilon=0.147, \delta=10^{-6})$-differential privacy vs. 95.2% for the non-private baseline. Through our experiments, we also show that our prompt-based approach is easily deployed with existing commercial~APIs.

paragraphs: Examples included in language-model prompts can contain sensitive information. This paper demonstrates that the concern is concrete through a simple, effective membership-inference attack on prompt data. It then develops private prompt-learning methods that aim to preserve the practicality of prompting without requiring full-model private fine-tuning.

For soft prompts, the authors show that private gradient descent on downstream data can learn the prompt parameters. Discrete text prompts require a different approach. An ensemble of language models receives different prompts and participates in a noisy vote. That vote transfers the ensemble's knowledge into a single public prompt while providing a privacy guarantee.

The resulting private prompting methods closely match non-private baselines in the reported experiments. With GPT3 on SST2, the paper reports 92.7% downstream accuracy under differential privacy with epsilon 0.147 and delta one millionth, compared with 95.2% for the non-private baseline. The experiments also demonstrate deployment through existing commercial APIs. These findings show a practical route to protecting prompt-derived information while retaining much of the measured task performance.
summary.tldr: Private gradient-based soft prompts and noisy ensemble voting for text prompts protect sensitive prompt data while closely matching tested non-private baselines.

title: Flocks of Stochastic Parrots: Differentially Private Prompt Learning for Large Language Models

abstract: Many tasks in explainable machine learning, such as data valuation and feature attribution, perform expensive computation for each data point and are intractable for large datasets. These methods require efficient approximations, and although amortizing the process by learning a network to directly predict the desired output is a promising solution, training such models with exact labels is often infeasible. We therefore explore training amortized models with noisy labels, and we find that this is inexpensive and surprisingly effective. Through theoretical analysis of the label noise and experiments with various models and datasets, we show that this approach tolerates high noise levels and significantly accelerates several feature attribution and data valuation methods, often yielding an order of magnitude speedup over existing approaches.

paragraphs: Feature attribution and data valuation can require expensive calculations for every example. This makes otherwise useful explanation methods difficult to apply to large datasets. Amortization offers a way to share that computational work: train a model to predict the desired attribution or valuation output directly.

The difficulty is obtaining accurate targets for training such a model. Computing enough exact labels may recreate the same expense that amortization is meant to avoid. This paper instead investigates training with noisy labels that are inexpensive to obtain. The authors analyze the label noise theoretically and test the approach across different models and datasets, finding that substantial noise can be tolerated.

The resulting approach accelerates several feature attribution and data valuation methods, often by an order of magnitude compared with existing approaches. These findings suggest that exact training targets are not always needed for useful amortized explanations. The contribution is a common strategy for reducing repeated explanation costs by learning from approximate targets, supported by both noise analysis and empirical evaluation.
summary.tldr: Training attribution predictors with inexpensive noisy labels tolerates substantial noise and often speeds up explanation methods by an order of magnitude.

title: Stochastic Amortization: A Unified Approach to Accelerate Feature and Data Attribution

abstract: Model-X knockoff has garnered significant attention among various feature selection methods due to its guarantees for controlling the false discovery rate (FDR). Since its introduction in parametric design, knockoff techniques have evolved to handle arbitrary data distributions using deep learning-based generative models. However, we have observed limitations in the current implementations of the deep Model-X knockoff framework. Notably, the "swap property" that knockoffs require often faces challenges at the sample level, resulting in diminished selection power. To address these issues, we develop "Deep Dependency Regularized Knockoff (DeepDRK)," a distribution-free deep learning method that effectively balances FDR and power. In DeepDRK, we introduce a novel formulation of the knockoff model as a learning problem under multi-source adversarial attacks. By employing an innovative perturbation technique, we achieve lower FDR and higher power. Our model outperforms existing benchmarks across synthetic, semi-synthetic, and real-world datasets, particularly when sample sizes are small and data distributions are non-Gaussian.

paragraphs: Feature selection aims to identify useful variables while limiting false discoveries. Model-X knockoffs are attractive because their framework provides guarantees for controlling the false discovery rate. Deep generative versions extend knockoff methods beyond parametric data settings, but the authors identify weaknesses in how existing implementations satisfy a required swap property at the sample level.

That property concerns the interchangeability required of original features and their knockoff counterparts. Problems maintaining it can reduce selection power, meaning fewer relevant features are detected. DeepDRK addresses this issue by casting knockoff generation as a learning problem exposed to adversarial attacks from multiple sources, together with a new perturbation technique.

The proposed distribution-free method seeks a better balance between controlling false selections and detecting useful features. Across synthetic, semi-synthetic, and real datasets, it achieves lower false discovery rates and higher power than the compared benchmarks. The reported advantages are particularly pronounced with small samples and non-Gaussian data, settings where the quality of learned knockoffs is especially consequential in the authors' evaluations.
summary.tldr: DeepDRK uses adversarial learning and perturbations to improve the balance between false discoveries and detection power in knockoff-based feature selection.

title: DeepDRK: Deep Dependency Regularized Knockoff for Feature Selection

abstract: Recently, vision model pre-training has evolved from relying on manually annotated datasets to leveraging large-scale, web-crawled image-text data. Despite these advances, there is no pre-training method that effectively exploits the interleaved image-text data, which is very prevalent on the Internet. Inspired by the recent success of compression learning in natural language processing, we propose a novel vision model pre-training method called Latent Compression Learning (LCL) for interleaved image-text data. This method performs latent compression learning by maximizing the mutual information between the inputs and outputs of a causal attention model. The training objective can be decomposed into two basic tasks: 1) contrastive learning between visual representation and preceding context, and 2) generating subsequent text based on visual representation. Our experiments demonstrate that our method not only matches the performance of CLIP on paired pre-training datasets (e.g., LAION), but can also leverage interleaved pre-training data (e.g., MMC4) to learn robust visual representations from scratch, showcasing the potential of vision model pre-training with interleaved image-text data.

paragraphs: Web content often mixes images and text in a sequence rather than presenting isolated image–caption pairs. Latent Compression Learning introduces a vision pretraining method designed to use this interleaved material. It connects visual representations to both the text that comes before an image and the text that follows it.

The training objective maximizes mutual information between a causal attention model's inputs and outputs. The authors decompose this objective into two tasks: contrastive learning between a visual representation and its preceding context, and generation of subsequent text from that representation. These tasks provide complementary training signals from the surrounding sequence.

Experiments show that the method matches CLIP's performance on paired pretraining data such as LAION. It also learns robust visual representations from scratch using interleaved data such as MMC4. The findings demonstrate that the same approach can work with paired examples while taking advantage of the richer arrangement of images and text found in interleaved material, expanding the forms of web data available for vision pretraining.
summary.tldr: Latent Compression Learning trains visual representations from interleaved images and text using preceding-context contrast and subsequent-text generation.

title: Vision Model Pre-training on Interleaved Image-Text Data via Latent Compression Learning

abstract: This paper concerns imitation learning (IL) in cooperative multi-agent systems.The learning problem under consideration poses several challenges, characterized by high-dimensional state and action spaces and intricate inter-agent dependencies. In a single-agent setting, IL was shown to be done efficiently via an inverse soft-Q learning process. However, extending this framework to a multi-agent context introduces the need to simultaneously learn both local value functions to capture local observations and individual actions, and a joint value function for exploiting centralized learning.In this work, we introduce a new multi-agent IL algorithm designed to address these challenges. Our approach enables thecentralized learning by leveraging mixing networks to aggregate decentralized Q functions.We further establish conditions for the mixing networks under which the multi-agent IL objective function exhibits convexity within the Q function space.We present extensive experiments conducted on some challenging multi-agent game environments, including an advanced version of the Star-Craft multi-agent challenge (SMACv2), which demonstrates the effectiveness of our algorithm.

paragraphs: Imitation learning becomes more complicated when several agents must cooperate. Each agent has local observations and actions, while successful coordination depends on interactions across the group. The resulting state and action spaces are large, and a learning method must connect individual decisions to a shared assessment of team behavior.

The paper extends inverse soft-Q learning to this setting by using mixing networks to combine decentralized Q functions into a joint value function. The local functions capture information associated with individual agents, while their aggregation enables centralized learning. This gives the algorithm a way to represent both individual behavior and collective dependencies within one learning framework.

The authors establish conditions on the mixing networks under which the imitation-learning objective is convex in the space of Q functions. This is a conditional result about that function space. Experiments on challenging multi-agent games, including SMACv2, demonstrate the algorithm's effectiveness and support the use of factorized value functions for cooperative imitation.
summary.tldr: The method combines individual agents' Q functions through mixing networks to enable centralized cooperative imitation learning.

title: Inverse Factorized Soft Q-Learning for Cooperative Multi-agent Imitation Learning

abstract: In this paper, we make the first attempt to align diffusion models for image inpainting with human aesthetic standards via a reinforcement learning framework, significantly improving the quality and visual appeal of inpainted images. Specifically, instead of directly measuring the divergence with paired images, we train a reward model with the dataset we construct, consisting of nearly 51,000 images annotated with human preferences. Then, we adopt a reinforcement learning process to fine-tune the distribution of a pre-trained diffusion model for image inpainting in the direction of higher reward. Moreover, we theoretically deduce the upper bound on the error of the reward model, which illustrates the potential confidence of reward estimation throughout the reinforcement alignment process, thereby facilitating accurate regularization.Extensive experiments on inpainting comparison and downstream tasks, such as image extension and 3D reconstruction, demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, showing significant improvements in the alignment of inpainted images with human preference compared with state-of-the-art methods. This research not only advances the field of image inpainting but also provides a framework for incorporating human preference into the iterative refinement of generative models based on modeling reward accuracy, with broad implications for the design of visually driven AI applications. Our code and dataset are publicly available at \url{https://prefpaint.github.io}.

paragraphs: Image inpainting fills missing regions, but agreement with a reference image does not directly express human aesthetic preference. PrefPaint trains an inpainting diffusion model using a reward learned from people’s judgments. The authors construct a dataset of nearly 51,000 images annotated with human preferences and use it to train that reward model.

Reinforcement learning then shifts the output distribution of a pretrained inpainting model toward higher predicted reward. The paper also derives an upper bound on reward-model error. This analysis addresses confidence in reward estimates during alignment and helps guide regularization, connecting the refinement process to the accuracy of the signal used to steer it.

Experiments cover inpainting comparisons and downstream tasks including image extension and 3D reconstruction. The authors report significant improvements in agreement with human preferences relative to state-of-the-art methods. The contribution combines a preference dataset, a reinforcement-learning procedure, and an analysis of reward accuracy, providing a framework for refining visual generation according to human aesthetic judgments.
summary.tldr: PrefPaint uses human-preference rewards and reinforcement learning to improve the aesthetic alignment of diffusion-based image inpainting.

title: PrefPaint: Aligning Image Inpainting Diffusion Model with Human Preference

abstract: In this paper, we introduce the \textbf{USCILab3D dataset}, a large-scale, annotated outdoor dataset designed for versatile applications across multiple domains, including computer vision, robotics, and machine learning. The dataset was acquired using a mobile robot equipped with 5 cameras and a 32-beam, $360^{\circ}$ scanning LIDAR. The robot was teleoperated, over the course of a year and under a variety of weather and lighting conditions, through a rich variety of paths within the USC campus (229 acres = $\sim 92.7$ hectares). The raw data was annotated using state-of-the-art large foundation models, and processed to provide multi-view imagery, 3D reconstructions, semantically-annotated images and point clouds (267 semantic categories), and text descriptions of images and objects within. The dataset also offers a diverse array of complex analyses using pose-stamping and trajectory data. In sum, the dataset offers 1.4M point clouds and 10M images ($\sim 6$TB of data). Despite covering a narrower geographical scope compared to a whole-city dataset, our dataset prioritizes intricate intersections along with denser multi-view scene images and semantic point clouds, enabling more precise 3D labelling and facilitating a broader spectrum of 3D vision tasks. For data, code and more details, please visit our website.

paragraphs: USCILab3D is an outdoor dataset built from a year of robot traversals around the USC campus. A teleoperated robot carried five cameras and a 32-beam LiDAR scanner with full surrounding coverage. Collection across varied paths, weather, and lighting provides repeated observations under changing conditions within the campus's roughly 92.7 hectares.

The dataset includes 10 million images and 1.4 million point clouds, totaling approximately six terabytes. Foundation models were used to annotate the raw observations. Processed outputs include multi-view imagery, 3D reconstructions, images and point clouds labeled with 267 semantic categories, and textual descriptions of images and objects. Pose and trajectory information support additional analyses.

Its stated tradeoff is geographical breadth for denser coverage: it covers less area than a whole-city dataset but emphasizes intricate intersections and rich multi-view observations. The authors describe this density as enabling more precise 3D labeling and a wider range of 3D vision tasks. The contribution is a long-term, multimodal resource for research across vision, robotics, and machine learning.
summary.tldr: USCILab3D provides a year of densely sampled campus imagery and LiDAR with semantic annotations, reconstructions, text, and trajectories.

title: USCILab3D: A Large-scale, Long-term, Semantically Annotated Outdoor Dataset

abstract: In many applications, we desire neural networks to exhibit invariance or equivariance to certain groups due to symmetries inherent in the data. Recently, frame-averaging methods emerged to be a unified framework for attaining symmetries efficiently by averaging over input-dependent subsets of the group, i.e., frames. What we currently lack is a principled understanding of the design of frames. In this work, we introduce a canonicalization perspective that provides an essential and complete view of the design of frames. Canonicalization is a classic approach for attaining invariance by mapping inputs to their canonical forms. We show that there exists an inherent connection between frames and canonical forms. Leveraging this connection, we can efficiently compare the complexity of frames as well as determine the optimality of certain frames. Guided by this principle, we design novel frames for eigenvectors that are strictly superior to existing methods --- some are even optimal --- both theoretically and empirically. The reduction to the canonicalization perspective further uncovers equivalences between previous methods. These observations suggest that canonicalization provides a fundamental understanding of existing frame-averaging methods and unifies existing equivariant and invariant learning methods. Code is available at https://github.com/PKU-ML/canonicalization.

paragraphs: When data have symmetries, a useful network should respond consistently to those symmetries. Invariance means its output stays unchanged, while equivariance means its output changes in a corresponding way. Frame averaging approaches obtain these properties by averaging over selected transformations that depend on the input. The paper asks how to design those selections in a principled way.

The authors connect frames to canonicalization: mapping an input to a standard representative form. This connection provides a way to analyze how much work different frames require and to establish whether particular frames are optimal. It also reveals equivalences between methods that previously appeared different, giving a common explanation for their behavior.

Using this perspective, the authors construct new frames for eigenvectors. They report theoretical and empirical improvements over existing approaches, with some of the proposed frames achieving optimality. The contribution is therefore both a design principle and a concrete application: canonical forms help explain existing symmetry methods and guide the construction of better ones.
summary.tldr: Connecting frame averaging to canonical forms provides a principled way to compare symmetry methods and design improved frames.

title: A Canonicalization Perspective on Invariant and Equivariant Learning

abstract: Motivated by applications of large embedding models, we study differentially private (DP) optimization problems under sparsity of _individual_ gradients. We start with new near-optimal bounds for the classic mean estimation problem but with sparse data, improving upon existing algorithms particularly for the high-dimensional regime. The corresponding lower bounds are based on a novel block-diagonal construction that is combined with existing DP mean estimation lower bounds.Next, we obtain pure- and approximate-DP algorithms with almost optimal rates for stochastic convex optimization with sparse gradients; the former represents the first nearly dimension-independent rates for this problem. Furthermore, by introducing novel analyses of bias reduction in mean estimation and randomly-stopped biased SGD we obtain nearly dimension-independent rates for near-stationary points for the empirical risk in nonconvex settings under approximate-DP.
