paragraphs: This paper studies private optimization when each individual gradient is sparse, motivated by large embedding models. The distinction matters because the assumed sparsity belongs to individual gradients, rather than being a general claim that every quantity in training is sparse. The goal is to exploit that structure when establishing differential privacy guarantees and optimization accuracy.

The authors first develop nearly optimal bounds for estimating a mean from sparse data, with particular improvements in high dimensions. They also derive corresponding lower bounds using a new block-diagonal construction. Together, the achievable bounds and lower bounds characterize how close the proposed methods come to the best possible performance.

These results support nearly optimal algorithms for stochastic convex optimization under both pure and approximate differential privacy. The pure-private result gives the first nearly dimension-independent rates for this problem. For nonconvex empirical risk, new analyses of mean-estimation bias and randomly stopped biased stochastic gradient descent yield nearly dimension-independent rates for finding near-stationary points under approximate privacy.
summary.tldr: Exploiting sparsity in individual gradients yields nearly optimal private optimization guarantees with reduced dependence on dimension.

title: Differentially Private Optimization with Sparse Gradients

abstract: The rise of large language models (LLMs) has significantly transformed both the construction and application of information retrieval (IR) systems. However, current interactions between IR systems and LLMs remain limited, with LLMs merely serving as part of components within IR systems, and IR systems being constructed independently of LLMs. This separated architecture restricts knowledge sharing and deep collaboration between them.In this paper, we introduce Self-Retrieval, a novel end-to-end LLM-driven information retrieval architecture.Self-Retrieval unifies all essential IR functions within a single LLM, leveraging the inherent capabilities of LLMs throughout the IR process.Specifically, Self-Retrieval internalizes the retrieval corpus through self-supervised learning, transforms the retrieval process into sequential passage generation, and performs relevance assessment for reranking.Experimental results demonstrate that Self-Retrieval not only outperforms existing retrieval approaches by a significant margin, but also substantially enhances the performance of LLM-driven downstream applications like retrieval-augmented generation.

paragraphs: Language models increasingly participate in information retrieval, but they often serve as individual components inside systems built separately from them. The paper argues that this separation limits knowledge sharing and close coordination. Self-Retrieval reorganizes the process so that one language model performs the essential retrieval functions.

The model first internalizes the retrieval corpus through self-supervised learning. It then treats retrieval as sequential passage generation and assesses relevance to rerank the results. These stages place corpus learning, passage production, and relevance assessment within a shared model, creating an end-to-end architecture around the language model's capabilities.

The reported experiments show a significant improvement over existing retrieval approaches. They also show substantial gains in downstream language-model applications such as retrieval-augmented generation. This connects the architectural change to both retrieval performance and the usefulness of retrieved material in a broader application. The paper's contribution is therefore an integrated retrieval design with empirical benefits at both stages of use.
summary.tldr: Self-Retrieval integrates corpus learning, passage retrieval, and reranking into one language model, improving retrieval and downstream applications in experiments.

title: Self-Retrieval: End-to-End Information Retrieval with One Large Language Model

abstract: We develop a neural network architecture which, trained in an unsupervised manner as a denoising diffusion model, simultaneously learns to both generate and segment images. Learning is driven entirely by the denoising diffusion objective, without any annotation or prior knowledge about regions during training. A computational bottleneck, built into the neural architecture, encourages the denoising network to partition an input into regions, denoise them in parallel, and combine the results. Our trained model generates both synthetic images and, by simple examination of its internal predicted partitions, semantic segmentations of those images. Without fine-tuning, we directly apply our unsupervised model to the downstream task of segmenting real images via noising and subsequently denoising them. Experiments demonstrate that our model achieves accurate unsupervised image segmentation and high-quality synthetic image generation across multiple datasets.

paragraphs: This paper develops a diffusion architecture that learns image generation and segmentation together without region annotations. Training uses only the denoising diffusion objective, so the segmentation behavior must arise from how the network solves its generation task. The model receives no prior knowledge about image regions during training.

The key intervention is a computational bottleneck built into the architecture. It encourages the network to partition an image into regions, denoise those regions in parallel, and combine their outputs. Because predicted partitions are part of this internal computation, examining them provides semantic segmentations of the synthetic images the trained model generates.

The same trained model can also segment real images without additional fine-tuning. It first adds noise to a real image and then denoises it, exposing partitions through that process. Experiments across multiple datasets report accurate unsupervised segmentation alongside high-quality generation. The approach makes segmentation an outcome of an architectural constraint within generative learning, allowing one training objective to support both tasks.
summary.tldr: A region-based computational bottleneck lets a diffusion model learn image generation and segmentation using only denoising supervision.

title: Factorized Diffusion Architectures for Unsupervised Image Generation and Segmentation

abstract: Multi-modal contrastive learning with language supervision has presented a paradigm shift in modern machine learning. By pre-training on a web-scale dataset, multi-modal contrastive learning can learn high-quality representations that exhibit impressive robustness and transferability. Despite its empirical success, the theoretical understanding is still in its infancy, especially regarding its comparison with single-modal contrastive learning. In this work, we introduce a feature learning theory framework that provides a theoretical foundation for understanding the differences between multi-modal and single-modal contrastive learning. Based on a data generation model consisting of signal and noise, our analysis is performed on a ReLU network trained with the InfoMax objective function. Through a trajectory-based optimization analysis and generalization characterization on downstream tasks, we identify the critical factor, which is the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), that impacts the generalizability in downstream tasks of both multi-modal and single-modal contrastive learning. Through the cooperation between the two modalities, multi-modal learning can achieve better feature learning, leading to improvements in performance in downstream tasks compared to single-modal learning. Our analysis provides a unified framework that can characterize the optimization and generalization of both single-modal and multi-modal contrastive learning. Empirical experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets further consolidate our theoretical findings.

paragraphs: The paper investigates why contrastive learning across two modalities can produce better representations than learning from one modality alone. Its aim is to explain differences in feature learning and downstream performance within a shared theoretical framework. This connects the empirical success of language-supervised multimodal learning to an analysis of what training actually learns.

The analysis assumes a data-generation model with signal and noise and studies a ReLU network trained using an InfoMax objective. By following the optimization trajectory and characterizing downstream generalization, the authors identify signal-to-noise ratio as a critical factor for both single-modal and multimodal learning. This makes the quality of the available signal central to understanding the comparison.

Within the framework, cooperation between modalities can improve learned features and thereby improve downstream-task performance. The claim is an explanation of how multimodal gains can arise under the analyzed setting, rather than a universal advantage for every pair of modalities. Experiments using synthetic and real-world datasets support the theoretical findings, linking the analysis to observed learning behavior.
summary.tldr: A feature-learning analysis identifies signal-to-noise ratio as central to when cooperation between modalities can improve contrastive learning.

title: On the Comparison between Multi-modal and Single-modal Contrastive Learning

abstract: Modern machine learning models are becoming increasingly expensive to train for real-world image and text classification tasks, where massive web-scale data is collected in a streaming fashion. To reduce the training cost, online batch selection techniques have been developed to choose the most informative datapoints. However, many existing techniques are not robust to class imbalance and distributional shifts, and can suffer from poor worst-class generalization performance. This work introduces REDUCR, a robust and efficient data downsampling method that uses class priority reweighting. REDUCR reduces the training data while preserving worst-class generalization performance. REDUCR assigns priority weights to datapoints in a class-aware manner using an online learning algorithm. We demonstrate the data efficiency and robust performance of REDUCR on vision and text classification tasks. On web-scraped datasets with imbalanced class distributions, REDUCR significantly improves worst-class test accuracy (and average accuracy), surpassing state-of-the-art methods by around 15\%.

paragraphs: Selecting only part of an incoming data stream can reduce the expense of training image and text classifiers. However, selecting informative examples does not automatically protect every class. Existing batch-selection methods can struggle with class imbalance and distribution shifts, leaving the worst-performing class with poor generalization even when training is more economical.

REDUCR addresses this problem through class-aware priority weights. An online learning algorithm assigns priorities to data points with their class information in mind, guiding which examples are retained for training. The objective is to reduce the data used while preserving performance on the class that generalizes least well.

Experiments on vision and text classification tasks demonstrate both data efficiency and robust performance. On web-scraped datasets with imbalanced classes, the authors report improvements in worst-class and average test accuracy, with gains of around 15% over state-of-the-art methods. These findings support incorporating class priorities into data selection when reducing training cost would otherwise risk uneven performance across categories.
summary.tldr: REDUCR selects training data using class-aware priorities to reduce training cost while protecting worst-class generalization.

title: REDUCR: Robust Data Downsampling using Class Priority Reweighting

abstract: Intervention Target Estimation (ITE) is vital for both understanding and decision-making in complex systems, yet it remains underexplored. Current ITE methods are hampered by their inability to learn from distinct intervention instances collaboratively and to incorporate rich insights from labeled data, which leads to inefficiencies such as the need for re-estimation of intervention targets with minor data changes or alterations in causal graphs. In this paper, we propose DeepITE, an innovative deep learning framework designed around a variational graph autoencoder. DeepITE can concurrently learn from both unlabeled and labeled data with different intervention targets and causal graphs, harnessing correlated information in a self or semi-supervised manner. The model's inference capabilities allow for the immediate identification of intervention targets on unseen samples and novel causal graphs, circumventing the need for retraining. Our extensive testing confirms that DeepITE not only surpasses 13 baseline methods in the Recall@k metric but also demonstrates expeditious inference times, particularly on large graphs. Moreover, incorporating a modest fraction of labeled data (5-10\%) substantially enhances DeepITE's performance, further solidifying its practical applicability. Our source code is available at https://github.com/alipay/DeepITE.

paragraphs: Intervention target estimation seeks to identify where an intervention acted within a causal system. Existing methods can struggle to share information across intervention instances or use labeled examples effectively. As a result, even modest changes to the data or causal graph may require estimating the targets again.

DeepITE approaches this problem with a variational graph autoencoder. Its framework learns jointly from examples involving different intervention targets and different causal graphs, using unlabeled data alone or combining it with labels. By learning across these examples, the model can identify targets in previously unseen samples and new causal graphs through inference, without retraining.

In the reported tests, DeepITE surpasses 13 baseline methods on Recall@k, a measure of target recovery among a selected set of candidates. It also provides fast inference, particularly for large graphs. Adding labels for 5–10% of the data substantially improves performance. These findings support the value of sharing learned information across intervention problems and incorporating even a modest amount of supervision.
summary.tldr: DeepITE learns across causal graphs and intervention examples to identify new intervention targets quickly, with further gains from limited labels.

title: DeepITE: Designing Variational Graph Autoencoders for Intervention Target Estimation

abstract: Gloss-free sign language translation (SLT) aims to develop well-performing SLT systems with no requirement for the costly gloss annotations, but currently still lags behind gloss-based approaches significantly. In this paper, we identify **a representation density problem** that could be a bottleneck in restricting the performance of gloss-free SLT. Specifically, the representation density problem describes that the visual representations of semantically distinct sign gestures tend to be closely packed together in feature space, which makes gloss-free methods struggle with distinguishing different sign gestures and suffer from a sharp performance drop. To address the representation density problem, we introduce a simple but effective contrastive learning strategy, namely SignCL, which encourages gloss-free models to learn more discriminative feature representation in a self-supervised manner. Our experiments demonstrate that the proposed SignCL can significantly reduce the representation density and improve performance across various translation frameworks. Specifically, SignCLachieves a significant improvement in BLEU score for the Sign Language Transformer and GFSLT-VLP on the CSL-Daily dataset by 39\% and 46\%, respectively, without any increase of model parameters. Compared to Sign2GPT, a state-of-the-art method based on large-scale pre-trained vision and language models, SignCLachieves better performance with only 35\% of its parameters. We will release our code and model to facilitate further research.

paragraphs: Gloss-free sign language translation avoids the costly gloss annotations used by other translation systems, but its performance still trails gloss-based approaches. This paper identifies a possible bottleneck in the visual representations learned by gloss-free models. Gestures with different meanings can occupy closely packed positions in feature space, making them difficult for the model to distinguish.

SignCL addresses this representation-density problem through self-supervised contrastive learning. The training strategy encourages more discriminative visual features, helping the model separate semantically distinct gestures. Because it changes the learning strategy without increasing the model's parameter count, its reported gains do not require enlarging the translation model.

On CSL-Daily, the reported BLEU improvements are 39% for the Sign Language Transformer and 46% for GFSLT-VLP. SignCL also outperforms Sign2GPT while using 35% of its parameters. These results support representation separation as a useful intervention across the evaluated systems, while the paper presents density as a potential bottleneck rather than the sole explanation for gloss-free translation's performance gap.
summary.tldr: SignCL improves gloss-free sign language translation by using contrastive learning to separate crowded gesture representations without adding model parameters.

title: Improving Gloss-free Sign Language Translation by Reducing Representation Density

abstract: General-purpose artificial intelligence (AI) systems are built on massive swathes of public web data, assembled into corpora such as C4, RefinedWeb, and Dolma. To our knowledge, we conduct the first, large-scale, longitudinal audit of the consent protocols for the web domains underlying AI training corpora. Our audit of 14,000 web domains provides an expansive view of crawlable web data and how codified data use preferences are changing over time. We observe a proliferation of AI-specific clauses to limit use, acute differences in restrictions on AI developers, as well as general inconsistencies between websites' expressed intentions in their Terms of Service and their robots.txt. We diagnose these as symptoms of ineffective web protocols, not designed to cope with the widespread re-purposing of the internet for AI. Our longitudinal analyses show that in a single year (2023-2024) there has been a rapid crescendo of data restrictions from web sources, rendering ~5\%+ of all tokens in C4, or 28%+ of the most actively maintained, critical sources in C4, fully restricted from use. For Terms of Service crawling restrictions, a full 45% of C4 is now restricted. If respected or enforced, these restrictions are rapidly biasing the diversity, freshness, and scaling laws for general-purpose AI systems. We hope to illustrate the emerging crises in data consent, for both developers and creators. The foreclosure of much of the open web will impact not only commercial AI, but also non-commercial AI and academic research.

paragraphs: The paper studies how websites communicate permission and restrictions around data used to train general-purpose AI. It audits 14,000 domains underlying major web corpora, tracking changes over time. The focus is on codified preferences, including Terms of Service and robots.txt, and whether these mechanisms provide consistent signals about acceptable use.

They separately report Terms of Service crawling restrictions covering 45% of C4.

The authors interpret these findings as evidence that existing web protocols are poorly suited to widespread reuse for AI. If respected or enforced, the restrictions affect the diversity, freshness, and scaling of available training data. The concern extends to academic and noncommercial research, while also exposing difficulties creators face in expressing meaningful data-use preferences.
summary.tldr: An audit of 14,000 web domains finds rapidly increasing AI data restrictions and inconsistent mechanisms for expressing consent.

title: Consent in Crisis: The Rapid Decline of the AI Data Commons

abstract: Image description datasets play a crucial role in the advancement of various applications such as image understanding, text-to-image generation, and text-image retrieval. Currently, image description datasets primarily originate from two sources. One source is the scraping of image-text pairs from the web. Despite their abundance, these descriptions are often of low quality and noisy. Another way is through human labeling. Datasets such as COCO are generally very short and lack details. Although detailed image descriptions can be annotated by humans, the high cost limits their quantity and feasibility. These limitations underscore the need for more efficient and scalable methods to generate accurate and detailed image descriptions. In this paper, we propose an innovative framework termed Image Textualization, which automatically produces high-quality image descriptions by leveraging existing mult-modal large language models (MLLMs) and multiple vision expert models in a collaborative manner. We conduct various experiments to validate the high quality of the descriptions constructed by our framework. Furthermore, we show that MLLMs fine-tuned on our dataset acquire an unprecedented capability of generating richer image descriptions, substantially increasing the length and detail of their output with even less hallucinations.

paragraphs: Image Textualization addresses a problem with the descriptions used to train image-related AI systems: readily available text often provides an unreliable or incomplete account of an image. Web descriptions can be noisy, while human-written captions are frequently brief. Hiring people to write detailed descriptions is possible, but its cost constrains how much data can be produced.

The proposed framework automatically creates detailed image descriptions by combining existing multimodal large language models with several specialist vision models. Multimodal models work with images and language, while the vision experts contribute visual analysis. The central idea is to make these models collaborate in producing descriptions, offering a way to expand detailed annotation without relying entirely on human labeling.

The authors report experiments supporting the quality of the generated descriptions. They also use the resulting dataset to fine-tune multimodal language models, which then produce substantially longer, more detailed descriptions with fewer hallucinations—claims about content that is not actually present. These findings suggest that the dataset can help models describe more of an image while reducing unsupported additions.
summary.tldr: Image Textualization combines multimodal language models and vision experts to generate detailed image descriptions that improve description richness and reduce hallucinations when used for fine-tuning.

title: Image Textualization: An Automatic Framework for Generating Rich and Detailed Image Descriptions

abstract: Pretraining data selection has the potential to improve language model pretraining efficiency by utilizing higher-quality data from massive web data corpora. Current data selection methods, which rely on either hand-crafted rules or larger reference models, are conducted statically and do not capture the evolving data preferences during pretraining. In this paper, we introduce *model-aware data selection with data influence models (MATES)*, where a data influence model continuously adapts to the evolving data preferences of the pretraining model and then selects the data most effective for the current pretraining progress. Specifically, we collect oracle data influence by locally probing the pretraining model and fine-tune a small data influence model to approximate it accurately. The data influence model then predicts data influence over the whole pretraining corpus and selects the most influential data for the next pretraining stage. Experiments of pretraining 410M and 1B models on the C4 dataset demonstrate that MATES significantly outperforms random data selection on extensive downstream tasks. It doubles the gains achieved by the state-of-the-art data selection approach that leverages larger reference models and reduces the total FLOPs required to reach certain performances by half. Further analyses validate the effectiveness of the locally probed oracle data influence and the approximation with data influence models. Our code is open-sourced at https://github.com/cxcscmu/MATES.

paragraphs: Training data can have different value at different points in language-model pretraining. MATES addresses this by updating data selection as the model develops. The motivation is that fixed rules or rankings from a larger reference model do not capture the evolving preferences of the particular model currently being trained.

The method locally probes the pretraining model to collect estimates of data influence, then finetunes a small model to approximate those estimates. This influence model scores the full corpus and selects influential data for the next training stage. Repeating the process lets selection respond to training progress while extending information from local probes across a much larger collection.

Experiments pretraining 410-million- and one-billion-parameter models on C4 show significant improvements over random selection on downstream tasks. MATES doubles the gains of the compared leading selection method and halves total FLOPs needed to reach certain performance levels. Additional analyses support both the local influence estimates and their learned approximation, reinforcing the case for adapting selection throughout pretraining.
summary.tldr: MATES adapts data selection to a language model's training progress and halves the reported compute needed to reach certain performance levels.

title: MATES: Model-Aware Data Selection for Efficient Pretraining with Data Influence Models

abstract: Federated Learning (FL) is a form of distributed learning that allows multiple institutions or clients to collaboratively learn a global model to solve a task. This allows the model to utilize the information from every institute while preserving data privacy. However, recent studies show that the promise of protecting the privacy of data is not upheld by existing methods and that it is possible to recreate the training data from the different institutions. This is done by utilizing gradients transferred between the clients and the global server during training or by knowing the model architecture at the client end. In this paper, we propose a federated learning framework for semantic segmentation without knowing the model architecture nor transferring gradients between the client and the server, thus enabling better privacy preservation. We propose \textit{BlackFed} - a black-box adaptation of neural networks that utilizes zero order optimization (ZOO) to update the client model weights and first order optimization (FOO) to update the server weights. We evaluate our approach on several computer vision and medical imaging datasets to demonstrate its effectiveness. To the best of our knowledge, this work is one of the first works in employing federated learning for segmentation, devoid of gradients or model information exchange. Code: https://github.com/JayParanjape/blackfed/tree/master

paragraphs: Federated learning allows institutions to collaborate without pooling their original datasets, but information exchanged during training can still expose private data. The paper points to reconstruction risks involving transferred gradients or knowledge of client model architectures. It addresses these concerns for semantic segmentation, where models assign categories to image regions at the pixel level.

BlackFed adapts client networks without exchanging gradients or model architecture information between clients and the server. It uses zero-order optimization to update client weights and first-order optimization to update server weights. This combination lets the client side operate as a black box while maintaining a federated learning process.

The authors evaluate the framework on several computer vision and medical imaging datasets and report that it is effective. They describe it as one of the first federated segmentation approaches to avoid both gradient and model-information exchange. Its privacy contribution is the removal of those information-sharing pathways; the abstract presents this as better privacy preservation, without claiming an unconditional guarantee against every form of data disclosure.
summary.tldr: BlackFed enables federated semantic segmentation without exchanging client gradients or model architecture information.

title: Federated Black-Box Adaptation for Semantic Segmentation

abstract: Sign language translation (SLT) addresses the problem of translating information from a sign language in video to a spoken language in text. Existing studies, while showing progress, are often limited to narrow domains and/or few sign languages and struggle with open-domain tasks. In this paper, we push forward the frontier of SLT by scaling pretraining data, model size, and number of translation directions. We perform large-scale SLT pretraining on different data including 1) noisy multilingual Youtube SLT data,2) parallel text corpora, and 3) SLT data augmented by translating video captions to other languages with off-the-shelf machine translation models. We unify different pretraining tasks with task-specific prompts under the encoder-decoder architecture, and initialize the SLT model with pretrained (m/By)T5 models across model sizes. SLT pretraining results on How2Sign and FLEURS-ASL\#0 (ASL to 42 spoken languages) demonstrate the significance of data/model scaling and cross-lingual cross-modal transfer, as well as the feasibility of zero-shot SLT. We finetune the pretrained SLT models on 5 downstream open-domain SLT benchmarks covering 5 sign languages. Experiments show substantial quality improvements over the vanilla baselines, surpassing the previous state-of-the-art (SOTA) by wide margins.

paragraphs: Sign language translation converts information in signed video into text in a spoken language. Existing systems often cover limited domains or few sign languages. This paper explores broader translation by increasing pretraining data, model size, and the number of translation directions within a shared modeling framework.

Pretraining combines noisy multilingual YouTube sign-language data, parallel text corpora, and additional translation pairs created by translating video captions into other languages. Task-specific prompts unify these tasks in an encoder-decoder architecture initialized from pretrained T5-family models at different sizes. This setup brings linguistic and video-based learning into a common training process.

Results on How2Sign and FLEURS-ASL#0, which covers ASL translation into 42 spoken languages, support the importance of scaling and transfer across languages and modalities. They also demonstrate the feasibility of zero-shot sign language translation. Fine-tuning on five open-domain benchmarks covering five sign languages produces substantial improvements over vanilla baselines and previous leading results. Together, the findings support shared large-scale pretraining as a route toward broader sign-language translation coverage.
summary.tldr: Scaling multilingual, multimodal pretraining improves open-domain sign language translation and demonstrates feasible zero-shot translation.

title: Scaling Sign Language Translation

abstract: Learning reliably safe autonomous control is one of the core problems in trustworthy autonomy. However, training a controller that can be formally verified to be safe remains a major challenge. We introduce a novel approach for learning verified safe control policies in nonlinear neural dynamical systems while maximizing overall performance. Our approach aims to achieve safety in the sense of finite-horizon reachability proofs, and is comprised of three key parts. The first is a novel curriculum learning scheme that iteratively increases the verified safe horizon. The second leverages the iterative nature of gradient-based learning to leverage incremental verification, reusing information from prior verification runs. Finally, we learn multiple verified initial-state-dependent controllers, an idea that is especially valuable for more complex domains where learning a single universal verified safe controller is extremely challenging. Our experiments on five safe control problems demonstrate that our trained controllers can achieve verified safety over horizons that are as much as an order of magnitude longer than state-of-the-art baselines, while maintaining high reward, as well as a perfect safety record over entire episodes. Our code is available at https://github.com/jlwu002/VSRL.

paragraphs: A controller can perform well during training yet remain difficult to verify formally. This paper combines reinforcement learning with safety verification for nonlinear systems represented by neural dynamics. Its safety target is a reachability proof over a finite horizon, while the learning process also seeks high overall performance.

Three components support that goal. A curriculum gradually extends the horizon over which safety is verified. Incremental verification reuses information from earlier verification runs as gradient-based learning updates the controller. Finally, the method learns multiple verified controllers associated with different initial states, helping address domains where one universally verified controller is especially difficult to obtain.

Across five safe-control problems, the authors report verified horizons up to an order of magnitude longer than state-of-the-art baselines while maintaining high reward. They also observe a perfect safety record over complete experimental episodes. These are complementary forms of evidence: the formal proofs cover finite horizons, while the full-episode safety record describes observed experimental behavior. The method therefore improves both verified reach and practical performance in the evaluated problems.
summary.tldr: Curriculum learning, incremental verification, and initial-state-specific controllers extend formally verified safety horizons while retaining high reward in evaluated control problems.

title: Verified Safe Reinforcement Learning for Neural Network Dynamic Models

abstract: The application of reinforcement learning (RL) involving interactions with individuals has grown significantly in recent years. These interactions, influenced by factors such as personal preferences and physiological differences, causally influence state transitions, ranging from health conditions in healthcare to learning progress in education. As a result, different individuals may exhibit different state-transition processes. Understanding individualized state-transition processes is essential for optimizing individualized policies. In practice, however, identifying these state-transition processes is challenging, as individual-specific factors often remain latent. In this paper, we establish the identifiability of these latent factors and introduce a practical method that effectively learns these processes from observed state-action trajectories. Experiments on various datasets show that the proposed method can effectively identify latent state-transition processes and facilitate the learning of individualized RL policies.

paragraphs: The same action can affect different people differently. In reinforcement learning applications involving individuals, personal preferences or physiological differences can influence how states change over time. These differences matter for choosing effective personalized actions, but the factors responsible are often hidden rather than directly recorded in the available data.

The paper studies whether those latent factors and the individualized transition processes they influence can be identified from observed state-action trajectories. It establishes an identifiability result and introduces a practical learning method. Identifiability addresses a foundational question: whether the observations can distinguish the hidden structure the method aims to recover, rather than merely support a predictive fit.

Experiments across several datasets show that the method can identify latent transition processes and support learning individualized policies. The significance is the connection between understanding a person's response dynamics and adapting the policy used for that person. Personalization here concerns how actions change future states, so recovering individual differences in those dynamics directly informs the subsequent reinforcement learning problem.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes identifiability of hidden individual factors and learns personalized state-transition processes to support individualized reinforcement learning.

title: Identifying Latent State-Transition Processes for Individualized Reinforcement Learning

abstract: With the rapid development of deep learning, the increasing complexity and scale of parameters make training a new model increasingly resource-intensive. In this paper, we start from the classic convolutional neural network (CNN) and explore a paradigm that does not require training to obtain new models. Similar to the birth of CNN inspired by receptive fields in the biological visual system, we draw inspiration from the information subsystem pathways in the biological visual system and propose Model Disassembling and Assembling (MDA). During model disassembling, we introduce the concept of relative contribution and propose a component locating technique to extract task-aware components from trained CNN classifiers. For model assembling, we present the alignment padding strategy and parameter scaling strategy to construct a new model tailored for a specific task, utilizing the disassembled task-aware components.The entire process is akin to playing with LEGO bricks, enabling arbitrary assembly of new models, and providing a novel perspective for model creation and reuse. Extensive experiments showcase that task-aware components disassembled from CNN classifiers or new models assembled using these components closely match or even surpass the performance of the baseline,demonstrating its promising results for model reuse. Furthermore, MDA exhibits diverse potential applications, with comprehensive experiments exploring model decision route analysis, model compression, knowledge distillation, and more.

paragraphs: Training new neural networks becomes increasingly resource-intensive as models grow. Model LEGO explores reusing parts of trained convolutional classifiers to construct models for specific tasks without training the newly assembled model. Its Model Disassembling and Assembling framework treats useful task-related components as building blocks that can be located, extracted, and recombined.

During disassembly, a notion of relative contribution helps identify components relevant to a task. During assembly, alignment padding and parameter scaling make those extracted components usable together in a new model. The approach is inspired by information pathways in biological vision, but its practical focus is on finding and combining task-aware computation already present in trained CNNs.

Experiments show that extracted components and assembled models can closely match or surpass the baseline's performance. The authors also explore decision-route analysis, compression, and knowledge distillation as applications. These results support component-level model reuse as a promising alternative source of task-specific models, with the reported evidence centered on components obtained from trained convolutional classifiers.
summary.tldr: Model LEGO extracts task-aware components from trained CNNs and recombines them into new models without additional training.

title: Model LEGO: Creating Models Like Disassembling and Assembling Building Blocks

abstract: Multimodal foundation models serve numerous applications at the intersection of vision and language. Still, despite being pretrained on extensive data, they become outdated over time.To keep models updated, research into continual pretraining mainly explores scenarios with either (1) infrequent, indiscriminate updates on large-scale new data, or (2) frequent, sample-level updates.However, practical model deployment often operates in the gap between these two limit cases, as real-world applications demand adaptation to specific subdomains, tasks or concepts --- spread over the entire, varying life cycle of a model. In this work, we complement current perspectives on continual pretraining through a research test bed and offer comprehensive guidance for effective continual model updates in such scenarios.We first introduce FoMo-in-Flux, a continual multimodal pretraining benchmark with realistic compute constraints and practical deployment requirements, constructed over 63 datasets with diverse visual and semantic coverage.Using FoMo-in-Flux, we explore the complex landscape of practical continual pretraining through multiple perspectives: (1) data mixtures and stream orderings that emulate real-world deployment settings, (2) methods ranging from simple fine-tuning and traditional continual learning strategies to parameter-efficient updates and model merging, (3) meta-learning-rate schedules and mechanistic design choices, and (4) model and compute scaling. Together, our insights provide a practitioner's guide to continual multimodal pretraining for real-world deployment. Benchmark and code is provided here: https://github.com/ExplainableML/fomo_in_flux.

paragraphs: Vision-language foundation models can become outdated after pretraining. Updating them in practice often means adapting to particular domains, tasks, or concepts at different points in their deployment. The paper argues that this setting falls between two common research extremes: occasional large updates using new data indiscriminately and frequent updates at the level of individual samples.

The authors introduce FoMo-in-Flux, a benchmark built from 63 datasets with varied visual and semantic content. It places continual multimodal pretraining within realistic compute constraints and deployment requirements. The benchmark makes it possible to study how changing data mixtures and the order of incoming data affect model updates across a model’s lifetime.

The study compares approaches including ordinary fine-tuning, traditional continual learning, parameter-efficient updates, and model merging. It also examines learning-rate schedules, other design decisions, and scaling of models and computation. Its stated contribution is a practical research framework and guidance drawn from these investigations, rather than a single update method claimed to be best in every deployment.
summary.tldr: FoMo-in-Flux benchmarks realistic continual vision-language pretraining and supports practical guidance on updating deployed models.

title: A Practitioner's Guide to Real-World Continual Multimodal Pretraining

abstract: In the era of foundation models, fine-tuning pre-trained models for specific downstream tasks has become crucial. This drives the need for robust fine-tuning methods to address challenges such as model overfitting and sparse labeling. Moleculargraph foundation models (MGFMs) face unique difficulties that complicate fine-tuning. These models are limited by smaller pre-training datasets and more severedata scarcity for downstream tasks, both of which require enhanced model generalization. Moreover, MGFMs must accommodate diverse objectives, including bothregression and classification tasks. To better understand and improve fine-tuningtechniques under these conditions, we classify eight fine-tuning methods into threemechanisms: weight-based, representation-based, and partial fine-tuning. Webenchmark these methods on downstream regression and classification tasks acrosssupervised and self-supervised pre-trained models in diverse labeling settings. Thisextensive evaluation provides valuable insights and informs the design of a refinedrobust fine-tuning method, ROFT-MOL. This approach combines the strengths ofsimple post-hoc weight interpolation with more complex weight ensemble fine-tuning methods, delivering improved performance across both task types whilemaintaining the ease of use inherent in post-hoc weight interpolation.

paragraphs: Molecular graph foundation models must adapt to downstream tasks with scarce labels and risks of overfitting. Their pretraining datasets are also relatively small, making generalization especially important. The paper studies robust fine-tuning under these conditions while accounting for the need to support both continuous-property regression and classification.

The authors organize eight fine-tuning methods into three mechanisms: methods operating on weights, methods operating on representations, and methods that fine-tune only part of a model. They compare these approaches across supervised and self-supervised pretrained models, multiple labeling settings, and both task types. This broad evaluation provides the basis for designing a refined method.

The resulting ROFT-MOL approach combines simple post-hoc weight interpolation with more complex weight-ensemble fine-tuning methods. The authors report improved performance for regression and classification while retaining the ease of use associated with post-hoc interpolation. The work contributes both an organized benchmark of adaptation strategies and a method informed by that comparison, addressing practical fine-tuning choices for molecular models with limited downstream data.
summary.tldr: RoFt-Mol benchmarks robust molecular-model fine-tuning and combines weight interpolation with ensemble-based methods to improve regression and classification.

title: RoFt-Mol: Benchmarking Robust Fine-tuning with Molecular Graph Foundation Models

abstract: It is common to reject undesired outputs of Large Language Models (LLMs); however, current methods to do so require an excessive amount of computation to re-sample after a rejection, or distort the distribution of outputs by constraining the output to highly improbable tokens. We present a method, Approximately Aligned Decoding (AprAD), to balance the distortion of the output distribution with computational efficiency, inspired by algorithms from the speculative decoding literature. AprAD allows for the generation of long sequences of text with difficult-to-satisfy constraints, while amplifying low probability outputs much less compared to existing methods. We show through a series of experiments that the task-specific performance of AprAD is comparable to methods that do not distort the output distribution, while being much more computationally efficient.

We present a method, Approximately Aligned Decoding (AprAD), to balance the distortion of the output distribution with computational efficiency, inspired by algorithms from the speculative decoding literature. AprAD allows for the generation of long sequences of text with difficult-to-satisfy constraints, while amplifying low probability outputs much less compared to existing methods. paragraphs: Rejecting an unwanted language-model output creates a tradeoff. Generating another candidate can require substantial computation, while forcing the model toward acceptable tokens can make otherwise unlikely outputs much more common. The paper addresses how to satisfy output constraints without paying too heavily in either computation or distortion of the model’s output distribution.

Approximately Aligned Decoding, or AprAD, draws inspiration from speculative decoding algorithms to balance these competing demands. It supports long text generation under constraints that are difficult to satisfy. A central aim is to limit how strongly the procedure amplifies low-probability outputs, preserving more of the model’s original distribution while avoiding the expense of repeated rejection and resampling.

In the reported experiments, AprAD achieves task-specific performance comparable to approaches that leave the output distribution undistorted, while using substantially less computation. It also amplifies unlikely outputs much less than existing methods. These findings support AprAD as an empirical compromise between computational efficiency and distribution preservation, rather than a claim that constrained generation becomes entirely distortion-free.
summary.tldr: AprAD makes constrained text generation more efficient while limiting the amplification of unlikely outputs.

title: Approximately Aligned Decoding

abstract: Recent deep clustering models have produced impressive clustering performance. However, a common issue with existing methods is the disparity between global and local feature structures. While local structures typically show strong consistency and compactness within class samples, global features often present intertwined boundaries and poorly separated clusters. Motivated by this observation, we propose **DCBoost, a parameter-free plug-in** designed to enhance the global feature structures of current deep clustering models. By harnessing reliable local structural cues, our method aims to elevate clustering performance effectively. Specifically, we first identify high-confidence samples through adaptive $k$-nearest neighbors-based consistency filtering, aiming to select a sufficient number of samples with high label reliability to serve as trustworthy anchors for self-supervision. Subsequently, these samples are utilized to compute a discriminative loss, which promotes both intra-class compactness and inter-class separability, to guide network optimization. Extensive experiments across various benchmark datasets showcase that our DCBoost significantly improves the clustering performance of diverse existing deep clustering models. Notably, our method improves the performance of current state-of-the-art baselines (e.g., ProPos) by more than 3\% and amplifies the silhouette coefficient by over $7\times$. **Code is available at [https://github.com/l-h-y168/DCBoost](https://github.com/l-h-y168/DCBoost).**

paragraphs: A clustering model can produce locally consistent neighborhoods even when its overall clusters remain poorly separated. DCBoost uses this mismatch as an opportunity: reliable local structure can supply a learning signal for improving the global representation. The method is presented as a parameter-free plug-in for existing deep clustering models.

It first selects high-confidence examples through an adaptive nearest-neighbor consistency filter. The goal is to obtain enough examples with reliable cluster labels to act as anchors for self-supervision. Those anchors then support a discriminative loss that encourages examples within a class to become more compact and different classes to become better separated.

Experiments across benchmark datasets report substantial improvements for diverse clustering models. The abstract highlights gains exceeding 3% for current state-of-the-art baselines such as ProPos and an increase of more than sevenfold in the silhouette coefficient. These results indicate improvements in both clustering performance and measured cluster separation. The central contribution is turning trusted portions of an existing representation into supervision that helps reorganize its broader structure.
summary.tldr: DCBoost uses reliable local neighborhoods as self-supervised anchors to improve global separation in existing deep clustering models.

title: You Can Trust Your Clustering Model: A Parameter-free Self-Boosting Plug-in for Deep Clustering

abstract: Weakly Supervised Video Anomaly Detection (WSVAD) has achieved notable advancements, yet existing models remain vulnerable to adversarial attacks, limiting their reliability. Due to the inherent constraints of weak supervision—where only video-level labels are provided despite the need for frame-level predictions—traditional adversarial defense mechanisms, such as adversarial training, are not effective since video-level adversarial perturbations are typically weak and inadequate. To address this limitation, pseudo-labels generated directly from the model can enable frame-level adversarial training; however, these pseudo-labels are inherently noisy, significantly degrading performance. We therefore introduce a novel Pseudo-Anomaly Generation method called Spatiotemporal Region Distortion (SRD), which creates synthetic anomalies by applying severe augmentations to localized regions in normal videos while preserving temporal consistency. Integrating these precisely annotated synthetic anomalies with the noisy pseudo-labels substantially reduces label noise, enabling effective adversarial training. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method significantly enhances the robustness of WSVAD models against adversarial attacks, outperforming state-of-the-art methods by an average of 71.0\% in overall AUROC performance across multiple benchmarks. The implementation and code are publicly available at [FrameShield (GitHub)](https://github.com/rohban-lab/FrameShield).

paragraphs: Weakly supervised video anomaly detection learns from labels attached to whole videos, even though it must identify anomalies in individual frames. This mismatch complicates adversarial defense. The authors find that video-level perturbations provide inadequate adversarial training, while using a model’s own frame-level predictions as labels introduces noise that harms performance.

FrameShield supplies more reliable training examples through Spatiotemporal Region Distortion. It creates synthetic anomalies by strongly modifying localized regions of normal videos while keeping the changes temporally consistent. Because these anomalies are deliberately generated, they come with precise annotations. Combining them with noisy model-generated labels substantially reduces label noise and enables effective frame-level adversarial training.

Across multiple benchmarks, the authors report improved resistance to adversarial attacks and an average 71.0% improvement over state-of-the-art methods in overall AUROC performance. This reported improvement should not be read as a percentage-point increase. The result supports using controlled synthetic anomalies to address the supervision problem that makes adversarial training difficult in this setting.
summary.tldr: FrameShield uses precisely labeled synthetic video anomalies to enable more effective adversarial training under weak supervision.

title: FrameShield: Adversarially Robust Video Anomaly Detection

abstract: Local field potentials (LFPs) can be routinely recorded alongside spiking activity in intracortical neural experiments, measure a larger complementary spatiotemporal scale of brain activity for scientific inquiry, and can offer practical advantages over spikes, including greater long-term stability, robustness to electrode degradation, and lower power requirements. Despite these advantages, recent neural modeling frameworks have largely focused on spiking activity since LFP signals pose inherent modeling challenges due to their aggregate, population-level nature, often leading to lower predictive power for downstream task variables such as motor behavior. To address this challenge, we introduce a cross-modal knowledge distillation framework that transfers high-fidelity representational knowledge from pretrained multi-session spike transformer models to LFP transformer models. Specifically, we first train a teacher spike model across multiple recording sessions using a masked autoencoding objective with a session-specific neural tokenization strategy. We then align the latent representations of the student LFP model to those of the teacher spike model. Our results show that the distilled LFP models consistently outperform single- and multi-session LFP baselines in both fully unsupervised and supervised settings, and can generalize to other sessions without additional distillation while maintaining superior performance. These findings demonstrate that cross-modal knowledge distillation is a powerful and scalable approach for leveraging high-performing spike models to develop more accurate LFP models.

paragraphs: Local field potentials capture brain activity at a broader scale than neural spikes and can offer advantages in stability, power use, and resistance to electrode degradation. Their aggregate nature also makes them difficult to model, often reducing predictive performance for variables such as motor behavior. This paper uses stronger spike models to improve LFP representations.

The approach first trains a spike transformer across multiple recording sessions using masked autoencoding and a tokenization strategy specific to each session. That pretrained model becomes a teacher. A student transformer processing LFP signals then learns to align its internal representations with those produced by the spike teacher.

The distilled students consistently outperform both single-session and multi-session LFP baselines in the reported unsupervised and supervised settings. They also transfer to other sessions without additional distillation while retaining superior performance. The result suggests that information learned from one neural recording modality can improve another, helping combine the representational strength of spike models with the practical advantages associated with LFP recordings.
summary.tldr: Distilling representations from spike transformers improves LFP models across learning settings and transfers to other recording sessions.

title: Cross-Modal Representational Knowledge Distillation for Enhanced Spike-informed LFP Modeling

abstract: The m-out-of-n bootstrap—proposed by \cite{bickel1992resampling}—approximates the distribution of a statistic by repeatedly drawing $m$ subsamples ($m \ll n$) without replacement from an original sample of size n; it is now routinely used for robust inference with heavy-tailed data, bandwidth selection, and other large-sample applications. Despite this broad applicability across econometrics, biostatistics, and machine-learning workflows, rigorous parameter-free guarantees for the soundness of the m-out-of-n bootstrap when estimating sample quantiles have remained elusive. This paper establishes such guarantees by analysing the estimator of sample quantiles obtained from m-out-of-n resampling of a dataset of length n. We first prove a central limit theorem for a fully data-driven version of the estimator that holds under a mild moment condition and involves no unknown nuisance parameters. We then show that the moment assumption is essentially tight by constructing a counter-example in which the CLT fails. Strengthening the assumptions slightly, we derive an Edgeworth expansion that delivers exact convergence rates and, as a corollary, a Berry–Esséen bound on the bootstrap approximation error. Finally, we illustrate the scope of our results by obtaining parameter-free asymptotic distributions for practical statistics, including the quantiles for random walk MH, and rewards of ergodic MDP's, thereby demonstrating the usefulness of our theory in modern estimation and learning tasks.

paragraphs: The paper studies quantile estimation using repeated resamples much smaller than the original dataset, drawn without replacement. Such resampling is useful in large-sample inference, but the authors identify a gap in rigorous guarantees that avoid unknown nuisance parameters. Their analysis supplies those guarantees for a fully data-driven estimator.

First, they prove a central limit theorem under a mild moment condition, giving an asymptotic distribution without unknown nuisance parameters. They then construct a counterexample where the theorem fails, showing that the moment requirement is essentially tight. This is a substantive boundary on the result: the guarantee depends on a condition that cannot simply be removed in general.

Under slightly stronger assumptions, an Edgeworth expansion yields exact convergence rates, and a Berry–Esséen bound quantifies bootstrap approximation error. The authors also derive parameter-free asymptotic distributions for practical statistics, including quantiles associated with random-walk Metropolis–Hastings and rewards in ergodic Markov decision processes. These applications connect the theoretical error guarantees to estimation problems involving stochastic computation and learning.
summary.tldr: The paper proves parameter-free asymptotic guarantees and convergence rates for resampled quantile estimators under explicit moment assumptions.

title: Small Resamples, Sharp Guarantees: Convergence Rates for Resampled Studentized Quantile Estimators

abstract: Molecular representation learning has emerged as a promising approach for modeling molecules with deep learning in chemistry and beyond. While 3D geometric models effectively capture molecular structure, they typically process single static conformers, overlooking the inherent flexibility and dynamics of molecules. In reality, many molecular properties depend on distributions of thermodynamically accessible conformations rather than single structures. Recent works show that learning from conformer ensembles can improve molecular representations, but existing approaches either produce unphysical structures through averaging or require restrictive molecular alignment. In this paper, we propose SymmetryPreserving Conformer Ensemble networks (SPiCE), which introduces two key innovations: (1) geometric mixture-of-experts for selective processing of scalar and vector features, and (2) hierarchical ensemble encoding that combines ensemblelevel representation with cross-conformer integration. Crucially, SPiCE ensures physically meaningful representations by maintaining joint equivariance to geometric transformations of individual conformers and conformer permutations. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SPiCE consistently outperforms existing conformer ensemble methods and state-of-the-art structural aggregation models across quantum mechanical and biological property prediction tasks.

paragraphs: Many molecular properties depend on a distribution of accessible three-dimensional shapes, called conformers. A model that processes only one static structure can overlook this flexibility. Existing ensemble approaches introduce other difficulties: averaging can produce unphysical structures, while aligning molecules can impose restrictive requirements.

SPiCE learns from conformer ensembles through two components. A geometric mixture of experts selectively processes scalar and vector features, while hierarchical encoding combines an overall ensemble representation with information exchanged across conformers. The network preserves joint equivariance under geometric transformations of individual conformers and permutations of their order, making its representations respond consistently to those changes.

Experiments cover quantum mechanical and biological property prediction. SPiCE consistently outperforms the compared conformer ensemble methods and state-of-the-art structural aggregation models. The contribution connects information sharing across molecular shapes with explicit symmetry preservation. Its reported success supports learning from the ensemble while respecting how each conformer's geometry and the ordering of the ensemble should affect the representation.
summary.tldr: SPiCE improves molecular property prediction by integrating multiple conformers while preserving their geometric and ordering symmetries.

title: Symmetry-Preserving Conformer Ensemble Networks for Molecular Representation Learning

abstract: The successful training of deep neural networks requires addressing challenges such as overfitting, numerical instabilities leading to divergence, and increasing variance in the residual stream. A common solution is to apply regularization and normalization techniques that usually require tuning additional hyperparameters. An alternative is to force all parameters and representations to lie on a hypersphere. This removes the need for regularization and increases convergence speed, but comes with additional costs. In this work, we propose a more holistic, approximate normalization via simple scalar multiplications motivated by the tight concentration of the norms of high-dimensional random vectors. Additionally, instead of applying strict normalization for the parameters, we constrain their norms. These modifications remove the need for weight decay and learning rate warm-up as well, but do not increase the total number of normalization layers. Our experiments with transformer architectures show up to 40% faster convergence compared to GPT models with QK normalization, with only 3% additional runtime cost. When deriving scaling laws, we found that our method enables training with larger batch sizes while preserving the favorable scaling characteristics of classic GPT architectures.

paragraphs: This paper develops an approximate normalization approach for Transformers. It addresses training problems such as numerical instability, overfitting, and increasing variation in the residual stream. Strictly placing parameters and representations on a hypersphere can help training but adds costs. The authors seek similar practical benefits using simpler operations and less rigid constraints.

Their approach uses scalar multiplications motivated by the observation that high-dimensional random-vector norms concentrate tightly. For parameters, it constrains norms instead of enforcing strict normalization. These changes remove the need for weight decay and learning-rate warm-up in the proposed setup, without increasing the total number of normalization layers. The method therefore changes how magnitudes are controlled throughout training.

Transformer experiments report up to 40% faster convergence than GPT models with QK normalization, with 3% additional runtime cost. The distinction matters: convergence speed and per-run computational overhead are separate measurements. Scaling-law investigations also find that the method supports larger training batches while preserving the favorable scaling behavior of classic GPT architectures. These are reported benefits of the evaluated training approach.
summary.tldr: Approximate normalization and parameter-norm constraints accelerate Transformer convergence in experiments with modest runtime overhead.

title: Learning in Compact Spaces with Approximately Normalized Transformer

abstract: Self-Taught Reasoners (STaR), synonymously known as Rejection sampling Fine-Tuning (RFT), is an integral part of the training pipeline of self-improving reasoning Language Models (LMs). The self-improving mechanism often employs random observation (data) sampling. However, this results in trained observation imbalance; inefficiently over-training on solved examples while under-training on challenging ones. In response, we introduce Adaptive STaR (AdaSTaR), a novel algorithm that rectifies this by integrating two adaptive sampling principles: (1) Adaptive Sampling for Diversity: promoting balanced training across observations, and (2) Adaptive Sampling for Curriculum: dynamically adjusting data difficulty to match the model's evolving strength. Across six benchmarks, AdaSTaR achieves best test accuracy in all instances (6/6) and reduces training FLOPs by an average of 58.6\% against an extensive list of baselines. These improvements in performance and efficiency generalize to different pre-trained LMs and larger models, paving the way for more efficient and effective self-improving LMs.

paragraphs: Self-taught reasoning methods improve language models through a training process that uses the models’ own generated reasoning. A common choice is to sample training problems randomly. The paper identifies an imbalance this can create: the model spends too much training effort on problems it already solves while receiving too little effective training on harder problems.

AdaSTaR changes how problems are selected using two adaptive principles. The first promotes diversity by balancing training across examples. The second provides a curriculum that adjusts problem difficulty to the model’s current ability. Together, these principles make the sampling process respond to learning progress, addressing both which examples receive attention and whether their difficulty is appropriate for the model.

Across six benchmarks, AdaSTaR achieves the best test accuracy among the compared methods in every case and reduces training computation by an average of 58.6%. The authors also report benefits across different pretrained language models and larger models. The results support adaptive data selection as a way to improve reasoning accuracy while spending substantially less computation in the evaluated self-improvement pipelines.
summary.tldr: AdaSTaR adapts training-example diversity and difficulty, achieving the best accuracy across six benchmarks while reducing training FLOPs by 58.6% on average.

title: AdaSTaR: Adaptive Data Sampling for Training Self-Taught Reasoners

abstract: Schrodinger Bridges (SBs) are diffusion processes that steer, in finite time, a given initial distribution to another final one while minimizing a suitable cost functional. Although various methods for computing SBs have recently been proposed in the literature, most of these approaches require computationally expensive training schemes, even for solving low-dimensional problems. In this work, we propose an analytic parametrization of a set of feasible policies for steering the distribution of a dynamical system from one Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM) to another. Instead of relying on standard non-convex optimization techniques, the optimal policy within the set can be approximated as the solution of a low-dimensional linear program whose dimension scales linearly with the number of components in each mixture. The proposed method generalizes naturally to more general classes of dynamical systems, such as controllable linear time-varying systems, enabling efficient solutions to multi-marginal momentum SBs between GMMs, a challenging distribution interpolation problem. We showcase the potential of this approach in low-to-moderate dimensional problems such as image-to-image translation in the latent space of an autoencoder, learning of cellular dynamics using multi-marginal momentum SBs, and various other examples. The implementation is publicly available at https://github.com/georgeRapa/GMMflow.

paragraphs: Schrödinger bridges describe diffusion processes that move one probability distribution to another within a fixed time while minimizing a cost. Computing them often requires expensive training, even in small problems. This paper focuses on distributions represented as Gaussian mixtures and develops an analytic family of policies that can carry out the required distribution change.

The key simplification is to approximate the best policy within that family through a low-dimensional linear program, avoiding standard non-convex optimization. Its dimension scales linearly with the number of components in each mixture. The scope of the optimization matters: the paper approximates the optimum within its chosen feasible family, rather than claiming an unrestricted solution to every bridge problem.

The construction also extends to controllable linear time-varying systems and supports multi-marginal momentum bridges, which interpolate distributions subject to multiple marginals. Demonstrations include image translation in an autoencoder's latent space and learning cellular dynamics. These low-to-moderate-dimensional examples show the potential of combining an analytic policy representation with a compact optimization problem to reduce computational demands.
summary.tldr: An analytic policy family reduces diffusion between Gaussian mixtures to a small linear program that approximates the best policy within that family.

title: Go With the Flow: Fast Diffusion for Gaussian Mixture Models

abstract: Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) have become powerful tools for complex problem solving, but their structured reasoning pathways can lead to unsafe outputs when exposed to harmful prompts. Existing safety alignment methods reduce harmful outputs but can degrade reasoning depth, leading to significant trade-offs in complex, multi-step tasks, and remain vulnerable to sophisticated jailbreak attacks. To address this, we introduce SAFEPATH, a lightweight alignment method that fine-tunes LRMs to emit a short, 8-token Safety Primer at the start of their reasoning, in response to harmful prompts, while leaving the rest of the reasoning process unsupervised. Empirical results across multiple benchmarks indicate that SAFEPATH effectively reduces harmful outputs while maintaining reasoning performance. Specifically, SAFEPATH reduces harmful responses by up to 90.0\% and blocks 83.3\% of jailbreak attempts in the DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B model, while requiring 295.9x less compute than Direct Refusal and 314.1x less than SafeChain. We further introduce a zero-shot variant that requires no fine-tuning. In addition, we provide a comprehensive analysis of how existing methods in LLMs generalize, or fail, when applied to reasoning-centric models, revealing critical gaps and new directions for safer AI.

It fine-tunes a model to produce a short, eight-token safety primer when faced with a harmful prompt, leaving the subsequent reasoning process unsupervised.

The authors evaluate whether that small intervention can influence the resulting output while maintaining reasoning performance. summary.tldr: SAFEPATH trains reasoning models to start harmful-prompt responses with a brief safety primer, reducing harmful outputs while preserving reasoning performance.

title: SAFEPATH: Preventing Harmful Reasoning in Chain-of-Thought via Early Alignment

abstract: Diffusion models have demonstrated remarkable success in high-fidelity image synthesis and prompt-guided generative modeling. However, ensuring adequate diversity in generated samples of prompt-guided diffusion models remains a challenge, particularly when the prompts span a broad semantic spectrum and the diversity of generated data needs to be evaluated in a prompt-aware fashion across semantically similar prompts. Recent methods have introduced guidance via diversity measures to encourage more varied generations. In this work, we extend the diversity measure-based approaches by proposing the *S*calable *P*rompt-*A*ware *R*eny *K*ernel *E*ntropy Diversity Guidance (*SPARKE*) method for prompt-aware diversity guidance. SPARKE utilizes conditional entropy for diversity guidance, which dynamically conditions diversity measurement on similar prompts and enables prompt-aware diversity control. While the entropy-based guidance approach enhances prompt-aware diversity, its reliance on the matrix-based entropy scores poses computational challenges in large-scale generation settings. To address this, we focus on the special case of \textit{Conditional latent RKE Score Guidance}, reducing entropy computation and gradient-based optimization complexity from the $\mathcal{O}(n^3)$ of general entropy measures to $\mathcal{O}(n)$. The reduced computational complexity allows for diversity-guided sampling over potentially thousands of generation rounds on different prompts. We numerically test the SPARKE method on several text-to-image diffusion models, demonstrating that the proposed method improves the prompt-aware diversity of the generated data without incurring significant computational costs. We release our code on the project page: [https://mjalali.github.io/SPARKE/](https://mjalali.github.io/SPARKE).

paragraphs: Generated images should vary meaningfully without confusing differences between unrelated prompts with diversity for one semantic request. SPARKE measures diversity conditionally on similar prompts, making guidance sensitive to the content users are asking for.

The method builds on Rényi kernel entropy and introduces conditional latent RKE guidance. In the relevant formulation, entropy computation and gradient-optimization complexity fall from O(n³) to O(n), making it practical to maintain diversity guidance across potentially thousands of generation rounds.

Experiments with several text-to-image diffusion models improve prompt-aware diversity without significant added computation. The contribution combines a more appropriate comparison group with efficient calculation: samples are encouraged to explore alternatives within related semantic contexts, while the guidance remains affordable as the generated collection grows. The result concerns measured diversity, which remains distinct from correctness or aesthetic quality of every output.
summary.tldr: SPARKE guides diffusion diversity relative to similar prompts with scalable conditional-entropy calculations.

title: SPARKE: Scalable Prompt-Aware Diversity and Novelty Guidance in Diffusion Models via RKE Score

abstract: Out-of-distribution (OOD) fine-tuning has emerged as a promising approach for anomaly segmentation. Current OOD fine-tuning strategies typically employ global-level objectives, aiming to guide segmentation models to accurately predict a large number of anomaly pixels. However, these strategies often perform poorly on small anomalies. To address this issue, we propose an instance-level OOD fine-tuning framework, dubbed LNOIB (Leaving No OOD Instance Behind). We start by theoretically analyzing why global-level objectives fail to segment small anomalies. Building on this analysis, we introduce a simple yet effective instance-level objective. Moreover, we propose a feature separation objective to explicitly constrain the representations of anomalies, which are prone to be smoothed by their in-distribution (ID) surroundings. LNOIB integrates these objectives to enhance the segmentation of small anomalies and serves as a paradigm adaptable to existing OOD fine-tuning strategies, without introducing additional inference cost. Experimental results show that integrating LNOIB into various OOD fine-tuning strategies yields significant improvements, particularly in component-level results, highlighting its strength in comprehensive anomaly segmentation.
