LNOIB integrates these objectives to enhance the segmentation of small anomalies and serves as a paradigm adaptable to existing OOD fine-tuning strategies, without introducing additional inference cost. Experimental results show that integrating LNOIB into various OOD fine-tuning strategies yields significant improvements, particularly in component-level results, highlighting its strength in comprehensive anomaly segmentation.

paragraphs: Anomaly segmentation identifies image regions that fall outside the distribution a model normally recognizes. Existing out-of-distribution fine-tuning objectives often emphasize correctly predicting many anomaly pixels overall. The paper analyzes why this global emphasis can leave small anomalous objects poorly segmented, even when the total pixel-level objective appears useful.

LNOIB changes the training focus by introducing an objective at the level of individual anomaly instances. It also adds a feature-separation objective because the representations of anomalies can be smoothed by surrounding in-distribution content. Together, these objectives address both how anomalies contribute to learning and how distinctly they are represented.

The framework can be integrated into existing out-of-distribution fine-tuning strategies without adding inference cost. Experiments with several such strategies show significant improvements, particularly when results are measured at the component level. This supports the importance of assessing whether individual anomalies are captured, alongside aggregate pixel coverage, and shows that training changes can improve small-anomaly segmentation without making deployment more expensive.
summary.tldr: LNOIB improves small-anomaly segmentation through instance-level training and feature separation without adding inference cost.

title: Leaving No OOD Instance Behind: Instance-Level OOD Fine-Tuning for Anomaly Segmentation

abstract: Reconstructing dynamic 3D scenes from monocular videos remains a fundamental challenge in 3D vision. While 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) achieves real-time rendering in static settings, extending it to dynamic scenes is challenging due to the difficulty of learning structured and temporally consistent motion representations. This challenge often manifests as three limitations in existing methods: redundant Gaussian updates, insufficient motion supervision, and weak modeling of complex non-rigid deformations. These issues collectively hinder coherent and efficient dynamic reconstruction. To address these limitations, we propose HAIF-GS, a unified framework that enables structured and consistent dynamic modeling through sparse anchor-driven deformation. It first identifies motion-relevant regions via an Anchor Filter to suppress redundant updates in static areas. A self-supervised Induced Flow-Guided Deformation module induces anchor motion using multi-frame feature aggregation, eliminating the need for explicit flow labels. To further handle fine-grained deformations, a Hierarchical Anchor Propagation mechanism increases anchor resolution based on motion complexity and propagates multi-level transformations. Extensive experiments on synthetic and real-world benchmarks validate that HAIF-GS significantly outperforms prior dynamic 3DGS methods in rendering quality, temporal coherence, and reconstruction efficiency.

paragraphs: Reconstructing a moving 3D scene from a single-camera video requires a representation that changes coherently over time. Extending Gaussian Splatting to this setting can involve unnecessary updates in static regions, weak motion supervision, and difficulty representing complex deformations. HAIF-GS addresses these issues through a sparse set of anchors that drive deformation.

An Anchor Filter first identifies regions where motion matters, suppressing redundant updates elsewhere. A self-supervised deformation module then combines features from multiple frames to induce anchor motion without explicit flow labels. For more detailed movement, hierarchical anchor propagation increases anchor resolution according to motion complexity and passes transformations across levels.

These components connect where the model allocates motion updates, how it learns movement, and how finely it represents deformation. Experiments on synthetic and real-world benchmarks report significant improvements over prior dynamic Gaussian Splatting methods in rendering quality, consistency across time, and reconstruction efficiency. The findings support structured anchor-based motion as a way to improve both reconstruction coherence and computational use.
summary.tldr: HAIF-GS uses filtered, hierarchically refined motion anchors to improve dynamic Gaussian Splatting reconstruction without explicit flow labels.

title: HAIF-GS: Hierarchical and Induced Flow-Guided Gaussian Splatting for Dynamic Scene

abstract: Solving time-dependent parametric partial differential equations (PDEs) remains a fundamental challenge for neural solvers, particularly when generalizing across a wide range of physical parameters and dynamics. When data is uncertain or incomplete—as is often the case—a natural approach is to turn to generative models. We introduce ENMA, a generative neural operator designed to model spatio-temporal dynamics arising from physical phenomena. ENMA predicts future dynamics in a compressed latent space using a generative masked autoregressive transformer trained with flow matching loss, enabling tokenwise generation. Irregularly sampled spatial observations are encoded into uniform latent representations via attention mechanisms and further compressed through a spatio-temporal convolutional encoder. This allows ENMA to perform in-context learning at inference time by conditioning on either past states of the target trajectory or auxiliary context trajectories with similar dynamics. The result is a robust and adaptable framework that generalizes to new PDE regimes and supports one-shot surrogate modeling of time-dependent parametric PDEs.

paragraphs: ENMA addresses prediction of physical systems described by time-dependent, parameterized partial differential equations. These systems can vary across physical parameters and dynamical regimes, while observations may be incomplete or uncertain. The paper introduces a generative neural operator to predict future spatial and temporal behavior under those conditions.

Its representation pipeline first uses attention to map irregularly sampled spatial observations into uniform latent representations. A spatial and temporal convolutional encoder compresses them further. A masked autoregressive transformer then predicts future dynamics token by token in this compressed space, using a flow-matching training loss. This connects irregular observations to a compact generative representation of evolving physical fields.

At inference time, ENMA can condition on earlier states from the target trajectory or on auxiliary trajectories with similar dynamics. That conditioning enables in-context adaptation using the supplied examples. The authors report generalization to new PDE regimes and support for one-shot surrogate modeling. The central contribution is a generative operator that combines flexible observation encoding with example-conditioned prediction of future dynamics.
summary.tldr: ENMA generates future PDE dynamics token by token in a compressed space, adapting through context from past states or related trajectories.

title: ENMA: Tokenwise Autoregression for Continuous Neural PDE Operators

abstract: Scene understanding in adverse conditions, such as fog, snow, and night, is challenging due to the visual appearance degeneration. In this context, we propose a Cross-modal Semantic Compensation Adaptation method (CroPe) for scene understanding. Distinct from the existing methods, which only use the visual information to learn the domain-invariant features, CroPe establishes a visual-textual paradigm which provides textual semantic compensation for visual features, enabling the model to learn more consistent representations. We propose the Complementary Perceptual Text Generation (CPTG) module which generates a set of multi-level complementary-perceptive text embeddings incorporating both generalization and domain awareness. To achieve cross-modal semantic compensation, the Reverse Chain Text-Visual Fusion (RCTVF) module is developed. By the unified attention and reverse decoding chain, compensation information is successively fused to the visual features from the deep (semantic dense) to shallow (semantic sparse) features, maximizing compensation gain. CroPe yields competitive results under all adverse conditions and significantly improves the state-of-the-art performance by 6.5 mIoU for ACDC-Night dataset and 1.2 mIoU for ACDC-All dataset, respectively.

paragraphs: Fog, snow, and darkness degrade the visual evidence needed to understand a scene. CroPe addresses this problem by supplementing visual features with textual semantic information. The aim is to help a model form more consistent representations across adverse conditions when appearance alone becomes less reliable.

Its text-generation module creates complementary text embeddings at multiple levels. These embeddings combine information intended to generalize across conditions with information sensitive to the particular domain. A second module then integrates this textual information into the visual representation using unified attention and a reverse decoding chain. Fusion proceeds from deeper features rich in semantic information toward shallower features with less semantic content.

This ordering makes semantic compensation part of the feature-processing pipeline, allowing textual information to support multiple levels of visual understanding. The authors report competitive results across the adverse conditions evaluated, with improvements over prior state-of-the-art performance of 6.5 mIoU on ACDC-Night and 1.2 mIoU on ACDC-All. These results support the usefulness of combining visual and textual representations for the studied adverse-scene tasks.
summary.tldr: CroPe supplements degraded visual features with multi-level textual information, improving scene understanding on adverse-condition benchmarks.

title: CroPe: Cross-Modal Semantic Compensation Adaptation for All Adverse Scene Understanding

abstract: Synthetic oversampling of minority examples using SMOTE and its variants is a leading strategy for addressing imbalanced classification problems. Despite the success of this approach in practice, its theoretical foundations remain underexplored. We develop a theoretical framework to analyze the behavior of SMOTE and related methods when classifiers are trained on synthetic data. We first derive a uniform concentration bound on the discrepancy between the empirical risk over synthetic minority samples and the population risk on the true minority distribution. We then provide a nonparametric excess risk guarantee for kernel-based classifiers trained using such synthetic data. These results lead to practical guidelines for better parameter tuning of both SMOTE and the downstream learning algorithm. Numerical experiments are provided to illustrate and support the theoretical findings.

We first derive a uniform concentration bound on the discrepancy between the empirical risk over synthetic minority samples and the population risk on the true minority distribution. We then provide a nonparametric excess risk guarantee for kernel-based classifiers trained using such synthetic data. These results lead to practical guidelines for better parameter tuning of both SMOTE and the downstream learning algorithm. Numerical experiments are provided to illustrate and support the theoretical findings.

paragraphs: When one class has relatively few examples, synthetic oversampling creates additional minority-class training samples. SMOTE and related methods are widely used for this purpose, but their practical success has outpaced theoretical understanding. This paper develops a framework for analyzing classifiers trained with these artificially generated examples.

Its first result bounds the discrepancy between error measured on synthetic minority samples and error on the actual minority population. The bound is uniform, providing control beyond the error of a single fixed classifier. This addresses a central issue in oversampling: good performance on generated examples needs a theoretical connection to performance on the distribution those examples are intended to represent.

The authors then establish an excess-risk guarantee for nonparametric kernel-based classifiers trained with synthetic data. Together, the results yield guidance for choosing parameters of both the oversampling procedure and the downstream classifier. Numerical experiments illustrate and support the theory, connecting the mathematical analysis to practical decisions about how synthetic minority examples should be used.
summary.tldr: The paper derives theoretical guarantees linking SMOTE-generated training data to minority-population error and kernel-classifier performance.

title: Concentration and excess risk bounds for imbalanced classification with synthetic oversampling

abstract: Learning the underlying dynamics of single cells from snapshot data has gained increasing attention in scientific and machine learning research. The destructive measurement technique and cell proliferation/death result in unpaired and unbalanced data between snapshots, making the learning of the underlying dynamics challenging. In this paper, we propose joint Velocity-Growth Flow Matching (VGFM), a novel paradigm that jointly learns state transition and mass growth of single-cell populations via flow matching. VGFM builds an ideal single-cell dynamics containing velocity of state and growth of mass, driven by a presented two-period dynamic understanding of the static semi-relaxed optimal transport, a mathematical tool that seeks the coupling between unpaired and unbalanced data. To enable practical usage, we approximate the ideal dynamics using neural networks, forming our joint velocity and growth matching framework. A distribution fitting loss is also employed in VGFM to further improve the fitting performance for snapshot data. Extensive experimental results on both synthetic and real datasets demonstrate that VGFM can capture the underlying biological dynamics accounting for mass and state variations over time, outperforming existing approaches for single-cell dynamics modeling.

VGFM builds an ideal single-cell dynamics containing velocity of state and growth of mass, driven by a presented two-period dynamic understanding of the static semi-relaxed optimal transport, a mathematical tool that seeks the coupling between unpaired and unbalanced data. To enable practical usage, we approximate the ideal dynamics using neural networks, forming our joint velocity and growth matching framework. paragraphs: Single-cell measurements provide snapshots of a population, but the measurement process destroys the observed cells. Researchers therefore cannot directly pair the same cells across time. Cell division and death also change population size, so learning biological dynamics requires explaining both changes in cell state and changes in population mass.

Velocity-Growth Flow Matching, or VGFM, models those two processes jointly. It constructs ideal dynamics containing a velocity for state transitions and a growth term for population mass. The construction draws on a two-period dynamic interpretation of semi-relaxed optimal transport, which connects datasets that are both unpaired and unbalanced. Neural networks then approximate these ideal dynamics for practical use.

VGFM also includes a distribution-fitting loss to improve agreement with observed snapshots. Experiments on synthetic and real datasets show that it can capture dynamics involving both state and mass variation, outperforming existing approaches in the reported evaluations. The contribution matters because a changing snapshot distribution can reflect several biological processes at once; explicitly modeling movement through cell states alongside growth gives the framework a way to account for both.
summary.tldr: VGFM jointly learns cell-state transitions and population growth from unpaired, unequal-sized single-cell snapshots.

title: Joint Velocity-Growth Flow Matching for Single-Cell Dynamics Modeling

abstract: On-device large models (LMs) reduce cloud dependency but expose proprietary model weights to the end-user, making them vulnerable to white-box model stealing (MS) attacks. A common defense is TEE-Shielded DNN Partition (TSDP), which places all trainable LoRA adapters (fine tuned on private data) inside a trusted execution environment (TEE). However, this design suffers from excessive host-to-TEE communication latency. We propose AegisGuard, a fine tuning and deployment framework that selectively shields the MS sensitive adapters while offloading the rest to the GPU, balancing security and efficiency. AegisGuard integrates two key components: i) RL-based Sensitivity Measurement (RSM), which injects Gaussian noise during training and applies a lightweight reinforcement learning to rank adapters based on their impact on model stealing; and (ii) Shielded-Adapter Compression (SAC), which structurally prunes the selected adapters to reduce both parameter size and intermediate feature maps, further lowering TEE computation and data transfer costs. Extensive experiments demonstrate that AegisGuard achieves black-box level MS resilience (surrogate accuracy around 39%, matching fully shielded baselines), while reducing end-to-end inference latency by 2–3× and cutting TEE memory usage by 4× compared to state-of-the-art TSDP methods.

paragraphs: Running large models on a user's device exposes model components to inspection and copying. One defense keeps privately fine-tuned LoRA adapters inside a trusted execution environment, a protected computing region. Protecting every adapter this way creates substantial communication delays between the protected environment and the rest of the device.

AegisGuard selects which adapters need protection most. During training, it introduces Gaussian noise and uses lightweight reinforcement learning to rank adapters by their effect on model stealing. It then shields the sensitive adapters and sends the others to the GPU. A second component structurally prunes protected adapters, reducing both their parameters and the intermediate representations that must be transferred.

In the reported experiments, the resulting system matches fully shielded baselines at roughly 39% surrogate accuracy, which measures the copying model's performance. It also reduces inference latency by a factor of two to three and TEE memory use by a factor of four against the compared methods. These findings support selective protection as an empirical security–efficiency tradeoff, rather than a claim that copying becomes impossible.
summary.tldr: AegisGuard selectively protects and compresses sensitive adapters, matching fully shielded model-stealing resilience in experiments while reducing latency and protected memory use.

title: AegisGuard: RL-Guided Adapter Tuning for TEE-Based Efficient & Secure On-Device Inference

abstract: We introduce and study new models for learning from contagion processes in a network. A learning algorithm is allowed to either choose or passively observe an initial set of seed infections. This seed set then induces a final set of infections resulting from the underlying stochastic contagion dynamics. Our models differ from prior work in that detailed vertex-by-vertex timestamps for the spread of the contagion are not observed. The goal of learning is to infer the unknown network structure. Our main theoretical results are efficient and provably correct algorithms for exactly learning trees. We provide empirical evidence that our algorithm performs well more generally on realistic sparse graphs.
originalAbstract: We introduce and study new models for learning from contagion processes in a network. A learning algorithm is allowed to either choose or passively observe an initial set of seed infections. This seed set then induces a final set of infections resulting from the underlying stochastic contagion dynamics. Our models differ from prior work in that detailed vertex-by-vertex timestamps for the spread of the contagion are not observed. The goal of learning is to infer the unknown network structure. Our main theoretical results are efficient and provably correct algorithms for exactly learning trees. We provide empirical evidence that our algorithm performs well more generally on realistic sparse graphs.

paragraphs: This paper asks how to recover an unknown network from contagion outcomes when detailed infection times are unavailable. The learner sees an initial set of infected vertices and the final set reached by a stochastic spreading process. It must infer network structure from these starting and ending sets, without observing the timing of each intermediate infection.

The authors introduce models covering two ways of obtaining the initial infections: the learner may actively choose them or passively observe them. This distinction separates settings where experiments can be designed from those where the available contagion events are simply recorded. In both cases, the information available is deliberately coarser than vertex-by-vertex timestamp histories.

The main theoretical results provide efficient, provably correct algorithms for exactly learning tree networks. The authors also give empirical evidence of good performance on realistic sparse graphs more generally. The distinction matters: exact recovery is theoretically established for trees, while the broader sparse-graph claim is experimental. The work shows that initial and final infection sets can retain enough information for rigorous network learning in the supported setting.
summary.tldr: Initial and final contagion sets enable provably exact learning of tree networks, with encouraging empirical results on more general sparse graphs.

title: Learning from Contagion (Without Timestamps)

abstract: For many tasks and data types, there are natural transformations to which the data should be invariant or insensitive. For instance, in visual recognition, natural images should be insensitive to rotation and translation. This requirement and its implications have been important in many machine learning applications, and tolerance for image transformations was primarily achieved by using robust feature vectors. In this paper we propose a novel and computationally efficient way to learn a local Mahalanobis metric per datum, and show how we can learn a local invariant metric to any transformation in order to improve performance.
originalAbstract: For many tasks and data types, there are natural transformations to which the data should be invariant or insensitive. For instance, in visual recognition, natural images should be insensitive to rotation and translation. This requirement and its implications have been important in many machine learning applications, and tolerance for image transformations was primarily achieved by using robust feature vectors. In this paper we propose a novel and computationally efficient way to learn a local Mahalanobis metric per datum, and show how we can learn a local invariant metric to any transformation in order to improve performance.

paragraphs: The paper addresses learning tasks where certain transformations should have little or no effect on how examples are compared. In visual recognition, rotation and translation are examples of changes for which such tolerance can be useful. The authors focus on incorporating this requirement into the distance used to compare data points.

Their method learns a local Mahalanobis metric for each datum. Such a metric determines how differences in feature coordinates contribute to distance, while making it local allows that rule to vary across the dataset. The approach therefore places transformation tolerance directly in the learned comparison rule, extending the emphasis on robust feature vectors described in the abstract.

The authors present the method as computationally efficient and show how a local metric can be made invariant to a chosen transformation to improve performance. The scope of the proposal is broad in the transformation it can accommodate. Its key contribution is the connection between a per-datum distance model and an explicit invariance requirement, making the desired insensitivity part of metric learning itself.
summary.tldr: The paper efficiently learns a separate Mahalanobis distance around each datum and incorporates invariance to chosen transformations.

title: Learning Local Invariant Mahalanobis Distances

abstract: When multiple views of data are available for a set of subjects, co-clustering aims to identify subject clusters that agree across the different views. We explore the problem of co-clustering when the underlying clusters exist in different subspaces of each view. We propose a proximal alternating linearized minimization algorithm that simultaneously decomposes multiple data matrices into sparse row and columns vectors. This approach is able to group subjects consistently across the views and simultaneously identify the subset of features in each view that are associated with the clusters. The proposed algorithm can globally converge to a critical point of the problem. A simulation study validates that the proposed algorithm can identify the hypothesized clusters and their associated features. Comparison with several latest multi-view co-clustering methods on benchmark datasets demonstrates the superior performance of the proposed approach.
originalAbstract: When multiple views of data are available for a set of subjects, co-clustering aims to identify subject clusters that agree across the different views. We explore the problem of co-clustering when the underlying clusters exist in different subspaces of each view. We propose a proximal alternating linearized minimization algorithm that simultaneously decomposes multiple data matrices into sparse row and columns vectors. This approach is able to group subjects consistently across the views and simultaneously identify the subset of features in each view that are associated with the clusters. The proposed algorithm can globally converge to a critical point of the problem. A simulation study validates that the proposed algorithm can identify the hypothesized clusters and their associated features. Comparison with several latest multi-view co-clustering methods on benchmark datasets demonstrates the superior performance of the proposed approach.

paragraphs: When the same subjects have several kinds of measurements, useful clusters may agree across those views while depending on different features in each one. This paper addresses that setting by jointly discovering subject groups and the feature subsets associated with them. It allows the underlying clusters to occupy different subspaces across views.

The proposed algorithm simultaneously decomposes multiple data matrices into sparse row and column vectors. Sparsity supports selecting relevant subjects and features within the decomposition, while the joint formulation maintains consistent subject grouping across views. Optimization uses proximal alternating linearized minimization, providing a procedure for handling these coupled sparse representations.

The convergence result is to a critical point of the optimization problem; it does not establish a globally optimal solution. A simulation study shows recovery of the hypothesized clusters and associated features. Comparisons on benchmark datasets report stronger performance than several recent multi-view co-clustering methods. Together, these findings support learning both shared grouping structure and view-specific feature relevance within one approach.
summary.tldr: A sparse multi-view co-clustering method jointly discovers consistent subject groups and their view-specific features, with convergence to a critical point.

title: Multi-view Sparse Co-clustering via Proximal Alternating Linearized Minimization

abstract: Bayesian optimization is a powerful tool for fine-tuning the hyper-parameters of a wide variety of machine learning models. The success of machine learning has led practitioners in diverse real-world settings to learn classifiers for practical problems. As machine learning becomes commonplace, Bayesian optimization becomes an attractive method for practitioners to automate the process of classifier hyper-parameter tuning. A key observation is that the data used for tuning models in these settings is often sensitive. Certain data such as genetic predisposition, personal email statistics, and car accident history, if not properly private, may be at risk of being inferred from Bayesian optimization outputs. To address this, we introduce methods for releasing the best hyper-parameters and classifier accuracy privately. Leveraging the strong theoretical guarantees of differential privacy and known Bayesian optimization convergence bounds, we prove that under a GP assumption these private quantities are often near-optimal. Finally, even if this assumption is not satisfied, we can use different smoothness guarantees to protect privacy.

The success of machine learning has led practitioners in diverse real-world settings to learn classifiers for practical problems. As machine learning becomes commonplace, Bayesian optimization becomes an attractive method for practitioners to automate the process of classifier hyper-parameter tuning. A key observation is that the data used for tuning models in these settings is often sensitive. Certain data such as genetic predisposition, personal email statistics, and car accident history, if not properly private, may be at risk of being inferred from Bayesian optimization outputs. To address this, we introduce methods for releasing the best hyper-parameters and classifier accuracy privately. Leveraging the strong theoretical guarantees of differential privacy and known Bayesian optimization convergence bounds, we prove that under a GP assumption these private quantities are often near-optimal. Finally, even if this assumption is not satisfied, we can use different smoothness guarantees to protect privacy.

paragraphs: Bayesian optimization automates the search for useful model hyperparameters. When the data used to evaluate those choices are sensitive, the optimization outputs can themselves expose information about the data. This paper focuses on that release step: how to disclose the selected hyperparameters and classifier accuracy while providing differential privacy.

The authors develop private release methods and analyze their usefulness by combining differential privacy guarantees with known convergence bounds for Bayesian optimization. Under a Gaussian process assumption, they prove that the privately released quantities are often near-optimal. The result links protection of the tuning data to the quality of the information practitioners receive.

The Gaussian process assumption matters to the stated near-optimality result. The paper also explains how other smoothness guarantees can protect privacy when that assumption does not hold. This distinguishes the conditions used to establish output quality from the alternative conditions available for privacy protection, while addressing the practical need to report useful results from sensitive model-tuning data.
summary.tldr: Private Bayesian optimization releases selected hyperparameters and accuracy with privacy guarantees and conditional near-optimality results.

title: Differentially Private Bayesian Optimization

abstract: We propose and study a row-and-column affine measurement scheme for low-rank matrix recovery. Each measurement is a linear combination of elements in one row or one column of a matrix X. This setting arises naturally in applications from different domains. However, current algorithms developed for standard matrix recovery problems do not perform well in our case, hence the need for developing new algorithms and theory for our problem. We propose a simple algorithm for the problem based on Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) and least-squares (LS), which we term alg. We prove that (a simplified version of) our algorithm can recover X exactly with the minimum possible number of measurements in the noiseless case. In the general noisy case, we prove performance guarantees on the reconstruction accuracy under the Frobenius norm. In simulations, our row-and-column design and alg algorithm show improved speed, and comparable and in some cases better accuracy compared to standard measurements designs and algorithms. Our theoretical and experimental results suggest that the proposed row-and-column affine measurements scheme, together with our recovery algorithm, may provide a powerful framework for affine matrix reconstruction.

Each measurement is a linear combination of elements in one row or one column of a matrix X. This setting arises naturally in applications from different domains. However, current algorithms developed for standard matrix recovery problems do not perform well in our case, hence the need for developing new algorithms and theory for our problem. We propose a simple algorithm for the problem based on Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) and least-squares (LS), which we term alg. In the general noisy case, we prove performance guarantees on the reconstruction accuracy under the Frobenius norm. In simulations, our row-and-column design and alg algorithm show improved speed, and comparable and in some cases better accuracy compared to standard measurements designs and algorithms. Our theoretical and experimental results suggest that the proposed row-and-column affine measurements scheme, together with our recovery algorithm, may provide a powerful framework for affine matrix reconstruction.

paragraphs: This paper studies reconstructing a low-rank matrix from measurements that each combine entries within one row or one column. Such measurements have a particular structure, and the authors report that algorithms designed for standard matrix recovery do not perform well in this setting. They therefore develop a matching reconstruction algorithm and theory.

The algorithm combines singular value decomposition with least squares. For a simplified version, the authors prove exact recovery using the minimum possible number of measurements when there is no noise. They separately establish reconstruction accuracy guarantees for noisy measurements, measuring error with the Frobenius norm, which summarizes discrepancies across matrix entries.

Simulations compare the proposed measurement design and algorithm with standard designs and methods. The new combination is faster, with comparable accuracy and sometimes better accuracy. The results support row-and-column measurements as a promising reconstruction framework. The strongest exact-recovery statement specifically concerns the simplified algorithm in the noiseless case, while the noisy analysis provides accuracy bounds.
summary.tldr: A reconstruction method tailored to row-and-column measurements offers recovery guarantees and faster simulated low-rank matrix reconstruction.

title: Low-Rank Matrix Recovery from Row-and-Column Affine Measurements

abstract: Despite recent breakthroughs in the applications of deep neural networks, one setting that presents a persistent challenge is that of "one-shot learning." Traditional gradient-based networks require a lot of data to learn, often through extensive iterative training. When new data is encountered, the models must inefficiently relearn their parameters to adequately incorporate the new information without catastrophic interference. Architectures with augmented memory capacities, such as Neural Turing Machines (NTMs), offer the ability to quickly encode and retrieve new information, and hence can potentially obviate the downsides of conventional models. Here, we demonstrate the ability of a memory-augmented neural network to rapidly assimilate new data, and leverage this data to make accurate predictions after only a few samples. We also introduce a new method for accessing an external memory that focuses on memory content, unlike previous methods that additionally use memory location-based focusing mechanisms.

title: Meta-Learning with Memory-Augmented Neural Networks

abstract: In recent years increasingly complex architectures for deep convolution networks (DCNs) have been proposed to boost the performance on image recognition tasks. However, the gains in performance have come at a cost of substantial increase in computation and model storage resources. Fixed point implementation of DCNs has the potential to alleviate some of these complexities and facilitate potential deployment on embedded hardware. In this paper, we propose a quantizer design for fixed point implementation of DCNs. We formulate and solve an optimization problem to identify optimal fixed point bit-width allocation across DCN layers. Our experiments show that in comparison to equal bit-width settings, the fixed point DCNs with optimized bit width allocation offer >20% reduction in the model size without any loss in accuracy on CIFAR-10 benchmark. We also demonstrate that fine-tuning can further enhance the accuracy of fixed point DCNs beyond that of the original floating point model. In doing so, we report a new state-of-the-art fixed point performance of 6.78% error-rate on CIFAR-10 benchmark.

paragraphs: More complex convolutional networks can improve image recognition while demanding more computation and storage. The authors design a quantizer and formulate an optimization problem that selects fixed-point bit widths across the network. This makes precision allocation a deliberate optimization decision instead of giving every layer the same bit width. The approach matters because the storage budget can be distributed across layers according to the allocation selected by that optimization.

summary.tldr: Optimizing bit widths across convolutional layers reduces model size without accuracy loss in the reported CIFAR-10 experiments.

title: Fixed Point Quantization of Deep Convolutional Networks

abstract: Recurrent neural networks, such as long-short term memory (LSTM) networks, are powerful tools for modeling sequential data like user browsing history (Tan et al., 2016; Korpusik et al., 2016) or natural language text (Mikolov et al., 2010). However, to generalize across different user types, LSTMs require a large number of parameters, notwithstanding the simplicity of the underlying dynamics, rendering it uninterpretable, which is highly undesirable in user modeling. The increase in complexity and parameters arises due to a large action space in which many of the actions have similar intent or topic. In this paper, we introduce Latent LSTM Allocation (LLA) for user modeling combining hierarchical Bayesian models with LSTMs. In LLA, each user is modeled as a sequence of actions, and the model jointly groups actions into topics and learns the temporal dynamics over the topic sequence, instead of action space directly. This leads to a model that is highly interpretable, concise, and can capture intricate dynamics. We present an efficient Stochastic EM inference algorithm for our model that scales to millions of users/documents. Our experimental evaluations show that the proposed model compares favorably with several state-of-the-art baselines.

paragraphs: Modeling user behavior directly as a sequence of individual actions can make an LSTM unnecessarily complex. Many actions may express similar intentions or topics, yet a large action space still demands many parameters. Latent LSTM Allocation addresses this mismatch by combining hierarchical Bayesian modeling with recurrent neural networks.

The model jointly groups actions into topics and learns how the resulting topic sequence changes over time. Each user is still represented through a sequence of actions, but temporal modeling operates over the inferred topics. Learning the grouping and dynamics together produces a concise, interpretable representation that can still capture intricate patterns of behavior.

The authors introduce an efficient stochastic EM inference algorithm that scales to millions of users or documents. Their experimental evaluations compare favorably with several state-of-the-art baselines. The contribution brings together interpretability, sequence modeling, and scalable inference: related actions can share a topic representation, allowing the temporal model to focus on changes among meaningful groups instead of handling every action separately.
summary.tldr: Latent LSTM Allocation jointly groups actions into topics and learns their temporal dynamics for concise, interpretable sequence modeling.

title: Latent LSTM Allocation: Joint Clustering and Non-Linear Dynamic Modeling of Sequence Data

abstract: The representation and learning benefits of methods based on graph Laplacians, such as Laplacian smoothing or harmonic function solution for semi-supervised learning (SSL), are empirically and theoretically well supported. Nonetheless, the exact versions of these methods scale poorly with the number of nodes $n$ of the graph. In this paper, we combine a spectral sparsification routine with Laplacian learning. Given a graph $G$ as input, our algorithm computes a sparsifier in a distributed way in $O(n\log^3(n))$ time, $O(m\log^3(n))$ work and $O(n\log(n))$ memory, using only $\log(n)$ rounds of communication. Furthermore, motivated by the regularization often employed in learning algorithms, we show that constructing sparsifiers that preserve the spectrum of the Laplacian only up to the regularization level may drastically reduce the size of the final graph. By constructing a spectrally-similar graph, we are able to bound the error induced by the sparsification for a variety of downstream tasks (e.g., SSL). We empirically validate the theoretical guarantees on Amazon co-purchase graph and compare to the state-of-the-art heuristics.

paragraphs: Graph Laplacian methods support tasks such as smoothing and semi-supervised learning, but exact computations become expensive as graphs grow. This paper combines these learning methods with spectral sparsification: constructing a smaller graph that preserves relevant spectral properties of the original Laplacian. The aim is to reduce computational demands while controlling the effect on learning.

The proposed distributed construction uses O(n log³ n) time, O(m log³ n) work, O(n log n) memory, and log n communication rounds, where n and m denote nodes and edges. A further idea connects sparsification to regularization. Preserving the spectrum only to the resolution required by the regularization level may substantially reduce the size of the resulting graph.

The authors bound the error introduced by sparsification for several downstream tasks, including semi-supervised learning. This links the quality of the smaller graph to the computations it will support. Experiments on an Amazon co-purchase graph validate the theoretical guarantees and compare the method with state-of-the-art heuristics.
summary.tldr: Regularization-aware spectral sparsification reduces graph size while providing error bounds for downstream Laplacian learning.

title: Improved large-scale graph learning through ridge spectral sparsification

abstract: In this paper, we model the problem of optimizing crowdfunding platforms, such as the non-profit Kiva or for-profit KickStarter, as a variant of the multi-armed bandit problem. In our setting, Bernoulli arms emit no rewards until their cumulative number of successes over any number of trials exceeds a fixed threshold and then provides no additional reward for any additional trials - a process reminiscent to that of a neuron firing once it reaches the action potential and then saturates. In the spirit of an infinite armed bandit problem, the player can add new arms whose expected probability of success is drawn iid from an unknown distribution – this endless supply of projects models the harsh reality that the number of projects seeking funding greatly exceeds the total capital available by lenders. Crowdfunding platforms naturally fall under this setting where the arms are potential projects, and their probability of success is the probability that a potential funder decides to fund it after reviewing it. The goal is to play arms (prioritize the display of projects on a webpage) to maximize the number of arms that reach the firing threshold (meet their goal amount) using as few total trials (number of impressions) as possible over all the played arms. We provide an algorithm for this setting and prove sublinear regret bounds.

paragraphs: The paper models crowdfunding as a decision problem about which projects to show potential funders. Each project has an unknown probability that a viewing produces a funding success. A project produces a reward only after its accumulated successes exceed a fixed threshold, and further attempts produce no additional reward once that threshold has been reached.

This creates a variant of the multi-armed bandit problem in which completing projects is the central objective. The platform can introduce new projects, whose success probabilities are drawn independently from the same unknown distribution. An unlimited supply of possible projects represents a setting where requests for funding greatly exceed the capital available.

The algorithm must allocate impressions across projects to bring as many as possible to their funding goals using as few total impressions as possible. The authors provide an algorithm and prove sublinear regret bounds for this setting. Such bounds mean that regret grows more slowly than the number of trials, supporting the algorithm's ability to learn effective allocation decisions within the proposed model.
summary.tldr: A bandit model for crowdfunding rewards completed funding goals, and the proposed allocation algorithm has sublinear regret guarantees.

title: Firing Bandits: Optimizing Crowdfunding

abstract: Motivated by settings such as hyper-parameter tuning and physical simulations, we consider the problem of black-box optimization of a function. Multi-fidelity techniques have become popular for applications where exact function evaluations are expensive, but coarse (biased) approximations are available at much lower cost. A canonical example is that of hyper-parameter selection in a learning algorithm. The learning algorithm can be trained for fewer iterations – this results in a lower cost, but its validation error is only coarsely indicative of the same if the algorithm had been trained till completion. We incorporate the multi-fidelity setup into the powerful framework of black-box optimization through hierarchical partitioning. We develop tree-search based multi-fidelity algorithms with theoretical guarantees on simple regret. We finally demonstrate the performance gains of our algorithms on both real and synthetic datasets.

paragraphs: Black-box optimization can be expensive when every candidate requires a full simulation or training run. Multi-fidelity methods use cheaper, biased approximations to obtain partial information. For hyperparameter tuning, training for fewer iterations costs less, but the resulting validation error is only a coarse indication of the error after training finishes.

This paper incorporates that tradeoff into hierarchical partitioning, a framework that organizes the search space into progressively refined regions. The authors develop tree-search algorithms that operate in the multi-fidelity setting. Their approach brings inexpensive approximate evaluations into a structured search procedure, making evaluation fidelity part of how the optimization problem is handled.

The algorithms come with theoretical guarantees on simple regret, which concerns the quality of the solution recommended by the search. Experiments on real and synthetic datasets also demonstrate performance gains. Together, the theory and experiments support combining hierarchical search with multiple evaluation fidelities when accurate evaluations are costly and cheaper approximations are available.
summary.tldr: Tree-based multi-fidelity optimization combines cheap approximate evaluations with hierarchical search and provides simple-regret guarantees.

title: Multi-Fidelity Black-Box Optimization with Hierarchical Partitions

abstract: A key challenge in complex visuomotor control is learning abstract representations that are effective for specifying goals, planning, and generalization. To this end, we introduce universal planning networks (UPN). UPNs embed differentiable planning within a goal-directed policy. This planning computation unrolls a forward model in a latent space and infers an optimal action plan through gradient descent trajectory optimization. The plan-by-gradient-descent process and its underlying representations are learned end-to-end to directly optimize a supervised imitation learning objective. We find that the representations learned are not only effective for goal-directed visual imitation via gradient-based trajectory optimization, but can also provide a metric for specifying goals using images. The learned representations can be leveraged to specify distance-based rewards to reach new target states for model-free reinforcement learning, resulting in substantially more effective learning when solving new tasks described via image based goals. We were able to achieve successful transfer of visuomotor planning strategies across robots with significantly different morphologies and actuation capabilities. paragraphs: Visual control needs representations that make goals meaningful and support planning toward them. Universal Planning Networks learn such representations by embedding differentiable planning inside a goal-directed policy. A forward model unfolds possible behavior in a latent space, and gradient-based trajectory optimization searches for an action plan within that representation.

The planning process and the representation are trained together using a supervised imitation-learning objective. This ties the learned space directly to the task of producing useful plans from demonstrations. The authors find that the resulting representations also provide a distance measure for goals expressed as images. That distance can define rewards for model-free reinforcement learning aimed at reaching new target states.

Using those image-goal rewards substantially improves learning on new tasks in the reported experiments. The authors also demonstrate successful transfer of visuomotor planning strategies between robots with substantially different shapes and actuation capabilities. These findings show that a representation learned through planning can remain useful beyond its original imitation task, supporting both new goal-directed learning and transfer across different robot bodies.
summary.tldr: Universal Planning Networks learn visual representations through differentiable planning that also support new image-goal tasks and transfer across robots.

title: Universal Planning Networks: Learning Generalizable Representations for Visuomotor Control

abstract: We consider online learning in episodic loop-free Markov decision processes (MDPs), where the loss function can change arbitrarily between episodes, and the transition function is not known to the learner. We show $\tilde{O}(L|X|\sqrt{|A|T})$ regret bound, where $T$ is the number of episodes, $X$ is the state space, $A$ is the action space, and $L$ is the length of each episode. Our online algorithm is implemented using entropic regularization methodology, which allows to extend the original adversarial MDP model to handle convex performance criteria (different ways to aggregate the losses of a single episode) , as well as improve previous regret bounds.

paragraphs: This paper studies online learning in episodic, loop-free Markov decision processes with unknown transitions. The loss function may change arbitrarily between episodes, so the learner faces both uncertainty about how actions move between states and an adversarial sequence of objectives. The analysis measures cumulative performance through regret.

The proposed algorithm uses entropic regularization. The authors establish a regret bound of order L times the number of states times the square root of the product of the number of actions and episodes, with logarithmic factors suppressed. For fixed state and action spaces and episode length, the square-root dependence on episode count gives sublinear growth in the bound.

The same methodology extends the adversarial MDP model to convex performance criteria, allowing different ways to aggregate losses within an episode. It also improves previous regret bounds. The contribution thus addresses both performance and expressiveness: it provides a stronger guarantee in the stated unknown-transition setting and supports a broader class of episode-level objectives.
summary.tldr: Entropic regularization yields improved regret bounds for unknown-transition adversarial MDPs and supports convex episode-level performance criteria.

title: Online Convex Optimization in Adversarial Markov Decision Processes

abstract: Decentralized stochastic optimization methods have gained a lot of attention recently, mainly because of their cheap per iteration cost, data locality, and their communication-efficiency. In this paper we introduce a unified convergence analysis that covers a large variety of decentralized SGD methods which so far have required different intuitions, have different applications, and which have been developed separately in various communities. Our algorithmic framework covers local SGD updates and synchronous and pairwise gossip updates on adaptive network topology. We derive universal convergence rates for smooth (convex and non-convex) problems and the rates interpolate between the heterogeneous (non-identically distributed data) and iid-data settings, recovering linear convergence rates in many special cases, for instance for over-parametrized models. Our proofs rely on weak assumptions (typically improving over prior work in several aspects) and recover (and improve) the best known complexity results for a host of important scenarios, such as for instance coorperative SGD and federated averaging (local SGD).

paragraphs: Decentralized training lets several workers learn from locally held data while exchanging information. Different methods vary in how often workers communicate and which workers communicate with each other. This paper brings many such methods into one convergence framework, connecting approaches that previously had separate analyses and motivations.

The framework includes local stochastic gradient updates, synchronous communication, and pairwise gossip, where workers exchange information in pairs. It also permits the communication network to adapt. The analysis covers smooth optimization problems with both convex and nonconvex objectives, and accounts for differences between workers' data distributions. Its rates connect the case of identically distributed data to the case of heterogeneous data.

The resulting guarantees recover and sometimes improve known complexity results for methods including cooperative SGD and federated averaging. Linear convergence is recovered in many special cases, including some overparameterized settings; it is not asserted for every covered problem. The contribution is a shared way to understand how local computation, communication structure, and data differences affect convergence under relatively weak assumptions.
summary.tldr: A unified analysis explains convergence across decentralized SGD methods with local updates, changing communication networks, and differing data distributions.

title: A Unified Theory of Decentralized SGD with Changing Topology and Local Updates

abstract: We develop a polynomial-time algorithm for identification of structural coefficients in linear causal models that subsumes previous efficient state-of-the-art methods, unifying several disparate approaches to identification in this setting. Building on these results, we develop a procedure for identifying total causal effects in linear systems.
originalAbstract: We develop a polynomial-time algorithm for identification of structural coefficients in linear causal models that subsumes previous efficient state-of-the-art methods, unifying several disparate approaches to identification in this setting. Building on these results, we develop a procedure for identifying total causal effects in linear systems.

paragraphs: The paper studies identification in linear causal models: determining structural coefficients within a model of causal relationships. These coefficients describe the relationships specified by the linear system. The central contribution is an identification algorithm whose running time is polynomial, making computational efficiency part of the result.

The algorithm subsumes earlier efficient state-of-the-art methods and brings together several previously separate approaches. Subsuming those methods means its identification capabilities encompass what those methods could handle. Unification matters because it places multiple approaches within a shared procedure. This is a claim about the reach of an efficient identification method within linear causal models, rather than a claim that every coefficient in every model is identifiable.

The authors then build on this result to develop a procedure for identifying total causal effects in linear systems. This extends the focus from individual structural coefficients to the overall effects represented by the system. The paper thus links efficient coefficient identification with a procedure addressing a broader causal quantity.
summary.tldr: The paper unifies earlier efficient identification methods in a polynomial-time algorithm for linear causal models and develops a procedure for total causal effects.

title: Efficient Identification in Linear Structural Causal Models with Auxiliary Cutsets

abstract: One principled approach for provably efficient exploration is incorporating the upper confidence bound (UCB) into the value function as a bonus. However, UCB is specified to deal with linear and tabular settings and is incompatible with Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL). In this paper, we propose a principled exploration method for DRL through Optimistic Bootstrapping and Backward Induction (OB2I). OB2I constructs a general-purpose UCB-bonus through non-parametric bootstrap in DRL. The UCB-bonus estimates the epistemic uncertainty of state-action pairs for optimistic exploration. We build theoretical connections between the proposed UCB-bonus and the LSVI-UCB in linear setting. We propagate future uncertainty in a time-consistent manner through episodic backward update, which exploits the theoretical advantage and empirically improves the sample-efficiency. Our experiments in MNIST maze and Atari suit suggest that OB2I outperforms several state-of-the-art exploration approaches.

paragraphs: An exploration bonus can encourage a reinforcement-learning agent to try actions whose value remains uncertain. Upper confidence bounds provide a principled way to construct such bonuses in tabular and linear settings. This paper addresses the difficulty of carrying that approach into deep reinforcement learning, where those formulations do not directly apply.

Optimistic Bootstrapping and Backward Induction constructs a bonus using a nonparametric bootstrap. The bonus estimates epistemic uncertainty for state-action pairs: uncertainty associated with what the learner has not yet established. The authors connect this construction theoretically to LSVI-UCB in the linear setting, grounding the proposed deep-learning method in an existing exploration framework.

The method also updates episodes backward so that uncertainty about future outcomes propagates in a time-consistent way. This component empirically improves sample efficiency. Experiments in MNIST maze and Atari suggest that the complete method outperforms several state-of-the-art exploration approaches, supporting the combination of bootstrap uncertainty estimates with coordinated backward updates.
summary.tldr: Bootstrap uncertainty bonuses and backward episodic updates provide a principled exploration method with promising deep reinforcement-learning results.

title: Principled Exploration via Optimistic Bootstrapping and Backward Induction

abstract: We study a class of convex-concave saddle-point problems of the form $\min_x\max_y ⟨Kx,y⟩+f_{\cal P}(x)-h^*(y)$ where $K$ is a linear operator, $f_{\cal P}$ is the sum of a convex function $f$ with a Lipschitz-continuous gradient and the indicator function of a bounded convex polytope ${\cal P}$, and $h^\ast$ is a convex (possibly nonsmooth) function. Such problem arises, for example, as a Lagrangian relaxation of various discrete optimization problems. Our main assumptions are the existence of an efficient {\em linear minimization oracle} ($lmo$) for $f_{\cal P}$ and an efficient {\em proximal map} ($prox$) for $h^*$ which motivate the solution via a blend of proximal primal-dual algorithms and Frank-Wolfe algorithms. In case $h^*$ is the indicator function of a linear constraint and function $f$ is quadratic, we show a $O(1/n^2)$ convergence rate on the dual objective, requiring $O(n \log n)$ calls of $lmo$. If the problem comes from the constrained optimization problem $\min_{x\in\mathbb R^d}\{f_{\cal P}(x)\:|\:Ax-b=0\}$ then we additionally get bound $O(1/n^2)$ both on the primal gap and on the infeasibility gap. In the most general case, we show a $O(1/n)$ convergence rate of the primal-dual gap again requiring $O(n\log n)$ calls of $lmo$. To the best of our knowledge, this improves on the known convergence rates for the considered class of saddle-point problems. We show applications to labeling problems frequently appearing in machine learning and computer vision.

Such problem arises, for example, as a Lagrangian relaxation of various discrete optimization problems. Our main assumptions are the existence of an efficient {\em linear minimization oracle} ($lmo$) for $f_{\cal P}$ and an efficient {\em proximal map} ($prox$) for $h^*$ which motivate the solution via a blend of proximal primal-dual algorithms and Frank-Wolfe algorithms. In case $h^*$ is the indicator function of a linear constraint and function $f$ is quadratic, we show a $O(1/n^2)$ convergence rate on the dual objective, requiring $O(n \log n)$ calls of $lmo$. If the problem comes from the constrained optimization problem $\min_{x\in\mathbb R^d}\{f_{\cal P}(x)\:|\:Ax-b=0\}$ then we additionally get bound $O(1/n^2)$ both on the primal gap and on the infeasibility gap. In the most general case, we show a $O(1/n)$ convergence rate of the primal-dual gap again requiring $O(n\log n)$ calls of $lmo$. To the best of our knowledge, this improves on the known convergence rates for the considered class of saddle-point problems. We show applications to labeling problems frequently appearing in machine learning and computer vision.

paragraphs: The paper studies convex-concave saddle problems, where one variable is minimized while another is maximized. The variables interact through a linear operator. The minimizing side includes a smooth convex function restricted to a bounded convex polytope, while the maximizing side can involve a nonsmooth convex function. Such formulations arise in relaxations of discrete optimization problems.

The approach assumes two efficient computational tools: a linear minimization oracle for the polytope-constrained side and a proximal map for the other side. It combines Frank-Wolfe updates with proximal primal-dual algorithms to exploit that asymmetric structure. In the general setting, the authors prove an O(1/n) primal-dual gap using O(n log n) oracle calls.

Stronger results hold in specified special cases. With a quadratic smooth function and an indicator of a linear constraint, the dual objective converges at O(1/n²). For the stated equality-constrained formulation, the primal and infeasibility gaps also have O(1/n²) bounds. The authors present these as improvements over known rates for the considered class and show applications to labeling problems.
summary.tldr: Combining Frank-Wolfe and proximal updates yields convergence guarantees for structured saddle problems, with faster rates under specified quadratic and constraint conditions.

title: One-sided Frank-Wolfe algorithms for saddle problems

abstract: Microfluidic biochips are being utilized for clinical diagnostics, including COVID-19 testing, because of they provide sample-to-result turnaround at low cost. Recently, microelectrode-dot-array (MEDA) biochips have been proposed to advance microfluidics technology. A MEDA biochip manipulates droplets of nano/picoliter volumes to automatically execute biochemical protocols. During bioassay execution, droplets are transported in parallel to achieve high-throughput outcomes. However, a major concern associated with the use of MEDA biochips is microelectrode degradation over time. Recent work has shown that formulating droplet transportation as a reinforcement-learning (RL) problem enables the training of policies to capture the underlying health conditions of microelectrodes and ensure reliable fluidic operations. However, the above RL-based approach suffers from two key limitations: 1) it cannot be used for concurrent transportation of multiple droplets; 2) it requires the availability of CCD cameras for monitoring droplet movement. To overcome these problems, we present a multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) droplet-routing solution that can be used for various sizes of MEDA biochips with integrated sensors, and we demonstrate the reliable execution of a serial-dilution bioassay with the MARL droplet router on a fabricated MEDA biochip. To facilitate further research, we also present a simulation environment based on the PettingZoo Gym Interface for MARL-guided droplet-routing problems on MEDA biochips.

summary.tldr: A multi-agent reinforcement-learning router coordinates droplets on sensor-equipped biochips and demonstrates reliable serial dilution on fabricated hardware.

title: Parallel Droplet Control in MEDA Biochips using Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning

abstract: In the domain generalization literature, a common objective is to learn representations independent of the domain after conditioning on the class label. We show that this objective is not sufficient: there exist counter-examples where a model fails to generalize to unseen domains even after satisfying class-conditional domain invariance. We formalize this observation through a structural causal model and show the importance of modeling within-class variations for generalization. Specifically, classes contain objects that characterize specific causal features, and domains can be interpreted as interventions on these objects that change non-causal features. We highlight an alternative condition: inputs across domains should have the same representation if they are derived from the same object. Based on this objective, we propose matching-based algorithms when base objects are observed (e.g., through data augmentation) and approximate the objective when objects are not observed (MatchDG). Our simple matching-based algorithms are competitive to prior work on out-of-domain accuracy for rotated MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, PACS, and Chest-Xray datasets. Our method MatchDG also recovers ground-truth object matches: on MNIST and Fashion-MNIST, top-10 matches from MatchDG have over 50% overlap with ground-truth matches.

paragraphs: Domain generalization asks whether a model trained in some environments can work in unseen ones. A common approach makes representations independent of the environment after accounting for the class label. This paper provides counterexamples showing that satisfying this condition alone does not ensure generalization, because important differences can remain among objects within the same class.

The authors use a structural causal model to distinguish an object's causal features from non-causal features changed by the domain. Their alternative objective matches representations of observations derived from the same underlying object across domains. They develop matching algorithms for observed object correspondences and MatchDG to approximate this objective when those correspondences are unavailable.

The algorithms achieve competitive out-of-domain accuracy on rotated MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, PACS, and Chest-Xray data. MatchDG also recovers meaningful object correspondences: its top ten matches overlap ground-truth matches by more than half on MNIST and Fashion-MNIST. These findings support matching within classes as a useful training objective, while the counterexamples establish why class-level invariance alone can be inadequate.
summary.tldr: Matching the same underlying objects across domains addresses a weakness of class-conditional invariance and yields competitive generalization results.

title: Domain Generalization using Causal Matching

abstract: Much of the work in the field of group fairness addresses disparities between predefined groups based on protected features such as gender, age, and race, which need to be available at train, and often also at test, time. These approaches are static and retrospective, since algorithms designed to protect groups identified a priori cannot anticipate and protect the needs of different at-risk groups in the future. In this work we analyze the space of solutions for worst-case fairness beyond demographics, and propose Blind Pareto Fairness (BPF), a method that leverages no-regret dynamics to recover a fair minimax classifier that reduces worst-case risk of any potential subgroup of sufficient size, and guarantees that the remaining population receives the best possible level of service. BPF addresses fairness beyond demographics, that is, it does not rely on predefined notions of at-risk groups, neither at train nor at test time. Our experimental results show that the proposed framework improves worst-case risk in multiple standard datasets, while simultaneously providing better levels of service for the remaining population. The code is available at github.com/natalialmg/BlindParetoFairness

paragraphs: Many group-fairness methods protect demographic groups specified before training. This paper argues that such a setup cannot anticipate every group that may later face poor service. It studies fairness through worst-case risk across potential subgroups, without requiring predefined demographic categories at either training or test time.

The proposed Blind Pareto Fairness method uses no-regret dynamics to recover a fair minimax classifier. Its objective reduces the worst-case risk of any potential subgroup meeting a sufficient-size requirement. At the same time, it guarantees the best possible service for the remaining population within the proposed fairness formulation. This connects protection for poorly served groups with the treatment of everyone else.

The subgroup-size qualification is part of the stated protection: the method’s claim concerns groups of sufficient size. Experiments on multiple standard datasets show improved worst-case risk together with better service for the remaining population. These findings support the usefulness of examining fairness beyond a fixed list of protected groups.
summary.tldr: Blind Pareto Fairness protects sufficiently large potential subgroups while optimizing service for the remaining population.

title: Blind Pareto Fairness and Subgroup Robustness

abstract: Knowledge distillation is a technique for improving a “student” model by replacing its one-hot training labels with a label distribution obtained from a “teacher” model. Despite its broad success, several basic questions — e.g., Why does distillation help? Why do more accurate teachers not necessarily distill better? — have received limited formal study. In this paper, we present a statistical perspective on distillation which provides an answer to these questions. Our core observation is that a “Bayes teacher” providing the true class-probabilities can lower the variance of the student objective, and thus improve performance. We then establish a bias-variance tradeoff that quantifies the value of teachers that approximate the Bayes class-probabilities. This provides a formal criterion as to what constitutes a “good” teacher, namely, the quality of its probability estimates. Finally, we illustrate how our statistical perspective facilitates novel applications of distillation to bipartite ranking and multiclass retrieval.

paragraphs: Knowledge distillation trains a student model using a teacher’s probabilities over classes instead of labels that put all their weight on one class. This paper asks why that replacement can help, and why a teacher with higher classification accuracy does not necessarily produce a better student. It approaches these questions through the statistics of the student’s training objective.

The central observation concerns an ideal teacher that supplies the true class probabilities. Such a teacher can reduce the variance of the objective the student learns from, which can improve performance. Real teachers only approximate those probabilities, so the authors establish a bias–variance tradeoff describing the value of these imperfect estimates.

This analysis makes probability estimation quality a formal criterion for choosing a useful teacher. Getting the winning class right does not by itself capture how helpful the full probability distribution will be for learning. The paper also illustrates how this perspective supports applications of distillation to bipartite ranking and multiclass retrieval, extending the statistical argument beyond ordinary classification.
summary.tldr: Distillation can help by reducing training-objective variance, with teacher probability quality governing a bias–variance tradeoff.

title: A statistical perspective on distillation

abstract: We consider learning Ising tree models when the observations from the nodes are corrupted by independent but non-identically distributed noise with unknown statistics. Katiyar et al. (2020) showed that although the exact tree structure cannot be recovered, one can recover a partial tree structure; that is, a structure belonging to the equivalence class containing the true tree. This paper presents a systematic improvement of Katiyar et al. (2020). First, we present a novel impossibility result by deriving a bound on the necessary number of samples for partial recovery. Second, we derive a significantly improved sample complexity result in which the dependence on the minimum correlation $\rho_{\min}$ is $\rho_{\min}^{-8}$ instead of $\rho_{\min}^{-24}$. Finally, we propose Symmetrized Geometric Averaging (SGA), a more statistically robust algorithm for partial tree recovery. We provide error exponent analyses and extensive numerical results on a variety of trees to show that the sample complexity of SGA is significantly better than the algorithm of Katiyar et al. (2020). SGA can be readily extended to Gaussian models and is shown via numerical experiments to be similarly superior.

paragraphs: This paper studies learning Ising tree structures when each node’s observations are corrupted by independent noise with unknown statistics that can differ across nodes. In this setting, the exact tree cannot generally be recovered. The attainable objective is partial recovery: identifying a structure in the equivalence class containing the true tree.

The authors strengthen the theoretical understanding of that objective in two directions. They derive a necessary sample-count bound, establishing an impossibility result when data are insufficient. They also improve a sample-complexity result so that its dependence on the minimum correlation changes from an inverse twenty-fourth power to an inverse eighth power.

The proposed Symmetrized Geometric Averaging algorithm, or SGA, makes partial recovery more statistically robust. Error-exponent analyses and numerical experiments across various trees show significantly better sample complexity than the earlier algorithm studied in the paper. SGA also extends readily to Gaussian models, where numerical experiments show similar superiority. The advance improves recovery within the identifiable equivalence class while respecting the stated obstacle to recovering the exact original tree.
summary.tldr: SGA improves the statistical efficiency of partial tree recovery under unknown node noise, alongside stronger sample-complexity bounds.

title: SGA: A Robust Algorithm for Partial Recovery of Tree-Structured Graphical Models with Noisy Samples

abstract: Pearl’s do calculus is a complete axiomatic approach to learn the identifiable causal effects from observational data. When such an effect is not identifiable, it is necessary to perform a collection of often costly interventions in the system to learn the causal effect. In this work, we consider the problem of designing the collection of interventions with the minimum cost to identify the desired effect. First, we prove that this prob-em is NP-complete, and subsequently propose an algorithm that can either find the optimal solution or a logarithmic-factor approximation of it. This is done by establishing a connection between our problem and the minimum hitting set problem. Additionally, we propose several polynomial time heuristic algorithms to tackle the computational complexity of the problem. Although these algorithms could potentially stumble on sub-optimal solutions, our simulations show that they achieve small regrets on random graphs.
