paragraphs: Some causal effects can be determined from observational data, while others require interventions that actively change the system. Those interventions can be costly. This paper studies how to choose a collection of interventions that makes a desired causal effect identifiable while minimizing the total cost of obtaining the necessary information.

The authors prove that the intervention-design problem is NP-complete. They then connect it to the minimum hitting set problem, using that relationship to develop an algorithm that can obtain an optimal solution or a logarithmic-factor approximation. This connection supplies an algorithmic route for a problem whose general computational difficulty rules out expecting an easy exact solution in every case.

To further address computational cost, the paper proposes several polynomial-time heuristics. These methods can return suboptimal intervention collections, but simulations on random graphs show small regrets. The findings provide both a formal characterization of the design problem and practical methods for tackling it. The heuristic evidence is empirical and concerns the simulated graphs, while the exact and approximation approaches offer different forms of solution guarantees.
summary.tldr: Minimum-cost causal intervention design is NP-complete, but a hitting-set connection enables exact, approximate, and practical heuristic approaches.

title: Minimum Cost Intervention Design for Causal Effect Identification

abstract: Noisy labels are inevitable yet problematic in machine learning society. It ruins the generalization of a classifier by making the classifier over-fitted to noisy labels. Existing methods on noisy label have focused on modifying the classifier during the training procedure. It has two potential problems. First, these methods are not applicable to a pre-trained classifier without further access to training. Second, it is not easy to train a classifier and regularize all negative effects from noisy labels, simultaneously. We suggest a new branch of method, Noisy Prediction Calibration (NPC) in learning with noisy labels. Through the introduction and estimation of a new type of transition matrix via generative model, NPC corrects the noisy prediction from the pre-trained classifier to the true label as a post-processing scheme. We prove that NPC theoretically aligns with the transition matrix based methods. Yet, NPC empirically provides more accurate pathway to estimate true label, even without involvement in classifier learning. Also, NPC is applicable to any classifier trained with noisy label methods, if training instances and its predictions are available. Our method, NPC, boosts the classification performances of all baseline models on both synthetic and real-world datasets. The implemented code is available at https://github.com/BaeHeeSun/NPC.

paragraphs: Incorrect training labels can lead a classifier to fit labeling errors and generalize poorly. Many approaches address this during classifier training, which creates a practical problem when the classifier is already trained and its training process is unavailable. This paper studies a separate correction step applied to the classifier’s predictions.

Noisy Prediction Calibration, or NPC, introduces a new kind of transition matrix and estimates it through a generative model. That matrix supports converting noisy predictions into estimates of the true labels. The method operates as post-processing, so its correction does not require participation in the original classifier learning procedure.

The authors prove a theoretical alignment with transition-matrix-based methods and report that NPC provides a more accurate route to estimating true labels empirically. It improves every evaluated baseline on both synthetic and real-world datasets. Its stated applicability includes classifiers trained with noisy-label methods, provided the training instances and their predictions are available. This requirement distinguishes avoiding classifier retraining from avoiding access to the training examples altogether.
summary.tldr: NPC uses a generative transition model to correct predictions after training, improving all evaluated noisy-label classifiers.

title: From Noisy Prediction to True Label: Noisy Prediction Calibration via Generative Model

abstract: In this work we investigate and demonstrate benefits of a Bayesian approach to imitation learning from multiple sensor inputs, as applied to the task of opening office doors with a mobile manipulator. Augmenting policies with additional sensor inputs{—}such as RGB + depth cameras{—}is a straightforward approach to improving robot perception capabilities, especially for tasks that may favor different sensors in different situations. As we scale multi-sensor robotic learning to unstructured real-world settings (e.g. offices, homes) and more complex robot behaviors, we also increase reliance on simulators for cost, efficiency, and safety. Consequently, the sim-to-real gap across multiple sensor modalities also increases, making simulated validation more difficult. We show that using the Variational Information Bottleneck (Alemi et al., 2016) to regularize convolutional neural networks improves generalization to heldout domains and reduces the sim-to-real gap in a sensor-agnostic manner. As a side effect, the learned embeddings also provide useful estimates of model uncertainty for each sensor. We demonstrate that our method is able to help close the sim-to-real gap and successfully fuse RGB and depth modalities based on understanding of the situational uncertainty of each sensor. In a real-world office environment, we achieve 96% task success, improving upon the baseline by +16%.

paragraphs: A mobile robot opening office doors must combine perception with physical action. Adding RGB and depth cameras supplies complementary information, but it also creates multiple ways for simulated sensor inputs to differ from real ones. The paper studies Bayesian imitation learning as a way to improve this transfer while making use of several sensors.

The method regularizes convolutional networks with a Variational Information Bottleneck. The authors find that this improves generalization to held-out domains and reduces the simulation-to-reality gap across sensor types. The learned embeddings also provide estimates of each sensor’s model uncertainty. These estimates help the policy combine RGB and depth information according to how uncertain each sensor is in the current situation.

In a real office environment, the method achieves 96% task success, with the abstract reporting a +16% improvement over its baseline. The contribution connects representation regularization with uncertainty-aware sensor fusion: the learned representation supports transfer, while its uncertainty information helps the robot use multiple inputs under changing conditions.
summary.tldr: Bayesian representation learning improves simulation-to-reality transfer and uncertainty-aware sensor fusion for a door-opening robot.

title: Bayesian Imitation Learning for End-to-End Mobile Manipulation

abstract: In black-box function optimization, we need to consider not only controllable design variables but also uncontrollable stochastic environment variables. In such cases, it is necessary to solve the optimization problem by taking into account the uncertainty of the environmental variables. Chance-constrained (CC) problem, the problem of maximizing the expected value under a certain level of constraint satisfaction probability, is one of the practically important problems in the presence of environmental variables. In this study, we consider distributionally robust CC (DRCC) problem and propose a novel DRCC Bayesian optimization method for the case where the distribution of the environmental variables cannot be precisely specified. We show that the proposed method can find an arbitrary accurate solution with high probability in a finite number of trials, and confirm the usefulness of the proposed method through numerical experiments.

Chance-constrained (CC) problem, the problem of maximizing the expected value under a certain level of constraint satisfaction probability, is one of the practically important problems in the presence of environmental variables. In this study, we consider distributionally robust CC (DRCC) problem and propose a novel DRCC Bayesian optimization method for the case where the distribution of the environmental variables cannot be precisely specified. paragraphs: Optimizing a black-box system can involve two kinds of variables: design choices that can be controlled and environmental conditions that fluctuate outside the decision-maker's control. A useful design must account for those fluctuations. Chance-constrained optimization expresses this by maximizing expected performance while requiring constraints to hold with a specified probability.

The paper addresses an additional uncertainty: the environmental probability distribution may itself be imprecisely known. It proposes a Bayesian optimization method for the distributionally robust version of the chance-constrained problem. This formulation incorporates uncertainty about the distribution into the search for a design, so the optimization is not based solely on one precisely specified environmental model.

The authors show that the proposed method can obtain a solution with arbitrarily high accuracy, with high probability, after finitely many trials. This is a probabilistic accuracy guarantee for the studied problem, rather than a claim that every run must succeed. Numerical experiments further support the method's usefulness for black-box optimization with uncertain environments and probabilistic constraints.
summary.tldr: The paper develops Bayesian optimization for probabilistic constraints when the distribution of uncontrollable environmental variables is uncertain.

title: Bayesian Optimization for Distributionally Robust Chance-constrained Problem

abstract: Learning representations of multimodal data that are both informative and robust to missing modalities at test time remains a challenging problem due to the inherent heterogeneity of data obtained from different channels. To address it, we present a novel Geometric Multimodal Contrastive (GMC) representation learning method consisting of two main components: i) a two-level architecture consisting of modality-specific base encoders, allowing to process an arbitrary number of modalities to an intermediate representation of fixed dimensionality, and a shared projection head, mapping the intermediate representations to a latent representation space; ii) a multimodal contrastive loss function that encourages the geometric alignment of the learned representations. We experimentally demonstrate that GMC representations are semantically rich and achieve state-of-the-art performance with missing modality information on three different learning problems including prediction and reinforcement learning tasks.

To address it, we present a novel Geometric Multimodal Contrastive (GMC) representation learning method consisting of two main components: i) a two-level architecture consisting of modality-specific base encoders, allowing to process an arbitrary number of modalities to an intermediate representation of fixed dimensionality, and a shared projection head, mapping the intermediate representations to a latent representation space; ii) a multimodal contrastive loss function that encourages the geometric alignment of the learned representations. We experimentally demonstrate that GMC representations are semantically rich and achieve state-of-the-art performance with missing modality information on three different learning problems including prediction and reinforcement learning tasks.

paragraphs: Multimodal models combine information from different channels, but those channels can have very different forms and some may be unavailable during use. This paper addresses the challenge of learning informative representations that remain useful when modalities are missing. Its method, Geometric Multimodal Contrastive learning, connects the channels through a shared representation space.

The architecture has two levels. Modality-specific encoders convert inputs into intermediate representations with a fixed dimensionality, supporting an arbitrary number of modalities. A shared projection head then maps those representations into a common latent space. A multimodal contrastive loss encourages geometric alignment there, making the relationship between representations an explicit part of the learning objective.

The authors evaluate the approach on three learning problems spanning prediction and reinforcement learning. They report semantically rich representations and state-of-the-art performance when modality information is missing. These findings support the combination of channel-specific processing and shared geometric alignment as a way to handle incomplete multimodal inputs. The reported robustness is demonstrated on those learning problems.
summary.tldr: GMC aligns modality-specific representations in a shared space to support strong performance when input modalities are missing.

title: Geometric Multimodal Contrastive Representation Learning

abstract: We propose a novel quadratic programming formulation for estimating the corruption levels in group synchronization, and use these estimates to solve this problem. Our objective function exploits the cycle consistency of the group and we thus refer to our method as detection and estimation of structural consistency (DESC). This general framework can be extended to other algebraic and geometric structures. Our formulation has the following advantages: it can tolerate corruption as high as the information-theoretic bound, it does not require a good initialization for the estimates of group elements, it has a simple interpretation, and under some mild conditions the global minimum of our objective function exactly recovers the corruption levels. We demonstrate the competitive accuracy of our approach on both synthetic and real data experiments of rotation averaging.

Our formulation has the following advantages: it can tolerate corruption as high as the information-theoretic bound, it does not require a good initialization for the estimates of group elements, it has a simple interpretation, and under some mild conditions the global minimum of our objective function exactly recovers the corruption levels. paragraphs: Group synchronization requires estimating group elements from relationships that may be corrupted. This paper approaches the problem by first estimating the levels of corruption and then using those estimates to solve the synchronization task. Its method, detection and estimation of structural consistency, or DESC, is formulated as a quadratic program.

The objective uses cycle consistency: relationships around a cycle should agree with the underlying group structure. This structural information supplies evidence about corruption without requiring a good initial estimate of the group elements. The authors also describe the framework as extendable to other algebraic and geometric structures.

The formulation can tolerate corruption up to the information-theoretic bound, and under stated mild conditions its global minimum exactly recovers the corruption levels. Exact recovery is thus tied to both those conditions and the global minimum of the objective. Synthetic and real rotation-averaging experiments show competitive accuracy, providing empirical support for using structural consistency to guide robust estimation.
summary.tldr: DESC uses cycle consistency and quadratic programming to estimate corruption and support robust group synchronization.

title: Robust Group Synchronization via Quadratic Programming

abstract: Kernel mean embedding is a useful tool to compare probability measures. Despite its usefulness, kernel mean embedding considers infinite-dimensional features, which are challenging to handle in the context of differentially private data generation. A recent work, DP-MERF (Harder et al., 2021), proposes to approximate the kernel mean embedding of data distribution using finite-dimensional random features, which yields an analytically tractable sensitivity of approximate kernel mean embedding. However, the required number of random features in DP-MERF is excessively high, often ten thousand to a hundred thousand, which worsens the sensitivity of the approximate kernel mean embedding. To improve the sensitivity, we propose to replace random features with Hermite polynomial features. Unlike the random features, the Hermite polynomial features are ordered, where the features at the low orders contain more information on the distribution than those at the high orders. Hence, a relatively low order of Hermite polynomial features can more accurately approximate the mean embedding of the data distribution compared to a significantly higher number of random features. As a result, the Hermite polynomial features help us to improve the privacy-accuracy trade-off compared to DP-MERF, as demonstrated on several heterogeneous tabular datasets, as well as several image benchmark datasets.

Their infinite-dimensional form is difficult to handle in differentially private generation. An earlier method, DP-MERF, uses finite random features, but the large number needed worsens the sensitivity of the resulting distribution summary.

This paper replaces random features with Hermite polynomial features. Their ordering provides the key advantage: lower-order features contain more distributional information than higher-order ones. Consequently, a relatively low-order collection can approximate the mean embedding more accurately than a much larger collection of random features, improving how compactly the distribution is represented.

The more informative representation helps improve the privacy–accuracy trade-off relative to DP-MERF. The authors demonstrate this on heterogeneous tabular datasets and image benchmarks. The contribution shows why feature selection matters for private generation: representation quality and sensitivity are connected, so an efficient summary can support better accuracy under privacy constraints without requiring an excessively large random-feature approximation.
summary.tldr: Ordered Hermite polynomial features provide compact distribution summaries that improve the demonstrated privacy–accuracy trade-off in private data generation.

title: Hermite Polynomial Features for Private Data Generation

abstract: Explaining graph neural networks (GNNs) has become more and more important recently. Higher-order interpretation schemes, such as GNN-LRP (layer-wise relevance propagation for GNN), emerged as powerful tools for unraveling how different features interact thereby contributing to explaining GNNs. GNN-LRP gives a relevance attribution of walks between nodes at each layer, and the subgraph attribution is expressed as a sum over exponentially many such walks. In this work, we demonstrate that such exponential complexity can be avoided. In particular, we propose novel algorithms that enable to attribute subgraphs with GNN-LRP in linear-time (w.r.t. the network depth). Our algorithms are derived via message passing techniques that make use of the distributive property, thereby directly computing quantities for higher-order explanations. We further adapt our efficient algorithms to compute a generalization of subgraph attributions that also takes into account the neighboring graph features. Experimental results show the significant acceleration of the proposed algorithms and demonstrate the high usefulness and scalability of our novel generalized subgraph attribution method.

paragraphs: Explaining a graph neural network can require understanding how features interact, rather than assigning importance to each feature independently. GNN-LRP addresses such interactions by attributing relevance to walks through nodes across network layers. However, obtaining a subgraph’s attribution appears to require adding contributions from exponentially many walks, making direct computation expensive as depth grows.

The paper shows that this exponential enumeration can be avoided. Its algorithms use message passing and the distributive property to combine the required quantities directly. This produces GNN-LRP subgraph attributions in time that grows linearly with network depth. The stated complexity improvement concerns depth specifically, rather than asserting linear cost in every aspect of the graph or model.

The authors also extend the algorithms to a generalized attribution that includes neighboring graph features. This allows explanations to account for context around the subgraph being assessed. Experiments report substantial acceleration and demonstrate the usefulness and scalability of the generalized method. The main advance makes interaction-based explanations more computationally accessible without requiring explicit enumeration of all contributing walks.
summary.tldr: Message-passing algorithms compute GNN-LRP subgraph attributions in time linear in network depth and extend them to include neighboring features.

title: Efficient Computation of Higher-Order Subgraph Attribution via Message Passing

abstract: Covariate-shift generalization, a typical case in out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization, requires a good performance on the unknown test distribution, which varies from the accessible training distribution in the form of covariate shift. Recently, independence-driven importance weighting algorithms in stable learning literature have shown empirical effectiveness to deal with covariate-shift generalization on several learning models, including regression algorithms and deep neural networks, while their theoretical analyses are missing. In this paper, we theoretically prove the effectiveness of such algorithms by explaining them as feature selection processes. We first specify a set of variables, named minimal stable variable set, that is the minimal and optimal set of variables to deal with covariate-shift generalization for common loss functions, such as the mean squared loss and binary cross-entropy loss. Afterward, we prove that under ideal conditions, independence-driven importance weighting algorithms could identify the variables in this set. Analysis of asymptotic properties is also provided. These theories are further validated in several synthetic experiments.

paragraphs: The paper studies generalization when the test distribution is unknown and differs from training through covariate shift. Independence-driven importance weighting methods had already shown empirical benefits for this problem in regression and neural networks. The authors seek a theoretical explanation for those benefits by interpreting the weighting procedure as a form of feature selection.

They define a minimal stable variable set: a smallest, optimal collection of variables for handling covariate-shift generalization under common losses, including mean squared error and binary cross-entropy. This definition makes the desired outcome precise. The question becomes whether a weighting algorithm can identify the variables belonging to that set.

The authors prove that independence-driven importance weighting could identify these variables under ideal conditions. They also analyze asymptotic properties and validate their theory with synthetic experiments. The result supplies a conditional explanation for previously observed effectiveness: these algorithms can work by finding a stable predictive subset. The ideal-condition qualification matters because the identification result is not presented as an unconditional guarantee for every dataset.
summary.tldr: Under ideal conditions, independence-driven importance weighting can identify a minimal stable set of predictive variables for covariate-shift generalization.

title: A Theoretical Analysis on Independence-driven Importance Weighting for Covariate-shift Generalization

abstract: Advances in differentiable numerical integrators have enabled the use of gradient descent techniques to learn ordinary differential equations (ODEs), where a flexible function approximator (often a neural network) is used to estimate the system dynamics, given as a time derivative. However, these integrators can be unsatisfactorily slow and unstable when learning systems of ODEs from long sequences. We propose to learn an ODE of interest from data by viewing its dynamics as a vector field related to another base vector field via a diffeomorphism (i.e., a differentiable bijection), represented by an invertible neural network (INN). By learning both the INN and the dynamics of the base ODE, we provide an avenue to offload some of the complexity in modelling the dynamics directly on to the INN. Consequently, by restricting the base ODE to be amenable to integration, we can speed up and improve the robustness of integrating trajectories from the learned system. We demonstrate the efficacy of our method in training and evaluating benchmark ODE systems, as well as within continuous-depth neural networks models. We show that our approach attains speed-ups of up to two orders of magnitude when integrating learned ODEs.

paragraphs: Learning differential equations from long sequences can make numerical integration slow and unstable. This paper changes how the dynamics are represented. It treats the target system as a vector field connected to a simpler base vector field through a differentiable, invertible transformation represented by an invertible neural network.

The method learns both the transformation and the dynamics of the base ordinary differential equation. This lets the neural network carry part of the complexity that would otherwise have to appear directly in the dynamics. By restricting the base equation to a form that is amenable to integration, the approach can make trajectory computation faster and more robust.

The authors evaluate the method on benchmark differential-equation systems and within continuous-depth neural networks, examining both training and evaluation. They report integration speedups of up to two orders of magnitude for learned equations. The mechanism behind the approach is the division of work between an integrable base system and a learned change of coordinates, with the reported speedup representing the upper end of the demonstrated results.
summary.tldr: An invertible neural network transforms an easy-to-integrate base ODE into richer learned dynamics, enabling reported integration speedups of up to 100-fold.

title: Learning Efficient and Robust Ordinary Differential Equations via Invertible Neural Networks

abstract: We study the online restless bandit problem, where each arm evolves according to a Markov chain independently, and the reward of pulling an arm depends on both the current state of the corresponding Markov chain and the pulled arm. The agent (decision maker) does not know the transition functions and reward functions, and cannot observe the states of arms even after pulling. The goal is to sequentially choose which arms to pull so as to maximize the expected cumulative rewards collected. In this paper, we propose TSEETC, a learning algorithm based on Thompson Sampling with Episodic Explore-Then-Commit. The algorithm proceeds in episodes of increasing length and each episode is divided into exploration and exploitation phases. During the exploration phase, samples of action-reward pairs are collected in a round-robin fashion and utilized to update the posterior distribution as a mixture of Dirichlet distributions. At the beginning of the exploitation phase, TSEETC generates a sample from the posterior distribution as true parameters. It then follows the optimal policy for the sampled model for the rest of the episode. We establish the Bayesian regret bound $\tilde {\mathcal{O}}(\sqrt{T})$ for TSEETC, where $T$ is the time horizon. We show through simulations that TSEETC outperforms existing algorithms in regret.

paragraphs: The paper studies sequential decisions among options whose hidden states evolve independently according to Markov chains. Rewards depend on both the selected option and its current state. The decision maker knows neither the transition rules nor the reward functions, and choosing an option does not reveal its state. Learning must therefore rely on observed actions and rewards.

TSEETC combines Thompson sampling with episodes that grow longer over time. Each episode begins with exploration, selecting options in round-robin order and updating a posterior represented as a mixture of Dirichlet distributions. For exploitation, the algorithm samples model parameters from that posterior and follows the sampled model’s optimal policy for the remainder of the episode.

The authors prove a Bayesian regret bound that grows approximately as the square root of the time horizon, up to logarithmic factors. Simulations also show lower regret than existing algorithms. The result supports a structured alternation between gathering information and committing to a sampled policy, even when the system’s evolving states remain unobserved throughout learning.
summary.tldr: TSEETC learns from actions and rewards alone in hidden-state restless bandits, achieving a Bayesian regret bound of approximately square-root growth.

title: Online Restless Bandits with Unobserved States

abstract: Score-based diffusion models learn to reverse a stochastic differential equation that maps data to noise. However, for complex tasks, numerical error can compound and result in highly unnatural samples. Previous work mitigates this drift with thresholding, which projects to the natural data domain (such as pixel space for images) after each diffusion step, but this leads to a mismatch between the training and generative processes. To incorporate data constraints in a principled manner, we present Reflected Diffusion Models, which instead reverse a reflected stochastic differential equation evolving on the support of the data. Our approach learns the perturbed score function through a generalized score matching loss and extends key components of standard diffusion models including diffusion guidance, likelihood-based training, and ODE sampling. We also bridge the theoretical gap with thresholding: such schemes are just discretizations of reflected SDEs. On standard image benchmarks, our method is competitive with or surpasses the state of the art without architectural modifications and, for classifier-free guidance, our approach enables fast exact sampling with ODEs and produces more faithful samples under high guidance weight.

paragraphs: Diffusion models generate data by reversing a noisy process, but numerical errors can accumulate and produce unnatural samples. Thresholding addresses this by projecting each intermediate sample back into the data domain. The paper identifies a mismatch when this corrective procedure is used during generation without being part of the training process.

Reflected Diffusion Models incorporate the domain constraint into the stochastic differential equation itself. The model reverses a reflected process that evolves within the data's support and learns its perturbed score through generalized score matching. The framework extends diffusion guidance, likelihood-based training, and ordinary differential equation sampling, and interprets thresholding schemes as discretizations of reflected stochastic equations.

On standard image benchmarks, the authors report performance competitive with or better than the state of the art without changing the architecture. For classifier-free guidance, they report fast exact sampling using ordinary differential equations and more faithful samples at high guidance weights. The approach connects a commonly used sampling correction to a training framework that explicitly accounts for the same data constraints.
summary.tldr: Reflected Diffusion Models build data-domain constraints into the diffusion process, aligning training with constrained sampling.

title: Reflected Diffusion Models

abstract: We introduce the concept of programmable feature engineering for time series modeling and propose a feature programming framework. This framework generates large amounts of predictive features for noisy multivariate time series while allowing users to incorporate their inductive bias with minimal effort. The key motivation of our framework is to view any multivariate time series as a cumulative sum of fine-grained trajectory increments, with each increment governed by a novel spin-gas dynamical Ising model. This fine-grained perspective motivates the development of a parsimonious set of operators that summarize multivariate time series in an abstract fashion, serving as the foundation for large-scale automated feature engineering. Numerically, we validate the efficacy of our method on several synthetic and real-world noisy time series datasets.

paragraphs: Predicting from noisy multivariate time series requires useful summaries of several quantities evolving together. This paper introduces programmable feature engineering: a framework that automatically generates many predictive features while allowing users to express their own inductive biases with little effort. The aim is to combine large-scale feature generation with a manageable way to influence what the features represent.

The framework starts from a fine-grained view of a time series as an accumulated sequence of small trajectory increments. Each increment is governed by a proposed spin-gas dynamical Ising model. This modeling perspective motivates a compact collection of operators that summarize multivariate trajectories at an abstract level, forming the building blocks of the feature-generation system.

The significance of those operators is that a small vocabulary can support many derived features, rather than requiring every summary to be designed separately. The authors numerically evaluate the method on several synthetic and real-world noisy time-series datasets and report evidence of its effectiveness. The stated contribution is a programmable framework for constructing predictive representations, with empirical support across those evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: A programmable feature-engineering framework uses a fine-grained dynamical view of time series to generate predictive summaries guided by user assumptions.

title: Feature Programming for Multivariate Time Series Prediction

abstract: As children grow older, they develop an intuitive understanding of the physical processes around them. Their physical understanding develops in stages, moving along developmental trajectories which have been mapped out extensively in previous empirical research. Here, we investigate how the learning trajectories of deep generative neural networks compare to children’s developmental trajectories using physical understanding as a testbed. We outline an approach that allows us to examine two distinct hypotheses of human development – stochastic optimization and complexity increase. We find that while our models are able to accurately predict a number of physical processes, their learning trajectories under both hypotheses do not follow the developmental trajectories of children.

paragraphs: Children acquire an intuitive understanding of physical processes through developmental stages. This paper asks whether deep generative neural networks develop physical knowledge along similar learning trajectories. The comparison concerns how abilities emerge over learning, rather than only whether a trained model eventually predicts a physical process accurately.

The authors outline an approach for examining two hypotheses about human development: stochastic optimization and increasing complexity. Physical understanding provides the testbed for comparing the models' learning paths with developmental patterns documented in earlier empirical research. This makes the order and progression of learned abilities central to the evaluation.

The models accurately predict several physical processes, but their learning trajectories under both hypotheses fail to match those of children. The finding separates successful prediction from a successful account of development: reaching useful behavior does not by itself reproduce the path children take. For the models and hypotheses examined, predictive competence therefore offers only part of what would be needed to explain the acquisition of human physical knowledge.
summary.tldr: The studied generative networks predict physical processes accurately but do not acquire those abilities along children's developmental trajectories.

title: The Acquisition of Physical Knowledge in Generative Neural Networks

abstract: It is widely believed that given the same labeling budget, active learning (AL) algorithms like margin-based active learning achieve better predictive performance than passive learning (PL), albeit at a higher computational cost. Recent empirical evidence suggests that this added cost might be in vain, as margin-based AL can sometimes perform even worse than PL. While existing works offer different explanations in the low-dimensional regime, this paper shows that the underlying mechanism is entirely different in high dimensions: we prove for logistic regression that PL outperforms margin-based AL even for noiseless data and when using the Bayes optimal decision boundary for sampling. Insights from our proof indicate that this high-dimensional phenomenon is exacerbated when the separation between the classes is small. We corroborate this intuition with experiments on 20 high-dimensional datasets spanning a diverse range of applications, from finance and histology to chemistry and computer vision.

paragraphs: Active learning chooses which examples to label, often favoring examples near a decision boundary. The usual hope is better prediction from the same labeling budget, despite additional computation. This paper investigates why margin-based selection can instead perform worse than passive learning when the data has many dimensions.

For logistic regression, the authors prove a high-dimensional setting in which passive learning outperforms margin-based active learning. The result persists even with noiseless data and sampling based on the Bayes-optimal decision boundary. Those conditions matter because they show that neither label noise nor an inaccurate sampling boundary is needed for the demonstrated failure.

The proof points to a mechanism distinct from explanations developed for low-dimensional problems. It also suggests that weaker separation between classes makes the phenomenon worse. Experiments on 20 high-dimensional datasets across several application areas corroborate that intuition. The result challenges a blanket preference for margin-based sampling: sophisticated example selection can lose its expected advantage under the high-dimensional conditions studied, even when the boundary information used for sampling is ideal.
summary.tldr: In the high-dimensional logistic-regression setting studied, passive learning can beat margin-based active learning even with noiseless labels and an optimal sampling boundary.

title: Margin-based sampling in high dimensions: When being active is less efficient than staying passive

abstract: Improving the deployment efficiency of transformer-based language models has been challenging given their high computation and memory cost. While INT8 quantization has recently been shown to be effective in reducing both the memory cost and latency while preserving model accuracy, it remains unclear whether we can leverage INT4 (which doubles peak hardware throughput) to achieve further latency improvement. In this study, we explore the feasibility of employing INT4 weight and activation (W4A4) quantization for language models. Our findings indicate that W4A4 quantization introduces no to negligible accuracy degradation for encoder-only and encoder-decoder models, but causes a significant accuracy drop for decoder-only models. To materialize the performance gain using W4A4, we develop a highly-optimized end-to-end W4A4 encoder inference pipeline supporting different quantization strategies. Our INT4 pipeline is $8.5\times$ faster for latency-oriented scenarios and up to $3\times$ for throughput-oriented scenarios compared to the inference of FP16, and improves the SOTA BERT INT8 performance from FasterTransformer by up to $1.7\times$. We provide insights into the failure cases when applying W4A4 to decoder-only models, and further explore the compatibility of INT4 quantization with other compression methods, like pruning and layer reduction.

paragraphs: Reducing language-model weights and activations to four-bit integers promises lower deployment costs, but higher peak hardware throughput does not automatically establish useful end-to-end speedups. This paper studies W4A4 quantization, asking both whether model accuracy survives the change and whether an optimized inference pipeline can realize the performance opportunity.

The accuracy findings differ by architecture. Encoder-only and encoder-decoder models show no or negligible degradation, whereas decoder-only models suffer a significant drop. The authors develop an optimized end-to-end W4A4 encoder inference pipeline supporting different quantization strategies, connecting the numerical representation to an implementation that delivers measured speed gains.

It also improves on FasterTransformer's state-of-the-art BERT INT8 performance by up to 1.7 times. The study further examines decoder-only failure cases and compatibility with pruning and layer reduction. Its findings make architecture and execution setting central to interpreting the benefits of INT4.
summary.tldr: W4A4 quantization delivers substantial encoder inference speedups, while the studied decoder-only models suffer significant accuracy loss.

title: Understanding Int4 Quantization for Language Models: Latency Speedup, Composability, and Failure Cases

abstract: This paper is concerned with the problem of nonlinear filtering, i.e., computing the conditional distribution of the state of a stochastic dynamical system given a history of noisy partial observations. Conventional sequential importance resampling (SIR) particle filters suffer from fundamental limitations, in scenarios involving degenerate likelihoods or high-dimensional states, due to the weight degeneracy issue. In this paper, we explore an alternative method, which is based on estimating the Brenier optimal transport (OT) map from the current prior distribution of the state to the posterior distribution at the next time step. Unlike SIR particle filters, the OT formulation does not require the analytical form of the likelihood. Moreover, it allows us to harness the approximation power of neural networks to model complex and multi-modal distributions and employ stochastic optimization algorithms to enhance scalability. Extensive numerical experiments are presented that compare the OT method to the SIR particle filter and the ensemble Kalman filter, evaluating the performance in terms of sample efficiency, high-dimensional scalability, and the ability to capture complex and multi-modal distributions.
originalAbstract: This paper is concerned with the problem of nonlinear filtering, i.e., computing the conditional distribution of the state of a stochastic dynamical system given a history of noisy partial observations. Conventional sequential importance resampling (SIR) particle filters suffer from fundamental limitations, in scenarios involving degenerate likelihoods or high-dimensional states, due to the weight degeneracy issue. In this paper, we explore an alternative method, which is based on estimating the Brenier optimal transport (OT) map from the current prior distribution of the state to the posterior distribution at the next time step. Unlike SIR particle filters, the OT formulation does not require the analytical form of the likelihood. Moreover, it allows us to harness the approximation power of neural networks to model complex and multi-modal distributions and employ stochastic optimization algorithms to enhance scalability. Extensive numerical experiments are presented that compare the OT method to the SIR particle filter and the ensemble Kalman filter, evaluating the performance in terms of sample efficiency, high-dimensional scalability, and the ability to capture complex and multi-modal distributions.

paragraphs: Nonlinear filtering estimates the distribution of a changing hidden state from a history of noisy, partial observations. Conventional sequential importance resampling particle filters can struggle when their weights degenerate, particularly with high-dimensional states or degenerate likelihoods. This paper explores a different way to update the state distribution.

The method estimates a Brenier optimal transport map that moves the current prior distribution to the posterior at the next time step. Its formulation does not require an analytical expression for the likelihood. It also allows neural networks to approximate complex distributions, including distributions with multiple modes, and uses stochastic optimization to support scalability.

The authors compare the transport approach with a sequential importance resampling particle filter and an ensemble Kalman filter in extensive numerical experiments. The evaluation examines sample efficiency, scaling with state dimension, and representation of complex or multimodal distributions. The contribution is an alternative filtering construction that brings transport maps and neural approximation into the sequential update, with experiments directed at the difficulties motivating it.
summary.tldr: The paper uses learned Brenier transport maps to update filtering distributions without requiring an analytical likelihood.

title: Nonlinear Filtering with Brenier Optimal Transport Maps

abstract: This paper proposes a novel online evaluation protocol for Test Time Adaptation (TTA) methods, which penalizes slower methods by providing them with fewer samples for adaptation. TTA methods leverage unlabeled data at test time to adapt to distribution shifts. Though many effective methods have been proposed, their impressive performance usually comes at the cost of significantly increased computation budgets. Current evaluation protocols overlook the effect of this extra computation cost, affecting their real-world applicability. To address this issue, we propose a more realistic evaluation protocol for TTA methods, where data is received in an online fashion from a constant-speed data stream, thereby accounting for the method’s adaptation speed. We apply our proposed protocol to benchmark several TTA methods on multiple datasets and scenarios. Extensive experiments shows that, when accounting for inference speed, simple and fast approaches can outperform more sophisticated but slower methods. For example, SHOT from 2020, outperforms the state-of-the-art method SAR from 2023 under our online setting. Our results reveal the importance of developing practical TTA methods that are both accurate and efficient.

paragraphs: Test-time adaptation lets a model adjust to distribution changes using unlabeled data encountered during deployment. More elaborate adaptation methods can improve predictions, but their extra computation takes time. The paper argues that evaluations which overlook this time cost can give an incomplete picture of how useful these methods will be in practice.

The proposed evaluation protocol supplies data as an online stream arriving at a constant speed. A slower method consequently receives fewer samples for adaptation. This makes adaptation speed part of the evaluation itself, linking the available learning opportunities to how quickly a method can process the stream.

The authors benchmark several methods across multiple datasets and scenarios. They find that simple, fast approaches can outperform more sophisticated, slower ones under this protocol; SHOT outperforming SAR is one reported example. The finding concerns performance under an explicit time constraint, showing that method rankings can change when computation affects access to adaptation data. It supports evaluating accuracy together with the speed needed to sustain it.
summary.tldr: Evaluating adaptation on a constant-speed data stream shows that faster, simpler methods can outperform slower, more sophisticated ones.

title: Evaluation of Test-Time Adaptation Under Computational Time Constraints

abstract: This work introduces reduced models based on Continuous Low Rank Adaptation (CoLoRA) that pre-train neural networks for a given partial differential equation and then continuously adapt low-rank weights in time to rapidly predict the evolution of solution fields at new physics parameters and new initial conditions. The adaptation can be either purely data-driven or via an equation-driven variational approach that provides Galerkin-optimal approximations. Because CoLoRA approximates solution fields locally in time, the rank of the weights can be kept small, which means that only few training trajectories are required offline so that CoLoRA is well suited for data-scarce regimes. Predictions with CoLoRA are orders of magnitude faster than with classical methods and their accuracy and parameter efficiency is higher compared to other neural network approaches.

paragraphs: Predicting how a physical system evolves often requires solving a partial differential equation repeatedly for different parameters or starting conditions. CoLoRA builds a reduced neural model for this task. It first pretrains a network for a given equation, then continuously changes a small, low-rank set of weights as time advances to predict new solution fields.

The central design choice is to approximate the solution locally in time. According to the authors, this allows the adapted weights to retain a small rank and reduces the number of training trajectories needed beforehand. The adaptation can follow data alone or use an equation-driven variational formulation. The latter provides Galerkin-optimal approximations, giving that version a stated mathematical optimality property.

The paper reports predictions that are orders of magnitude faster than classical methods, together with better accuracy and parameter efficiency than other neural approaches. Its practical appeal is the combination of rapid prediction at new physics parameters and initial conditions with limited offline training data. The small evolving adaptation is what connects the reduced model’s flexibility to its efficiency.
summary.tldr: CoLoRA continuously adapts low-rank neural weights to predict PDE solutions quickly from relatively few training trajectories.

title: CoLoRA: Continuous low-rank adaptation for reduced implicit neural modeling of parameterized partial differential equations

abstract: In-Context Learning (ICL) has been a powerful emergent property of large language models that has attracted increasing attention in recent years. In contrast to regular gradient-based learning, ICL is highly interpretable and does not require parameter updates. In this paper, we show that, for linearized transformer networks, ICL can be made explicit and permanent through the inclusion of bias terms. We mathematically demonstrate the equivalence between a model with ICL demonstration prompts and the same model with the additional bias terms. Our algorithm (ICLCA) allows for exact conversion in an inexpensive manner. Existing methods are not exact and require expensive parameter updates. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach through experiments that show the exact incorporation of ICL tokens into a linear transformer. We further suggest how our method can be adapted to achieve cheap approximate conversion of ICL tokens, even in regular transformer networks that are not linearized. Our experiments on GPT-2 show that, even though the conversion is only approximate, the model still gains valuable context from the included bias terms.

paragraphs: In-context learning lets a language model use demonstrations supplied in its prompt without updating its parameters. This paper asks whether the effect of those demonstrations can instead be incorporated into the model itself. For transformers with linearized attention, the authors show that adding bias terms can make that contextual information explicit and permanent.

Their algorithm, ICLCA, converts demonstration prompts into additional biases. The mathematical result establishes equivalence between the prompted linearized model and the same model equipped with those terms. Exactness is the important distinction: in this setting, the conversion preserves the effect of the demonstrations rather than merely learning an approximation through expensive parameter updates.

Experiments demonstrate exact incorporation of context tokens in a linear transformer. The authors also suggest an adaptation for ordinary, nonlinearized transformers, where conversion is approximate. GPT-2 experiments show that the added biases still convey useful context in that case. The paper thus separates an exact result for linearized architectures from an empirically useful approximation for a regular transformer.
summary.tldr: ICLCA exactly converts demonstration prompts into bias terms for linearized transformers and provides an approximate adaptation tested on GPT-2.

title: Exact Conversion of In-Context Learning to Model Weights in Linearized-Attention Transformers

abstract: We introduce AnyTool, a large language model agent designed to revolutionize the utilization of a vast array of tools in addressing user queries. We utilize over 16,000 APIs from Rapid API, operating under the assumption that a subset of these APIs could potentially resolve the queries. AnyTool primarily incorporates three elements: an API retriever with a hierarchical structure, a solver aimed at resolving user queries using a selected set of API candidates, and a self-reflection mechanism, which re-activates AnyTool if the initial solution proves impracticable. AnyTool is powered by the function calling feature of GPT-4, eliminating the need for training external modules. We also revisit the evaluation protocol introduced by previous works and identify a limitation in this protocol that leads to an artificially high pass rate. By revising the evaluation protocol to better reflect practical application scenarios, we introduce an additional benchmark, termed AnyToolBench. Experiments across various datasets demonstrate the superiority of our AnyTool over strong baselines such as ToolLLM and a GPT-4 variant tailored for tool utilization. For instance, AnyTool outperforms ToolLLM by +35.5% in terms of average pass rate on ToolBench.

Its setting includes more than 16,000 APIs from Rapid API, under the assumption that some subset could potentially solve the request. The challenge is to find useful candidates, use them effectively, and recover when an attempted solution is impracticable.

summary.tldr: AnyTool combines hierarchical API retrieval, task solving, and self-reflection to improve tool use across a collection of more than 16,000 APIs.

title: AnyTool: Self-Reflective, Hierarchical Agents for Large-Scale API Calls

abstract: This paper introduces SceneCraft, a Large Language Model (LLM) Agent converting text descriptions into Blender-executable Python scripts which render complex scenes with up to a hundred 3D assets. This process requires complex spatial planning and arrangement. We tackle these challenges through a combination of advanced abstraction, strategic planning, and library learning. SceneCraft first models a scene graph as a blueprint, detailing the spatial relationships among assets in the scene. SceneCraft then writes Python scripts based on this graph, translating relationships into numerical constraints for asset layout. Next, SceneCraft leverages the perceptual strengths of vision-language foundation models like GPT-V to analyze rendered images and iteratively refine the scene. On top of this process, SceneCraft features a library learning mechanism that compiles common script functions into a reusable library, facilitating continuous self-improvement without expensive LLM parameter tuning. Our evaluation demonstrates that SceneCraft surpasses existing LLM-based agents in rendering complex scenes, as shown by its adherence to constraints and favorable human assessments. We also showcase the broader application potential of SceneCraft by reconstructing detailed 3D scenes from the Sintel movie and guiding a video generative model with generated scenes as intermediary control signal.

paragraphs: SceneCraft turns text descriptions into Python scripts that Blender can execute to render scenes containing up to a hundred 3D assets. The main challenge is arranging those assets coherently. The system first builds a scene graph that records spatial relationships, providing a blueprint before it commits those relationships to numerical positions.

It then writes scripts that translate the blueprint into layout constraints. After rendering, a vision-language model examines the resulting image and helps refine the scene through repeated revisions. SceneCraft also collects common script functions into a reusable library, supporting continued improvement without expensive tuning of the language model’s parameters.

Evaluations report better constraint adherence and more favorable human assessments than existing language-model agents for complex scene rendering. The paper additionally demonstrates reconstruction of detailed scenes from the Sintel movie and use of generated scenes as intermediate controls for a video-generation model. These results illustrate how explicit planning, executable code, visual feedback, and reusable functions can work together in a scene-generation agent.
summary.tldr: SceneCraft converts text into Blender scenes through scene-graph planning, code generation, visual refinement, and a reusable library of script functions.

title: SceneCraft: An LLM Agent for Synthesizing 3D Scenes as Blender Code

abstract: Deep Neural Nets (DNNs) have become a pervasive tool for solving many emerging problems. However, they tend to overfit to and memorize the training set. Memorization is of keen interest since it is closely related to several concepts such as generalization, noisy learning, and privacy. To study memorization, Feldman (2019) proposed a formal score, however its computational requirements limit its practical use. Recent research has shown empirical evidence linking input loss curvature (measured by the trace of the loss Hessian w.r.t inputs) and memorization. It was shown to be $\sim3$ orders of magnitude more efficient than calculating the memorization score. However, there is a lack of theoretical understanding linking memorization with input loss curvature. In this paper, we not only investigate this connection but also extend our analysis to establish theoretical links between differential privacy, memorization, and input loss curvature. First, we derive an upper bound on memorization characterized by both differential privacy and input loss curvature. Secondly, we present a novel insight showing that input loss curvature is upper-bounded by the differential privacy parameter. Our theoretical findings are further validated using deep models on CIFAR and ImageNet datasets, showing a strong correlation between our theoretical predictions and results observed in practice.

paragraphs: Measuring how much a neural network memorizes its training examples can be computationally expensive. Earlier empirical work connected memorization to input loss curvature, measured by the trace of the loss Hessian with respect to inputs. That curvature measure was reported to be roughly three orders of magnitude cheaper than computing a formal memorization score.

This paper develops theoretical links behind that empirical connection and extends them to differential privacy. The authors derive an upper bound on memorization involving both privacy and input loss curvature. They also show that input loss curvature is upper-bounded by the differential privacy parameter. These are bounding relationships connecting the quantities, rather than claims that they are identical measures.

Experiments with deep models on CIFAR and ImageNet show a strong correlation between the theoretical predictions and observed results. The work therefore gives theoretical support to a computationally attractive way of studying memorization, while connecting that analysis to privacy. Its contribution brings previously observed curvature relationships into a framework that also accounts for differential privacy.
summary.tldr: The paper derives bounds linking memorization, input loss curvature, and differential privacy, supported by experiments on CIFAR and ImageNet.

title: Unveiling Privacy, Memorization, and Input Curvature Links

abstract: Offline Reinforcement Learning (RL) commonly suffers from the out-of-distribution (OOD) overestimation issue due to the distribution shift. Prior work gradually shifts their focus from suppressing OOD overestimation to avoiding overly conservative learning from suboptimal behavior policies to improve generalization. However, most approaches explicitly delimit boundaries for OOD actions based on the support in the dataset, which can potentially impede the data near these boundaries from acquiring realistic estimates. This paper investigates how to loosen the rigid demarcation of OOD boundaries, adaptively extracting knowledge from empirical data to implicitly improve the model’s generalization to nearby unseen data. We introduce an adversarial data splitting (ADS) framework that enforces the model to generalize the distribution shifts simulated from the train/validation subsets splitting of the dataset. Specifically, ADS is modeled as a min-max optimization problem inspired by meta-learning and solved by iterating over the following two steps. First, we train the model on the train-subset to minimize its loss on the validation-subset. Then, we adversarially generate the "hardest" train/validation subsets with the maximum distribution shift, making the model incapable of generalization at that splitting. We derive a generalization error bound for theoretically understanding ADS and verify the effectiveness with extensive experiments. Code is available at https://github.com/DkING-lv6/ADS.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning must learn from an existing dataset, where actions outside the observed distribution can receive overly optimistic estimates. Restricting those actions can help, but rigid boundaries around the dataset's support may also hinder realistic estimates near the boundary. This paper seeks a more adaptive way to learn about nearby unseen data.

Adversarial data splitting, or ADS, creates distribution shifts within the available dataset. Its min-max procedure alternates between training a model on one subset to reduce loss on a validation subset and constructing a difficult split that maximizes the distribution shift and exposes generalization failures. The model is therefore trained against increasingly challenging differences between its training and validation data.

The authors derive a generalization error bound to help explain the framework and report extensive experiments supporting its effectiveness. The approach matters because it makes distribution shift part of the learning procedure itself. Rather than relying solely on a fixed distinction between observed and unobserved actions, ADS uses difficult internal splits to encourage generalization beyond the training subset.
summary.tldr: Adversarial data splitting improves offline reinforcement learning generalization by training against difficult distribution shifts constructed within the dataset.

title: Improving Generalization in Offline Reinforcement Learning via Adversarial Data Splitting

abstract: We study the question of volume optimality in split conformal regression, a topic still poorly understood in comparison to coverage control. Using the fact that the calibration step can be seen as an empirical volume minimization problem, we first derive a finite-sample upper-bound on the excess volume loss of the interval returned by the classical split method. This important quantity measures the difference in length between the interval obtained with the split method and the shortest oracle prediction interval. Then, we introduce EffOrt, a methodology that modifies the learning step so that the base prediction function is selected in order to minimize the length of the returned intervals. In particular, our theoretical analysis of the excess volume loss of the prediction sets produced by EffOrt reveals the links between the learning and calibration steps, and notably the impact of the choice of the function class of the base predictor. We also introduce Ad-EffOrt, an extension of the previous method, which produces intervals whose size adapts to the value of the covariate. Finally, we evaluate the empirical performance and the robustness of our methodologies.

paragraphs: Conformal regression produces prediction intervals, but their usefulness depends on their length as well as their coverage. This paper studies how close split conformal intervals come to the shortest oracle interval. It treats the difference in length as excess volume loss, making interval efficiency the central quantity of interest.

The authors interpret calibration as an empirical volume-minimization problem and derive a finite-sample upper bound on excess volume loss for classical split conformal regression. They then introduce EffOrt, which changes the learning stage so that the base prediction function is chosen with the final interval length in mind. The analysis connects predictor learning with the later calibration step.

That connection reveals how the choice of predictor function class affects the resulting interval efficiency. The authors also propose Ad-EffOrt, which allows interval sizes to vary with the covariates, and evaluate the methods’ empirical performance and robustness. The contribution is a framework for studying and improving interval length across both learning and calibration, rather than treating the predictor as unrelated to the size of the eventual uncertainty interval.
summary.tldr: EffOrt selects predictors to reduce conformal interval length, supported by excess-volume bounds and an extension with input-dependent interval sizes.

title: On Volume Minimization in Conformal Regression

abstract: Constructing robust simulators is essential for asking "what if?" questions and guiding policy in critical domains like healthcare and logistics. However, existing methods often struggle, either failing to generalize beyond historical data or, when using Large Language Models (LLMs), suffering from inaccuracies and poor empirical alignment. We introduce G-Sim, a hybrid framework that automates simulator construction by synergizing LLM-driven structural design with rigorous empirical calibration. G-Sim employs an LLM in an iterative loop to propose and refine a simulator’s core components and causal relationships, guided by domain knowledge. This structure is then grounded in reality by estimating its parameters using flexible calibration techniques. Specifically, G-Sim can leverage methods that are both likelihood-free and gradient-free with respect to the simulator, such as gradient-free optimization for direct parameter estimation or simulation-based inference for obtaining a posterior distribution over parameters. This allows it to handle non-differentiable and stochastic simulators. By integrating domain priors with empirical evidence, G-Sim produces reliable, causally-informed simulators, mitigating data-inefficiency and enabling robust system-level interventions for complex decision-making.

paragraphs: A simulator intended to answer what-if questions needs a plausible account of how a system works and parameters that agree with observations. The paper argues that existing approaches can struggle with either generalizing beyond historical data or keeping language-model-generated simulations empirically accurate. G-Sim combines structural design and data-based calibration to address these problems together.

An LLM repeatedly proposes and revises the simulator's components and causal relationships, using domain knowledge as guidance. Calibration then estimates parameters for that structure from empirical evidence. The framework supports direct parameter estimation through gradient-free optimization, as well as simulation-based inference that produces a posterior distribution over parameters.

These calibration options can work without a simulator likelihood or derivatives, allowing G-Sim to accommodate stochastic and non-differentiable simulators. The authors present the combination as a way to improve reliability and data efficiency while supporting system-level interventions. Its central contribution is a construction process in which domain-informed structural proposals are paired with empirical parameter fitting, making both sources of information part of the resulting simulation.
summary.tldr: G-Sim combines LLM-designed simulator structures with empirical, potentially gradient-free calibration for what-if analysis.

title: G-Sim: Generative Simulations with Large Language Models and Gradient-Free Calibration

abstract: We investigate the use of large language models (LLMs) to simulate human responses to survey questions, and perform uncertainty quantification to gain reliable insights. Our approach converts imperfect, LLM-simulated responses into confidence sets for population parameters of human responses, addressing the distribution shift between the simulated and real populations. A key innovation lies in determining the optimal number of simulated responses: too many produce overly narrow confidence sets with poor coverage, while too few yield excessively loose estimates. To resolve this, our method adaptively selects the simulation sample size, ensuring valid average-case coverage guarantees. It is broadly applicable to any LLM, irrespective of its fidelity, and any procedure for constructing confidence sets. Additionally, the selected sample size quantifies the degree of misalignment between the LLM and the target human population. We illustrate our method on real datasets and LLMs.

paragraphs: Language models can simulate survey answers, but their responses may follow a different distribution from those of the target human population. This paper studies how to turn imperfect simulated responses into confidence sets for human population parameters. The central concern is making the uncertainty reflect that mismatch rather than treating simulated answers as interchangeable with human answers.

The number of simulated responses creates a tradeoff. Too many can produce confidence sets that are overly narrow and fail to cover the target adequately; too few produce loose estimates. The proposed method selects the simulation sample size adaptively and establishes valid average-case coverage guarantees. This qualification concerns coverage on average, rather than an unconditional guarantee for every individual survey setting.

The approach applies to any language model, regardless of its fidelity, and to any confidence-set construction procedure. The selected sample size also quantifies misalignment between the model and the human population. Illustrations using real datasets and language models show how sample-size selection can serve both uncertainty quantification and assessment of the simulation’s population mismatch.
summary.tldr: Adaptively choosing how many survey responses to simulate yields average-case coverage guarantees while quantifying mismatch with the human population.

title: Uncertainty Quantification for LLM-Based Survey Simulations

abstract: Audio-visual speech recognition (AVSR) has become critical for enhancing speech recognition in noisy environments by integrating both auditory and visual modalities. However, existing AVSR systems struggle to scale up without compromising computational efficiency. In this study, we introduce MoHAVE (Mixture of Hierarchical Audio-Visual Experts), a novel robust AVSR framework designed to address these scalability constraints. By leveraging a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architecture, MoHAVE activates modality-specific expert groups, ensuring dynamic adaptation to various audio-visual inputs with minimal computational overhead. Key contributions of MoHAVE include: (1) a sparse MoE framework that efficiently scales AVSR model capacity, (2) a hierarchical gating mechanism that dynamically utilizes the expert groups based on input context, enhancing adaptability and robustness, and (3) remarkable performance across robust AVSR benchmarks, including LRS3 and MuAViC transcription and translation tasks, setting a new standard for scalable speech recognition systems.

paragraphs: Audio-visual speech recognition combines sound and visual information to improve recognition in noisy environments. Increasing model capacity can help, but existing systems face a computational challenge when scaling up. MoHAVE addresses that challenge with a mixture-of-experts architecture designed around the two input modalities.

The framework organizes experts into modality-specific groups and uses hierarchical gating to select them according to the input context. Because the mixture is sparse, the model can expand its available capacity while activating only selected experts. The gating mechanism connects computational allocation to the audio-visual evidence available for a particular input, supporting adaptation with limited additional overhead.

The authors report strong performance on robust audio-visual benchmarks, including LRS3 and MuAViC transcription and translation tasks. The contribution combines the architecture for scaling capacity with a routing mechanism intended to preserve efficiency and robustness. Its stated findings support context-dependent use of specialized expert groups as a way to handle varied audio-visual inputs while avoiding the computational burden of using all model capacity on every example.
summary.tldr: MoHAVE routes audio-visual inputs through selected expert groups to scale robust speech recognition with limited computational overhead.

title: MoHAVE: Mixture of Hierarchical Audio-Visual Experts for Robust Speech Recognition

abstract: Safe offline reinforcement learning aims to develop policies that maximize cumulative rewards while satisfying safety constraints without the need for risky online interaction. However, existing methods often struggle with the out-of-distribution (OOD) problem, leading to potentially unsafe and suboptimal policies. To address this issue, we first propose Constrained Implicit Q-learning (CIQL), a novel algorithm designed to avoid the OOD problem. In particular, CIQL expands the implicit update of reward value functions to constrained settings and then estimates cost value functions under the same implicit policy. Despite its advantages, the further performance improvement of CIQL is still hindered by the inaccurate discounted approximations of constraints. Thus, we further propose Constraint-Conditioned Implicit Q-learning (C2IQL). Building upon CIQL, C2IQL employs a cost reconstruction model to derive non-discounted cumulative costs from discounted values and incorporates a flexible, constraint-conditioned mechanism to accommodate dynamic safety constraints. Experiment results on DSRL benchmarks demonstrate the superiority of C2IQL compared to baseline methods in achieving higher rewards while guaranteeing safety constraints under different threshold conditions.

paragraphs: Safe offline reinforcement learning seeks policies that earn rewards while respecting safety constraints, using existing data rather than risky online interaction. A central difficulty is evaluating behavior outside the data distribution, which can produce unsafe or ineffective decisions. The paper first introduces Constrained Implicit Q-learning, or CIQL, to address this issue by extending implicit reward-value updates to constrained learning.

CIQL also estimates cost values under the same implicit policy, connecting reward and safety evaluation to a common behavior. However, its further improvement is hindered by approximating constraints with discounted costs. Discounting reduces the weight assigned to later costs, so the quantity being estimated can differ from the undiscounted cumulative cost relevant to a constraint.

C2IQL adds a reconstruction model that derives undiscounted cumulative costs from discounted values. It also conditions decisions on constraints, allowing the method to accommodate changing safety thresholds. On DSRL benchmarks, it achieves higher rewards than the evaluated baselines while satisfying safety constraints across different thresholds. These findings support both more accurate cost accounting and adaptation to the requested constraint.
summary.tldr: C2IQL combines implicit offline learning, reconstructed cumulative costs, and constraint conditioning to improve rewards while meeting tested safety thresholds.

title: C2IQL: Constraint-Conditioned Implicit Q-learning for Safe Offline Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Shapelets are discriminative subsequences (or shapes) with high interpretability in time series classification. Due to the time-intensive nature of shapelet discovery, existing shapelet-based methods mainly focus on selecting discriminative shapes while discarding others to achieve candidate subsequence sparsification. However, this approach may exclude beneficial shapes and overlook the varying contributions of shapelets to classification performance. To this end, we propose a Soft sparse Shapes (SoftShape) model for efficient time series classification. Our approach mainly introduces soft shape sparsification and soft shape learning blocks. The former transforms shapes into soft representations based on classification contribution scores, merging lower-scored ones into a single shape to retain and differentiate all subsequence information. The latter facilitates intra- and inter-shape temporal pattern learning, improving model efficiency by using sparsified soft shapes as inputs. Specifically, we employ a learnable router to activate a subset of class-specific expert networks for intra-shape pattern learning. Meanwhile, a shared expert network learns inter-shape patterns by converting sparsified shapes into sequences. Extensive experiments show that SoftShape outperforms state-of-the-art methods and produces interpretable results.
