paragraphs: Shapelets are short patterns in a time series that help distinguish classes and can make classification easier to interpret. Finding and processing them is expensive, so existing approaches often keep selected shapes and discard others. SoftShape addresses the possibility that discarded shapes still carry useful information and that shapes contribute unequally to classification.

Its soft sparsification block assigns contribution scores and forms soft representations of the shapes. Lower-scored shapes are merged into a single shape, retaining their information in aggregated form. This reduces the number of representations passed onward while preserving a role for subsequences that would otherwise be removed.

A second block learns temporal patterns both within individual shapes and across shapes. A learnable router activates a subset of class-specific expert networks for within-shape learning, while a shared expert processes sequences constructed from the sparsified shapes to learn cross-shape patterns. Experiments show that SoftShape outperforms the compared state-of-the-art methods and produces interpretable results. Its contribution combines selective computation with a softer treatment of less influential patterns.
summary.tldr: SoftShape improves time-series classification by merging weaker shapes and selectively learning patterns within and across the resulting representations.

title: Learning Soft Sparse Shapes for Efficient Time-Series Classification

abstract: As multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) progresses towards solving larger and more complex problems, it becomes increasingly important that algorithms exhibit the key properties of (1) strong performance, (2) memory efficiency, and (3) scalability. In this work, we introduce Sable, a performant, memory-efficient, and scalable sequence modelling approach to MARL. Sable works by adapting the retention mechanism in Retentive Networks (Sun et al., 2023) to achieve computationally efficient processing of multi-agent observations with long context memory for temporal reasoning. Through extensive evaluations across six diverse environments, we demonstrate how Sable is able to significantly outperform existing state-of-the-art methods in a large number of diverse tasks (34 out of 45 tested). Furthermore, Sable maintains performance as we scale the number of agents, handling environments with more than a thousand agents while exhibiting a linear increase in memory usage. Finally, we conduct ablation studies to isolate the source of Sable’s performance gains and confirm its efficient computational memory usage. All experimental data, hyperparameters, and code for a frozen version of Sable used in this paper are available on our website: https://sites.google.com/view/sable-marl. An improved and maintained version of Sable is available in Mava: https://github.com/instadeepai/Mava.

paragraphs: Multi-agent reinforcement learning becomes more demanding as tasks involve more agents and longer histories. A useful model must preserve decision quality while controlling the memory needed to process their observations. Sable addresses these requirements through a sequence-modeling approach designed for multi-agent observations and temporal reasoning.

The method adapts the retention mechanism from Retentive Networks. This provides computationally efficient processing together with long-context memory, allowing the model to use information across time. The architectural aim is to make access to that history compatible with larger agent populations, so that temporal reasoning does not prevent scaling.

Across six environments, Sable significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods on 34 of 45 tested tasks. It also maintains performance in scaling experiments involving more than a thousand agents, with memory usage increasing linearly. Ablations investigate the sources of its gains and confirm its efficient memory use. The results support the combined performance and scalability claims within these evaluations, while the task count makes clear that the reported superiority is not universal.
summary.tldr: Sable adapts retention-based sequence modeling for multi-agent learning, improving most tested tasks and scaling beyond a thousand agents with linear memory growth.

title: Sable: a Performant, Efficient and Scalable Sequence Model for MARL

abstract: Scaling up inference-time compute has proven to be a valuable strategy in improving the performance of Large Language Models (LLMs) without fine-tuning. An important task that can benefit from additional inference-time compute is self-repair; given an initial flawed response or guess, the LLM corrects its own mistake and produces an improved response or fix. We leverage the in-context learning ability of LLMs to perform self-repair in the coding domain. The key contribution of our paper is an approach that synthesises and selects an ordered set of golden example pairs, or AuPairs, of these initial guesses and subsequent fixes for the corresponding problems. Each such AuPair is provided as a single in-context example at inference time to generate a repaired solution. For an inference-time compute budget of $N$ LLM calls per problem, $N$ AuPairs are used to generate $N$ repaired solutions, out of which the highest-scoring solution is the final answer. The underlying intuition is that if the LLM is given a different example of fixing an incorrect guess each time, it can subsequently generate a diverse set of repaired solutions. Our algorithm selects these AuPairs in a manner that maximises complementarity and usefulness. We demonstrate the results of our algorithm on 5 LLMs across 7 competitive programming datasets for the code repair task. Our algorithm yields a significant boost in performance compared to best-of-$N$ and self-repair, and also exhibits strong generalisation across datasets and models. Moreover, our approach shows stronger scaling with inference-time compute budget compared to baselines.

paragraphs: An LLM can spend additional computation trying to repair a flawed code solution. AuPair makes those attempts more useful by changing the repair example supplied to the model on each attempt. It uses in-context learning, so the repair strategy operates at inference time without requiring model fine-tuning.

The method synthesizes and selects an ordered collection of examples pairing an incorrect solution with its subsequent fix. For a budget of N model calls, it uses N such pairs, supplying one pair per call to produce N repaired candidates. It then returns the highest-scoring candidate. Selection aims to make the examples complementary and useful, with the intuition that different repair demonstrations encourage diverse proposed fixes.

The authors evaluate the approach using five LLMs and seven competitive programming datasets. They report significant improvements over best-of-N and self-repair, strong generalization across datasets and models, and stronger scaling as inference budgets increase. These findings suggest that the choice of repair demonstrations can materially affect how much benefit additional model calls provide.
summary.tldr: AuPair selects complementary examples of code fixes to improve the diversity and effectiveness of repeated LLM repair attempts.

title: AuPair: Golden Example Pairs for Code Repair

abstract: Transformers have emerged as the dominant architecture in the field of deep learning, with a broad range of applications and remarkable in-context learning (ICL) capabilities. While not yet fully understood, ICL has already proved to be an intriguing phenomenon, allowing transformers to learn in context—without requiring further training. In this paper, we further advance the understanding of ICL by demonstrating that transformers can perform full Bayesian inference for commonly used statistical models in context. More specifically, we introduce a general framework that builds on ideas from prior fitted networks and continuous normalizing flows and enables us to infer complex posterior distributions for models such as generalized linear models and latent factor models. Extensive experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate that our ICL approach yields posterior samples that are similar in quality to state-of-the-art MCMC or variational inference methods that do not operate in context. The source code for this paper is available at https://github.com/ArikReuter/ICL_for_Full_Bayesian_Inference

paragraphs: Bayesian inference represents uncertainty through a posterior distribution rather than returning only one fitted answer. This paper asks whether transformers can perform that richer form of inference through in-context learning. In this setting, the model uses information supplied in its context without undergoing additional training for the particular inference problem.

The authors introduce a framework combining ideas from prior fitted networks and continuous normalizing flows. Its purpose is to produce samples from complex posterior distributions for commonly used statistical models. The examples covered include generalized linear models and latent factor models, extending the investigation beyond obtaining a single prediction or parameter estimate.

Experiments on real-world datasets find that the resulting posterior samples have quality similar to those produced by leading Markov chain Monte Carlo and variational inference methods. Those comparison methods do not operate in context. The result supports the possibility of learning a reusable inference procedure inside a transformer, with demonstrated posterior quality for the statistical models and datasets studied.
summary.tldr: A transformer framework performs Bayesian inference in context, producing posterior samples comparable in quality to established inference methods in experiments.

title: Can Transformers Learn Full Bayesian Inference in Context?

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) that integrate multiple input roles (e.g., system instructions, user queries, external tool outputs) are increasingly prevalent in practice. Ensuring that the model accurately distinguishes messages from each role—a concept we call role separation—is crucial for consistent multi-role behavior. Although recent work often targets state-of-the-art prompt injection defenses, it remains unclear whether such methods truly teach LLMs to differentiate roles or merely memorize known triggers. In this paper, we examine role-separation learning: the process of teaching LLMs to robustly distinguish system and user tokens. Through a simple, controlled experimental framework, we find that fine-tuned models often rely on two proxies for role identification: (1) task type exploitation, and (2) proximity to begin-of-text. Although data augmentation can partially mitigate these shortcuts, it generally leads to iterative patching rather than a deeper fix. To address this, we propose reinforcing invariant signals that mark role boundaries by adjusting token-wise cues in the model’s input encoding. In particular, modifying position IDs helps the model learn clearer distinctions and reduces reliance on superficial proxies. By focusing on this mechanism-centered perspective, our work illuminates how LLMs can more reliably maintain consistent multi-role behavior without merely memorizing known prompts or triggers.

paragraphs: Language models receive messages with different roles, including system instructions, user requests, and tool outputs. Reliable behavior requires distinguishing those roles. This paper examines whether fine-tuning teaches models that distinction or encourages them to recognize incidental patterns associated with particular roles in the training examples.

In controlled experiments focused on system and user tokens, the authors identify two shortcuts: using task type as a clue to role, and relying on proximity to the beginning of the text. Data augmentation partially reduces these behaviors, but the authors find that it generally leads to repeated patching. The underlying role distinction can remain entangled with superficial cues.

The proposed intervention strengthens invariant role-boundary signals through changes to token-level input encoding. In particular, modifying position IDs helps models distinguish roles more clearly and reduces shortcut reliance. The findings support investigating how role information is encoded, alongside which examples appear during training. The demonstrated improvement concerns clearer role learning, providing a mechanism-focused direction for more consistent behavior across multi-role inputs.
summary.tldr: The paper identifies shortcuts in LLM role learning and reduces them by strengthening role-boundary cues through input encoding.

title: The Illusion of Role Separation: Hidden Shortcuts in LLM Role Learning (and How to Fix Them)

abstract: Neural Processes (NPs) are deep probabilistic models that represent stochastic processes by conditioning their prior distributions on a set of context points. Despite their advantages in uncertainty estimation for complex distributions, NPs enforce parameterization coupling between the conditional prior model and the posterior model. We show that this coupling amounts to prior misspecification and revisit the NP objective to address this issue. More specifically, we propose Rényi Neural Processes (RNP), a method that replaces the standard KL divergence with the Rényi divergence, dampening the effects of the misspecified prior during posterior updates. We validate our approach across multiple benchmarks including regression and image inpainting tasks, and show significant performance improvements of RNPs in real-world problems. Our extensive experiments show consistently better log-likelihoods over state-of-the-art NP models.

paragraphs: Neural Processes are probabilistic models that use a set of observed context points to describe a stochastic process. They are useful for representing uncertainty in complex distributions. This paper examines a problem in their construction: the conditional prior and posterior models are coupled through their parameterization, which the authors show amounts to a misspecified prior.

Rényi Neural Processes change the training objective to reduce the influence of that misspecification during posterior updates. The method replaces the usual KL divergence with Rényi divergence. The central intervention is therefore in how the prior and posterior are compared during learning, dampening the effect of an imperfect prior on the updated probabilistic model.

The authors evaluate the approach on several benchmarks, including regression and image inpainting, and report significant improvements on real-world problems. Across their experiments, Rényi Neural Processes consistently achieve better log-likelihoods than the compared state-of-the-art Neural Process models. These findings support revisiting the divergence in the learning objective as a practical way to address the identified prior-modeling issue.
summary.tldr: Rényi Neural Processes replace KL divergence to reduce the impact of prior misspecification and improve predictive log-likelihoods.

title: Rényi Neural Processes

abstract: Inverse problems (IPs) involve reconstructing signals from noisy observations. Recently, diffusion models (DMs) have emerged as a powerful framework for solving IPs, achieving remarkable reconstruction performance. However, existing DM-based methods frequently encounter issues such as heavy computational demands and suboptimal convergence. In this work, building upon the idea of the recent work DMPlug, we propose two novel methods, DMILO and DMILO-PGD, to address these challenges. Our first method, DMILO, employs intermediate layer optimization (ILO) to alleviate the memory burden inherent in DMPlug. Additionally, by introducing sparse deviations, we expand the range of DMs, enabling the exploration of underlying signals that may lie outside the range of the diffusion model. We further propose DMILO-PGD, which integrates ILO with projected gradient descent (PGD), thereby reducing the risk of suboptimal convergence. We provide an intuitive theoretical analysis of our approaches under appropriate conditions and validate their superiority through extensive experiments on diverse image datasets, encompassing both linear and nonlinear IPs. Our results demonstrate significant performance gains over state-of-the-art methods, highlighting the effectiveness of DMILO and DMILO-PGD in addressing common challenges in DM-based IP solvers.

paragraphs: Inverse problems reconstruct an underlying signal from noisy observations. Diffusion models provide a useful framework for this reconstruction, but existing solvers can require substantial computation and converge to suboptimal solutions. Building on DMPlug, the paper introduces DMILO and DMILO-PGD to improve the practicality and effectiveness of diffusion-based reconstruction.

DMILO uses intermediate layer optimization to reduce DMPlug's memory burden. It also introduces sparse deviations that expand the range of signals accessible through the model. This matters when the underlying signal lies outside the diffusion model's original range: reconstruction gains some flexibility to explore beyond what the unmodified model can represent.

DMILO-PGD combines intermediate layer optimization with projected gradient descent to reduce the risk of suboptimal convergence. The paper provides intuitive theoretical analysis under appropriate conditions and evaluates both methods across diverse image datasets with linear and nonlinear inverse problems. The reported gains over state-of-the-art methods support addressing memory demands, representational restrictions, and optimization behavior together, while the theoretical conclusions remain conditional.
summary.tldr: DMILO and DMILO-PGD improve diffusion-based inverse-problem solving through intermediate-layer optimization, sparse deviations, and projected gradient descent.

title: Integrating Intermediate Layer Optimization and Projected Gradient Descent for Solving Inverse Problems with Diffusion Models

abstract: Language models are pretrained on sequences that blend statistical regularities, which make text fluent, with factual associations between specific tokens, which encode knowledge of facts. While recent works suggest that generalization depends critically on the interaction of these two streams, such as the diversity of the contexts in which facts appear, these effects remain difficult to study systematically. This paper introduces a flexible synthetic testbed that combines a statistical stream of generic tokens with an abstract factual stream of source-target token pairs, enabling fine-grained control over their interaction, such as their composition into a sequence (contextual structure) or the level of context diversity carrying the facts at training time. Through controlled experiments, we find that higher contextual diversity delays in-distribution factual learning, while low diversity can harm out-of-distribution generalization in ways that depend on the contextual structure. As a result, the optimal diversity level depends on the training budget. Beyond factual recall failures, we also identify failures in statistical generalization as we study how the interplay between contextual design and diversity level impacts different aspects of generalization. Furthermore, through a series of controlled interventions on the model components, we trace failure in different aspects of generalization to distinct optimization bottlenecks, highlighting the importance of the embedding and unembedding layers. Overall, our synthetic framework allows us to isolate effects that would be confounded in large-scale studies, offering a controlled testbed for future investigations.

paragraphs: Language-model training mixes statistical patterns with factual associations, making their separate effects difficult to study. This paper builds a synthetic testbed with generic tokens for statistical structure and source-target token pairs for facts. Researchers can control both how these streams are arranged and how varied the contexts carrying facts are.

Controlled experiments reveal a trade-off. Greater contextual diversity delays factual learning on the training distribution, while limited diversity can damage generalization outside that distribution. The latter effect depends on contextual structure. Consequently, the most useful diversity level depends on the training budget, rather than following a simple rule that more diversity is always better.

The study also finds failures in statistical generalization, beyond difficulties recalling facts. Interventions on model components connect different failures to distinct optimization bottlenecks and highlight the importance of embedding and unembedding layers. These findings come from the controlled synthetic setting. Its contribution is the ability to isolate interactions among context design, diversity, and optimization that would be entangled in large-scale pretraining studies.
summary.tldr: A synthetic pretraining testbed shows that contextual diversity trades off learning speed and generalization, with the best level depending on training budget.

title: Facts in Stats: Impacts of Pretraining Diversity on Language Model Generalization

abstract: In this paper, we identify a semantic decomposition in robot action sequences, separating task-level motion intent from execution-level refinements. By analyzing actions in the spectral domain using the discrete cosine transform (DCT), we observe that low-frequency components capture global motion trajectories, while high-frequency components encode precise timing, alignment, and contact behaviors. Motivated by this structure, we propose Causal Spectral Policy (CSP), which models action generation as a causal coarse-to-fine process: coarse motion is predicted from observation and language, and fine corrections are generated conditionally on the realized trajectory. Across simulation and real-world evaluations, CSP consistently outperforms strong baselines on precision-sensitive manipulation tasks. Additionally, we propose human-inspired teleoperation noise injection as a data augmentation method under which our approach demonstrates strong robustness to noisy demonstrations

paragraphs: Robot actions combine broad movement with small adjustments needed for accurate execution. This paper analyzes action sequences using the discrete cosine transform, which separates their slower and faster variations. The authors observe a meaningful pattern: low-frequency components describe overall trajectories, while high-frequency components capture precise timing, alignment, and contact behavior.

Causal Spectral Policy turns that observation into a hierarchy for generating actions. It first predicts coarse motion from observations and language, then generates fine corrections conditioned on the realized trajectory. This ordering gives the refinement stage a concrete motion to work with. The architecture therefore represents the dependency between task-level intent and the adjustments required to execute that intent precisely.

Across simulation and real-world evaluations, the policy consistently outperforms strong baselines on manipulation tasks that require precision. The authors also introduce a demonstration-augmentation method that injects noise inspired by human teleoperation, under which the approach shows strong robustness. Together, the results support organizing action prediction around broad trajectories and their dependent corrections, including when demonstrations contain noise.
summary.tldr: Causal Spectral Policy predicts broad robot motions before trajectory-dependent fine corrections, improving precision-sensitive manipulation.

title: Hierarchical Policy Learning via Spectral Decomposition

abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models have become a leading approach for decoupling parameter count from computational cost in large language models, yet effectively scaling MoE performance remains a challenge. Prior work shows that fine-grained experts enlarge the space of expert combinations and improve flexibility, but they also impose substantial routing overhead, creating a new scalability bottleneck. In this paper, we explore a complementary axis for scaling—how expert outputs are aggregated. We theoretically show that replacing the standard weighted-summation aggregation with structural aggregation expands the expert-combination space without altering the experts or router, and enables possible multi-step reasoning within a single MoE layer. To this end, we propose DAG-MoE, a sparse MoE framework that employs a lightweight module to automatically learn the optimal aggregation structure among the selected experts. Extensive experiments under standard language modeling settings show that DAG-MoE consistently improves performance in both pretraining and fine-tuning, surpassing traditional MoE baselines.

paragraphs: Mixture-of-experts models increase available model capacity while activating only selected experts for each input. Making experts smaller and more numerous can create additional combinations, but also increases routing overhead. This paper explores another way to improve such models: changing how the selected experts’ outputs are assembled.

Standard aggregation combines expert outputs through a weighted sum. The authors theoretically show that structural aggregation can expand the space of expert combinations without changing the experts or router. They also argue that it makes multi-step reasoning within one mixture-of-experts layer possible. DAG-MoE implements this idea through a lightweight module that learns the aggregation structure among selected experts.

Experiments in standard language modeling settings show consistent improvements over traditional mixture-of-experts baselines during both pretraining and fine-tuning. The findings identify aggregation as a useful additional design choice for scaling performance. The possibility of multi-step reasoning is part of the structural argument; the reported empirical result is improved language modeling performance, rather than direct proof that every layer performs such reasoning.
summary.tldr: DAG-MoE learns structured combinations of expert outputs, expanding their possible interactions and improving reported pretraining and fine-tuning performance.

title: DAG-MoE: From Simple Mixture to Structural Aggregation in Mixture-of-Experts

abstract: In many real-world networks, relationships are inherently directional, yet most graph neural networks (GNNs) assume undirected edges, and naïve adaptations of undirected GNNs to directed graphs amplify oversmoothing and gradient pathologies that cap model depth. Unitary graph convolutions (UniConv) provably prevent representational collapse and oversmoothing, but cannot incorporate edge directionality or edge features. In this paper, we introduce a directed unitary GNN with edge features (Dune), which retains these guarantees while overcoming UniConv’s limitations by incorporating edge directionality and edge features. Dune keeps gradient norms bounded at any number of layers, allowing it to benefit from neural network depth, unlike existing directed GNNs. The same unitary operator can be embedded in hybrid architectures with graph transformers, where its wavelike propagation supplies positional information and reduces the importance of random-walk or Laplacian-based encodings. We prove that Dune avoids exponential oversmoothing that plagues existing directed GNNs and empirically show that it achieves state-of-the-art performance on 12 directed-graph benchmarks while remaining trainable beyond 100 layers, improving performance by up to 18 percentage points over strong baselines. Our results establish unitary convolutions as a scalable, geometry-aware foundation for deep learning on directed graphs.

paragraphs: Directed graphs encode relationships whose orientation matters, but adapting undirected graph networks can worsen oversmoothing and gradient problems. Unitary graph convolutions already offer guarantees against representational collapse, yet the existing UniConv formulation cannot incorporate edge direction or features. Dune extends this approach to include both while retaining its protective guarantees.

There, wavelike propagation provides positional information and reduces the importance of separate random-walk or Laplacian encodings.

The empirical study reports state-of-the-art performance on 12 directed-graph benchmarks, trainability beyond 100 layers, and improvements of up to 18 percentage points over strong baselines. These findings support using depth in directed graph models without the same collapse behavior. The theoretical guarantees concern stability and oversmoothing, while the benchmark results establish the reported task-performance benefits.
summary.tldr: Dune extends unitary graph convolutions to directed edges and edge features, combining stability guarantees with strong results beyond 100 layers.

title: Unitary Convolutions for Message-passing and Positional Encodings on Directed Graphs

abstract: We study consumer utility maximization in an online random-order model where strategic agents arrive sequentially. To circumvent strong impossibility results for utility maximization, we turn to the framework of learning-augmented mechanism design. Crucially, we show that the types of predictions commonly used in learning-augmented mechanism design (such as predictions of agent values or the optimal value) are not useful for utility maximization, where payments are directly at odds with the objective. Instead, we identify that a qualitatively different kind of prediction suffices: the identity of the highest-valued agent. First, we provide a deterministic truthful mechanism for our online setting by adapting offline randomized techniques. Then, we augment our mechanism with predictions. When the predictions are correct, we achieve a constant approximation to the optimal solution under full information (consistency), and even when predictions are arbitrarily bad, we guarantee a constant approximation to the best implementable solution (robustness).

paragraphs: The paper studies consumer utility when strategic agents arrive one at a time in random order. Payments work against this objective, creating strong obstacles for mechanism design. The authors investigate whether predictions can help, and show that familiar predictions of agent values or the optimal value are not useful for this purpose in their setting.

They identify a different sufficient prediction: the identity of the highest-valued agent. The construction begins with a deterministic truthful online mechanism adapted from randomized offline techniques. Predictions then augment this mechanism, linking the information supplied by learning to the decisions made as agents arrive.

The resulting guarantees distinguish two benchmarks. With correct predictions, the mechanism achieves a constant approximation to the full-information optimum. Even with arbitrarily poor predictions, it retains a constant approximation to the best implementable solution. The second benchmark is therefore different from the first. The contribution shows how predicting the right kind of information can provide both benefits from accurate advice and a fallback guarantee when that advice fails.
summary.tldr: Predicting the highest-valued agent’s identity enables a truthful online mechanism with distinct consistency and robustness guarantees for consumer utility.

title: Knowing Who, Not How Much: Learning-Augmented Mechanisms for Consumer Utility Maximization

abstract: Artificial intelligence has achieved remarkable breakthroughs in fields such as text, image, and video analysis, with deep learning serving as the mainstream paradigm. Trained deep learning models can be integrated into various applications either through fine-tuning or without any modification. While this practice promotes the advancement of artificial intelligence, it also raises concerns regarding intellectual property protection and information security risks. Therefore, it is necessary to propose relevant methods to measure the similarity between models. Existing code clone detection techniques are insufficient to address this issue. In this paper, we provide the first definition of model cloning and design a method for model similarity detection. The framework characterizes model topology at the structural level based on normalized computational graphs, and at the weight level, it employs a method that does not require explicit parameter alignment to measure the statistical similarity of weight parameters. Experiments on a synthetic model clone benchmark dataset and real-world open-source models demonstrate that the proposed method can accurately detect similar models. This method provides a unified and extensible quantitative foundation for model lineage analysis, model retrieval, and intellectual property protection of models.

paragraphs: Reusing trained models, either directly or through fine-tuning, makes it useful to measure how closely two models are related. The paper studies this as model cloning, motivated by model lineage, intellectual property, and information security. It introduces a definition of model cloning and a detection framework designed for trained neural networks.

The framework examines two complementary aspects of a model. At the structural level, it represents computation through normalized graphs, allowing model topology to be compared. At the weight level, it measures statistical similarity between learned parameters without requiring explicit parameter alignment. Together, these views account for both how a model computes and the numerical values it has learned.

Experiments on a synthetic clone benchmark and real-world open-source models show that the method can accurately identify similar models. The contribution is a unified, extensible quantitative basis for comparing models beyond existing code-clone detection techniques. This supports applications such as finding related models, studying their lineage, and informing model intellectual property protection.
summary.tldr: The paper detects model similarity by combining normalized computational graphs with weight statistics that do not require explicit parameter alignment.

title: An In-Depth Study on Deep Learning Model Cloning

abstract: Understanding how and why large language models (LLMs) fail is becoming a central challenge as models rapidly evolve and static evaluations fall behind. While automated probing has been enabled by dynamic test generation, existing approaches often discover isolated failure cases, lack principled control over exploration, and provide limited insight into the underlying structure of model weaknesses. We propose ProbeLLM, a benchmark-agnostic automated probing framework that elevates weakness discovery from individual failures to structured failure modes. ProbeLLM formulates probing as a hierarchical Monte Carlo Tree Search, explicitly allocating limited probing budgets between global exploration of new failure regions and local refinement of recurring error patterns. By restricting probing to verifiable test cases and leveraging tool-augmented generation and verification, ProbeLLM grounds failure discovery in reliable evidence. Discovered failures are further consolidated into interpretable failure modes via failure-aware embeddings and boundary-aware induction. Across diverse benchmarks and LLMs, ProbeLLM reveals substantially broader, cleaner, and more fine-grained failure landscapes than static benchmarks and prior automated methods, supporting a shift from case-centric evaluation toward principled weakness discovery

paragraphs: Finding a single incorrect model response does not necessarily explain the broader weakness behind it. ProbeLLM aims to organize automated evaluation around recurring failure modes. It addresses a problem with both static benchmarks and existing dynamic probing: they can expose errors without systematically mapping the structure of model weaknesses.

The framework treats probing as a hierarchical Monte Carlo Tree Search. It allocates a limited testing budget between exploring new regions of failure and examining familiar error patterns more closely. Test generation and verification use tools, and probing is restricted to verifiable cases. These choices make reliable evidence part of the search process itself.

ProbeLLM then consolidates discovered failures using failure-aware embeddings and boundary-aware induction to produce interpretable failure modes. Across diverse models and benchmarks, it reports broader, cleaner, and more detailed failure landscapes than static evaluations and prior automated approaches. The contribution is a connected process for deciding where to test, checking that observed errors are valid, and turning individual mistakes into structured descriptions of recurring weaknesses.
summary.tldr: ProbeLLM combines budgeted search, verifiable tests, and failure consolidation to diagnose structured patterns of language-model weakness.

title: ProbeLLM: Automating Principled Diagnosis of LLM Failures

abstract: Deep learning surrogates for 3D Partial Differential Equations (PDEs) often fail to generalize across geometric transformations because they depend heavily on specific coordinate systems. While equivariant networks offer a solution, they typically rely on local operations in the spatial domain, making the global receptive field—essential for PDE dynamics—computationally expensive. Conversely, Fourier Neural Operators (FNOs) efficiently capture global interactions, yet establishing 3D equivariance within them remains impractical due to the prohibitive cost of spectral group convolutions. To bridge this gap, we introduce EqGINO, a geometrically robust framework that enforces isotropy in the spectral domain. By design, EqGINO guarantees exact equivariance to the discrete symmetries inherent to the discretized computational domain. Beyond this discrete guarantee, our structural prior enables effective generalization to arbitrary continuous orientations even with a limited number of SE(3)-transformed training samples. Consequently, our method robustly models coordinate-invariant physical laws on complex irregular 3D geometries. Our code is available at https://github.com/sung-won-kim/EqGINO

paragraphs: A learned model of a physical system should respond consistently when the geometry is reoriented. Many neural surrogates for three-dimensional partial differential equations depend too strongly on their coordinate system. Networks designed around symmetry address this issue, but combining symmetry with the global interactions needed for these equations can be computationally expensive.

EqGINO builds on Fourier neural operators, which efficiently represent interactions across a whole domain. It imposes isotropy in the spectral representation, providing a way to incorporate geometric structure without the prohibitive spectral group convolutions described in the paper. The resulting architecture guarantees exact equivariance for the discrete symmetries supported by its discretized computational domain.

The distinction between discrete and continuous transformations matters here. For arbitrary continuous orientations, the abstract claims effective generalization rather than exact equivariance. It reports that the structural prior supports this generalization with relatively few training examples transformed by three-dimensional rotations and translations. The approach therefore combines global interaction modeling with a precise discrete symmetry guarantee and broader empirical geometric robustness on complex, irregular three-dimensional domains.
summary.tldr: EqGINO combines Fourier neural operators with exact discrete equivariance and effective generalization to continuous orientations for 3D physical modeling.

title: EqGINO: Equivariant Geometry-Informed Fourier Neural Operators for 3D PDEs

abstract: Agent development kits (ADKs) provide effective platforms and tooling for constructing agents, and their designs are critical to the constructed agents’ performance, especially the functionality for agent topology, tools, and memory. However, current ADKs either lack sufficient functional support or rely on humans to manually design these components, limiting agents’ generalizability and overall performance. We propose OpenSage, the first ADK that enables LLMs to automatically create agents with self-generated topology and toolsets while providing comprehensive and structured memory support. OpenSage offers effective functionality for agents to create and manage their own sub-agents and toolkits. It also features a hierarchical, graph-based memory system for efficient management and a specialized toolkit tailored to software engineering tasks. Extensive experiments across three state-of-the-art benchmarks with various backbone models demonstrate the advantages of OpenSage over existing ADKs. We also conduct rigorous ablation studies to demonstrate the effectiveness of our design for each component. We believe OpenSage can pave the way for the next generation of agent development, shifting the focus from human-centered to AI-centered paradigms. Our code is available at https://github.com/opensage-agent/opensage-adk.

paragraphs: OpenSage is an agent development kit designed to let language models construct more of their own working organization. The paper argues that agent performance depends heavily on how agents, tools, and memory are arranged, yet existing kits either provide insufficient support or leave these decisions to human developers.

The system allows agents to create and manage sub-agents and toolkits, including generating their own topology and toolsets. It pairs this functionality with hierarchical, graph-based memory intended to support efficient, structured information management. A specialized toolkit supports software-engineering tasks. These components give the model facilities for both organizing work and retaining information within the resulting agent system.

Experiments across three benchmarks and several backbone models report advantages over existing agent development kits. Ablation studies examine the effectiveness of individual design components. The findings support the usefulness of the combined development infrastructure in those evaluations. The authors' broader ambition is a shift toward AI-directed agent construction, with automatic organization and tool creation taking on responsibilities commonly handled manually.
summary.tldr: OpenSage lets LLM agents generate and manage their own sub-agents and tools, supported by structured graph-based memory.

title: OpenSage: Self-programming Agent Generation Engine

abstract: Recent progress in Reinforcement Learning (RL) provides a principled approach to optimizing Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models, facilitating a shift from trajectory imitation to active learning in the task environment. Despite improvements in control precision, most RL optimizers remain task-specific, which reduces VLA models from generalist controllers to policies that overfit to a narrow set of tasks. In this study, we conduct an in-depth analysis of this phenomenon and highlight the importance of cross-task feature representations for improving the generalizability of VLA models. Motivated by this finding, we introduce DyGRO-VLA, a two-stage optimization framework that 1) effectively captures cross-task latent representations based on information-theoretic principles, and 2) dynamically refines policy optimization via a mixture-of-RL-residuals. DyGRO-VLA enables the RL optimizer to exploit task-relevant latent information while strategically mitigating adverse interference on the learned representations throughout the optimization process. We evaluate our approach on LIBERO, RoboTwin2 benchmarks, and further validate it on real world, demonstrating consistent improvements over strong baselines under multi-task training and distribution shift. Our project page is available at DyGRO-VLA.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning lets vision-language-action models improve by interacting with task environments. However, optimizing for particular tasks can weaken the broad competence that makes these models useful as generalist controllers. This paper examines that problem and identifies representations shared across tasks as important to maintaining generalization during reinforcement learning.

DyGRO-VLA uses a two-stage framework. The first stage captures cross-task latent representations using information-theoretic principles. The second dynamically refines policy optimization through a mixture of reinforcement-learning residuals. Together, these stages allow updates to use task-relevant information while reducing harmful interference with the representations already learned across tasks.

Evaluations on LIBERO and RoboTwin2, together with real-world validation, report consistent improvements over strong baselines in multi-task training and distribution-shift settings. The findings support the paper's focus on what optimization preserves as well as what it changes. Improving control for individual tasks is paired with protecting shared information that helps the controller operate across a broader task collection.
summary.tldr: DyGRO-VLA combines cross-task representation learning with adaptive reinforcement-learning updates to improve multi-task control and generalization.

title: DyGRO-VLA: Cross-Task Scaling of Vision–Language–Action Models via Dynamic Grouped Residual Optimization

abstract: Multi-view clustering aims to obtain a consensus clustering by integrating complementary and consistent information from multiple views. However, two critical challenges still exist in variational methods: (1) view heterogeneity and noise often make fusion unreliable; (2) ambiguous posteriors and misassigned boundary samples impact the clustering performance. To address these issues, we propose Dual-stage Contrastive Learning-enhanced Multi-view Variational Clustering (DCL-MVC), which integrates contrastive learning into both the fusion and representation stages. Firstly, at the fusion stage, we introduce a fusion-then-attention mechanism to capture cross-view interactions and learn view-level attention weights for building a unified and reliable fused representation, and further introduce instance-level contrastive learning to enforce cross-view alignment at the instance level. Secondly, we focus on boundary samples with uncertain posteriors and refine their cluster assignments by using cluster-center contrastive loss to enlarge inter-cluster margins, while leveraging prototypical contrastive learning with a confidence-aware curriculum to promote intra-cluster compactness at the representation stage. Extensive experiments on six real-world datasets demonstrate consistent improvements over strong baselines and validate the contribution of each component.

paragraphs: DCL-MVC aims to cluster examples described through multiple views into a shared grouping. Different views can contribute complementary information, but noise and differences between them can make fusion unreliable. A second problem arises near cluster boundaries, where uncertain assignment probabilities can lead to examples being placed in the wrong group.

The method introduces contrastive learning at two stages. During fusion, it first combines information and then applies attention to learn how much weight to give each view. An instance-level contrastive objective encourages representations of the same example across views to align. This stage targets the reliability of the shared representation before refining cluster structure.

During representation learning, a cluster-center contrastive loss increases separation between clusters, while prototypical contrastive learning encourages examples within a cluster to become more compact. A confidence-aware curriculum guides this process, with particular attention to uncertain boundary examples. Experiments on six real-world datasets report consistent gains over strong baselines and support the contribution of each component. The results connect improved cross-view fusion with more decisive cluster assignments.
summary.tldr: DCL-MVC uses contrastive learning during both multi-view fusion and cluster refinement to improve alignment and resolve uncertain assignments.

title: Dual-stage Contrastive Learning-enhanced Multi-view Variational Clustering

abstract: We study a simple yet principled modification of classical Q-learning that clips the value estimate in the Bellman backup by a threshold $\lambda$. The resulting algorithm, clipped Q-learning, is motivated by a key theoretical insight: the clipped Bellman backup is an unbiased one-sample estimation of a robust Bellman operator arising naturally from a transition-regularized MDP framework. This formulation corresponds to optimizing performance against a specific class of adversarial dynamics perturbations at the test time that reallocate transition probability mass away from high-value states, thereby inducing conservative but stable decision making. Under this interpretation, clipped Q-learning can be viewed as tracking the fixed point of the robust Bellman equation and learning policies that hedge against adversarial dynamics shifts at test time. We analyze two clipped Q-learning variants with an optimistic exploration bonus and establish polynomial regret guarantees, demonstrating statistical efficiency. Beyond the tabular setting, our framework suggests that value clipping is a modular mechanism that can be incorporated into general value-based RL algorithms with function approximation. As a proof of concept, we evaluate a clipped Double DQN algorithm on a control task and observe robustness improvements consistent with our theoretical predictions.

The theoretical result is that this clipped update provides an unbiased single-sample estimate of a robust Bellman operator arising from a transition-regularized decision-process formulation.

The corresponding robustness concerns a particular class of adversarial changes to environment dynamics: transition probability is moved away from high-value states. Under this interpretation, clipped Q-learning learns against that adverse possibility, producing more conservative decisions. The claim is specific to this perturbation class, rather than a guarantee against every possible environmental change. The authors also analyze two variants with optimistic exploration bonuses and establish polynomial regret guarantees.

Beyond tabular problems, the framework suggests that clipping could serve as a modular addition to value-based algorithms using function approximation. A clipped Double DQN experiment on one control task provides a proof of concept, showing robustness improvements consistent with the theory. The contribution connects a simple numerical operation to a precise objective for hedging against adverse dynamics.
summary.tldr: Clipped Q-learning has a theoretical interpretation as learning robustly against specific adverse changes in transition probabilities.

title: Clipped Q-Learning: Your Value Clipping Is Secretly A Robust Operator

abstract: Reliable long-horizon precipitation nowcasting requires preserving fine-scale echo structures while maintaining coherent transport. Although Rectified Flow (RF) can generate detail-preserving future sequences, numerical ODE integration compounds velocity estimation errors and induces progressive off-manifold drift, causing morphological distortions at extended lead times. We propose Physically-guided Data-space Rectified Flow (PDRF), which re-parameterizes the generative ODE in data space: the network predicts the clean future sequence, analytically inducing a coupled vector field with an implicit restoring effect that suppresses drift. We also introduce a soft Semi-Lagrangian teacher based on an advection prior to regularize large-scale transport, while allowing local growth/decay/deformation to be learned from data. Experiments on four public benchmarks demonstrate consistent improvements in event-based skill and better preservation of intense-echo morphology over long horizons.

The paper identifies this accumulation as a source of drift away from plausible sequences and distortion of echo morphology at later forecast times.

That prediction analytically determines a coupled vector field with an implicit restoring effect, helping suppress drift. The physical guidance remains soft so the network can learn local growth, decay, and deformation from observations. The approach therefore combines a generative parameterization intended to resist accumulated error with transport guidance that still leaves room for locally evolving precipitation.
summary.tldr: PDRF predicts clean future precipitation sequences and adds soft transport guidance to reduce drift and preserve intense-echo structure.

title: Physically-Guided Data-Space Rectified Flow for Precipitation Nowcasting

abstract: While flow-based generative models have demonstrated strong performance across a wide range of domains, deploying them in safety-critical physical systems remains challenging due to strict constraint requirements. Existing approaches typically enforce safety through post-hoc corrections, which incur substantial computational overhead and may distort the learned distribution. We propose PolyFlow, a polytope-constrained flow matching framework that embeds constraints directly into the model and flow dynamics. PolyFlow introduces a discrete-time flow formulation and a projection-free architecture, which eliminate the numeration error and guarantee strict satisfaction of arbitrary polyhedral constraints, without the need for expensive iterative solvers. Experimental results show that PolyFlow achieves zero constraint violation while maintaining high distributional fidelity across a range of planning and control tasks. Compared to state-of-the-art constrained generation baselines, PolyFlow significantly reduces inference latency and demonstrates a favorable trade-off between safety, efficiency, and generative quality.

The guarantee concerns the specified polyhedral constraints, which are the form of safety requirement explicitly represented within the framework.
summary.tldr: PolyFlow builds polyhedral constraints into flow generation, achieving zero reported violations and lower inference latency in planning and control experiments.

title: PolyFlow: Safe and Efficient Polytope-Constrained Flow Matching with Constraint Embedding and Projection-free Update

abstract: The quadratic computational complexity of self-attention remains a fundamental bottleneck for scaling Large Language Models (LLMs) to long contexts, particularly during the pre-filling phase. In this paper, we rethink the causal attention mechanism from the perspective of information flow. Due to causal constraints, tokens at initial positions participate in the aggregation of every subsequent token. However, existing sparse methods typically apply a uniform top-$k$ selection across all token positions within a layer, ignoring the cumulative dependency of token information inherent in causal architectures. To address this, we propose Stem, a novel, plug-and-play sparsity module aligned with information flow. First, Stem employs the Token Position-Decay strategy, applying position-dependent top-$k$ within each layer to retain initial tokens for recursive dependencies. Second, to preserve information-rich tokens, Stem utilizes the Output-Aware Metric. It prioritizes high-impact tokens based on approximate output magnitude. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that Stem achieves superior accuracy with reduced computation and pre-filling latency. Code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/stem-254ENLXL.

paragraphs: Long-context attention is expensive, especially while a model processes its input before generating output. Sparse attention reduces that work by selecting fewer tokens, but uniform selection rules can overlook how information accumulates in a causal model. Early tokens can contribute to many later token representations, creating dependencies across positions.

Stem introduces a plug-and-play sparsity module built around that information flow. Its Token Position-Decay strategy varies the number of retained tokens by position within a layer, helping preserve early-token information involved in recursive dependencies. Its Output-Aware Metric additionally prioritizes tokens according to their approximate contribution to output magnitude.

These two choices address complementary questions: how token position affects information flow, and which tokens have substantial output impact. The evaluations report better accuracy alongside reduced computation and pre-filling latency. The findings support treating causal structure as part of the sparsity decision, so attention selection can preserve influential information while reducing the work required to process long inputs.
summary.tldr: Stem makes sparse attention sensitive to token position and output impact, improving accuracy while reducing computation and pre-filling latency.

title: Stem: Rethinking Causal Information Flow in Sparse Attention

abstract: Natural language interfaces can greatly benefit the accessibility and usability of optimization modeling, and recent advances in large language models (LLMs) show promise in automatically translating textual problem descriptions into executable solver formulations. However, a key challenge for existing approaches is to ensure that the inferred formulation correctly implements the intended task, even if it may execute without errors. We introduce VeriSimpl, a solver–LLM framework for robust natural-language-to-optimization formalization. Our approach is based on the idea of simplification-based verification, where the optimization solver is leveraged to generate simplified diagnostic queries about a candidate formulation to allow the LLM to tractably reason about the correctness of the formulation with respect to the task description. We present such simplification strategies along different dimensions with respect to problem constraints and decision variables, which allow the LLM to reason locally under fixed global contexts. Evaluations on a range of optimization benchmarks show how our approach provides consistent improvements in accuracy over existing methods, while also providing a novel high-precision self-verification signal.

paragraphs: A solver formulation can execute successfully while representing the wrong optimization problem. VeriSimpl addresses this gap when language models translate natural-language descriptions into executable formulations. Its goal is to check whether the mathematical model reflects the intended task, beyond whether the resulting formulation can run without errors.

The framework couples an LLM with an optimization solver through simplification-based verification. The solver generates simplified diagnostic queries about a candidate formulation, giving the LLM smaller questions to reason through against the original description. Simplification strategies operate on constraints and decision variables, allowing local checks while holding the surrounding global context fixed.

Across optimization benchmarks, VeriSimpl consistently improves accuracy over existing methods and provides a high-precision self-verification signal. The findings support making formulation checking more tractable through targeted simplification. They also show a useful role for the solver within the verification process: it helps construct diagnostic questions that enable the language model to assess the meaning of its own proposed formulation.
summary.tldr: VeriSimpl uses solver-generated simplified questions to help LLMs verify that optimization formulations match their natural-language descriptions.

title: VeriSimpl: Robust Optimization Modeling from Natural Language using Simplification-based Verification

abstract: We study beyond worst case analysis for the $k$-means problem where the goal is to model typical instances of $k$-means arising in practice. Existing theoretical approaches provide guarantees under certain assumptions on the optimal solutions to $k$-means, making them difficult to validate in practice. We adopt the manifold hypothesis, where data obtained in ambient dimension $D$ concentrates around a low dimensional manifold of intrinsic dimension $d$, as a reasonable assumption to model real world clustering instances. We identify key geometric properties of datasets which have theoretically predictable scaling laws depending on the quantization exponent $\varepsilon = 2/d$ using techniques from optimum quantization theory. We show how to exploit these regularities to design a fast seeding method called $\operatorname{Qkmeans}$ which provides $O(\rho^{-2} \log k)$ approximate solutions to the $k$-means problem in time $O(nD \log k) + \widetilde{O}(\rho^{-1}k^{1+\gamma})$; where the exponent $\gamma = \varepsilon + \rho$ for an input parameter $\rho < 1$. This allows us to obtain new runtime - quality tradeoffs. We perform a large scale empirical study across various domains to validate our theoretical predictions and algorithm performance to bridge theory and practice for beyond worst case data clustering.

paragraphs: The paper seeks a theory of k-means clustering that better reflects practical datasets than worst-case analysis. Instead of assuming properties of an unknown optimal clustering, it assumes that high-dimensional observations concentrate around a lower-dimensional manifold. This shifts attention toward geometric properties of the data that can be examined empirically.

Using optimum quantization theory, the authors identify geometric scaling laws tied to intrinsic dimension. They exploit those regularities in Qkmeans, a fast method for selecting initial cluster centers. An input parameter controls a tradeoff between runtime and approximation quality, while intrinsic dimension affects the exponent in part of the computational cost.

The stated runtime includes a term proportional to the number of points, ambient dimension, and logarithm of the number of clusters, plus an additional cluster-dependent term. Its approximation guarantee also depends on the tradeoff parameter. A large empirical study across domains examines both the predicted scaling behavior and algorithm performance. The contribution connects a concrete geometric assumption to tunable guarantees for practical clustering initialization.
summary.tldr: Qkmeans uses geometric scaling laws under the manifold hypothesis to offer new speed–quality tradeoffs for k-means initialization.

title: Fast k-means Seeding Under The Manifold Hypothesis

abstract: Aligning large language models to human preferences is inherently multidimensional, yet most pipelines collapse heterogeneous signals into a single objective. We seek to answer what it would take to simultaneously align a model across various domains spanning those with: verifiable rewards, non-verifiable subjective preferences, and complex interactive scenarios. Such multi-objective alignment setups are often plagued by individual objectives being at odds with each other, resulting in inefficient training and limited user control during inference. To address these issues, we propose Multi-Action-Head ALignment with PRM-guided DecOding (MAHALO), a unified framework that standardizes PRM training across verifiable and non-verifiable settings for step-level supervision, performs vectorized multi-objective alignment with Multi-Action-Head DPO, and enables controllable inference through objective-specific weighting and PRM-guided decoding. Experiments across math reasoning, human values alignment, and multi-turn tutoring show that MAHALO jointly improves multiple objectives simultaneously with limited interference, while remaining generalizable and adaptable across domains and offering flexible user control at inference time. Our code is available at: https://github.com/pearls-lab/multiobj-align.

paragraphs: Aligning a language model involves several objectives that can conflict, including objectively checkable outcomes, subjective preferences, and goals within interactive exchanges. Combining all these signals into one score can make training inefficient and limit users' ability to adjust priorities later. MAHALO provides a unified framework for retaining and coordinating multiple objectives across these settings.

The framework standardizes training for process reward models, which provide supervision at individual steps. It combines this with Multi-Action-Head Direct Preference Optimization to perform vectorized multi-objective alignment. During inference, objective-specific weights and process-reward-guided decoding let the system adjust how different goals influence its output. This connects the training objectives with controls available when the model is used.

Experiments cover mathematical reasoning, human-values alignment, and multi-turn tutoring. MAHALO improves multiple objectives simultaneously with limited interference and demonstrates generalization and adaptability across domains. The findings indicate that heterogeneous reward signals can be coordinated while preserving flexible inference-time control; they do not imply that all conflicts between objectives disappear.
summary.tldr: MAHALO coordinates verifiable and subjective alignment objectives while allowing users to adjust objective priorities during inference.

title: Simultaneous Multi-objective Alignment Across Verifiable and Non-verifiable Rewards

abstract: In embodied vision, Goal-Oriented Navigation (GON) requires robots to locate a specific goal within an unexplored environment. The primary challenge of GON arises from the need to construct a Bird’s-Eye-View (BEV) map to understand the environment while simultaneously localizing an unobserved goal. Existing map-based methods typically employ self-centered semantic maps, often facing challenges such as reliance on complete maps or inconsistent semantic association. To this end, we propose Plug-and-Play Label Map Diffusion (PLMD), which defines a novel map completion diffusion model based on Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models (DDPM). PLMD generates obstacle and semantic labels for unobserved regions through a diffusion-based completion process, thereby enabling goal localization even in partially observed environments. Moreover, it mitigates inconsistent semantic association by leveraging structural consistency between known and unknown obstacle layouts and integrating obstacle priors into the semantic denoising process. By substituting predicted labels for unobserved regions, robots can accurately localize the specified objects. Extensive experiments demonstrate that PLMD (I) effectively expands the region of unknown maps, (II) integrates seamlessly into existing navigation strategies that rely on semantic maps, (III) achieves state-of-the-art performance on three GON tasks. Code is available at: https://github.com/FrankZxShen/PLMD.

paragraphs: Goal-oriented navigation requires a robot to find a specified target in an environment it has not fully explored. Map-based approaches must build a spatial representation while also estimating where an unseen goal might be. This paper introduces PLMD, a diffusion-based method that completes missing parts of a bird's-eye-view map with predicted obstacle and semantic labels.

The method generates labels for unobserved regions through a denoising diffusion process. It uses structural consistency between known and unknown obstacle layouts, then incorporates obstacle priors into semantic denoising. This connects predictions about what occupies a location with predictions about the surrounding physical layout, addressing inconsistent semantic associations in partially observed maps.

The completed labels support goal localization before the entire environment has been observed. Experiments show that PLMD extends maps into unknown regions, integrates into existing navigation strategies that use semantic maps, and achieves state-of-the-art performance on three goal-oriented navigation tasks. Its plug-and-play contribution is therefore a map-completion component that supplies existing navigation systems with useful predictions about unseen space.
summary.tldr: PLMD predicts obstacle and semantic labels in unseen map regions, helping existing navigation systems locate goals in partially explored environments.

title: Plug-and-Play Label Map Diffusion for Universal Goal-Oriented Navigation

abstract: We investigate the origins of massive activations in large language models (LLMs) and identify a specific layer named the Massive Emergence Layer (ME Layer), that is consistently observed across model families, where massive activations first emerge and subsequently propagate to deeper layers through residual connections. We show that, within the ME Layer both the RMSNorm and the FFN parameters jointly contribute to the emergence of massive activations. Once formed, the massive activation token representation remains largely invariant across layers, reducing the diversity of hidden representations passed to the attention module. Motivated by this limitation, we propose a simple and effective method to reduce the rigidity of the massive activation token. Our approach consistently improves LLM performance across multiple tasks, including instruction following and math reasoning, in both training free and fine tuning settings. Moreover, we show that our method mitigates attention sinks by selectively weakening their influence, elucidating their origin at the hidden state level and shedding new light on principled mitigation strategies.

paragraphs: Some internal activations in language models become unusually large. This paper traces where those values first arise, identifying a Massive Emergence Layer across the model families studied. After appearing there, the activations travel into deeper layers through residual connections. This focuses the explanation on a particular point of origin and the mechanism that carries its effects forward.

Within that layer, the authors find that RMSNorm and feed-forward network parameters jointly contribute to the large activations. The affected token representation then changes relatively little across subsequent layers. That persistence reduces the variety of hidden representations supplied to attention, linking the activation phenomenon to a specific restriction on the model’s internal processing.

The proposed intervention reduces this rigidity. The authors report consistent improvements across multiple tasks, including instruction following and mathematical reasoning, both without additional training and with fine-tuning. They also find that selectively weakening these representations mitigates attention sinks. Together, the findings connect an observable attention behavior to its hidden-state origins and identify a practical intervention point.
summary.tldr: The paper traces massive activations to a particular layer and reduces their rigidity to improve performance and mitigate attention sinks.

title: A Single Layer to Explain Them All: Understanding Massive Activations in Large Language Models

abstract: Data selection studies the problem of identifying high-quality subsets of training data. While some existing works have considered selecting the subset of data with top-$m$ Data Shapley or other semivalues as they account for the interaction among every subset of data, other works argue that Data Shapley can sometimes perform ineffectively in practice and select subsets that are no better than random. This raises the questions: (I) Are there certain "Shapley-informative" settings where Data Shapley consistently works well? (II) Can we strategically utilize these settings to select high-quality subsets consistently and efficiently? In this paper, we propose a novel data selection framework, NASH (Non-linear Aggregation of SHapley-informative components), which (I) decomposes the target utility function (e.g., validation accuracy) into simpler, Shapley-informative component functions, and selects data by optimizing an objective that (II) aggregates these components non-linearly. We demonstrate that NASH substantially boosts the effectiveness of Shapley/semivalue-based data selection with minimal additional runtime cost.

This raises the questions: (I) Are there certain "Shapley-informative" settings where Data Shapley consistently works well? (II) Can we strategically utilize these settings to select high-quality subsets consistently and efficiently? We demonstrate that NASH substantially boosts the effectiveness of Shapley/semivalue-based data selection with minimal additional runtime cost.

paragraphs: Data selection aims to retain a useful subset of training examples. One approach assigns each example a Data Shapley value or a related semivalue, then selects the highest-scoring examples. These values account for interactions across subsets, but earlier work has found cases where the resulting selection performs no better than random. This paper investigates how to use such information more effectively.

The proposed NASH framework decomposes the target utility, such as validation accuracy, into simpler component functions that are informative for Shapley-based selection. It then optimizes an objective that combines those components nonlinearly. The approach changes both the level at which usefulness is analyzed and how the resulting signals are assembled into a selection objective.

The authors report substantial improvements in the effectiveness of Shapley- and semivalue-based selection with minimal additional runtime. The finding supports a more structured use of data valuations: useful component-level information can contribute to better subset choices through nonlinear aggregation. It does not require interpreting the original top-scoring-example strategy as consistently effective across all settings.
summary.tldr: NASH improves Shapley-based data selection by decomposing utility into informative components and combining them nonlinearly.

title: Is Data Shapley Not Better than Random in Data Selection? Ask NASH

abstract: Recently, zero-shot 3D scene understanding via 2D Vision-Language Models (VLMs) has gained increasing research interest due to their promising spatial reasoning capabilities. Typically, multiple 2D views are sampled from a 3D point cloud and fed into pre-trained VLMs to answer a given question. This paradigm highlights the critical role of input context quality and raises the challenge of retaining as many task-relevant 3D details as possible under a limited input budget. We propose KeyVT, a hierarchical approach for input context collection at both the view and token levels. Specifically, we combine pixel features with camera parameters and assess view importance based on both semantic content and geometric position, resulting in spatially consistent and task-relevant views. Furthermore, we address redundancy among patches across selected views by identifying representative tokens under the optimal transport (OT) framework, where view tokens and key tokens are formulated as two discrete distributions in the embedding space. These key tokens are expected to cover all view features by minimizing the OT distance. We evaluate our framework on three widely used benchmarks, demonstrating significant improvements over existing tuning-free methods and performance comparable to training-based approaches.

We propose KeyVT, a hierarchical approach for input context collection at both the view and token levels. Specifically, we combine pixel features with camera parameters and assess view importance based on both semantic content and geometric position, resulting in spatially consistent and task-relevant views. paragraphs: A pretrained two-dimensional vision-language model can answer questions about a three-dimensional scene by inspecting views rendered from its point cloud. The challenge is selecting enough relevant scene information within a limited input budget. KeyVT addresses this at two levels: which views to include and which tokens to retain from those views.

View selection combines pixel features with camera parameters, evaluating both semantic relevance and geometric position. This encourages views that are useful for the question and spatially consistent. Token selection then reduces redundancy across the chosen images. An optimal transport formulation treats view tokens and representative key tokens as two discrete distributions in embedding space and minimizes the distance between them to encourage feature coverage.

On three benchmarks, KeyVT significantly improves over existing tuning-free methods and achieves performance comparable to training-based approaches. The findings show that organizing the input context can materially improve zero-shot 3D question answering. The method connects scene-level coverage with token-level compression, addressing both the choice of visual perspectives and repeated information within them.
summary.tldr: KeyVT selects geometrically informed views and representative visual tokens to improve zero-shot 3D question answering within a limited input budget.

title: Zero-Shot 3D Question Answering via Hierarchical View-to-Token Transportation

abstract: Diffusion models have shown remarkable performance on diverse generation tasks. Recent work finds that imposing representation alignment on the hidden states of diffusion networks can both facilitate training convergence and enhance sampling quality, yet the mechanism driving this synergy remains insufficiently understood. In this paper, we investigate the connection between self-supervised spectral representation learning and diffusion generative models through a shared perspective on perturbation kernels. On the diffusion side, samples (e.g., images, videos) are produced by reversing a stochastic noise-injection process specified by Gaussian kernels; on the spectral representation side, spectral embeddings emerge from contrasting positive and negative relations induced by random perturbation kernels. Motivated by this, we propose a self-supervised spectral representation alignment method to facilitate diffusion model training. In addition, we clarify how joint spectral learning can benefit diffusion training from a geometric perspective. Furthermore, we find that the optimization of the spectral alignment objective is in an equivalent form of diffusion score distillation in the representation space. Building on these findings, we integrate a spectral regularizer into diffusion training objectives to improve the performance of diffusion models on multiple datasets. Experiments across images and 3D point clouds show consistent gains in generation quality.
originalAbstract: Diffusion models have shown remarkable performance on diverse generation tasks. Recent work finds that imposing representation alignment on the hidden states of diffusion networks can both facilitate training convergence and enhance sampling quality, yet the mechanism driving this synergy remains insufficiently understood.
