On the diffusion side, samples (e.g., images, videos) are produced by reversing a stochastic noise-injection process specified by Gaussian kernels; on the spectral representation side, spectral embeddings emerge from contrasting positive and negative relations induced by random perturbation kernels. Motivated by this, we propose a self-supervised spectral representation alignment method to facilitate diffusion model training. In addition, we clarify how joint spectral learning can benefit diffusion training from a geometric perspective. Furthermore, we find that the optimization of the spectral alignment objective is in an equivalent form of diffusion score distillation in the representation space. Building on these findings, we integrate a spectral regularizer into diffusion training objectives to improve the performance of diffusion models on multiple datasets. Experiments across images and 3D point clouds show consistent gains in generation quality.

This paper investigates a connection between diffusion generation and self-supervised spectral representation learning. Both processes can be examined through the kernels that describe how data is randomly perturbed.

Diffusion models reverse a noise-injection process governed by Gaussian kernels. Spectral representation learning uses positive and negative relationships arising from perturbation kernels to form embeddings. Drawing on this shared structure, the authors propose self-supervised spectral alignment and explain its potential benefits geometrically. They also find that optimizing the alignment objective has an equivalent form to diffusion score distillation in representation space.

The practical method adds a spectral regularizer to the diffusion training objective. Experiments on images and three-dimensional point clouds show consistent improvements in generation quality across multiple datasets. The work therefore combines a conceptual explanation of representation alignment with a training modification, connecting the geometry of learned representations to the process used to generate samples.
summary.tldr: A shared perturbation-kernel perspective motivates spectral representation regularization that improves diffusion generation on images and 3D point clouds.

title: Revisiting Spectral Representations in Generative Diffusion Models

abstract: Deep multi-view graph clustering (DMGC) typically leverages graph neural networks for representation learning, but most existing methods excessively depend on local and static graph structures and only utilize simplistic cross-view fusion strategies. To this end, this paper proposes Attribute-aware Bidirectional Structural Refinement (ABSR) and Pseudo-label Guided Multi-level Fusion (PGMF) for DMGC, termed APGC. Specifically, ABSR selectively strengthens high-quality connections and suppresses semantically conflicting relationships, achieving bidirectional refinement of the graph structure based on attribute similarity. It incorporates global attribute semantics into the graph structure, thereby promoting the homophilic connections for discriminative graph representation learning. Guided by reliable pseudo-labels, PGMF achieves adaptive weighted fusion at both the node-level and the view-level, effectively balancing the differentiated contributions of multi-view information. Experiments on six homophilic and heterophilic datasets demonstrate the superior clustering performance of the proposed APGC method. The code of APGC could be available at https://github.com/TianxiangZhao0474/APGC.git.

paragraphs: Multi-view graph clustering groups nodes using several views of graph information. Existing methods can depend too heavily on fixed local connections and combine views too simply. APGC addresses these issues by modifying which relationships the model relies on and adapting how much information it takes from different nodes and views.

Its structural refinement module uses attribute similarity to strengthen useful connections and suppress relationships whose semantics conflict. Incorporating global attribute information promotes links between similar nodes, helping the graph neural network learn representations that distinguish clusters. The refinement is bidirectional in the sense that it can both reinforce and weaken connections, rather than merely adding more structure.

A second module uses reliable pseudo-labels to guide weighted fusion at both the node level and the view level. This allows different information sources to contribute unequally where appropriate. Experiments on six datasets, including graphs that connect similar nodes and graphs that connect dissimilar nodes, show superior clustering performance. The results support jointly refining graph structure and learning how to combine multiple views.
summary.tldr: APGC improves multi-view graph clustering by refining connections using attributes and adaptively combining information with pseudo-label guidance.

title: Deep Multi-view Graph Clustering via Attribute-aware Bidirectional Structural Refinement and Pseudo-label Guided Multi-level Fusion

abstract: Augmenting Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) with world models is promising for robotic policy learning but faces challenges in jointly predicting states and actions due to the modality gap. To address this, we propose DUal-STream diffusion (DUST), a world-model augmented VLA framework featuring a multimodal diffusion transformer that maintains separate modality streams while enabling cross-modal knowledge sharing. In addition, DUST utilizes independent noise perturbations and a decoupled flow matching loss to learn cross-modal causal relationships. We further introduce an asynchronous sampling method for action and vision tokens that enhances performance through inference-time scaling. Experimental results on simulated benchmarks like RoboCasa and GR-1 show that DUST achieves up to 6% gains over state-of-the-art VLA and world-modeling baselines, with inference-time scaling providing an additional 2–5% improvement. In real-world tasks using the Franka Research 3, DUST outperforms baselines by 10% in success rate. Finally, we demonstrate that DUST enables effective transfer learning through both pretraining on action-free videos and joint-training with heterogeneous robot and human datasets.

paragraphs: A robot policy can benefit from predicting both what action to take and how the world will change. Combining these predictions is difficult because visual states and actions are different kinds of information. DUST addresses this gap with a multimodal diffusion transformer that keeps vision and action in separate streams while allowing information to pass between them.

The training procedure applies independent noise perturbations and uses a decoupled flow-matching loss to learn causal relationships across modalities. At inference, an asynchronous sampling method handles action and vision tokens on different schedules. This provides a way to improve performance through additional inference-time computation while retaining the separation between the two streams.

On RoboCasa and GR-1 simulations, the authors report gains of up to 6% over leading vision-language-action and world-modeling baselines, with inference-time scaling adding 2–5%. On Franka Research 3 tasks, they report a 10% success-rate improvement over baselines. DUST also supports transfer through action-free video pretraining and joint training on heterogeneous robot and human datasets.
summary.tldr: DUST separates but connects visual and action diffusion streams, improving robotic performance and supporting transfer from varied video and interaction data.

title: Dual-Stream Diffusion for World-Model Augmented Vision-Language-Action Model

abstract: Generating runnable front-end code from UI screenshots is a long-standing goal in automated software engineering. Existing MLLM-based methods predominantly focused on HTML/CSS, leaving multi-framework generation for React/Vue/Angular underexplored. Naively modifying prompts leads to substantial performance gaps across multi-framework and highly framework-specific error modes. To address this, we propose MulFCoder, a framework-conditioned multi-agent method that explicitly encodes framework constraints to bring multi-framework differences into a decidable rule space. MulFCoder orchestrates four agents: Grounder constructs an ElementTable, ContentTable, and macro-layout regions from detected UI elements; Planner builds a DOM-like hierarchical layout tree, produces a task schedule, and derives a framework-specific file Contract; Writer generates structured file writes or patches within a restricted edit window; Judger enforces lightweight, framework-conditioned constraints to accept or reject updates and trigger bounded repairs, preventing drift and deadlocks without expensive builds. Experiments demonstrate that MulFCoder substantially improves compilation success rate and reduces framework-specific errors, with particularly pronounced gains on Angular.

paragraphs: Turning a screenshot into runnable front-end code requires more than reconstructing its visual layout. React, Vue, and Angular impose different structural requirements, and simply changing a prompt can produce framework-specific failures. MulFCoder makes those requirements explicit through rules that guide a coordinated four-agent generation process.

The Grounder organizes detected interface elements, content, and broad layout regions. The Planner converts that information into a hierarchical layout tree, a task schedule, and a framework-specific file contract. The Writer then produces structured file edits within a restricted window. The Judger checks lightweight constraints, accepts or rejects changes, and initiates bounded repairs without relying on expensive builds.

This division connects screenshot interpretation to concrete restrictions on how code is planned, written, and repaired. The framework-conditioned checks are intended to prevent drift and deadlocks during the process. Experiments report substantially higher compilation success and fewer framework-specific errors, with especially pronounced improvements for Angular. The findings support treating framework differences as explicit generation constraints rather than expecting a generic screenshot-to-code prompt to handle them implicitly.
summary.tldr: MulFCoder coordinates four agents around explicit framework rules to improve screenshot-to-code compilation success across front-end frameworks.

title: MulFCoder: Framework-conditioned Multi-agent for MLLM-based Multi-framework Front-end Code Generation

abstract: Policy gradient methods rely on a baseline to measure the relative advantage of an action. In Actor-Critic LLM training (e.g., PPO), this baseline is typically estimated by a Value Model as large as the policy. However, as the policy evolves, the value model requires expensive, synchronous training. To avoid this overhead, GRPO eliminates the value model by using the average reward of group rollouts as the baseline; yet, this necessitates extensive sampling to maintain stability. In this paper, we propose $V_0$, a Generalist Value Model capable of estimating the expected performance of any model on unseen prompts without parameter updates. We reframe value estimation by treating the policy’s dynamic capability as an explicit context input, leveraging a history of instruction-performance pairs to dynamically profile the model. Acting as a resource scheduler, $V_0$ predicts success rates prior to rollout during GRPO training for efficient sampling budget allocation. During deployment, it functions as a router dispatching instructions to the most cost-effective model. Empirical results demonstrate that $V_0$ significantly outperforms heuristic budget allocation and achieves a Pareto-optimal performance-cost trade-off in LLM routing.

paragraphs: Reinforcement-learning systems need a baseline for judging how good a response is relative to expectation. Maintaining a large value model can require expensive synchronized training as the policy changes. Estimating a baseline from groups of sampled responses avoids that model but can demand extensive sampling for stability.

V₀ estimates expected model performance on unseen prompts without updating its parameters. It takes a history of instruction–performance pairs as context, using that history to characterize the policy’s current capabilities. This makes the changing policy an explicit input to prediction rather than something that must be tracked solely through updates to the value model’s weights.

During GRPO training, V₀ predicts success before rollouts and guides allocation of the sampling budget. During deployment, it routes instructions to a cost-effective model. Experiments show substantial improvements over heuristic budget allocation and a Pareto-optimal performance–cost trade-off in routing. These results connect capability prediction to two resource decisions: where to spend training samples and which model to use for an instruction.
summary.tldr: V₀ uses a model’s performance history to predict success without parameter updates, guiding training budgets and cost-effective deployment routing.

title: $V_0$: A Generalist Value Model for Any Policy at State Zero

abstract: Current Video-LLM approaches for Video Temporal Grounding (VTG) typically rely on direct timestamp generation from an unstructured visual-token stream, often leading to brittle numerics and inconsistent boundaries. To address this, we propose Foresee-to-Ground (F2G), a framework that reformulates VTG as a verifiable Identify-then-Measure problem. F2G integrates Predictive Temporal Perception with Evidence-Driven Reasoning: it learns boundary-sensitive temporal representations to build a video-wide evidence pool of candidate event segments, and exposes these segments to the LLM as citable evidence units that bind boundary prediction to explicit event hypotheses. By decoupling event identification from precise boundary measurement, F2G stabilizes grounding and makes predictions verifiable. Extensive experiments demonstrate that F2G consistently improves grounding accuracy across diverse benchmarks, transfers robustly across different Video-LLM backbones, and preserves general video understanding capabilities. Our project is available at https://github.com/zelion2003/Foresee-to-Ground.

paragraphs: Video temporal grounding asks a model to locate an event's boundaries within a video. Existing video language models often generate timestamps directly from an unstructured sequence of visual tokens. The paper identifies this direct numerical prediction as a source of unstable timestamps and inconsistent boundaries, and proposes separating event identification from boundary measurement.

Foresee-to-Ground learns temporal representations that are sensitive to event boundaries. It uses them to construct a video-wide collection of candidate event segments, which the language model can reference as explicit evidence. Each boundary prediction is consequently tied to a proposed event segment, giving the reasoning process a concrete temporal object to identify and measure.

The authors report consistent grounding improvements across multiple benchmarks and robust transfer across different video language model backbones, while retaining general video understanding capabilities. The significance is both predictive and procedural: the framework improves event localization while making the basis of a prediction inspectable through its associated evidence segment. Its stated verifiability comes from this explicit connection between event hypotheses and boundaries.
summary.tldr: Foresee-to-Ground improves video event localization by identifying explicit candidate segments before measuring their temporal boundaries.

title: Foresee-to-Ground: From Predictive Temporal Perception to Evidence-Driven Reasoning for Video Temporal Grounding

abstract: Graph foundation models (GFMs) aim to reuse a single backbone across diverse graph domains, yet their transfer is often uneven and can exhibit negative transfer. While most prior work improves transfer through architectural or adaptation choices, we ask a data-centric question: which properties of two graph domains determine how much a fixed representation model changes its outputs? Using a graphon-based continuous limit for dense graphs, we show that for both set-based and message-passing tokenizations, any Lipschitz backbone admits an explicit decomposition of cross-domain output shift into (i) graph-specific finite-sample approximation terms and (ii) an intrinsic, relabeling-invariant domain discrepancy capturing structural mismatch. A key ingredient is positional-encoding (PE) stability: we establish stability guarantees for spectral PEs and highlight contrasting behaviors of eigenvector- versus subspace-based PEs. Experiments on synthetic and real graphs validate the theory and translate the decomposition into guidance for data curation in GFM transfer.

paragraphs: Graph foundation models aim to reuse one backbone across graph domains, but transfer can be uneven or harmful. This paper asks which properties of the data explain changes in a fixed model’s outputs. It shifts attention toward the relationship between source and target graph structure, rather than changing the model architecture or adaptation procedure.

Using a graphon-based continuous limit for dense graphs, the authors decompose cross-domain output shift into finite-sample approximation terms and an intrinsic domain discrepancy. The discrepancy captures structural mismatch independently of node relabeling. The result applies to Lipschitz backbones under both set-based and message-passing tokenizations, making the model’s regularity and the dense-graph setting explicit parts of the theoretical framework.

Positional-encoding stability is central to the analysis. The paper establishes stability guarantees for spectral encodings and identifies contrasting behavior between eigenvector-based and subspace-based constructions. Experiments on synthetic and real graphs validate the theory and connect the decomposition to data-curation guidance. The contribution separates effects associated with finite graph sampling from those associated with underlying domain structure when studying transfer.
summary.tldr: A dense-graph theory separates cross-domain output shifts into finite-sample effects and structural mismatch, offering guidance for graph-model transfer.

title: When Do Graph Foundation Models Transfer? A Data-Centric Theory

abstract: Indirect reciprocity, which means helping those who have helped others, is difficult to sustain among decentralized, self-interested LLM agents without reliable reputation systems. We address this challenge with the Agentic LInguistic Gossip Network (ALIGN), an automated framework that enables decentralized agents to form reputations, evaluate trustworthiness, and coordinate social norms by strategically sharing open-ended gossip with hierarchical tones. We demonstrate that ALIGN consistently improves indirect reciprocity and resists malicious entrants by identifying and ostracizing defectors. Notably, we find that stronger reasoning capabilities in LLMs lead to more incentive-aligned cooperation, whereas chat models often over-cooperate even when strategically suboptimal. These results suggest that leveraging LLM reasoning through decentralized gossip is a promising path for maintaining social welfare in agentic ecosystems. Our code is available at https://github.com/shuhui-zhu/ALIGN.

paragraphs: Indirect reciprocity means helping someone because they have helped others. Sustaining this behavior among decentralized, self-interested language-model agents requires some way to assess reputations. ALIGN investigates whether strategically shared linguistic gossip can supply that information and support cooperation without a centralized reputation system.

The framework lets agents exchange open-ended gossip with hierarchical tones, form reputations, judge trustworthiness, and coordinate social norms. In the reported evaluations, it consistently improves indirect reciprocity and resists malicious entrants by identifying and excluding defectors. Reputation formation therefore affects who receives cooperation, making exchanged judgments part of the agents' strategic decision process.

The authors also find that stronger reasoning capabilities lead to cooperation that better matches incentives. Chat models often cooperate excessively even when doing so is strategically unfavorable. This distinction matters because a higher amount of cooperation does not by itself demonstrate better decisions for self-interested agents. The findings suggest decentralized gossip combined with reasoning as a promising mechanism for maintaining social welfare in agent populations.
summary.tldr: ALIGN uses decentralized gossip to build agent reputations, improve indirect reciprocity, and identify defectors in the reported evaluations.

title: Talk, Judge, Cooperate: Gossip-Driven Indirect Reciprocity in Self-Interested LLM Agents

abstract: Image forgery is rapidly evolving, rendering forensic traces increasingly subtle and readily attenuated by post-processing. Although vision-language prompting can inject priors, open-ended LLM-generated prompts are difficult to constrain, and naive language descriptions can introduce semantic perturbations. To address these challenges, we propose Forensic Prompting with Dual-Action policy optimization (FPDA) for vision-language forgery detection and localization, where the Forensic Prompting Module (FPM) constructs a structured and reproducible forensic prompt bank and supports optional text input as a reliability-aware cue for stable conditioning. Moreover, Dual-Action Policy Optimization (DAPO) is applied to learn sample-adaptive evidence usage by routing forensic prompts and scheduling localization refinement on a per-image basis, stabilizing discriminative cues and improving mask spatial consistency. Extensive experiments are conducted on multiple public datasets covering manual manipulations, diffusion content, face forgeries, and text-enabled settings, demonstrating favorable detection and localization performance over representative state-of-the-art methods under comparable evaluation protocols.

paragraphs: FPDA addresses both detecting image forgery and identifying its location. The paper motivates its approach by noting that forensic traces are increasingly subtle and can be weakened by post-processing. Language prompts can supply useful prior information, but unconstrained generated prompts and naive descriptions can also disturb the semantic evidence used for detection.

Its Forensic Prompting Module creates a structured, reproducible bank of forensic prompts. Optional text is incorporated as a cue whose reliability informs conditioning. A second component, Dual-Action Policy Optimization, learns how to use evidence for each image. Its two actions route forensic prompts and schedule refinement of the localization result, aiming to stabilize discriminative clues and improve the spatial consistency of predicted masks.

The evaluation covers manual image manipulations, diffusion-generated content, face forgeries, and settings with text input. Under comparable evaluation protocols, the authors report favorable detection and localization performance against representative leading methods. The approach links controlled language guidance with adaptive visual refinement, so that prompt choice and localization effort respond to the particular image.
summary.tldr: FPDA combines structured forensic prompts with per-image policy decisions to improve forgery detection and localization.

title: Forensic Prompting with Dual-Action Policy Optimization for Vision-Language Forgery Detection and Localization
An Evaluation on Feature Selection for Text Clustering

abstract: In many real-world classification problems the input contains a large numberof potentially irrelevant features. This paper proposes a new Bayesian framework for determining the relevance of input features. Thisapproach extends one of the most successful Bayesian methods for featureselection and sparse learning, known as Automatic Relevance Determination(ARD). ARD finds the relevance of features by optimizing the model marginallikelihood, also known as the evidence. We show that this can lead tooverfitting. To address this problem, we propose Predictive ARD based onestimating the predictive performance of the classifier. While the actualleave-one-out predictive performance is generally very costly to compute, theexpectation propagation (EP) algorithm proposed by Minka provides an estimateof this predictive performance as a side-effect of its iterations. We exploitthis in our algorithm to do feature selection, and to select data points in asparse Bayesian kernel classifier. Moreover, we provide two other improvementsto previous algorithms, by replacing Laplace's approximation with thegenerally more accurate EP, and by incorporating the fast optimizationalgorithm proposed by Faul and Tipping. Our experiments show that our methodbased on the EP estimate of predictive performance is more accurate on testdata than relevance determination by optimizing the evidence.

paragraphs: The paper studies Bayesian feature selection for classifiers with many potentially irrelevant inputs. Standard automatic relevance determination, or ARD, assesses relevance by optimizing the model's marginal likelihood, also called evidence. The authors show that this objective can lead to overfitting and propose choosing relevance through estimated predictive performance instead.

Their Predictive ARD method uses expectation propagation to obtain an estimate of leave-one-out predictive performance as a byproduct of its iterations. Computing the actual leave-one-out performance is generally expensive, so this estimate makes the predictive criterion practical. The method uses it both to select input features and to select data points in a sparse Bayesian kernel classifier.

The approach also replaces a Laplace approximation with the generally more accurate expectation propagation approximation and incorporates a fast optimization algorithm. Experiments report better test accuracy than relevance determination based on evidence optimization. The finding supports prediction-oriented relevance selection in the evaluated settings, with the computational contribution being the reuse of an estimate already produced during approximate inference.
summary.tldr: Predictive ARD uses expectation propagation estimates to select relevant features and data points, improving test accuracy over evidence-based relevance selection in experiments.

title: Predictive automatic relevance determination by expectation propagation

abstract: Recently, several manifold learning algorithms have been proposed, such as ISOMAP (Tenenbaum et al., 2000), Locally Linear Embedding (Roweis & Saul, 2000), Laplacian Eigenmap (Belkin & Niyogi, 2001), Locality Preserving Projection (LPP) (He & Niyogi, 2003), etc. All of them aim at discovering the meaningful low dimensional structure of the data space. In this paper, we present a statistical analysis of the LPP algorithm. Different from Principal Component Analysis (PCA) which obtains a subspace spanned by the largest eigenvectors of the global covariance matrix, we show that LPP obtains a subspace spanned by the smallest eigenvectors of the local covariance matrix. We applied PCA and LPP to real world document clustering task. Experimental results show that the performance can be significantly improved in the subspace, and especially LPP works much better than PCA.

In this paper, we present a statistical analysis of the LPP algorithm. Different from Principal Component Analysis (PCA) which obtains a subspace spanned by the largest eigenvectors of the global covariance matrix, we show that LPP obtains a subspace spanned by the smallest eigenvectors of the local covariance matrix. We applied PCA and LPP to real world document clustering task. Experimental results show that the performance can be significantly improved in the subspace, and especially LPP works much better than PCA.

paragraphs: Dimensionality reduction seeks a smaller representation that retains meaningful structure in data. This paper analyzes Locality Preserving Projection, or LPP, from a statistical perspective. Its central result explains the subspace selected by LPP through a covariance matrix, making the method easier to compare with Principal Component Analysis.

PCA selects a subspace associated with the largest eigenvectors of the global covariance matrix. The authors show that LPP instead selects one associated with the smallest eigenvectors of a local covariance matrix. This identifies a precise mathematical distinction between the two methods: both the covariance information used and the selected end of its eigenvector spectrum differ.

The authors apply PCA and LPP to a real-world document-clustering task. The experiments show that using a reduced subspace can significantly improve clustering performance, with LPP performing much better than PCA in that evaluation. The findings connect the statistical distinction to a practical result, supporting the usefulness of the local representation for the document-clustering problem studied.
summary.tldr: LPP selects small-eigenvalue directions of a local covariance matrix and substantially outperforms PCA in the reported document-clustering experiment.

title: Statistical and computational analysis of locality preserving projection

abstract: Motivated by value function estimation in reinforcement learning, we study statistical linear inverse problems, i.e., problems where the coefficients of a linear system to be solved are observed in noise. We consider penalized estimators, where performance is evaluated using a matrix-weighted two-norm of the defect of the estimator measured with respect to the true, unknown coefficients. Two objective functions are considered depending whether the error of the defect measured with respect to the noisy coefficients is squared or unsquared. We propose simple, yet novel and theoretically well-founded data-dependent choices for the regularization parameters for both cases that avoid data-splitting. A distinguishing feature of our analysis is that we derive deterministic error bounds in terms of the error of the coefficients, thus allowing the complete separation of the analysis of the stochastic properties of these errors. We show that our results lead to new insights and bounds for linear value function estimation in reinforcement learning.

paragraphs: The paper studies linear systems whose coefficients are observed with noise, motivated by estimating value functions in reinforcement learning. An estimated solution can fit the noisy system yet leave an error in the true system. The authors evaluate that error using a matrix-weighted two-norm of the residual under the unknown true coefficients.

They consider penalized estimators with two objectives: one squares the residual norm computed from noisy coefficients, while the other leaves it unsquared. For both, they propose data-dependent choices of regularization parameters that avoid splitting the data. This gives a theoretically supported way to set the penalty using the available observations.

The analysis derives deterministic error bounds expressed in terms of coefficient-estimation errors. This separates the behavior of the estimator from the probabilistic analysis of how those coefficient errors arise. The authors then apply the results to linear value-function estimation, obtaining new bounds and insights for reinforcement learning. The separation makes the general inverse-problem analysis directly useful for that motivating application.
summary.tldr: Data-dependent regularization choices and deterministic error bounds improve the theoretical treatment of noisy linear systems and reinforcement-learning value estimation.
